# Jeremiah 21-52

## CHAPTER 21

**Verse 1.** *{The word that came unto Jeremiah from the LORD,}* As chap. 18.1. This chapter contains an answer returned from God, upon occasion of a motion made by King Zedekiah to the prophet, to enquire of God, or address himself unto him, in behalf of the king, and the state, in regard of the Chaldean forces that were set down before the city, v. 1,2. and the answer is directed, 1. To the whole state of the city, v. 4,7. 2. To the people, v. 8,10. 3. To the king and rulers, ver. 11,12. all closed up with a denunciation of utter destruction and devastation, notwithstanding their imaginary strength, v. 13,14.

*{when King Zedekiah sent unto him, Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the Priest, saying;}* Thus Zedekiah, though an evil king, and one that would not take any wholesome and safe advice from God's prophet, 2 Chr. 36.12. ch. 38.15. yet in times of distress, is glad to send here unto him, as at other times also afterward, ch. 37.3. & 38.14. but not as Ezekiah to Esay, out of a heart touched with sincere sorrow and remorse for his sins, 2 Kin. 19.1. Esa. 33.2. but as Pharao to Moses, for the removal of judgments, if it might be, Exod. 9.28.

*{Pashur the son of Melchiah}* One of the same name with the former, that so abused the prophet, ch. 20.1. but of another house and course; for he, that Pashur, was of the family of Immer, which was the sixteenth rank, 1 Chr. 24.14. whereas this Pashur was of the family of Melchias, which was the first rank, 1 Chr. 24.9. and a man, in likelihood, of a better and milder disposition than that other.

*{Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah}* Of his race, which made up the twentieth course, 1 Chr. 24.18. Of the same party; see further, chap. 29.25,29. & 37.3.

**Verse 2.** *{Enquire, I pray thee, of the LORD for us;}* Or, *Entreat God for us;* seek to him in our behalf: for so the word is commonly used, Deut. 4.29. Esa. 55.6. Ezek. 36.37. where it would much better be rendered, *required, or requested, or sought unto*, than *enquired of;* which suits not well there.

*{(for Nebuchadrezzar, King of Babylon, maketh war against us)}* Nebuchadrezzar; so is he called oft in this prophecy; as ch. 25.9. who is elsewhere commonly termed Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 1.1. and by the Greeks and Latins, *Nabuchodonosor;* and he was now set down with his forces before Jerusalem, v. 5. the cause and ground of his invading the land, and besieging the city, see 2 Kin. 24.17,20. & 25.1,2. 2 Chr. 36.10,13.

*{if so be that the LORD will deal with us, according to his wondrous works}* Or, *it may be the Lord will deal with us, &c.* for that is the proper and most usual notion of the term here used; as Zeph. 2.3. this they speak as hoping that God might be induced, especially upon Jeremie's entreaty, to show favor unto them, and work some strange deliverance for them, as he had done formerly for Ezekiah, upon the prayer of Esay, 2 Chr. 32.20,21. (for that deliverance they seem to have a more special eye unto) and for other of his servants at other times, 2 Chron. 14.9,15. and 20.12,25. So Psal. 44.1. but in vain do wicked wretches hope for relief and succor from him, whom they regard not to serve, by whom they refuse to be ruled, ch. 2.27,28.

*{that he may go up from us}* That Nebuchadrezzar who now besieges us, may be compelled to break up his siege, and so depart from us; as Sennacherib was sometime enforced to do, Esa. 37.36,37. *go up*, that is, *rise;* raise his siege: or rather simply, *depart, go away;* as ch. 37.5. So ch. 4.7,13. 1 Kin. 15.19.

**Verse 3.** *{Then said Jeremiah unto them}* Heb. *And Jeremiah said;* as ch. 20.9. *{Thus shall ye say to Zedekiah:}* Or, *Thus say;* as ch. 19.3.

**Verse 4.** *{Thus saith the LORD God of Israel;}* That God, from whom you expect protection, as being a part, yea, the principal part of his Israel, see chap. 19.3.

*{Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war, that are in your hand, wherewith ye fight against the King of Babylon, and against the Chaldeans, which besiege you without the walls,}* I will be so far from relieving and succoring you, that I will turn the weapons that you fight with, from your enemies, upon, or against yourselves, by setting you together by the ears amongst yourselves. See chap. 13.14. or, I will turn them back; and cause them to recoil, without doing of any damage at all unto them. See Psal. 89.41. So that all your fighting against them, shall be in vain, and to no purpose. See chap. 32.2. Heb. *I am turning back, or turning about;* as *bringing*, ch. 19.15. and *wherewith ye are fighting* with him, and them, as ch. 37.10. and *wall*, for, *walls*, as Ezek. 38.11.

*{and I will assemble them in the midst of this city.}* Or, *I will bring them* (who are yet without the walls) *into this city.* So is the word used, Exod. 9.19. *that is not brought into the house:* and Deut. 22.2. *thou shalt bring it into the midst of thine house;* that is, simply, *home to thine house;* where we have together, both the notion of the verb, and the form also here used.

**Verse 5.** *{And I myself will fight against you, with an outstretched, and with a strong arm, in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath.}* So far will I be from defending you or this city, as in former times I have done, Esa. 37.35. & 38.6. Heb. *fight with you*, for, *against you;* as before, v. 4. *an out-stretched-hand;* a term borrowed from the manner of stretching out the hand furnished with some offensive weapon to strike the enemy in fight, Josh. 8.18,19.26. So Esa. 9.12,21. of the *arm*, see the like, Exod. 6.6. Psal. 136.12. and this carriage of God towards them, complained of, Lam. 2.3,4.

**Verse 6.** *{And I will smite the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast}* Or, *I will slay* (as chap. 18.21.) *those that abide* in it: for the word signifies as well to *abide*, as to *dwell*, Judg. 5.16. ch. 39.14. and would so be here rendered, as it is vers. 9. Heb. *and the man, and the beast;* and, for, *both;* as chap. 17.26.

*{they shall die of a great pestilence.}* See ch. 16.4. & 18.21.

**Verse 7.** *{And afterward, saith the LORD, I will deliver Zedekiah King of Judah, and his servants, and the people, and such as are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those that seek their life;}* See ch. 15.2. & 34.20,21.

*{and his servants}* So Chap. 22.2. & 36.31.

*{and such as are left}* Or, *even such;* as Chap. 19.12. *hand*, for, *power;* and *soul*, for, *life;* as ch. 20.13. & 38.16.

*{and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword:}* He, that is, the king of Babylon, *shall smite*, that is, slay them; as v. 6. yet not Zedekiah himself, chap. 34.4. but his sons, his principal and chief officers, and other of the priests and people, ch. 39.6. & 52.7,9. *with the edge of the sword.* Heb. *mouth;* as Deut. 13.15. Luk. 21.24.

*{he shall not spare them, nor have pity, nor have mercy.}* Of the cruel carriage of the Chaldeans toward this people, see 2 Chr. 36.17. Esa. 47.6. ch. 6.23. Lam. 5.12,13.

**Verse 8.** *{And unto this people thou shalt say;}* Or, *And say to this people;* or, *Say also to this people;* as v. 3.

*{Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will set before you the way of life, and the way of death.}* Or, *I set before you.* Heb. *I am giving before you: giving;* as, *turning*, vers. 4. and, *to give*, for, *to set;* as Deut. 30.19. where see the like. I show you how you may escape; by yielding yourselves unto Nebuchadrezzar, ch. 38.17. and how you will bring destruction upon yourselves, if you stand it out against him, chap. 27.8.

**Verse 9.** *{He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence:}* See v. 6. ch. 38.2. the disjunctive would do better here (as also, ch. 20.4,17. and verse 13. than the copulative; because the participle prefixed is singular, though collective: for some were to perish by one of the three, and some by another, not each one by all three. See ch. 15.2.

*{but he that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans, that besiege you, shall live,}* Heb. *and;* as chap. 20.9. *he that goeth out;* to wit, of the city; to yield himself into their hands (so chap. 38.2. & 2 Kin. 24.12. *Jehoiachin went out unto him*) *and falleth to the Chaldeans*, (as ch. 37.13. *thou fallest to the Chaldeans*) *shall live:* shall escape.

*{and his life shall be unto him for a prey.}* A proverbial form of speech, importing as much, as he shall save, or gain his life: his life shall be to him, as some booty gotten in fight, in regard of the joy he may have of it, say some, Psal. 119.162. or in regard of the achievement and possession of it, as others rather; his life seeming to be as it were new acquired, and gotten again to him, and himself repossessed of that, which seemed in a manner utterly lost before: as 2 Cor. 2.8,9. Heb. 11.17,18. for lawful prey is deemed good purchase, Esa. 49.24. See the use of this form again, chap. 38.2. & 39.18. & 45.5.

**Verse 10.** *{For I have set my face against this city, for evil, and not for good, saith the LORD;}* Or, *I have set my face upon this city* (and so Psal. 34.16. as the particle is well rendered, Neh. 9.10. & 13.21. Est. 3.6. that it may sort the better with either member of the distribution ensuing) *for evil and not for good.* So ch. 39.16. & 44.11,27. Amos 9.4.

*{it shall be given into the hand of the King of Babylon}* *hand*, for, *power;* as vers. 7.

*{and he shall burn it with fire}* He shall cause it to be burnt. So chap. 38.23. & 39.8.

**Verse 11.** *{And touching the house of the King of Judah, say;}* Or, *And unto the house of the King.* So the text precisely has it. To those of the king's court, that are in place of judicature, or in offices thereunto belonging.

*{say}* Supplied; as Esa. 8.19.

*{Hear the word of the LORD;}* Or, *Hear the word of the Lord, O house of David;* annexing the compellation unto this clause, though prefixed to the words ensuing, v. 12. as Psal. 96.12,13. & 98.8,9.

**Verse 12.** *{O house of David}* You of the court that was David's sometime, and that come many of you from his stock: see, Esa. 7.2,13. c. 13.13. & 22.2.

*{Thus saith the LORD, execute justice in the morning;}* Imitate him of whose house you are, who sat constantly doing judgment and justice to all his people, 2 Sam. 8.15. 1 Chr. 18.14. So chap. 22.3. Heb. *Judge in the morning judgment.* Either do it timely, not spending the morning in eating and drinking, when you should be about matter of judicature, Eccl. 10.16,17. for in the morning did the people use to repair for justice to the place of judicature, Exod. 18.13. or, do it diligently, every morning; morning after morning, as Amos 4.4. daily without failing. See David, Psal. 101.8.

*{and deliver him that is spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor}* Right the oppressed against those that oppress them, and make a spoil of them. See Psal. 72.4,11,13. & 82.3,4. *hand*, for, *power;* as before, v. 7,10.

*{lest my fury go out like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.}* Implying, that their neglect of justice, and default therein, was one of the main sins that would be the cause of their utter and irrecoverable ruin, if it were not speedily reformed, Esa. 1.23. & 59.4,14,15. ch. 5.28. & 6.6,7. & 22.17. See the like expressions, chap. 4.4. & 17.24.

**Verse 13.** *{Behold, I am against thee, O Inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain, saith the LORD, which say, who shall come down against us? or who shall enter into our habitation?}* In the close of this answer returned to the messengers of Zedekiah, God, by the prophet meets with these their presumptuous conceits, whereby they imagined their city to be, in regard of its situation, and fortifications, an impregnable piece, able to withstand any the greatest forces, or force, that could be raised, or made against it; which to put them from, the Lord tells them, that he will come himself against them, as in the head of those that invade and assault them, and do that, which they fondly and vainly suppose not to be feasible. See v. 5.

*{Behold, I am against thee}* Heb. no more but, *I unto thee* (for so the word most commonly signifies) or, *against thee:* a defective speech in this prophet not infrequent. So ch. 23.30,31,32. & 50.31. & 51.25. and it may as well be rendered, *I am coming to thee;* as in way of answer, to that their insolent demand: *who will*, or, *can come at us?* as if he had said, I will come myself to you, against whom there is no standing out, or withstanding, Psal. 76.7. See the like, Obad. 3,4.

*{O Inhabitant}* Heb. *Inhabitress;* that is, Jerusalem, whereof as a city he uses oft to speak, in the feminine form. So ch. 10.17. & 22.23.

*{of the valley}* For it stood in a vale, environed with mountains, Psalm 125.2. and they strain it too far, who would have it so termed, in regard of what God intended to do with it; to wit, to destroy and bring it down into the vale.

*{and rock of the plain}* Or, as some, *of the rock of the plain:* for though it were situate in the midst of a lower ground, yet stood it, the upper part of it especially, on a rocky rising, or hill, having much plain ground round about it. See chap. 17.3. as also, Josh. 15.8.

*{which say}* Trusting overmuch in this their situation: the word is here masculine, and plural, as intending the citizens, or inhabitants of the city, who used insolently thus to speak.

*{who shall come down against us?}* Who dare come to sit down before our city, or to join battle with us? *come down:* a military term, as the Jewish critics observe; having in it a notion, as some of them, either of sitting down in siege, or lying in ambush: as 2 King. 6.9. *the Syrians are couched there;* or, as others, of coming down into the plain to join battle there: as 1 Sam. 26.10. *he shall descend into battle, and perish*, 1 Sam. 26.10. the verb seems to be here in a notion of *daring;* as Esay 10.14. Zach. 1.21.

*{or}* Heb. *and;* as before, verse 9.

*{who shall enter into our habitations?}* Or, *who can enter upon our dwellings?* as, *who shall stand?* for, *who can stand?* Psal. 76.7. See the like vaunt, ch. 49.4. & Obad. 3.

**Verse 14.** *{But I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings;}* Heb. *And;* which some render here, *for;* and so the copulative is used, Psalm 60.11. But I should rather retain the copulative itself, as knitting this to the former branch vers. 13. I will come to you, and when I come, I will punish you. I will come on visiting, when I come, to your smart. Heb. *I will visit upon thee;* as ch. 9.25. that is, in my visitation of you, inflict penal things upon you, such as your wicked courses do justly deserve, Psal. 28.4. and 62.12. Prov. 1.31. chap. 17.10.

*{and I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof, and it shall devour all things round about it.}* Here by *the forest thereof;* to wit, of Jerusalem, some understand their woods or groves, and high places thereunto belonging, wherein they had exercised their idolatry, ch. 3.2. Others, the inferior towns and cities round about it, like so many tufts of trees in a wood or forest, ch. 19.15. Others, mount Lebanon, being one of the boundaries of the promised land. See Esa. 37.24. Others, the goodly and stately buildings of the city, that stood as thick as trees in a forest, and were built with timber fetched from the forest of Lebanon. See chap. 22.7,15,23. Zach. 11.1. Of this fire threatened, see ch. 17.27. kindled, see 2 Chr. 36.19. ch. 52.13. *there* is a change of the person; as ch. 16.12.

## CHAPTER 22

**Verse 1.** *{Thus saith the LORD;}* It is evident enough, as we shall afterwards also further show on ch. 27.1. that the sermons or prophecies in this book recorded, were not ranged according to the times, at which they were delivered; for the relation made in the chapter next foregoing, is of somewhat done in Zedekiah's reign, in the time of the siege of the city; whereas the subject matter of this chapter seems to consist of such things as concerned Jehoahaz, v. 10,12. Jehoiakim, v. 18. and Jeconiah, v. 24. all of them foregoing the reign of Zedekiah. Howbeit, a learned late writer rendering the words, *Thus said the Lord;* (wherein I also willingly concur with him, and so do for the like, chap. 19.1.) does thence infer, that Jeremy should together at the same time when he delivered the former answer returned to Zedekiah, here relate, what messages he had been beforetime sent withal, either unto, or concerning those other kings his predecessors; and that for this end, to show that God now threatened to do no otherwise with Zedekiah, than as he had done with those other before him. But the whole file and series of the context, and frame of this chapter, seems to carry it another way.

*{Go down}* This, say some, because he was in the temple, when God gave him this injunction; and he was to go down therefore thence, ere he could repair to the king's house. But of this there is no necessity. For the words of ascent and descent are oft used of motion from place to place, without any special regard had to the situation of either. So Judg. 5.14. *from Machir came down* (for, *came forth*) *the Scribes:* and, *they went down* (for, *went*) *to the top of the rock*, Judg. 15.11,12. See on Esay 38.8. It may therefore be well rendered here, simply, *Go*, as ch. 18.2. and yet, *Go down to the Potters house*, would sound better there than *Go down to the Kings house*, will do, with us at least, here.

*{to the house of the King of Judah;}* The words may import the house, or palace, in general, that the kings of Judah did keep court in successively: but the question is, who then kept court there, when Jeremy was with the errand here recorded sent thither. To pass by the conceit of the late writer above mentioned, who supposes it to have been then the court of Zedekiah; and that the whole discourse throughout this chapter, is no other, than a relation of matters already past and gone. The most deem it to have been all delivered at the same time in the reign of Jehoiakim; but to contain matter of prediction, partly concerning Jehoiakim himself, vers. 18. and partly concerning Jeconiah his son, v. 24. I conceive the chapter to contain two several prophecies, or messages, of two several dates: the former, from ver. 3. to v. 19. delivered in Jehoiakim's reign; the latter, from v. 20. to 30. delivered in the reign of Jeconiah. The former by the subject matter of it, appears to have been delivered, while Jehonaz, or Jehoachaz, being deposed, yet survived in captivity, v. 10,11,12. and while Jehoiakim also was yet alive, whether at home, or abroad in captivity, uncertain; but retaining still the royal title: for it foretells also his death, v. 18. and, consequently, within the compass of his reign.

*{and speak there this word}* Heb. *and thou shalt speak* (as ch. 1.17. & 17.27.) *this word there;* that is, *this commandment*, or *precept:* as, *ten words*, for, *ten commandments*, or, *precepts*, Deut. 10.4. for with an injunction he begins, v. 3. or, *this word*, that is, *this thing;* as ch. 7.22,23. and, *no vain word*, for, *no vain thing*, Deut. 32.47. *Speak this* (to wit, that here follows) *there:* so v. 4.

*{And say.}* Heb. *Thou shalt say;* as ch. 19.3.

**Verse 2.** *{Hear the word of the LORD;}* As ch. 17.20. & 19.3. & 21.11.

*{O King of Judah}* *O Jehoiakim.* See on v. 1,18.

*{that sittest upon the Throne of David,}* Succeeding him in the kingdom of Judah. See ch. 17.25. & 21.12.

*{thou, and thy Servants,}* *Thou*, as the principal; *and thy servants*, that is, your officers and attendants: as ch. 21.7. for they also oftentimes are instrumental, and overforward in wrongdoing, as well as their masters, Neh. 5.15. Prov. 29.12. Zeph. 1.9.

*{and thy people}* Those that in any kind appertain to your family, Josh. 24.15. ch. 21.12. or such of the people as repair to you for audience, and for matter of justice: but the former here rather.

*{that enter in by these gates.}* The court or palace gates, v. 1. that go in and out by them: as c. 17.19. the one here put for both: as c. 17.23,27.

**Verse 3.** *{Thus saith the LORD,}* God's message now follows to the king and his retinue: consisting of, first an injunction, backed with a double sanction, of promise, v. 4. of menace, v. 5. 2. a denunciation of destruction, with the ground of it, v. 6,9. 3. a prediction of Jehoachaz his death in captivity, v. 10,12. 4. A sharp reprehension of Jehoiakim, for his oppressions; wherein he swerved from his father's righteous and religious steps, v. 13,17. together with a prediction of his ignominious end, v. 18,19.

*{Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver ye the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor:}* The injunction concerning the due execution of justice. See the same in effect, c. 21.12. and of the terms here used, Esa. 56.1.

*{and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow:}* Heb. *and stranger, orphan, and* (for, *or:* as ch. 21.13.) *widow, oppress not, wrong not:* these God especially gives a charge of, both because such commonly are most exposed to wrong, and such as he has therefore taken into his more special protection, Exo. 22.21,22. ch. 7.6.

*{neither shed innocent blood in this place.}* See ch. 7.6.

**Verse 4.** *{For if ye do this thing indeed,}* If carefully, or diligently you do this. Heb. *if doing ye do* (as ch. 7.5.) *this word;* as v. 1. So ch. 26.2. & 22.17.

*{then shall there enter in by the gates of this house, Kings sitting upon the Throne of David, riding in chariots, and on horses, he and his Servants and his people.}* See the same in effect, chap. 17.25. Heb. *Sitting for David upon his Throne.*

*{he and his servants, and his people}* Each of them, to wit, those kings successively, and their retinue. See ver. 2.

**Verse 5.** *{But if ye will not hear these words,}* Heb. *And* ch. 21.3. *if ye will* *not herein obey me:* *to hear* for *to obey;* as ch. 7.23. and *words* for *things*, as Deut. 30.1. and 32.46.

*{I swear by myself, saith the LORD}* God swears by himself, because he has none greater than himself to swear by, Heb. 6.12. and what he thus swears, binding by so solemn an oath, shall undoubtedly be fulfilled, Psal. 110.4. & 132.11. Heb. 6.17,18.

*{that this house shall become a desolation.}* Heb. *shall be unto desolation*, as ch. 7.32. that is threatened to the king's court and palace here that is elsewhere threatened to the temple, God's own house, 1 Kin. 9.7,8. cha. 7.14. though they swerve from the text here, that refer this and that which follows here ver. 6. unto that.

**Verse 6.** *{For thus saith the LORD unto the Kings house of Judah}* Heb. *concerning*, as (cha. 12.14. See ver. 11,18.) *the house of the King of Judah:* and consequently concerning the whole kingdom and state, whereof that was the royal seat.

*{Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon: yet surely I will make thee a wilderness, and cities which are not inhabited.}* Because the judgment threatened might seem to them very unlikely to be effected, trusting partly to their wealth, and partly to their strength, arising as well from the natural situation of the place, as from their works and fortifications about it; see ch. 17.3. & 21.13. God further here tells them, that though their land were as wealthy as Gilead, and their structures as strong and impregnable, as if they were situate on the highest part of Mount Lebanon; yet he would reduce their whole land and head city to a wild wilderness; and make the other cities about it like a vast desert.

*{Thou art Gilead unto me}* Or, *Though thou beest as Gilead to me:* the particle both of concession and similitude is wanting; as Job 13.15. the one; and ch. 5.8. the other: as *Gilead;* that is, like to it for wealth: for the land of Gilead was not only a fat and rich soil of itself, but a region abounding with such precious commodities of balm and spicery, as did, by trade and traffic in those kind of merchandise, much enrich her inhabitants. See Gen. 37.25. Numb. 32.1. of the ground of the name see Gen. 31.47. *unto me;* that is, as some, in my esteem and account: though I well know and grant you so to be. Others, *unto me;* that is, *before me*, or in my sight: whereof more anon. Others, *by me*, (as some render the particle, ch. 15.8,15.) through my blessing upon you; whereby you have been enriched, and are grown up to this height of wealth and strength, Deut. 8.18. Prov. 10.22. Ezek. 16.14. but I suppose the form here used to be only an elegant redundancy; not unlike the same, ch. 5.7. and 12.9.

*{the head of Lebanon}* This some join to the former, as spoken, not of Jerusalem, or the king's court, but of Gilead; and of the king's court only as by Gilead resembled: and they say that *Gilead* is called *the head of Lebanon*, near unto which it lay, because it was esteemed a principal part of the land thereabout: whereunto the Jewish doctors add, that as the city of Gilead was the head city of those parts, so Jerusalem was the head city of the kingdom of Judah; and the king's court, or Sion, the head of Jerusalem; sometime termed Lebanon, Zach. 11.1. *head* for *chief:* as Exod. 30.23. Others again say, that Gilead is called *the head of Lebanon*, because at the south end of it does mount Lebanon begin. So *head* should be used here for *beginning;* as Esa. 51.20. Lam. 2.19. but these things are overforcibly stretched unto Gilead; nor is the *head* of a mountain anywhere used for the first *rise*, but for the *top* of it rather, Isa. 2.2. Amos 9.3. I rather therefore concur with those who conceive in these words another resemblance to be used, distinct from the former, wherein the king's house, or Sion, whereon it stood, is said to be for loftiness and stateliness, as *the head*, that is, *the top of Lebanon;* that goodly high mountain, stored with abundance of fair and tall cedars, and other the like choice timber trees, Isa. 14.8. & 37.24. see v. 23. Nor can I assent to those who expound both this and the former; as if it were said, *Thou* Jerusalem *art in my sight*, as *Gilead*, as some waste place; as respecting the present estate of Gilead, by the Assyrians laid waste, 2 King. 15.29. or *as the top of Lebanon:* as a parcel of some wild forest, inhabited, not by men, but by wild beasts: supposing the meaning to be, either that God no more than so regarded it for the present, Amos 9.7. or that God would make it like unto those two places, by laying it waste, and dispeopling of it: and so it should be as that, which they parallel with this, ch. 7.12,14.

*{yet surely I will make thee a wilderness,}* Heb. *if I make thee not a wilderness:* the usual form of an oath. See Isa. 5.9. & 22.14. and the like menaces, ch. 9.10,12. Some insert the note of similitude both here and in the next member; *as a wilderness;* and *as cities:* expressed also, ch. 9.11. Hos. 2.5.

*{and cities which are not inhabited}* Like such cities: and then there is a defect, both of the note of similitude, as before; and of the relative also; as ch. 15.14,18. Howbeit, some render it, *and thy cities shall not be inhabited;* the cities round about you shall be dispeopled: but the former seems the more familiar.

**Verse 7.** *{And I will prepare destroyers against thee,}* Or, *For* (as Isa. 9.11.) *I have prepared* (Heb. *sanctified*, as Esa. 13.3. chap. 6.4.) *destroyers* (the Chaldeans, ch. 4.7.) *against thee:* to come against you and destroy you, ch. 44.18. & 6.20.

*{every one with his weapons}* Heb. *a man* (for *each one;* as ch. 18.11.) *and his instruments*, for *with his instruments:* as Isa. 5.14. ch. 1.13. So v. 14. and so rather than *weapons*, to keep to the similitude of fellers or hewers with axes and hatchets, such as trees are wont to be felled and hewn down with, Psal. 74.5,6. See ch. 46.23.

*{and they shall cut down thy choice cedars, and cast them into the fire.}* Heb. *the choice of thy cedars;* as Isa. 37.24. Your fair buildings made of the choicest cedars, ch. 21.14. v. 13. and he speaks of them, as if they were felling some part of Lebanon. So Isa. 10.34.

**Verse 8.** *{And many nations shall pass by this city, and they shall say, every man to his neighbour,}* Or, *And when many nations* (men of divers nations) *passing by this city*, (or the place where it stood) *shall say one to another.* Heb. *a man to his friend*, or *familiar;* as ch. 9.4. So Gen. 11.3,7. Mal. 3.16.

*{Wherefore hath the LORD done thus unto this great City?}* So Deu. 29.24. 1 King. 9.8. See Lam. 4.12.

**Verse 9.** *{Then they shall answer,}* Or, *They shall answer;* or, *It shall be answered:* for the verb is indefinite. This answer shall be returned them that make the demand, v. 8. Heb. *And they shall say*, for *It shall be said:* as Ezek. 36.35. See the like syntax, Lev. 9.24. ch. 13.12,13. & 16.10,11.

*{Because they have forsaken the Covenant of the LORD their God, and worshipped other gods, and served them.}* So Deut. 28.25. 1 King. 9.9. cha. 1.16. & 9.13,14. & 16.11.

**Verse 10.** *{Weep not for the dead, neither bemoan him; but weep sore for him that goeth away; for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.}* These words some take as spoken in general of the persons of those times; to wit, that there was little cause to mourn for those that should then die, whether by some natural or violent death; more cause to bewail those that surviving them should go into captivity, where they should live in continual slavery, and much misery, without hope of ever seeing their own country again, ch. 8.3. & 16.6,7. Ezek. 24.16,17,21,22. Rev. 9.6. & 14.13. not unlike that of our Savior, Luk. 23.28. Others, and so the most understand it, as having reference to some particular person and prince, or persons and princes: the former whereof, the words next ensuing, v. 11. do sufficiently confirm: and of these, some understand the former branch of Josiah, slain in fight by Pharao-Nechoh; for the loss of whom, grievous lamentation not without good and great ground, was generally made, 2 Chr. 35.24,25. Zach. 10.12. but the prophet here tells them, that howsoever in regard of their own interest, they had cause to bewail the loss of so worthy and godly a governor; yet in regard of him there was no such cause of mourning; for that he died with honor, was departed to peace, and taken away from the sight of such evils as were to ensue, 2 King. 22.20. Esay 57.1,2. the latter they conceive to be meant of Jehoachaz, whom the people set up upon his father's decease, but having sat little above three months, was by Pharao-Nechoh deposed, and carried captive into Egypt, where he died, 2 King. 22.30,34. 2 Chr. 36.1,4. v. 11. Ezek. 19.4. and this way, as the most probable, the greater part of these go. Some only swerve a little from the rest; expounding the whole passage of Jehoachaz, as more to be lamented in regard of his captivity, than of his decease: but this seems not so probable as the former; which some also of the Jewish commenters approve. Howbeit, a learned chronologer, departing herein from both, supposes Jehoiakim in this latter branch intended, who was carried away captive, towards, at least, if not unto, Babylon; nor was to return unto Jerusalem again. See further on v. 1,18. And again, some of the Jewish doctors would have Jehoiakim deciphered in the former branch, who died by the way, being drawn out of Jerusalem, but never carried to Babylon, 2 Chr. 36.6. whereof see more on v. 18. Jeconiah; and as some, also, Zedekiah in the latter branch; because both carried captive to Babylon, where they both died. 2 King. 24.15. & 25.7. But the current of the context, with the consent of the best interpreters, leads rather the way before mentioned.

*{weep not}* That is, not so much: as, *I spake not*, ch. 7.22.

*{for the dead}* As if his state were worthy lamentation, 1 Thess. 4.13.

*{neither bewail him}* Or, *nor condole with others for him.* See ch. 16.7.

*{but}* A defect of the adversative: as ch. 5.3.

*{weep sore}* Or, *weep seriously*, or *sadly:* weep to the purpose. Heb. *weeping weep*, as Esa. 30.19.

*{for him that is gone away}* Heb. *that goeth* for *is gone;* to wit, into captivity: as v. 11.

*{he shall return no more, nor see}* Heb. *he shall not return any more, and shall see;* that is, *he shall no more return to see:* as Josh. 24.9. cha. 10.4. & 14.19. or *he shall never see again:* as Gen. 26.18. Zach. 4.1.

*{his native country.}* Heb. *the land of his nativity:* as Gen. 11.28. & 24.7.

**Verse 11.** *{For thus saith the LORD touching Shallum the son of Josiah King of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more:}* There is no small dispute and debate about this *Shallum*, who he should be. The most suppose him to be *Jehoachaz:* one of the Jewish doctors, to confirm this opinion, produces that place of the Chronicles, 1 Chron. 3.15. where Josiah is said to have had four sons, *Johanan*, or *Jochanan, Joakim*, or *Jehoiakim, Zedekiah*, and *Shallum;* and this *Shallum*, says he, must needs be *Jehoachaz;* for one of Josiah his sons was Jehoachaz, and there is no other left to be this Shallum but he. But against this is objected, that *Shallum* here mentioned is said to be Josiah's *fourth* son; whereas Jehoachaz was his second son at least, the next to Jehoiakim, who appears to have been the eldest, being born two years before Jehoachaz. See 2 King. 23.31,36. Others therefore acknowledging this *Shallum* to be Jehoachaz, suppose him to be the same with *Johanan, Jochanan*, or *John* (for these names are all one. See chap. 40.8.) whom they suppose to have had two several names, (as divers others in Scripture; whereof, see on Isa. 1.1. *Uzziah*) *Jehoachaz* and *Jochanan;* and as they imagine a third also in this place, *Shallum.* So the same person is called *Shelomoh*, and *Jedidiah*, and *Lemuel*, 2 Sam. 12.24,25. Prov. 31.1. Howbeit, they suppose him to be here called *Shallum;* not from his birth, but afterward in regard of the shortness of his reign, continuing not above ten days more than three months, 2 King. 23.11. partly, from another of that name king of Israel, who reigned but a month, 2 King. 15.13. and partly, from his younger son, who bore also the same name, and deceased it may be before him, as more worthy to bear that name than he, and to succeed him in the same. Besides, they hold him to be termed Josiah's *first-born*, 1 Chron. 3.15. not in regard of priority of birth, (for Jehoiakim, as has been said, was the elder of the twain) but in regard of his primacy in the royal succession, being through the favor of the people preferred to the crown before his elder brother, 2 King. 23.30. And this way the most and best of ours go. But of the Jewish interpreters, the most run other ways: and some of them would have this *Shallum* to be Zedekiah, said to be, both the *third* of Josiah's sons in regard of his birth, and again the *fourth* of them in regard of his reign: for of Josiah's issue Jehoachaz reigned first, then Jehoiakim, then Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah; and in the fourth place Zedekiah: and they add that therefore he was called *Shallum*, because the kingdom of Judah ended and expired in him, at his downfall seeming to give out its last breath, Lam. 4.20. But the text in the genealogy expressly mentions them as two several persons; *sons of Josiah, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum.* Some other of them therefore justly rejecting this, would have this *Shallum* to be *Jehoiachin*, or *Jeconiah;* for both names he bears in Scripture; called, say they, *the son of Josiah*, here termed *his father;* and reckoned among his issue, because he was his son's son; as *Belshazzar*, or *Baltasar*, is said to be *the son* of Nebuchadnezzar, and Nebuchadnezzar is called his father, Dan. 5.18,22. But this also is very improbable; for in the next place there follows, *the sons of Joakim, Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son.* So that Jeconiah therefore and Shallum are two several persons there; the nephew the one, the uncle the other. In the last place therefore, that learned chronologer before mentioned, by *Shallum* understands here that fourth son of Josiah; by the party here said to be gone into captivity, *Jehoiakim:* and he thus renders the text; *For thus saith the Lord* (not, *touching*, or *concerning, Shallum;* though the particle be sometime so used; as Psal. 2.7. & 69.27. v. 18. but as it is most commonly taken) *unto Shallum, the son of Josiah King of Judah, who reigneth in the room of Josiah his father;* (as speaking to him of some other) *He that is gone out from this place*, (to wit, Jehoiakim your brother, gone in captivity to Babylon) *shall return no more hither.* This he thus endeavors to clear. Jehoiakim set up by Pharao-Nechoh, 2 King. 23.34. was afterward by Nebuchadnezzar, Necho's adversary invaded, and compelled to hold from him; unto whom he continued loyal some three years, but began then to rebel against him, 2 King. 24.1. whereupon Nebuchadnezzar again invaded the land, surprised the city, took him prisoner, and *bound him in fetters to carry him unto Babylon*, 2 Chr. 36.6. yea, in likelihood did accordingly carry him thither. See Ezek. 19.9. where during his captivity and restraint, his brother Shallum, as viceroy in the minority of his son Jeconiah, governed the kingdom; and is therefore here said *to reign in the room of Josiah his father*, unto Jehoiakim's decease. Now whereas the people were possessed with a strong persuasion, that Jehoiakim should at length return back from his exilement; God sends the prophet here to Shallum, who ruled in likelihood as Jehoiakim had done, as to reprove him also for his evil government, so withal to assure him, that Jehoiakim should never see Jerusalem again, but should die in the land of his captivity. Had we any record of this Shallum's viceroyship, I should somewhat incline to this learned man's opinion. As it stands, I leave it to the consideration of other learned.

**Verse 12.** *{But he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more.}* Or, *For* (so the particle alone most commonly signifies; and so v. 11. but usually with an addition) *he shall dye in the place unto which he hath been led captive;* (for these indefinites are best rendered passively. So v. 6. Isa. 47.1. Mal. 1.4.) *and shall see this land no more;* and much less then this court, or this city, v. 10,11.

**Verse 13.** *{Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong:}* This reprehension ushered in with a woe, like that Isa. 5.8. & Habb. 2.9,12. is by the most deemed to concern Jehoiakim; and the main current of the context carries it that way: for they force it too much that would divert it, either unto Shallum, or any other.

*{his chambers}* Properly *upper-chambers;* and the word is therefore rendered *a loft*, 1 Kin. 17.19. and the Greek fitly answering it, *an upper-room*, Mark 14.15.

*{by unrighteousness, and by wrong}* Heb. *by not justice*, or *righteousness, and by not judgment*, or *right;* that is, without either, or contrary unto either, unjustly, wrongfully: as Prov. 16.8. Ezek. 22.29. either he that builds with money gotten by oppression and wrong dealing; or by dealing unjustly and wrongfully with those whom he employs about his buildings: the next way, either of them, not to build up a house, but to ruin and pull down the building, Habb. 2.9.13.

*{that useth his neighbours service without wages, and giveth him not for his work.}* The detaining, and denial much more of the workman's wages, and laborer's hire, being forbidden, and condemned as a sin that cries unto heaven for vengeance, Lev. 19.13. Deut. 24.14,15. Jam. 5.4. Heb. *that serveth himself of his neighbour* (as ch. 25.14. Exod. 1.14. compels him to serve or work for him) *freely*, (without hire or due consideration) *and giveth him not his work;* that is, hire or wages for his work: as Job 34.11. Esa. 49.4.

**Verse 14.** *{That saith}* Thinks with himself: as ch. 12.13.

*{I will build me a wide house, and large chambers;}* Or, *a spacious house* (Heb. *an house* of *spaces*, or *measures*, or *dimensions:* as, *men of dimensions*, for square and tall men, Num. 13.32. 2 Sam. 21.20. Isa. 45.14.) *with wide*, or *windy*, (*well-aired*, or as some render it, *through-aired*) *chambers.* Heb. *widened*, or *winded;* for the participle here used comes from a root, that has a notion sometime of *dilating* or *widening:* whence a word used for *space*, when applied unto place, Gen. 32.16. for *respite*, when applied unto time, Exod. 8.15. sometime of *breathing*, or, *drawing breath* for refreshment, rendered *refresh*, 1 Sam. 16.23. Job 32.20. and to this the old Greek and Latin refer it; as also the Jewish critics, expounding it of summer rooms or lodgings, fitted for fresh air: opposed to winter ones, Amos 3.15. the copulative for the relative: as chap. 11.16. vers. 7.

*{and cutteth him out windows,}* To let in both air and light, to make the rooms not large only and lightsome, but well aired also, as before; though some render the words, *that teareth my windows;* as if the word had a pronoun affixed to it: supposing that Jehoiakim had mangled and defaced the windows of God's temple, to adorn and beautify his own building therewith; as Ezekiah sometime pulled off the gold from the doors and pillars thereof, to make up the sum of money required of him to satisfy the king of Assyria, 2 Kin. 18.16. But this carries with it no great probability: *to cut out windows* seems no more here than to make open spaces, by cutting of the walls, wherein to set frames of windows; for the letting in as well of fresh air, as of light: and the plural, though irregular, is found in this form, as well with divers other words, as here with this. So 2 Chr. 3.11.9. Isa. 19.9. & 20.4. See the like, ch. 18.14. In the word *him*, or *to him;* as also in the word, *me*, or, *to me*, as the Hebrew has either, there seems an elegant redundancy: the like whereunto see ch. 2.21. & 5.5. & 12.8. & 16.20.

*{and it is cieled with cedar}* Or, *and that cieled with cedar;* to wit, the large house before mentioned; as was God's house that Solomon built, and his own, 1 King. 6.15,16. & 7.3. the like use of the copulative see chap. 17.4,10,11. & 20.5.

*{and painted with vermilion.}* Heb. *anointed with Shashar;* which the Jewish critics both here, and Ezek. 23.14. expound one of them *minium*, or *vermilion;* and so the Chaldee and the Greek: another *sinopis*, or *sinopel*, which come all to one; and so the old Latin: yet a late learned interpreter would have it to be *indico;* which colors and dyes not red, but sky color, or blue. See *Pliny* l. 35. c. 6. and he supposes it to have had its name, as with the Greeks and Latins, from *India*, out of which country it was brought into those parts: so with the Hebrews from the *Sasuri*, a people of that country, mentioned by *Pliny*, l. 6. c. 19. This may be not improbable, though the main current of interpreters go the other way: but that which the same writer adds concerning the sense of the place, as if the meaning were, that Jehoiakim having mangled and torn, not the windows only of God's temple, but some of the cedar ceiling of it also wherewith to beautify his palace, should to conceal his sacrilege, color it over with indigo; and so renders the text, *that teareth away my windows and cedar-ceiling, and then coloureth them over with Indico;* to me seems to carry with it no great probability.

**Verse 15.** *{Shalt thou reign because thou closest thyself in cedar?}* Do you Jehoiakim who are not reformed by God's judgment upon your brother Jehoachaz, v. 10,12. think to establish your throne and prolong your reign, by stately buildings raised from cruel oppression, and by wrongful dealing erected? v. 13,14. or do you think that a ceiling of cedar can secure you against the forcible assaults of a potent enemy, coming furnished with commission from God to execute vengeance on you for your violent and injurious carriages? for he seems to allude in the verb here used, unto a word that signifies *a coat of mail*, or *a brigandine*, Exod. 28.32. & 39.23. as speaking of one that should think himself sufficiently armed, when instead of such an armor, he had got a case of slit cedar about him. For neither can I here accord with that learned interpreter, who rendering the text; *Shalt thou reign because thou minglest thy self with that cedar?* to wit, says he, which you have torn from my temple, mingling yours and mine together, joining sacred and profane materials the one with the other, for the making up of your building: True it is, that the word seems to have a notion of *intermingling* of persons, or other things one with another, chap. 12.5. in which place and this only, it is found in the form here used: but this sense seems but harshly to be here wrung from the text. Nor is it likely, that either the priest, or people, would suffer the very ceiling of the temple to be so defaced; which in tearing or taking down, could not but be much mangled, and made very unserviceable for any exquisite employment. As far, I suppose, also do they swerve from the true sense of the place, who following the old Latin, rendering the words; *Shalt thou reign, because thou comparest thy self to a cedar?* Some of them conceive his haughtiness to be taxed, in deeming himself like to some tall cedar; a tree as well goodly to sight, and great of growth, as also well rooted, and of long continuance: as of Assur, Ezek. 31.3. Others, his presumption, in comparing himself with his father Josiah, a cedar of God's own planting: as Ezek. 17.21,22. and making account to do as well as he did. But these also seem as wide as the former. If any need were of swerving from the received interpretation, I should rather choose to render the words to this purpose; *Shalt thou reign, that thou environest thy self with cedar?* Do you expect and make account to continue your reign, that you are so busy in building yourself such a goodly, brave, and strong palace; when as God purposes, ere long, to send you packing out of this place? v. 18,19. So it might be not unlike the check given unto Shebna for his building, Isa. 22.16,19. and the places might well be paralleled. But in regard of what next follows, I adhere rather to that which was first propounded.

*{did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice?}* He directs the present king to another manner of foundation, for the firm grounding, and sure settling of a throne, or state: that which Solomon also suggests, when he tells us, That *by justice and judgement, and truth and mercy, and beneficence, the throne is supported, and the state established*, Prov. 16.12. and 20.28. and 29.4,14. and points him to a pattern and precedent of it in his father Josiah, one that was studious and careful, as of the advancement and settlement of God's service, so likewise of the due administration and execution of justice; and through God's blessing therefore upon him, and his government, enjoyed a long time of peace and prosperity, and passed the time of his reign in tranquility and quietness: the words may well be rendered; *Did not thy father eat and drink, when he administered judgement and justice?* did he not *eat and drink;* that is, live cheerfully and comfortably, free from carking cares, distracting thoughts, and distrustful fears, Eccles. 2.24. and 3.13. and 9.7. Mat. 11.18,19. See of Potiphar, Gen. 39.6. *when he administered judgement and justice?* So to *do judgement and justice* is used of David, 2 Sam. 18.15. 1 Chr. 18.14. See vers. 3. Chap. 21.12. the conjunction copulative, for the adverb of time: as 1 King. 11.25. *he vexed Israel, and reigned over Syria;* that is, *when*, or, *while, he reigned over Syria.* So the words would there be read. Est. 2.21. *In those dayes, and Mordecai sate in the Kings gate;* for, *when*, or, *while he sate there;* as it is well there rendered. See also, Esai 36.9. Chap. 17.4.

*{and then it was well with him?}* We need not bring this clause within compass of the demand, as our version does: Nor need we with some interpreters, who cut the demand overshort, concluding it at *eat and drink;* (*Did not thy father eat and drink?*) annex it to the former branch, rendering the words, *Surely he executed judgement and justice;* and *then* was it *well with him:* it contains an enunciation entire of itself; importing a ground, or reason of what was before said, he well might, as he did also, then live cheerfully and comfortably; though he had no such stately palace, as you are now building, which is but a presage of your downfall, Prov. 16.18. and 17.19. and 18.12. for it fared well with him, he was successful and prosperous in all his undertakings: as Psal. 1.3. Heb. *then was good to him.* So Deut. 5.33. and 19.13. Psal. 128.2. Esai 3.10. vers. 16.

**Verse 16.** *{He judged the cause of the poor and the needy: then it was well with him.}* Or, *When* (as vers. 21.) *he judged the cause* (Heb. *judged the judgement;* as Chap. 5.28. and 30.13.) *of the poor and needy* (as Psal. 72.4,12,13.) or, *when the cause of the poor and needy was judged* (for the verb may well be taken indefinitely, when justice was indifferently and impartially administered to all sorts, even to the meanest, Deut. 16.18,20.) *then was it well:* then were all things successful, it went well with the state: for by due administration of *judgement doth a King establish a land*, Prov. 29.4. and cause a state to flourish; and the clause here seems to reach further than before, vers. 15.

*{was not this to know me? saith the LORD.}* Heb. *that;* that was indeed to show by his deeds and carriage, by the effects and fruits of it, that his professed knowledge of God was sound and sincere, when he followed those courses that he knew God delighted in, and were pleasing in his sight, chap. 9.24. Mic. 6.8. Jam. 1.27. 1 Joh. 2.6. the contrary hereunto, see Chap. 9.3. Hos. 4.1. Tit. 1.16. 2 Tim. 3.5. 1 Joh. 2.4. The old Latin, though in effect for the matter agreeing here with this, yet swerves somewhat from the words of the text, rendering it thus, *Was it not therefore because he knew me:* and the Greek yet far further, rendering both this, and the foregoing branches, all in the negative: *they do not thus, because they know not me.* As also do they mangle the text overmuch, that make two members of this concluding clause, rendering the words thus, *Is not this? the knowledge of it is with me:* as if it were said, Is not that true that I charge you with? vers. 14. though you deny it, and others may be ignorant of it, yet I know and take notice of it: as Chap. 7.11. and 13.27. But the course of the context will not bear this; and it offers too much force to a familiar expression.

**Verse 17.** *{But thine eyes and thine heart are not but for thy covetousness}* Heb. *upon thy lucre*, or, *gain*, Prov. 1.19. Ezek. 33.31. You, contrary to the disposition and practice of your religious father, are wholly addicted unto, and set upon your lucre and gain, not regarding by what wrongful and cruel practices you compass it: to *set the heart and eyes* upon ought, in Scripture, is greedily to affect it, and eagerly to pursue it, Psalm 62.10. Prov. 23.5.

*{and for to shed innocent blood,}* Or, *and upon shedding of innocent blood.* Heb. *and upon innocent blood to shed it:* a defect of the pronoun; as Chap. 17.21. So in the last member, see vers. 1.

*{and for oppression}* Heb. *upon oppression.*

*{and for violence to do it.}* Or, *upon doing of violence.* Heb. *upon incursion*, or, *contrition, to do it*, as before: to act and exercise it at your pleasure: the word here used, the Jewish critics, some of them, expound *incursion;* from a root that signifies *to run;* whence it is used for *a course*, or *race*, 2 Sam. 18.27. See Chap. 8.6. and so it should signify a violent *incursion*, or assault, made upon a man's person. Others of them expound it, *a contrition*, or breaking to pieces, from a word of that notion, Psal. 74.14. applied to violent courses exercised upon the persons of the poor, Amos 4.1. and herein both agree, that the former word rendered *oppression*, has reference properly to men's goods, the latter rendered *violence* here, to their persons; especially where they are found coupled together: as Deut. 28.33. 1 Sam. 12.3,4. Hos. 5.11. where this latter seems to be made matter of greater vexation and evil usage than the former.

**Verse 18.** *{Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah King of Judah}* Having given in the charge against Jehoiakim, he passes now to his doom. *Therefore;* because you are altogether thus wickedly bent, as vers. 17. carrying yourself clean contrary to your religious father's courses, vers. 15,16. *thus saith the Lord;* the Lord has passed this heavy doom and sad sentence upon you: the particle commonly signifies *unto:* but here rather, *concerning*, as vers. 11. Gen. 20.2. and it is spoken in way of denunciation of a thing to come; not in way of relation of somewhat formerly denounced, and already executed, as a learned writer would have it. See on vers. 1.

*{Jehoiakim}* The name given him by Pharaoh-Nechoh, whereas before he was called *Eliakim*, 2 King. 23.34. he is also called *Joakim*, by an abbreviation, 1 Chronicles 3.15. as, *Oshea*, for, *Jehoshua*, Numb. 13.8. a name for signification well agreeing with the former. He was the eldest son of Josiah; howsoever the people had preferred his brother, two years younger than him to the crown before him; whereof see before on vers. 11. but Necho at his return, reversed their choice, and settled it upon the right heir, 2 Kings, 23.30,33,34.

*{They shall not lament for him}* For all his stately structures and buildings, he shall not have so much as any solemn funeral, or honorable sepulture: there shall no lamentation be made for him; for the verb is indefinite here; as also chap. 16.6. See the contrary promised to Zedekiah, chap. 34.5.

*{saying, Ah my brother, or, Ah Sister;}* as they were wont to say upon the decease, and at the burial of some near of kin of either sex; or whom they esteemed of as such, 1 Kings 13.30. Heb. *and, Ah Sister:* the copulative in a disjunctive notion, as v. 3. for it is a little too far fetched, which some would draw from the word *sister;* as if it were said, that neither he nor his queen should be lamented.

*{they shall not lament for him, saying,}* As before.

*{Ah Lord, or, Ah his glory.}* Or, *his magnificence.* See Esay 30.30. he shall not be lamented either by kindred, or by subjects: who were wont to use such expressions at the funerals of their kings. See Chap. 34.5.

**Verse 19.** *{He shall be buried with the burial of an Ass; drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.}* *with the burial of an Asse;* that is, as an ass is wont to be buried: as, *with the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorra*, Chap. 49.18. that is, in such manner as they were overthrown. His corpse shall not come into the sepulcher of his ancestors, 1 Kings 13.22. nor shall have any stately interment, such as kings usually have, Esay 14.18. it shall not have so much as a place of ordinary burial among the graves of the common people, Chap. 26.23. but shall be cast out like some carrion, as the carcass of an ass, into some remote place, where it may not, as it lies rotting there, infect, or annoy people with its stench. So of the king of Babylon, Esai 14.19. But in what manner, or in what place this doom was executed upon the corpse of Jehoiakim is questioned. For first, to some it seems that he was buried; because it is said of him, *he slept with his fathers*, 2 Kings 24.6. which to reconcile, some say, that he was buried by his people; but after taken up again by the Chaldeans, and so cast forth without the city: but it is very unlikely the Chaldeans, having surprised the city, would suffer the present king's corpse being slain by them, to be buried, when as they dealt so barbarously with the corpses of their former kings, as to pull the remains of them out of their monuments, where they had long lain quiet, and lay them open to the light, ch. 8.1,2. and though the phrase of *sleeping with their fathers*, be commonly used of those, whose bodies are laid up in some monument among their ancestors, yet the form of itself imports no more, than to die, as his progenitors before him did, Psalm 49.19. and does not necessarily imply any communion either in sepulture, or in place of sepulture with them: whence also *to sleep* with one's *fathers*, and *to be buried* with them are mentioned as two distinct things, 2 Chr. 15.18. and 16.20. That Jehoiakim's corpse therefore was ever committed to the ground, there is none, either sound proof from that phrase, or probability of the thing itself. But where he died and was thrown out, is further doubted, and is more doubtful. Some suppose that he died at Jerusalem, being there slain, and that he was afterward *cast forth without the walls;* where his corpse lay buried, that which the words themselves may here seem to import: and Joseph the Jew in his *Antiquities*, lib. 10. cap. 8. accordingly, in likelihood grounding on this place, relates. But others rather suppose, that being carried away captive to Babylon he there died, and was after his decease used there in such ignominious manner, as is here foretold: for both in the sacred story it is said of him, that Nebuchadnezzar came against him, and having taken him, bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon, 2 Chr. 36.6. nor have we any more added further of him there: in the prophecies of Ezekiel, it is further said of him, that *they put him in ward chained, and brought him to the King of Babylon:* and so secured him, that *his voyce was no more heard on the mountains of Israel*, Ezek. 19.9. as for that which they press to prove that he should be slain in Jerusalem; because it is said here that he should be *cast forth without the gates of Jerusalem*, as the old Latin renders it: the words should rather be read *far beyond* (Heb. *from beyond*) *the gates of Jerusalem:* the rather mentioned in likelihood, because by his curious buildings there, he seemed to make full account, as to live and reign long, so at length when he died, to lay his bones there: whereas the prophet from God tells him, that his corpse should be *dragged out*, (as chap. 49.20.) *and cast forth farre beyond the gates* of that city. So is the word used without the particle here prefixed, Gen. 19.9. *Stand aloof off;* and with it, Amos 5.27. *I will carry you captive farre beyond Damascus.* Hereunto may be added, that the word *gates*, is frequently used for *cities;* as Deut. 15.7. & 16.5. & 17.2. *in any of thy gates*, for, *in any of thy cities:* and so, *farre beyond the the gates of Jerusalem*, may be, *far beyond the cities of Judah;* called also *the cities of Jerusalem*, Chap. 34.1. and so it would be as much in effect, as far beyond all the coasts of Judea. See of the casting out of his corpse further, Chapter 36.30.

*{drawn and cast forth.}* The two verbs here used, are of an infinitive form: the former sometime signifying simply, *to drag out*, or, *draw away*, 2 Sam. 17.13. Chap. 49.20. sometime, *to drag to and fro*, as dogs use to do with a carcass, when they have seized on it, whence it is rendered *to tear*, Chap. 15.3. the old Latin here renders it, *rotten:* building I suppose on the use of the word, Chap. 38.11,12. but there also the word rather denotes *castclouts*, as our version renders it: or, *worn*, or, *ragged*, than *rotten;* though such also those there mentioned were: the latter word generally signifies *to cast forth*, or, *cast out:* and if the former word be taken in its latter notion, there should be an inversion in the terms here used; for a carcass must first be cast out, ere it can be so dragged, and torn with dogs: but it seems rather to be used here in the former notion, for dragging of a corpse forth of the place, where the party died; as they use to do among the Romans, with the bodies of malefactors executed in the prison, or elsewhere made away, into some more remote and disgraceful place, some laystall, or the like. So the words may be rendered; *As an asse is buried, so shall he be buried; being dragged and cast out, far beyond the gates of Jerusalem.* Heb. *dragging* dragged; *and casting* cast out. Of which form, both defective, and yet emphatical, see on Esay 59.13.

**Verse 20.** *{Go up to Lebanon and cry, and lift up thy voice in Bashan, and cry from the passages}* Whether the rest of this chapter be one continued prophecy with the former, or another distinct from it, seems somewhat doubtful. See on verse 2. Certain it is, that as the former part of it concerns Jehoiakim, and his wicked courses, together with the wretched end and issue thereof; so this latter concerns Jehoiachin or Jeconiah, his son, who succeeded him in the kingdom, 2 Kings 24.6. 2 Chron. 36.8. and the Jewish state shortly to suffer under him, whose destituted and distressed condition is here prophesied, together with the cause of it, their refusal to hearken unto wholesome advice in the time of their prosperity, verse 20–23. then Jeconiah's disgraceful exilement is denounced, with the cutting off of the royal dignity from any of his issue, verse 21–30.

**Verse 21.** *{Go up to Lebanon and cry;}* An abrupt entrance into a new discourse not unlike unto that. *Open thy dores, O Lebanon.* Zach. 11.1. The speech is directed unto Jerusalem, or the Jewish state, spoken to, as to a woman of some state, but in distress, verse 23. and called upon therefore to get up into some high and eminent place, whence she may be heard at distance, calling for friends and assistance to come in to her succor and relief: but withal implying, that though she turned herself every way, and made outcries on every side yet all would be in vain: for that those, from whom she expected aid, should be in as bad case as herself.

*{Lebanon and Bashan}* Two high hills. Psal. 68.15. from the latter whereof, the whole fat and rich soil and country about it had its name, Psal. 136.20. These two, say some, because they looked towards Assyria, from whence they expected aid against the Chaldeans. And it is true that of the Assyrians they had sometime made use against the Syrians, 2 Kings 16.7. but that they ever sought to them for help against the Chaldeans, I nowhere find; and suppose therefore that the eminency of those hills, and the vicinity of them, is alone here respected.

*{lift up thy voice}* Or, *cry aloud.* Heb. *give*, or, *give out thy voyce;* as Prov. 2.3. Chap. 2.15.

*{from the passages}* The old Latin, *to those that pass by;* not regarding the prefixed particle. The Greek, *to the sea-coast*, or, *to beyond the sea;* cutting the word in pieces. Others render it, *at*, or, *beyond the fords;* to wit, those of Sichor, or Nilus, towards Egypt, Chap. 2.18,26. But I find not where the word here found is used for *fords*, or, *passages;* though some other words springing from the same root sometime are: for *sides* indeed it is frequently found used, Exod. 32.15. 1 Kings 4.24. See on Esay 7.20. Besides it is not here, *at*, or, *unto*, or *beyond*, but, *from*, the place specified, whatever it be: and will not therefore so well suit with the Egyptian fords. Others therefore render it, *on every side;* *from*, or, *on, all sides*, as Chap. 49.32. Others, *from the ends;* to wit, of the land as the word is used in the Syriac, Mat. 12.42. Luke 11.31. Howbeit, all things well weighed, I concur with those, that take the word here for a proper name: the mount *Abarim*, a place of special note in the confines of Moab, by which the Israelites passed in their journey to Canaan, from the top whereof Moses saw that land, Numb. 27.12. & 33.47,48. Deut. 32.49. this the rather because of the other two mountains of note. *For all thy lovers are destroyed:* According to this version, the meaning of the words before going should be; not that she should get up into those places to call in help, as yet all interpreters generally take it; but bewail rather there with lamentable outcries, the forlorn condition both of herself, and of her friends and allies; as Chap. 3.21. & 7.29. I should therefore rather render the words; *But thy lovers are all destroyed;* so is the particle used, Chap. 2.27,34. & 14.12,13. *thy lovers*, your friends and wonted assistants, Chap. 4.30. are all ruined (Heb. *broken;* as 2 Chron. 14.13.) before you, by the Chaldeans already. See 2 Kings 24.7. and all your looking about you therefore and crying for help to any of them, is but in vain, Lam. 1.16,17.

**Verse 21.** *{I spake unto thee in thy prosperity; but thou saidst, I will not hear:}* Or, *When I spake unto thee in the height of thy prosperity*, (Heb. *in thy prosperities*, or *tranquilities:* for, these plurals have their emphasis. See on Esay 58.11. chap. 14.1.) *thou saidst, I will not hear;* you refused to obey. See chap. 2.31. & 6.16,17. a defect of the adverb of time, as vers. 16. and, *to hear*, for, *to obey*, as Chap. 7.23,24. See of God's gracious dispensations in this kind, a large and pithy discourse of Elihu, Job 33.14–28.

*{this has been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice.}* Heb. *this thy way* (as Prov. 1.19. & 30.20.) *from thy youth that thou hast not heard*, or, *wouldst not hearken to, my voyce.* You have been refractory and rebellious ever since I first molded you into a state, Deut. 9.7. & 31.27. Esay 48.8. Chap. 2.24,25. & 32.30. Of their *youth*, see Chap. 2.2.

**Verse 22.** *{The wind shall eat up all thy pastors;}* Your rulers shall all vanish or pass away, like wind, Psal. 78.39. Prov. 10.25. or, they shall be blown away like chaff before the wind, Psal. 1.4. & 83.13. Chap. 4.11,12. Hos. 13.3. or, be blasted, as grass, grain, or fruit, with such a wind as shrivels or withers it away, Psal. 103.15,16. Esay 40.6,7. alluded to Hag. 1.9. or all your hopes of help from foreign forces shall prove windy and vain, altogether uneffectual and unable to produce ought for your good, Hos. 8.7. & 12.1. and this last way the most go: but then it should rather have been; *they feed upon wind;* as Hos. 11.1. (which the old Latin yet seems to have intended, rendering it, *wind shall feed them*) than *the wind feed upon them.* I conceive therefore to be meant the second or third way; though both come much home to one, and the Chaldee taking after the second, gives it, *the wind shall disperse them*, and carry them away: that which is elegantly expressed, Hos. 4.19. where it is said, *the wind hath bound them up in her wings:* though I prefer rather the third; as alluding to some malignant blast, that mars and spoils all that it meets with, Gen. 41.6. Ezek. 19.12. Howsoever, the phrase here denotes both a sudden and utter destruction, as of things, so whether borne away or blasted. There is an elegant antanaclasis, or variety of notions, in the same word here twice used to a divers sense, as if it were said, *All thy feeders*, (so are *Shepherds* in Hebrew termed, as Psal. 23.1.) or *all that feed thee*, (as your shepherds should do, Ezek. 34.2.) *shall the wind feed on:* not, *feed* them; but *feed on* them: as, *death shall feed upon them*, Psal. 49.14. that is, devour, destroy, and consume them, as our English here well renders it. So that the word has a notion of *ruling* and governing in the former place: as 2 Sam. 5.2. 1 Chron. 11.2. a notion of *depasturing* and destroying in the latter; as the like is, Ezek. 34.10. *I am coming against the shepherds*, or, *feeders*, and, I *will make them to cease feeding the flock:* *nor shall the feeders*, or, *shepherds, feed any more upon them.* So it should be rendered: for it follows; *for I will deliver my flock from their mouthes that they may not be meat for them;* that is that they may not be devoured and destroyed by them. See also chap. 23.2. Howbeit, by *Pastors*, or *Feeders*, I conceive rather to be understood their *rulers* and governors, as chap. 3.15. & 10.21. & 23.2. than with the Jewish doctors, such foreign nations, as were called their *lovers*, verse 20. though by them they made account that they were fed, maintained and kept in life, Esay 57.10. Hos. 2.5. for of them again in the next branch apart.

*{and thy lovers shall go into captivity;}* Those that you and your rulers relied upon for succor and support, (see verse 20.) shall become captives and exiles as well as yourself; for of them also had the Chaldean king captives in Babylon, chap. 52.31,32.

*{surely then shalt thou be ashamed and confounded for all thy wickedness.}* When you shall find yourself wholly destitute of all help and relief, either from your princes at home, or your friends and confederates abroad, amidst all those evils which by your wicked courses you have brought upon yourself, Chap. 2.17,19,37. & 4.18.

**Verse 23.** *{O Inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars,}* Heb. *O Inhabitress:* as chap. 10.17. & 21.13. for he speaks to the people and state of Jerusalem, as to some stately and haughty lady. See verse 20. said here to dwell in Lebanon, (so is the city itself termed, Zach. 11.1.) not so much, as some, in regard of the vicinity of that mountain, reckoned not as a boundary only, but as a part also of the promised land, Deut. 1.7. & 3.25. as of their present condition, living and carrying themselves as loftily and haughtily, as if they sat roosting on the top of Lebanon, verse 6. as also in regard of their buildings, consisting much, the great men's palaces especially, of choice cedar wood brought from Lebanon, ver. 7,14,15.

*{how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travel?}* Heb. *as of one bringing forth.* So Psal. 48.6. Esay 13.8. & 42.14. what will all your pomp and state, or all your goodly buildings with their rich and gorgeous furniture avail you? what will become of it all? or what comfort shall you have of it, when you shall be in these distresses? no more than a woman in travail full of pains and throes, unable to find ease, or to procure delivery, (see Esay 26.17,18. & 37.3.) can have any joy or comfort of any such outward ornaments or bravery, while she continues in that condition. So Chap. 6.24. & 13.21. See also the like demand, Esay 10.3. or how lovely and amiable, for all your present gallantry, will you then appear in the eyes of those, that now seem enamored with you, and whom you repute as your paramours? See Chap. 4.30.

**Verse 24.** *{As I live, saith the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim King of Judah, were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence.}* From the state in general, and the distresses thereof denounced, God by the prophet descends more specially to the person of Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah, foretelling, and that also solemnly, confirmed with an oath, the ruin and downfall of him and his, with the utter cessation of the royal power in regard of him, or any of his posterity.

*{As I live}* Heb. no more but, *I live.* So chap. 46.18. Ezek. 5.11. & 14.13. and, *I live for ever*, Deut. 32.40. As when men swore by the Lord one to another, they used commonly that form, *The Lord liveth*, Chap. 42. & 5.16. God, swearing by himself, ver. 5. uses the like defective form; yet not unfitly supplied, as our version yields it: as if it were said, *As sure as I live.*

*{saith the LORD;}* As verse 5.16. for as for that learned writer, who would have it rendered, *said the Lord;* as if it were a relation only of some former denunciation, enough has been said before, on verse 1.4.11.

*{though Coniah}* Heb. *Coniahu;* as *Zidkijahu*, Chap. 1.3. & 21.1. He is sometime called *Jehojacin*, 2 King. 24.8. 2 Chr. 36.8. and sometime, *Jeconiah*, 1 Chron. 3.16,17. and in the Gospel, according to the Greek usage, *Jechonias* Mat. 1.11,12. whence in this place, the first letter of his name taken off, in a kind of scorn and contempt, to note his vileness and baseness, (see on verse 28.) as nicking his name, or giving him (so we use to speak) a *nickname*, *Coniah* or, *Coniahu;* as names so terminated were commonly expressed. See Esay 1.1. Howbeit, that conceit of a learned commenter, that the initial letter of his name should be taken away, because it is one of the letters of God's name, which he was not worthy to bear any part of, is frivolous and unsound: for neither was that initial letter in his name, or the notation of it, any letter of God's name, being a formative only of that verb, whereof that his name in part consisted; and not that one letter of God's name alone, but the whole name of God, to wit, *Jah*, remains and appears still in this his name, notwithstanding, that detraction; the name still importing, one *prepared*, or *established, by God:* that which his father's names, both the one and the other, do in the latter notion also import. And as little ground has the same author's surmise, concerning the change both of the father's name, and the son's; to wit, that as whereas the father's name was at first *Helioakim*, Pharaoh-Necho contracted it, and made it *Aeliakim;* so Nebuchadnezzar in like manner when he had surprised Jeconiah, altered his name, and by paring away the first syllable of it, made it *Coniah;* which the prophet here uses: for neither appears it, that his father ever had such a compound name as he supposes; nor that the King of Babylon ever thus altered the name of Jeconiah: somewhat over-curious and groundless also is that of another late writer, who would have the initial letter of his name *Coniahu*, here mentioned, to be taken off, in token of the diminution of his estate; the latter syllable *hu*, being added to it, in way of contempt, as if it were said, *that Coniah:* for it is no more *that Coniah*, than *that Jeshaiah*, or *that Ezekiah*, or, *that Uzziah*, or, *that Jeremiah*, or the like, which have usually the same adjection. See Esai 1.1. & Chap. 1.1.

*{were the signet on my right hand,}* Though he were as near and dear to me, as a king's sealing ring, that is most carefully carried about and kept, worn commonly, yea continually, on some finger, not of the hand indifferently and indefinitely, but more specially of his right hand; the better and the more principal hand, (*the right hand;* as, *the right eye* also, Matthew 5.29,30.) yet such is his vileness and baseness that I can no longer endure him, but would pluck him off, and cast him from me; so offensive is he to me, Mat. 18.8,9. See Cant. 8.6. Hag. 2.13.

*{would I pluck thee thence}* A passage from person to person; as Esay 2.19. & 22.18,19. Chap. 16.12. & 21.14.

**Verse 25.** *{And I will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life,}* An elegant antanaclasis again. I will pluck you off my *hand;* cast you out of my protection and custody; and I will deliver you up into the *hand*, that is, the power, as (Chap. 19.7. & 20.4,5.) of them that seek your life. Heb. *thy soul.* So Chap. 21.7. & 34.20. Howbeit, it seems that albeit he were delivered up into the power of persons so affected, yet that they did not make use of that power for the taking away of his life, God in his secret providence so disposing it, that the line of David should in his issue, though deprived of royal dignity, be continued unto the times of the Messias our Savior. See Chap. 52.31,32. 2 Kings 25.27,28. Mat. 1.12.

*{and into the hand of them, whose face thou fearest,}* Or, *of whom thou art afraid;* as it is rendered, Chap. 39.17. where is a promise to another of the contrary. (Heb. *from the face of whom thou fearest*) So Chap. 1.8,17.

*{even into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon, and of the Chaldeans.}* Or, *into the hand*, I *say*, Heb. *and*, as Esay 58.17. Chap. 19.12. See 2 Kings 24.12.

**Verse 26.** *{And I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee, into another country where ye were not born, and there shall ye die}* Heb. *I will throw thee out*, (the same term that is used of Shebna, Esay 22.17.) *and thy mother that bare thee*, (*Nehushta* the daughter of *Elnathan*, 2 Kings 24.8. (of whom, see Chap. 13.18.) *into another countrey*, (a *strange land:* as, *other gods*, for, *strange gods*, verse 9. and, *other tongues*, for, *strange tongues*, Esay 28.11. See verse 28.) *which ye were not born there*, (to wit, into Chaldea; an elegant redundancy frequent in that language, See the like, verse 27. Chap. 23.3.) *and there shall ye dye:* as before of Jehoachaz, verse 12. See the complement hereof concerning the captivity of Jehoiachin and his mother, 2 Kings 24.15. 2 Chron. 36.10.

**Verse 27.** *{But to the land that they desire to return, thither shall they not return.}* Heb. *And* (as verse 5.) *unto the land which they lift up their soul* (as Exod. 32.15. Psal. 24.4.) *to return there*, (as verse 26.) *thither shall they not return.* See chap. 44.14. the same threatening delivered in the same terms: and of Jehoachaz the like, verse 10,11. a change of the person again here, as before, verse 24,25.

**Verse 28.** *{Is this Coniah a despised broken idol? is he a vessel in which is no pleasure? Wherefore are they cast out he and his seed, and are cast into a land, which they know not?}* These words some conceive to be spoken in the person of the Jewish people, complaining of the disgraceful usage of their king, as if he were some sorry picture or image fallen in pieces, or some old foul and filthy pot or pan past use, and therefore thrown out at doors, and cast into the highway or street, for every one that passes by to trample upon: and expostulating concerning it, what the reason might be, that he and his should be so contumeliously used; or, as some of them would have it, objecting it to Jeremy, thereby to disprove the truth of his prophecy concerning Jeconiah, that it could not be, that God should so meanly esteem of him, or set so light by him, as either to deal so reproachfully with him, or to permit him so to be dealt with. Others would have it to be the speech of the prophet himself, expressing his grief upon the consideration, and at the contemplation of this Jeconiah his ignominious condition, that no more account than so should be made of him. But I conceive them rather to be the words of God himself, demanding what the reason was, why he should be thus used, as he had before threatened he should be; and implying that it was for no other cause, than for his wicked courses, wherein he followed his father Jehoiakim, treading just in his steps, 2 Kings 24.9. See the very like, Chap. 2.14,17.

*{this man}* Spoken in way of contempt and disgrace; as we use to say, *this fellow.* So Tertullus of Paul, Acts 24.5. that which shows this not to be the speech, either of the prophet, who speaking in his own person, would not in likelihood use such language of him; and much less of the people.

*{Coniah}* Heb. *Coniahu:* as before, verse 24.

*{a despised broken idol}* An idol, which when a man discovers the vanity of it, and he now perceives it to be unable to stead him in his necessity, he then breaks and casts away, or that by casting away is broken, Esay 2.20. & 17.9. & 30.22. or, some old picture or image, that being either fallen in pieces of itself, or broken by casualty, or otherwise dashed to pieces, is now of little worth, and of as little regard.

*{a vessel in which is no pleasure}* Heb. *a vessel, no desire*, or, *delight in it.* So Chap. 48.8.
