**Verse 40.** *{And I will bring an everlasting reproach upon you, and a perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.}* Heb. *I will give*, or, *put* (as Ezek. 37.7.) *upon you a reproach of perpetuity, and a shame perpetuity;* that is, such as shall stick to them, and abide by them forever. See the like, Chapter 20.11.

## CHAPTER 24

**Verse 1.** *{The LORD shewed me}* Heb. *Made me to see;* as Amos 7.1,4,8. and 8.1. to wit, in a vision, as Esay 6.1.

*{and behold, two baskets of figs were set before the Temple of the LORD}* The word *dud* here after used ver. 2. whereof this questionless is the plural: and in the Chaldee *duda* with *aleph*, 2 Kings 4.38. signifies sometime, *a pot*, or, *caldron*, 1 Sam. 2.14. 1 Chron. 35.13. and so some of the Jewish doctors here render it: sometime, *a basket*, or, *a maund*, 2 Kings 10.7. and so the Chaldee, whom other of them rather follow, here expresses it: agreeable to that in the Law, Deut. 26.2. hence the plural *dudae* in a contracted form in regard of its regiment. which in his entire shape would be *dudaim*, a word of signification very uncertain, used Cant. 7.14. and contracted as this here, Genesis 30.14,15,16. but such as seems to have no affinity at all with this no more than *sir*, for *a pot*, Exod. 16.3. with *sir*, for *a thorn*, Esay 34.13. or then *tsir*, for *a messenger*, Prov. 13.17. and *tsir*, for, *pain*, or, *torment*, Esay 21.7. and *tsir*, for *an hinge*, Prov. 26.14. and *tsir*, for *an image*, Esay 45.16. for it is absurd to imagine, that wheresoever the letters are found the same, the word must of necessity be the same, as well for sense, as for sound. As for the redundancy of *aleph*, in this *dudaim*, and *dudae*, from *dud:* the Jewish critic upon the place directs us for the like unto *lulaoth*, for *loops*, Exodus 26.5. from *lul* whence *lulim*, for *winding stairs*, 1 Kings 6.8. and the like superfluity of *aleph* may be observed, in *chalaim*, for *jewels*, Cant. 7.1. as also in *tachaluim*, and *tachalue*, for *diseases*, and *diseased*, chapter 14.18. and 16.4. and in *betsaoth*, for *meeres*, or *miry places*, Ezek. 47.11. though our English manner of pronunciation express it not: as also in some verbs; as in *heeznichu, they have driven away*, Esay 19.6. and in *egalti, I have polluted*, Esay 63.3. and as *aleph* is, beside the common analogy found added in these; so is it in like manner found wanting in others; as in *sherith*, for *a remnant*, 1 Chr. 11.38. in *maccolet*, for *meat*, 1 Kings 5.11. in *maleph, a teacher*, Job 35.11. and many other the like: And though it should be objected (as I see not why it should) that none of these are in all respects parallel to this, it might well be answered, that some irregularities have no match; as beside divers of those before pointed to, so that of *baitim* or *battim*, for *houses* from *bait*, for *an house*, and *banim*, for *sons* from *ben*, for *a son:* and the like therefore may be here: yea, whether it have any match or no, certain it is, that the two *dudae* here mentioned are no other than those, whereof it is immediately after subjoined, *the one dud*, and *the other dud:* and this word *dud* having a plain and known sense, it is but a needless work to hunt after any other far-fetched notion for it, when we have already one at hand.

*{were set}* Heb. only *set.* *Behold two baskets of Figs set*, or *standing:* for the word is a participle, not a verb; as Ezekiel 21.16.

*{before the Temple of the LORD}* As presented unto him for first fruits or the like, Deut. 26.2.

*{after that Nebuchadrezzar the King of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim King of Judah, with the Carpenters and Smiths from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon}* The date of this prophecy, and time of the apparition which from hence appears to have been about the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah. See 2 Kings 24.12,14–16. 2 Chr. 36.10. Chap. 29.2.

*{Nebuchadrezzar}* See Chap. 29.2.

*{Jeconiah}* Called also *Coniah*, Chap. 22.24,25. and elsewhere, Jehojacin, 2 Kings 24.8.

*{with the Carpenters}* The word here used is rendered *crafts-men*, 2 Kings 24.14,16. and it comprehends as well as *Carpenters, Masons* also and *Smiths.* See on Esay 3.3. & 40.19. & 41.7. Heb. *and the crafts-men:* nor need the particle be altered; but the noun is taken collectively, as also the next is.

*{Smiths}* About this word more doubt is made, because in the notion wherein it is here used, it is not oft found and but in this story: in the rest of the Scripture not at all: it signifies properly *an inclosure;* (whence it is used for *a prison*, Psalm 142.7. Esay 24.22. & 42.7.) or *an incloser:* and so both the ancient Greek and old Latin render it: and from some such notion the Chaldee constantly reads it *doore-keepers*, or *Porters*, such as *shut the doors*, Mal. 1.10. yet some of the Jewish critics, *noblemen, men of price*, or *worth:* as from a word that is used for *gold* Job 28.15. or another, not much differing from that, that signifies, *purified*, or *refined*, and is never found used but of *gold*, 1 Kings 6.20,21. & 7.49,50. & 10.21. 2 Chronicles 4.20,22. & 9.20. but why *noblemen* and *crafts-men* should be in this story yoked together, I suppose little reason can be rendered; and as little for that which some other would have, that these should by these be meant *wise* men and *counsellours:* or, as others, men *skilful in the Law:* either so termed by the former title, because all others *are silent*, when they speak Job 29.9,10. or by the latter, because what they *shut*, none can open or assoil, Esay 22.22. but these seem trifling niceties, though delivered by such as are deemed to be of the greatest among the Jewish masters. And as far from the truth may that well be deemed, which a late writer has of military men, men skillful in *entrenching* and raising of works, either to secure besiegers, and to straiten the besieged, or to strengthen the besieged against the besiegers: to which purpose he tells us, that those who are so termed here, are in the Book of the Kings termed, *valiant men and warriours;* but he was herein much mistaken; for these are there in the same terms mentioned and those other after them. Others therefore would have the word to signify *workmen of special note* and reckoning, in regard of their skill and cunning, such as those called the *skilful artificers*, the word before used Esay 3.3. I suppose with some of the ancients, that this latter word signifies properly *gold-smiths*, or such as *enclose*, that is, set stones in gold, or other metal. Though that be not improbable, which one of the middle age suggests, who by the former word seems to understand *Smiths*, by the other *masons;* so called, because their employment is in raising of walls for *enclosing* of cities and other places of habitation, or special use otherwise, Cant. 4.12. The Chaldeans, says he, dealt with them as the Philistines formerly, that left not *a smith* in Israel, 1 Sam. 13.19. So in like manner the Chaldeans carried away from them, as the *Smiths*, that they might not furnish them with weapons, Esay 54.16. so the *Masons* also, that they might not repair again those breaches which they had made in the walls of the city: though it may be questionable whether they made any at all then, Jehojacin yielding himself to him, as under Zedekiah they did afterward, 2 Kings 25.19.

**Verse 2.** *{One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe:}* Heb. *The one basket of figs very good, as figs of the rath ripe ones;* that is, says the Jewish commenter, as the figs of such fig trees, as bring rath ripe figs; which are usually for their forwardness, much esteemed and desired. See Esai 28.4. Hos. 9.10.

*{and}* Or, *but;* as Chap. 23.14. Mal. 1.3.

*{the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten they were so bad.}* Heb. *the other of figs very bad* (as before) *which shall not be eaten* (the indicative potentially; as Job 6.7. so also verse 3.8.) *for badness;* as *for fear*, Job 22.4. So verse 3.8. See Chapter 29.37. where the same, in effect, is found.

**Verse 3.** *{Then said the LORD unto me}* Heb. *And the Lord said*, as Chapter 23.33.

*{what seest thou Jeremiah?}* See Chapter 1.11.

*{and I said, figs, the good figs, very good; and the evil figs very evil, they cannot be eaten they are so evil.}* Or, *the bad figs very bad, that cannot be eaten, they are so bad:* for of such things we use not the word *evil:* and the word is, first and last, the same, both here, and verse 2.

**Verse 4.** *{Again, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,}* Heb. *And* (as Hosea 11.6.) *the Word of the Lord was to me:* as Chapter 1.1,11.

**Verse 5.** *{Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel,}* That has not yet so cast off all care of the seed of Jacob, or regard to them, as that he should cease wholly to be their God, Esay 41.9. and 44.21. Chapter 31.36,37. and 34.26.

*{Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the Land of the Chaldeans for their good.}* Here God begins to inform the prophet what by this apparition was meant, and what by those two maunds of figs, so diversely conditioned, was intended.

*{will I acknowledge}* Or, *do I own*, or take special *notice* of, Heb. *know;* and so the word is used, Psalm 1.6. and 37.18. Math. 7.23. Joh. 10.14.

*{them that are carried away captive of Judah,}* Those that were carried away captive with Jeconiah, vers. 1. Heb. *the captivity of Judah;* as Chap. 28.4. and 29.22. and 40.1. So, *the captivity of Sion*, Psal. 126.1.

*{whom I have sent out of this place}* Whom I have, using Nebuchadnezzar as my instrument, sent out of this city, as Chap. 29.20.

*{for their good.}* So the words read, should import the truth of that, which is indeed an undoubted truth, that afflictions, deportations, and the worst of things, work for the good of the godly, Psal. 119.67,71. Rom. 8.28. 1 Cor. 11.30,32. Phil. 1.12,19. and so this clause should have reference to God's sending of them out, in these words, *I have sent out;* yet it may rather have reference to the foregoing words, of God's *owning*, or *taking notice* of them, in those words, *I will own*, or *take notice* of them, *whom I have* so *sent out for good:* for the Hebrew has no more. So Chap. 21.10. *I will set my face against them for evil, and not for good:* the former seems to have some strength from that which follows, vers. 9. the latter from what immediately is subjoined, vers. 6. As for that which some hence gather, that God should approve of Jeconiah's yielding himself to Nebuchadnezzar, as done in obedience to the like command with that, Chap. 21.8,9. and 38.17,18. neither is it very probable, nor has it place here.

**Verse 6.** *{For}* Heb. *And;* which need not here be altered.

*{I will set mine eyes upon them}* Heb. *eye;* as Psalm 33.18. for which *eyes*, Psalm 34.15.

*{for good}* As Neh. 5.19. and 13.31. So ver. 5.

*{and I will bring them again to this land}* So Chapter 12.16. and 15.16.

*{and I will build them, and not pull them down, and I will plant them, and not pluck them up.}* So Chap. 42.10. See more of these metaphors, Chap. 1.10. and 18.7,9. a defect of the pronoun in the latter member, is supplied from the former; as Chapter 8.10. and 9.10.

**Verse 7.** *{And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD;}* So to know me, as to acknowledge me for their God, and to carry themselves accordingly for matter of obedience towards me. So Deut. 30.6. Chap. 32.39. Ezek. 11.19. and 36.27. 1 Timothy 5.20.

*{and they shall be my people, and I will be their God,}* Heb. *And they shall be to me for people, and I will be unto them for God.* Such a mutual relation, and entire communion, shall be between me and them, that it shall appear that I regard them as their God, and they carry themselves toward me, as my people. So Chap. 7.23. and 30.22. and 31.33. and 32.38. the ancient covenant being between me and them renewed, Gen. 17.7,19. Exod. 20.3,5,6. Deut. 26.17,18.

*{for they shall return unto me with their whole heart.}* Or, *when* (as Chap. 10.2. & 11.23.) *they shall return unto me* (by repentance and amendment of their ways, Esay 55.6.) *with their whole heart:* not feignedly, as in former times, Chap. 3.10. Psal. 78.36,37. but sincerely, Psal. 119.2,10. Chap. 29.13.

**Verse 8.** *{And as the evil figs which cannot be eaten they are so evil}* Or, *But as the bad figs which are so bad, that they cannot be eaten*, as verse 2,3.

*{(surely thus saith the LORD)}* So is the particle *ci* used Chapter 22.22.

*{so will I give Zedekiah the King, and his Princes, and the residue of Jerusalem, that remain in this land, and them that dwell in the land of Egypt}* Or, *So will I give up*, or, *deliver;* as v. 9.

*{the residue of Jerusalem}* That remained still there left behind by Nebuchadnezzar, when he carried Jeconiah with those other away, v. 1.

*{that dwell in the land of Egypt}* Whither many in likelihood, had fled for succor and protection, upon the Babylonian invasion as before times they had done the like, Esay 30.2. and 31.1. and as others also did afterward, against God's express charge to the contrary, Chap. 42.15.18. 2 Kings 25.26.

**Verse 9.** *{And I will deliver them}* Or, *I will*, I *say* (as Esay 55.1. and 58.10. and 59.17.) *give them up*, or *deliver them;* as verse 8.

*{to be removed into all the Kingdoms of the earth for their evil.}* Heb. *I will give them for a removal* (or, *make them a removal;* make a removal of them) *for evil* (as Chap. 21.10. and as, *for good*, v. 5,6.) *unto all the Kingdomes of the earth:* to be driven to and fro from place to place, or dispersed into all places, Chap. 15.4. and 29.18. and 34.17. of old threatened, Deut. 28.25. fulfilled, Lam. 1.8. yet some render the word here used, *vexation;* to be vexed and molested, 2 Chr. 29.8. Esay 29.18. Hab. 2.7. But the word here used, and elsewhere in this prophecy, seems the same in notion with that in Moses, though the letters be transposed: whereof, see on Ch. 23.31.

*{to be a reproach and a proverb}* Heb. *for a reproach, and for a proverb*, or, *by-word.* So Deut. 28.37. 1 King. 9.7.

*{a taunt and a curse}* Heb. *for a taunt, and for a curse:* as Chap. 26.6. and 29.22. See on Esai 65.15.

*{in all places whither I shall drive them.}* Heb. *which I shall drive them there*, or *thither.* So Chap. 8.3. and 16.15. and 23.23. and 29.18. and 32.37.

**Verse 10.** *{And I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence among them,}* These come not by chance, but by mission, commission, or permission from God. So Chap. 14.11. & 34.17. Ezek. 14.21.

*{till they be consumed}* So is the word used, Josh. 10.20. Ch. 27.8. and 44.12.

*{from off the land,}* As Deut. 4.26. 2 Chr. 33.8.

*{that I gave unto them, and to their fathers}* So Chap. 7.14. and 23.39.

## CHAPTER 25

**Verse 1.** *{The word that came to Jeremiah}* Heb. *The word* (to wit, of the Lord) *which was to Jeremiah;* as Chap. 1.1. Or, *The word that was to Jeremiah;* to wit, from the Lord: as Chap. 11.1.

*{concerning all the people of Judah,}* As Esai 1.1.

*{in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah King of Judah,}* By the date of this prophecy, compared together with that next before, Chap. 24. and the next following, Chap. 26. that appears, which formerly has been observed, Chap. 22. that the prophecies, or sermons, in this book recorded are not disposed, or ranked, according to the precise order of time wherein they were delivered, that foregoing, in time coming after this; and that following, some time before it.

*{that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon.}* Or, *which was:* the demonstrative for the relative. But hence some doubt arises concerning the composure of the first year of Nebuchadnezzar with the fourth of Jehoiakim: whereas Dan. 1.1. it is said that *in the third year of Jehoiakims reign* Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem, besieged and took it. To which answer is given by some, that the *third* year mentioned in Daniel, is not the *third* year of Jehoiakim's reign, but the *third* year of the Sabbatical course; the like whereunto they suppose to be found, Chap. 28.1. But whatsoever may be said of this latter place, whereof further when we come to it, that of Daniel seems too express for the year of Jehoiakim's reign, that it cannot be so avoided. And others rather answer, that the first year of Nebuchadnezzar's absolute reign, wherein he reigned after his father's decease, concurred (as it oft falls out) partly with the latter part of Jehoiakim's third year, and partly with the former part of his fourth, and that it may well be therefore, that in the latter part of Jehoiakim's third year, he might advance toward Jerusalem, or arrive and sit down there, and surprise it in the beginning of his fourth. So Don Joseph upon Daniel. For Jehoiakim was set up by Pharaoh-Nechoh in the room of Jehoachaz his brother, 2 King. 23.34. but Nebuchadnezzar having abandoned the power of Pharaoh in those parts, 2 King. 25.7. about this third and fourth of Jehoiakim's reign came to Jerusalem, took the city, and took away divers choice youths of the blood royal to be trained up for attendance on him in his court at Babylon. Dan. 1.3. yet left Jehoiakim enjoying the crown and kingdom still, only holding now from him, as from Nechoh he did formerly; until about three years after, when finding disloyalty in him, he returned again, took him captive and carried him to Babylon, 2 King. 25.1,2. 2 Chr. 36.6. Ezek. 19.9. See the like to this, Chap. 52.28. For Joseph the Jew, with those that follow him are far out of the way, who in his *Jewish antiquities*, l. 10, c. 7. writes, that this first invasion of Judea by Nebuchadnezzar, was in the fourth year of his reign, and the eighth of Jehoiakim's; which the calculations of the sacred records do evidently refel. Nor shall we need to have recourse to that which a learned writer suggests, to wit, that in Daniel the words may be rendered, *After the third year of Jehoiakims reign;* because the particle there used does so signify, Exod. 2.23. and Num. 28.26. Since that such use of it in these computations is unusual: and the other way is familiar.

**Verse 2.** *{The word which Jeremiah the Prophet spake unto all the people of Judah, and unto all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying,}* Unto all those, that out of all parts of the land, repaired to Jerusalem, (for it is not to be imagined that he went up and down to publish it from town to town, or from city to city) as well as unto those that had their places of abode there, because it concerned all of them, as well the one as the other, vers. 1. and the former part of this prophecy is concerning them in particular; denouncing their destruction, vers. 8–11. for their obstinacy in their wicked courses, notwithstanding the manifold admonitions and warnings from time to time given them, both by Jeremy, and other God's messengers, vers. 3–7. and yet promising a restitution at seventy years end, vers. 12–14. for the latter part is more general, containing a denunciation of the like judgment against sundry several nations at large reckoned, the King of Babylon himself, by whom they were to suffer, not excepted, vers. 15.38.

**Verse 3.** *{From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon King of Judah, even unto this day,}* (*that is, the three and twentieth year*) *{the word of the LORD hath come unto me;}* To convince them of their obstinacy, he relates how assiduous and sedulous God himself by his prophets, and his prophets from him, for a long time had been, in admonishing them of their wicked courses, and endeavoring to reclaim them from the same; but all to no purpose, without any fruit, or good effect.

*{From the thirteenth year of Josiah}* So is the time of his calling to the prophetical function precisely fixed, Chap. 1.2.

*{the son of Ammon}* So Chap. 1.2.

*{this is the three and twentieth year}* Heb. *this three and twentieth year;* which need not be altered, nor put into any parenthesis: for twelve entire years being taken from the *thirty* and *one* of Josiah, 2 Kings 22.1. there will *eighteen* (with some advantage in likelihood) remain; whereunto if we add *six months*, 2 Kings 23.31. together with the *third*, near expiring, or *fourth* beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, the sum of *twenty and three* will arise. So this prophecy seems to have been delivered much about the time of Nebuchadnezzar's first invasion of Judea, and surprising of Jerusalem, or very shortly after it; and to be of the same date with that recorded, Chap. 36.1.

*{and I have spoken unto you rising early, and speaking}* I have not failed to deliver faithfully to you, what I received from God; and that with all sedulity, assiduity and diligence, for so much this form of speech imports. See Chap. 7.13,25. withal alluding, as some think, to the time of the morning meeting for God's solemn service, Numb. 28.4. 2 Kings 3.20. Luke 21.36. Acts 2.15. at which time it is not unlikely that the prophet usually preached, there being then the greatest concourse of people in the temple: but the allusion seems more general unto all sorts of diligent and industrious persons, that rise early to attend and follow their several employments in their several places: magistrates, to sit in judgment, merchants to attend their trade, workmen and laboring men to follow their day's work, Psal. 101.8. & 104.23. & 127.2. Chap. 21.12.

*{but ye have not hearkened}* Heb. *and* (as chap. 23.14.) *ye heard not:* you would not hear; that is, be admonished and obey, Psal. 81.11. Chap. 7.23,24.

**Verse 4.** *{And the LORD hath sent unto you all his servants the Prophets, rising early and sending them,}* See chap. 7.25. So also, chap. 29.19.

*{but ye have not hearkened nor inclined your ear to hear}* See chap. 7.24,26.

**Verse 5.** *{They said}* Heb. *Saying;* as chap. 18.1. God saying by them whom he sent, verse 4. for the speech runs as spoken by him, verse 7.

*{Turn ye again now every one from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings}* I labored by them to reduce you to repentance, and to amendment of life, 2 Kings 17.13. chap. 18.11. & 35.15. to reclaim you especially from your idolatrous courses, which you have always been much addicted unto, verse 6.

*{and dwell in the land}* Or, *so shall ye dwell in the land*, as Psal. 37.3. *and be fed: and dwell*, for, *so shalt thou be fed*, and, *so shalt thou dwell.*

*{that the LORD hath given unto you, and to your fathers}* As Chapter 23.9.

*{for ever and ever}* Heb. *to from age and unto age:* but the first particle, as in the like forms, (as Chap. 2.25.) is redundant: as also is the copulative before the latter, as Chap. 7.7. and this clause may have reference both here and there, either to their continuance in the land, as Psal. 37.27. or to the extent of God's gift and grant: as Gen. 17.8.

**Verse 6.** *{And go not after other gods to serve them, and to worship them,}* As both you and your fathers have from time to time done, Chapter 16.11.

*{and provoke me not to anger with the works of your hands,}* Heb. *and anger me not.* So Chapter 7.18,89. *with the works of your hands;* your idols, Psal. 78.40,58. & 106.29. Chap. 32.30. & 44.8. or your wicked courses in general; as verse 14. Psal. 28.4. Hag. 2.14.

*{and I will do you no hurt.}* Heb. *I will not do evil to you.* As 1 Sam. 26.11. Those evils that I have threatened to bring upon you, shall be reversed and withheld, Chap. 1.6. & 6.19. & 11.11. & 19.3,15. See Chap. 18.8.

**Verse 7.** *{Yet ye have not hearkened unto me, saith the LORD;}* Heb. *And* (as chap. 23.21.) or, *But;* as verse 4. see there.

*{that ye might provoke me to anger}* Heb. *anger me.* as verse 6. See Chap. 7.18.

*{with the works of your hands}* See verse 6.

*{to your own hurt}* Not to mine; whom no evil of yours can reach unto, nor do the least harm, Job 35.6,8. Chap. 7.19. Heb. *for evil to you;* that is, *to yourselves:* as Prov. 9.12. chap. 5.19. & 23.8.

**Verse 8.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Because ye have not heard my words,}* That is not hearkened to him, and yielded obedience to them; but refused and rejected them, as Chap. 7.19. for had they not heard? yes undoubtedly. See verse 3,4. heard they had, (which aggravated their guilt) but obeyed they had not. See Rom. 10.16,18,19.

**Verse 9.** *{Behold, I will send and take all the families of the North}* What is termed *sending* and *taking* here, is expressed by *calling*, Chap. 1.15. and those here called *the families of the North*, are called *the kingdoms of the North* there: *family*, for, *kindred:* as Chap. 8.3. those of the several kingdoms and nations subject to the Chaldean monarch (whose country lay to the north of Judea, Chap. 1.14. & 6.22.) and serving under him; whom by a secret instinct, God would cause to come as readily and unanimously unto this service, as if he had sent some messengers to them to invite them thereto, or some leaders to bring them on. See the like Esay 13.2,4. Heb. *I am sending and will take;* that is, *I am sending to take*, as Josh. 24.5. to take them up for this service, and bring them thereunto.

*{and Nebuchadnezzar the King of Babylon my servant;}* Heb. *and to Nebuchadnezzar.* I will send to him as well as to them; to bring them to him, (whom I intend to employ as my commander in chief for this expedition, to do me special service therein: as Chap. 27.6. & 43.10. Ezek. 29.18,20.) and to bring him and them together against this land, and the neighboring countries. Thus does the Lord show himself to be *the Lord* of hosts, verse 8. and that he has all the creatures even wicked men, and the devils themselves, at command, Psal. 119.91. & 148.8. making use of them, even without their privity, and beside their purposes, Esay 10.5,7. and 45.4,5. for his own glory, the correction and dejection of some, and the restitution and advancement of others, Prov. 16.4,5. Esay 40.5. & 45.4.

*{and will bring them against this land, and against the Inhabitants thereof,}* He speaks as if he himself were coming in the head of Nebuchadnezzar's forces against them. See chap. 15.8. & 21.5,13.

*{and against all these nations round about,}* That you may not in vain expect or hope for any help against him from them. Whence it appears that Nebuchadnezzar had not as yet made entire conquest of those neighboring nations, when this prophecy was delivered; whom yet having subdued, he made use of afterward against Judah and Jerusalem, when Jehoiachim proved disloyal to him, 2 Kings 24.1,2. he having at that time taken away from the Egyptian all the power and interest that he had in those parts, and the regions thereabout as far as to Euphrates, 2 Kings 24.7.

*{and will utterly destroy them}* Heb. *make a cherem*, or *anathema, of them;* as Esay 37.11. So Chap. 50.16.

*{and make them an astonishment, and an hissing,}* See chap. 19.8. So verse 18.

*{and perpetual desolations}* Heb. *desolations of perpetuity;* that is, of long continuance: as Esay 58.12. So verse 18.

**Verse 10.** *{Moreover, I will take from them}* Or, *I will also take from them.* Heb. *And* (which may well here be retained) *I will cause to perish from them;* as Obad. 8.

*{the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness,}* All such mirth as they had wont to have, and to make by music instrumental or vocal, at their feasts, and merry meetings, Amos 6.5. See the like threatening, Chap. 7.34. Ezek. 26.13. Hos. 2.11. Rev. 18.22.

*{the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride,}* Such songs and solemn speeches as virgins and others, were wont to entertain the bridegroom and bride with, Psal. 45.1. Mat. 25.1. or wherewith they used mutually to solace themselves one with another, Cant. 2.8,14. See also chap. 7.34. Rev. 18.23. See also Chap. 33.11.

*{the sound of the millstones}* Heb. *the voyce of the mill:* and so also Rev. 18.22. that which some understand, simply of the noise that the millstones in grinding are wont to make: alluded to Eccles. 12.4. implying that bread corn, and bread itself consequently, (see Zach. 9.16.) and together with it, whatsoever supply they had of means, wherewith to maintain, not jollity alone, but life and subsistence, should be taken away: as Esay 3.1. But some others understand it of such songs as women use to sing, to pass the time away, while they wrought at the handmill, Exod. 11.5. Mat. 24.41. Luke 17.35. of which kind of ditties, we have some yet extant in the monuments of the ancient Greeks. And some again going also this way, restrain to the songs used by such at the grinding of corn for flour to make bride cakes and spiced bread with for weddings; because it is joined here with such wedding solemnities: but that seems of little weight, since that in that parallel place of John where all these particulars are recited, it is subjoined not to weddings, but to artificers; nor is it adjoined to the former place. I concur rather with the first. Of the word here rendered *mill-stones* see on Esay 57.2.

*{and the light of the candle}* Heb. *light of candle*, or, *candle-light;* and so Rev. 18.24. a note of desolation, and of a place desolate, and utterly abandoned, where no candlelight at all is to be seen: and its needlessly therefore restrained, to the enervating of the text, unto such torches, tapers or lamps, and other like lights, as they had wont to accompany the bridegroom with, brought to the bridal house by night, Mat. 25.1.

**Verse 11.** *{And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment;}* Heb. *all this land* (to wit, Judea) shall be *unto devastation,* *unto astonishment*, or *desolation;* as it is also commonly taken, and rendered, chap. 2.15. & 4.7. & 18.16. and so would rather here: and though the root it comes of, have sometime also a notion of *astonishment*, Lev. 26.32. Chap. 2.12. Ezek. 26.16. where it may seem to be not amiss so rendered, vers. 9. yet I suppose that but a groundless nicety of a learned writer, who would have the noun here used, and thence deduced, to be not a simple, but a compound term, and to signify, *there what?* or *what is there?* as taken from the usual speech of folk, who seeing a place strangely defaced and wasted, are wont to say, *what is there here?* or *what have we here?*

*{and these nations}* Neighboring upon you round about, to wit, the Philistines, Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, and Aramites, or Syrians, vers. 9.

*{shall serve the King of Babylon}* Not some one king of Babylon alone, but three of them successively, one after another. See Chap. 27.7.

*{seventy years}* The term and time of the Jewish captivity, together with the servitude of those other neighboring nations, under the Chaldean monarchy, is here precisely set down, as for the further confirmation of the truth of this prophecy, so more especially, for the better support of the faithful during the time of their captivity, and nourishing in them an hopeful expectation of their undoubted deliverance, when that term of years should be expired, Dan. 9.3. Concerning the determination whereof, the agreement seems to be more general, the Holy Ghost having in the sacred records expressly fixed it upon the first year of Cyrus his absolute reign, 2 Chr. 36.22. Ezr. 1.1. But about the time, or term from which those years commence is doubt made by divers. For some begin them at the date of this present prophecy, from the fourth year of Jehoiakim's reign, vers. 1. about which time Nebuchadnezzar having given a great overthrow unto Pharaoh-Necho king of Egypt, Chap. 46.2. did afterward also upon this occasion invade Judea; Pharaoh Necho had gone to recover Carchemish from the King of Assyria, 2 King. 23.29. and 2 Chr. 35.20. and having by the way slain Josiah in fight; upon his return from thence entering upon Judea, he put down Jehoachaz, whom the people had made king in his father's room, and set up Jehoiakim, his brother, in his stead, 2 King. 33.29,30,33,34. but Nebuchadnezzar having met with the Egyptian, and given him the fore-mentioned overthrow, struck into Judea, came to Jerusalem, took it, as may seem, without any notable resistance, and compelled Jehoiakim to renounce his tenure from the crown of Egypt, and to hold it, which Jehoiakim was content to do, from him, 2 King. 24.1. And from this surprisal of Jerusalem, in Jehoiakim's third and fourth year, vers. 1. Dan. 1.1. do divers writers make these seventy years to commence. But howsoever it be true indeed that at that time the Chaldean gave order to some of his ministers to bring with him unto Babylon some young striplings of the blood royal and princely alliance; to be trained up for his service and attendance in his court there, whereof Daniel was one, Dan. 1.3,4. yet neither did he then either carry away captive, or depose Jehoiakim, who continued his reign seven years after that, 2 Kings 23.36. 2 Chr. 36.5. neither is there mention in the sacred records, either of any great devastation at that time made in the land, or of any considerable number, that should then be carried away captive. Others therefore choose rather to fix it at the eleventh year of Zedekiah; at which time that kingdom and state seemed to draw its last breath, Lam. 4.20. for then was the city not only surprised and sacked, but together with the temple, and the king's palace, a great part of it burnt down, the state royal dissolved, and a more general deportation of the people of the land than had at any time been before, 2 King. 25.4.21. 2 Chr. 36.17–20. Chap. 52.5–30. This further to confirm, they allege that saying, 2 Chr. 36.20,21. that *those which had escaped the sword, were carried away to Babylon, where they were servants to him* (to wit, Nebuchadnezzar) *and his sons, untill the reign of the Kingdom of Persia: to fulfill the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her Sabbaths: for so long as she lay desolate, she kept Sabbath, untill the seventy years were fulfilled.* But hereunto is answer given, the end, or uttermost term of the land's sabbatizing after it began to lie waste is there specified, and it is said only to have sabbatized so long as it so lay waste: but neither is mention made of the beginning of those seventy years, nor that the land lay in that manner waste that whole seventy years time, from that year commencing: and the like they find in the same chapter, where it is said of Jehojacin, that *he reigned three months and ten dayes, and when the year came about*, or expired, *Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon*, 2 Chr. 36.9,10. yet is not the meaning, that he reigned an entire year; but that when that year went out, the three last months whereof only with a few days over he reigned, this his surprisal fell out. Others therefore lastly, with whom I concur, begin them at the captivity of Jeconiah, or Jehojacin, Chap. 22.24–[reference ending unclear]. at what time Nebuchadnezzar in the eighth year of his reign took him prisoner, having sat little above *three months* in the royal seat, together with *his mother, his Princes, and his officers*, and carried them away with him to Babylon: and besides them *all the Inhabitants of Jerusalem*, and *all the men of might or valour in the land*, some *seven thousand* in number, and *all the artificers, and smiths*, or *masons, a thousand*, and *all that were strong and fit for war, ten thousand* in all; leaving none save of the poorest sort of people behind, 2 King. 24.8–16. And this beginning of the seventy years captivity we have both from Jeremy and Ezekiel: for Jeremy himself, the fittest and best able to fix the head of this account, writing unto those that were in captivity at Babylon, being carried thither with Jeconiah, in the time of Zedekiah's reign, Chap. 29.1,2,3. tells them expressly, that *when as seventy years should be accomplished, God would visit them, and bring them back to their own countrey again*, Chap. 29.10. as also, Ezek. 4.1. the captivity is said to have begun *eleven years* before the sacking of the city under Zedekiah: for the *fourteenth year after the sacking of the citie*, is said expressly to be *the twenty and fifth year of their captivity:* And again, the first tidings are said to have been brought unto him abiding among the captives at Babylon, of the surprisal of the city, by one that had escaped thence, *in the twelfth year* of their captivity, Chap. 33.21. which comes up just to Jeconiah's deportation, the eleven years of Zedekiah's reign coming between, 2 King. 24.18. and 25.2–4. whereby it evidently appears, that the years of their captivity were reckoned, neither from the fourth of Jehoiakim, nor from the eleventh of Zedekiah, but between them both, from the deportation of the people together with Jehojacin, or Jeconiah.

**Verse 12.** *{And it shall come to pass when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the King of Babylon, and that nation, saith the LORD, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans:}* Thus the destruction of Babylon, and the deliverance of God's people out of that captivity, Chap. 29.10. do concur in time exactly the one with the other. See Esai 1.1.

*{it shall come to pass}* Heb. *it shall be;* as Chap. 17.24.

*{when seventy years are accomplished}* Of these seventy, six and thirty complete, are of Nebuchadnezzar's reign; for so we find that the first year of Evil-Merodac his son's reign concurred with the seven and thirtieth year of Jehojacin's captivity, 2 King. 25.27. Chap. 52.31. the other thirty and four are to be divided between Evil-Merodac, and Belshazzar, (the latter of which reigned two, at least, complete; for of his third is mention made, Dan. 8.1.) unless some vexation, or usurpation, as some deem, came between their two reigns. See Chap. 27.7. and out of Berosus his *Chaldean storie*, Joseph the Jew in his fifth book *against Apion.* For as for the Jewish doctors that will give Evil-Merodac only twenty three, and to make up the sum reckon from the first of Nebuchadnezzar, and the fourth of Jehoiakim, taking in the whole forty five of Nebuchadnezzar's reign; they seem to go but on mere surmise for the former, and to cross the prophet's own computation in the latter, see on vers. 11.

*{that}* Supplied, as Esai 4.7.

*{I will punish for their iniquity}* Heb. *I will visit upon them their iniquitie;* as Exod. 34.7. Chap. 23.2,34. as he will *visit* his people then in mercy, Chap. 29.10. so he will *visit* their oppressors then in wrath for the wrong done by them to his people. See Esai 47.6. and 51.22,23. Chap. 27.18. and 51.35,36. So Gen. 15.13,14. Esai 10.12.

*{the King of Babylon}* Not Nebuchadnezzar, but one of his issue and successors in that empire, Belshazzar. See on Esai 14.4–19.

*{that nation}* The Chaldeans, Chap. 6.22. and 24.5. together with their land; by destruction the one, by devastation the other.

*{and will make it perpetual desolations.}* Heb. *put it unto desolations*, or *devastations of perpetuity*, or *diuturnity;* as vers. 9. See Esai 13.19. and 14.23. Chap. 50.40. and 51.26.

**Verse 13.** *{And I will bring upon that land all my words that I have pronounced against it, even all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah hath prophesied against all the nations.}* Hence some gather, that those ensuing prophecies from chap. 46. to 51. the two last whereof do at large foretell and describe the ruin of Babylon, were preached before this: and the ancient Greek therefore does here, after these words, insert them, in a confused way. But hereof there is no necessity.

*{And}* Or, *So;* as Chap. 11.18. vers. 14.

*{against all the nations}* See the title prefixed at Chap. 45.1.

**Verse 14.** *{For many nations, and great Kings, shall serve themselves of them also:}* As many nations with their kings shall for a time serve them; so after the term of that monarchy run out, they shall serve themselves of them. Whence some observe, that these *seventy years* are to commence, not so much from the utter desolation of the land of Judea, and those other countries hereafter mentioned, as from their servitude, see on v. 11.

*{many nations}* The Medes and Persians with others subject to them, and serving under them, Esai 13.4. Dan. 5.28,31. yet the word in the original is ambiguous to *many*, or *great.* So Psal. 25.11.

*{great Kings}* Darius and Cyrus: under whose conduct those forces consisting of divers nations against Babylon, see Esai 21.7,9. and 43.14. and 45.1.

*{shall serve themselves of them}* Heb. *have served upon them;* which the old Latin following, renders the words; *because they served* *them when they were many nations, and great Kings:* and this some expound, as if the reason were here rendered, why the nations before-mentioned, vers. 13. should so suffer, to wit, because they had served against God's people under the Chaldeans: which though true of some of them hereafter mentioned, 2 King. 24.2. Psal. 137.7. yet of some of them, the Egyptians especially, is not true, Chap. 37.5. and others therefore say, because that God's people had served them, and they had dealt rigorously and cruelly with them: to which purpose, a learned writer cites one of the Jewish doctors, who should so expound the place; but the Jewish commenter, whom he cites, says no such matter: he rather directly controls it; for first he observes, that the verb of the time past is put here for the future, as our version well renders it; then that the word of *service* (which this author also in part admits) in the syntax here used signifies, not to *serve* one, but to *exact service* of one, or to *serve* oneself *upon* one, (of which see on Chap. 30.8. and 34.10. as also, see Ezek. 34.27.) and lastly, that the words are meant of the kings of Media and Persia, with their people, who should have the Chaldeans to serve them, as they had done with others before: and this exposition is confirmed by that parallel place, Chap. 37.7.

*{of them also.}* Heb. *upon them: upon them also*, as they have done upon others: or, *even upon them;* as Esai 57.6,7. howsoever it may seem a matter very unlikely at present.

*{and I will recompence them according to their deeds, according to the works of their own hands.}* Or, *so:* as vers. 13. or, *thus*, as Chap. 7.34. *will I repay them*, or, *render unto them;* as the word is rendered, Chap. 51.24.

**Verse 15.** *{For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me;}* Or, *For thus said the Lord, the God of Israel unto me;* to wit, at that time when he delivered me the foregoing message, vers. 1.

*{Take the wine cup of this fury at mine hand}* Or rather, *Take this wine-cup of wrath.* Heb. *heat*, or *fervour:* whence some render it, *this smoaking wine-cup;* an argument of anger, Esai 6.4. See Rev. 14.10,11. Esai 51.17,22. *from my hand.* Those judgments and afflictions that God allots, especially out of anger and wrath to any, are in Scripture frequently compared to a cup of some hot, or heady drink that does exceedingly distemper. See Psalm 11.6. and 60.3. and 75.8. Job 21.20. Lam. 4.21. Ezek. 23.32–34. Such a cup in a vision is reached out to Jeremy, and he enjoined taking it out of God's hand, to go with it unto the nations hereafter mentioned, and to render it unto them.

*{and cause all the nations to whom I send thee to drink it}* Heb. *make to drink it all the nations whom I am sending thee unto them:* an elegant redundancy, very common in this language: so 1 King. 21.11.

**Verse 16.** *{And they shall drink it, and be moved, and be mad: because of the sword that I will send among them.}* The effects of this drink, together with an explication of it, what it is: see further, vers. 27,29.

*{they shall drink it}* They shall be enforced to drink of it, whether they will, or no, vers. 28. or, *that they may drink it;* as Chap. 22.10. and 23.18,21. Mal. 1.9.

*{and be moved;}* None of them being so strong, as to be able to bear it; but shall be overcome with it: as Chap. 23.9. the word may well be rendered, *They shall be tossed*, or, *shall toss themselves* to and fro. See Chap. 5.22. as men unquiet and restless by occasion of drink that disturbs their brains, or being in a distemper of frenzy, are wont to do, Prov. 23.34.

*{and be mad}* As men that are mad drunk. So Ezek. 23.34. chap. 51.7.

*{because of the sword}* Heb. *from before*, or, *from the face of;* that is, by reason of; as Chap. 23.9.

*{the sword}* That is, hostile invasion with fire and sword: so is the term *sword*, commonly taken, Lev. 26.25. Esai 1.20. Ezek. 30.4. and that is the cup, or wine of God's wrath, the smoking liquor, before-mentioned. So vers. 27,29.

*{I shall send}* For by his appointment, and with his commission, it comes, Chap. 47.6,7. Ezek. 14.17.

**Verse 17.** *{Then took I the cup at the Lords hand}* Or, *So* (as v. 14. Heb. *And;* So Chap. 43.2,5.) *I took the cup from the Lords hand:* being by his hand, in vision, reached out to me, vers. 15.

*{and made all them to drink, unto whom the LORD had sent me}* As vers. 15. either in vision, or by denunciation. See Chap. 27.4. vers. 30. For that conceit of a learned writer seems to me nothing probable, that the prophet should go up and down with a cup in his hand, and travel to so many several nations, and so far remote one from another with it; enough to have taken up a main part of his life.

**Verse 18.** *{To wit, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah}* Thus judgment usually begins at God's own house, with God's own people, Ezek. 9.6. 1 Pet. 4.27.

*{and the Kings thereof, and the Princes thereof}* The kings thereof successively, Jehoiakim, Jehojacin, and Zedekiah, Ch. 22.18,19,24,25. and 21.7. See chap. 27. vers. 19.20,25.

*{to make them a desolation, and astonishment, an hissing, and a curse.}* Heb. *to give them unto desolation*, &c. See on Chap. 24.9. vers. 9.

*{(as it is this day)}* Or, *as appeareth this day.* So chap. 4.20,38. and 8.18. 1 King. 8.24. whence some gather, that this prophecy was delivered after the captivity of Jehojacin: but the date of it, vers. 1. directly controls this. Nor can I accord with those, who would have this prophecy to be of a diverse date from the former: the series of the context, vers. 15. it seeming not well to admit it: and with those much less, who would have it spoken in a prophetical strain, in the time present, as of a thing to come, but as sure to be, as if it were already done, and to be seen, even at present; because I nowhere meet with this form so used. Others suppose that this clause has relation not to the time when the prophecy was first uttered; but the time when it was afterward penned and published in writing, being made up in one volume together with the rest of his prophecies; which yet to me seems no more probable than the former. I suppose it was shortly after the Chaldean irruption in the third and fourth of Jehoiakim, ver. 1. Dan. 1.1. when the land being questionless of necessity much plundered by so great an army as Nebuchadnezzar in all likelihood brought with him, after it had not long before by Pharaoh Nechoh been so pillaged, the city surprised, the crown tossed from one head to another, and enforced to hold from the Egyptian one while, and the Chaldean another while; that dismal work began then to break forth and discover itself, that afterward grew to its higher growth in Jehojacin's captivity; and to its full height in the expiring reign of Zedekiah. See 2 King. 23.32,37. and 24.15,16. and 25.1,21.

**Verse 19.** *{Pharaoh King of Egypt, and his servants, and his Princes, and all his people.}* *Pharaoh-Nechoh*, ch. 46.2. & *Pharaoh-Hophra*, ch. 44.30. his successor. *Egypt* comes in the first place because the Jewish people relied principally upon them, presuming much upon succors and safeguards, which they promised unto themselves from them, ch. 37.5. Ezek. 29.6,7,16. and the prophet may seem the rather therefore to insist upon particulars concerning them, their *Princes, servants* and *people;* (because though their king might miscarry, yet the state might stand, managed by the peers and officers of state and their strength consisting in the multitude of their people, might not be much impaired) to put them out of all hope of support, or shelter from thence. See Chap. 40. Ezek. 29. and 30. and 31.

**Verse 20.** *{And all the mingled people;}* Concerning the term here used, interpreters much differ; the word is used sometime for *a mixture* of persons, or people, a promiscuous multitude, Chap. 50.37. and with the *r* only lengthened in the same notion, Exod. 12.38. Neh. 13.3. to which purpose some understand it here. So some of the Jewish doctors, affirming hereby to be understood a mixture of people, consisting of divers nations, that were embodied together: but who in particular, or where abiding, they tell us not. But some others deem it to have reference to the nations ensuing, as generally comprehending the people, in this verse and the next, by name more particularly there recited; and here so termed, because, say they, their borders and confines were intermixed the one with the other. Others, going the same way for notion of the term, understand it as having reference to the verse before-going; of such people as were mingled in their places of habitation with the Egyptians, or bordered near upon them, and were in confederacy with them: to which purpose the Chaldee paraphrast expresses it by a term, that is deemed to import *auxiliaries;* which may seem therefore to take in the Cushites, who are oft mentioned as borderers upon Egypt. See Esai 18.1. confederates with it, and assistants to it, Esai 20.4. Ezek. 30.4,6. where in the 5. verse, also the word here used is found: and this the rather may carry some probability with it, because the Cushites in all this catalogue are not at all mentioned. Howbeit, others take the word here to signify *Arabia*, as sometime in this very form it does (though for the most part, with a very small variation, as vers. 24. but sometime also without any such variation; as appears by 1 King. 10.19. compared with 2 Chr. 9.14. and whereas it might be objected, that *Arabic* is expressly mentioned apart vers. 24. it is answered, that there is mention made of those that lived under some royal government, either in *Arabia* the *fertile;* or in *Arabia* the *desart;* here such of them are intended, as were under no settled government, but lived wildly, wandering from place to place; and withal, which has some hint of the former notion, were a mixture of divers nations. To which purpose, also, some draw in here that of Tidal, called *King of nations*, Gen. 14.1. In a matter so ambiguous, I shall forbear to determine ought, leaving it to the decision of the learned.

*{and all the Kings of the land of Uz}* Or *Uts:* of which name there are three several parties mentioned in Scripture; and accordingly three several places deemed to have borne that name. The first and ancientest of them was the son of Aram, Genes. 10.23. whose posterity are supposed to have dwelt in that part of Syria, wherein Damascus is situated, 2 Sam. 8.5. Esai 7.8. the large valley bordering upon it, retaining still in the Arabic language the name of *Gauta*, by a change of letters not unusual: as *Gaza*, for, *Azzah*, Act. 8.26. *Gomorra*, for, *Ammirah*, Esai 1.9. and *Tyre* for, *Tsor*, Esai 23.1. *Tanes* for, *Tsoan*, Esai 30.4. The second was the son of Nachor, Abraham's brother, whose posterity are deemed to have taken up their abode in some part of Arabia the desert, near to Chaldea, the place of Job's habitation, Job 1.1. where he had such bad neighbors, the Chaldeans on the one side, and the Sabeans on the other, Job 1.15,17. the region by the Greeks termed *Ausitis*, and the inhabitants thereof, by Ptolemy, *Æsitæ*; or as some rather think *Ausitæ*. The third was by Dishan the issue of Seir, Gen. 36.28. those of his posterity seated themselves, as some think, in some part of Arabia the stony; either within, or very near unto the land of Idumea, Lam. 4.21. and of these I conceive that the Prophet here speaks.

*{and all the kings of the land of the Philistines}* See Chap. 47.1. These were of the race of Cham, by Mitsraim his son, the Egyptians’ progenitor. Gen. 10.6,13,14. 1 Chr. 1.8,11,12. those of his posterity in succeeding ages bordered to the west upon the land of Judea. See Esay 2.6. and 9.12.

*{and Ashkelon, and Azza, and Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod}* Or, *even of Ashkelon and Azza*, etc. as Chap. 19.12. and 23.9. for these were all several Princes in the Philistines’ country, See 1 Sam. 6.17. where these four are reckoned up among the five, which *Gath* here omitted, makes up there. the reason whereof may be, because that albeit, it had a King in former times, 1 Sam. 21.10. yet it may seem, in progress of time, before Jeremiah’s days, either to have been swallowed up in some one of the other four, or to have been utterly ruined by some foreign force. See Amos 6.2. of *Ashkelon*, see chap. 47.5,7.

*{Azzah}* Rendered *Gaza*, after the Greek pronunciation of it, 1 Sam. 6.17. and chap. 47.5. See on the words foregoing.

*{the remnant of Ashdod}* By the Greeks, and Latins, termed *Azotus*, Act. 8.40. And it is here said *the remnant* of it, as some suppose, because it had been much impaired and wasted by Psammetichus, father to Pharaoh-Nechoh, who a long time besieged it. See Herodote, lib. 2. or as it may well be, by Tartan, a Commander under Sargon King of Assyria, who seems not to have besieged it only, as Psammetichus did, but to have surprised also, and sacked it, Esay 20.1.

**V. 21.** *{Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon.}* These, the posterity of Esau, the first of them, Gen. 36.1. of Lot the other two, Gen. 19.37,38. did border near upon one another, Deut. 2.8,9. and they were as near borderers, so bad neighbors also from time to time unto God’s people. See Psal. 83.6,7,8. Of the ruin of Edom, see further, Chap. 49.7. Moab, Chap. 48. of Ammon, Chap. 49.1.

**V. 22.** *{And all the kings of Tyrus,}* Heb. *Tsor.* see Esay 23.1. and on v. 10. either Kings of several colonies from thence sent abroad, and countries thence peopled; of which sort Carthage is generally acknowledged to have been one; or petty Kings, that held from, and were as vassals unto the hereditary crown of that State; or, *Kings*, for, *Princes*, and *Rulers*, as chap. 17.20. and 19.3. and 22.5. the rather here so termed for their great state and wealth, Esay 23.8. See chap. 47.4. Ezek. 26.17,18.

*{and all the kings of Sidon}* Heb. *Tsidon.* Greek, *Sidon*, Mat. 11.21. A neighboring city to Tyrus: whereof see on Esay 23.2,12. they are found oft joined together, in regard of their vicinity, Mat. 11.21. and 15.21.

*{and all the kings of the Isles which are beyond the Sea}* Or, *of the lands*, or *countries*, or *regions* (as Esay 20.6. and 24.1. and 42.4. and 49.1.) or *the coast* (for the Hebrew term is singular) *that are*, or *that is* (and this rather) *besides the Sea*, or *by the Sea-side*; as the word is used, Deut. 1.1. whereby some (taking the words according to our Version) suppose Greece & Italy to be meant, divided from Judah by the midland Sea. Others, Rhodes and Cyprus, and those other Islands toward the bottom of that Sea, which they tell us were surprised and subdued by Nebuchadnezzar, but no record is produced for either of these; nor is there any great probability of either; and less yet of the former. I conceive therefore rather to be hereby meant those Parts of Syria that coasted all along upon the midland sea. See chap. 49.23.

**V. 23.** *{Dedan}* Of this name we find two persons in Scripture: the one Cham’s issue by Chush, and Raamah, Gen. 10.7. the other of Abraham’s posterity by Jokshan, Gen. 25.3. of whom, see Esay 21.13. This present passage seems to concern the place where the posterity of the latter was seated; which is deemed to have been part of Idumea. See chap. 49.28.

*{and Tema}* *Tema* was one of Ishmael’s race, Gen. 25.15. the land that his posterity inhabited in some part of Arabia, was from him so termed: whereof see Job 6.19. Esay 21.14. where the Dedanites, and the Temaites, are together mentioned.

*{and Buz}* The name of one of Nachor’s posterity, Gen. 22.21. of which Family Elihu, one of Job’s friends was, Job 32.1,6.

*{and all that are in the utmost corners}* Heb. *cutted off of a corner:* whereof see on chap. 9.26. as also, chap. 49.32. where they seem to be placed either within, or near upon Idumea, and the Kingdom of Hazor.

**Ver. 24.** *{And all the kings of Arabia}* Reckoned among those that brought gold and silver to Solomon. So 2 Chr. 9.14. See on Esay 21.13.

*{and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert}* Or, *of Arabia;* as well those that inhabit Arabia the fertile, as those, that abide under kingly government in Arabia the waste. See on vers. 20. which some conceive to be the Kedarens, mentioned, Chap. 49.28. said there to dwell *without gates, or bars;* that is, without walled towns, or fenced cities, in tents removable from place to place, Chap. 49.31. Esay 13.20. The old Latin renders it, *of the West;* and the word indeed commonly signifies *the evening*, Gen. 5.8. and one derived from it, *the West*, or *evening coast:* because the Sun setting in the *West*, produces the evening, Psalm 103.12. Esay 59.19. But where the word itself is so used, I find not.

**V. 25.** *{And all the kings of Zimri}* The posterity of *Zimram*, the son of Abraham by Keturah, Genes. 25.2. *m* being lost, as in *Maria*, for, *Miriam*, or *Mariam*, Math. 1.16,18. with Luke 1.27. and *Gehenna*, for *Gehinnom*, Math. 5.22,30. they seem to have been those *Zamarens*, a people of Arabia, mentioned by Pliny, lib. 6. cap. 28.

*{and all the kings of Elam}* The Persians descended of Sem, Gen. 10.22. See on Esay 22.6. and afterward, chap. 49.34.

*{and all the kings of the Medes}* Heb. *of Madai:* the son of Japhet, Gen. 10.2. from whom the *Medes* are descended, joined with the Persians, Dan. 5.28. and 6.8,12.

**V. 26.** *{And all the kings of the North far and near one with another:}* Under the present Chaldean Government, chap. 1.15. v. 9. Heb. *a man to his brother:* as Gen. 26.31. 2 King. 7.6. chap. 13.14. but *to* here for, *with;* as Lam. 3.41.

*{and all the Kingdoms of the world, which are upon the face of the earth.}* In those regions and countries commonly known in those times unto parts, and with whom any ordinary commerce then was; as Esay 34.2. Act. 2.5.

*{and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them}* That by *Sheshach* is meant Babylon, appears plainly from chap. 51.41. the King whereof is said to drink last; because the rest were to drink; as before him, so by him, and he afterward by some of them, vers. 9,12,14. But why Babylon should be thus termed, or how it should come to have this name given it, is questioned. Whereunto the Jewish Masters answer, that Sheshac and Babel, the letters of the Alphabet, being traversed and transposed, are all one. For of this trick, or device, they have two sorts; one, that they call *Albam;* whereof see on Esay 7.6. another, which they call *Athbash*, or *Atbas*, in which two whole sets of letters being placed, the one in a direct order above; the other under backward, beneath on this wise,

אבגדהוזחטיכלמנסעפצקרשת

תשרקצפעסנמלכיטחזוהדגבא

they interchange them, as they stand in order, the upper for the lower, and the lower for the upper: and thus *shin* being put for *beth*, and *caph* for *lamed*, for *Babel* you have *sheshac;* and this trick some suppose, that the Prophet should use on purpose to darken the Prophecy, for fear lest if he should have expressly named Babylon, the King of Babylon, then being set down before the city, should use more rigor and violence against it. But neither was this Prophet afraid freely to deliver God’s message, and that in plain terms also, as afterward he did again and again, chap. 27.6,7. and 29.10. and 50.1. and 51.1,41,64. nor does this prophecy seem to have been delivered until Jehoiakim had yielded himself unto Nebuchadnezzar, content now to hold the crown from him. See on vers. 18. nor are the penmen of Scripture acquainted with such tricks as these, being but late (to speak of) Talmudical devices. Others therefore suppose, that there might be some other great and famous city in Chaldea so termed from the first founder of it, because they find a King of Egypt to have been of the like name, 2 Chr. 12.2. But this seems to be a very groundless conjecture. Others therefore think rather, and with more probability, that Babylon is thus termed from an idol, called *Sheshac*, or *Shak*, from which *Mishael* was by the King of Babylon’s Chamberlain termed *Meshac*, Dan. 1.7. which they worshiped, and whose festival they were celebrating what time the city was by Cyrus surprised. Whereof see more on chap. 51.41. though what a learned Writer has here, that *Sheshac* in the Babylonian language signifies *to feast;* & *share*, *feastivals*, I find not by any author asserted. True it is, that Atheneus in his *Supper-sophisters*, l. 14. relates from Berosus, in his *Babylonian*, and Ctesius in his *Persian story*, that a feast called the *Sacean-festival*, was wont to be held at Babylon for eleven days together: not unlike to the Greeks and Romans *Saturnalia:* and it is not improbable, that in the time of this festival, Babylon was taken: of which more hereafter. But that the word *Sheshac* in that language has any such general signification, is neither by the relator, nor by the Authors whom he cites, averred.

*{shall drink}* In this phrase is deemed to be some allusion to that fatal banquet, at which Belshazzar was slain, Dan. 5.1,30. there is in more likelihood an allusion thereunto, chap. 51.39,57. where God says, that he will *make their feast for them, and make them so drunk, that they shall sleep an everlasting sleep:* but here the same term is used promiscuously of them all, and of him no more than of the rest with him.

**V. 27.** *{Therefore shalt thou say unto them,}* Or, *Say thou unto them;* as Chap. 19.3,11. to wit, in the public delivery of this prophecy.

*{Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel.}* As Chap. 19.15.

*{Drink ye, and be drunken, and spew, and fall, and rise no more.}* Heb. *and ye shall not rise.* Drink till you be so drunk that you spew again (as Esay 19. 14. & 28. 8. Habb. 2. 16.) and so stagger as (as Psal. 107. 27.) that you fall, and so fall, that you be not able to rise and recover yourselves again, Esay 26. 19. chap. 51. 61. as, *Sleep and not wake again,* chap. 51. 39, 57. the imperative in way of prediction, save in the last word, where yet it is to run in the same tenor with the rest. See the like, ver. 34. compared with ver. 36. as the future enunciative in way of injunction in the words before-going.

*{because of the sword that I will send among you}* As ver. 6.

**Verse 28.** *{And it shall be, if so be they shall refuse to take the cup at thine hand to drink}* Assure them from me, that according to your denunciation, drink it they all shall, as well one as another, though they be never so loath and unwilling to come to it; or conceive themselves free enough, and safe enough from being forced thereunto.

*{If so be}* Or, *when;* as chap. 13. 21. or, *that* if: with a defect of the conditional: as 2 Sam. 19. 7. chap. 12. 5. but the former here rather.

*{at thine hand}* Heb. *from;* as verse 17.

*{then shalt thou say unto them;}* Or, *that thou shalt say unto them;* as chap. 1. 9. & 16. 11.

*{Thus saith the LORD of hosts, ye shall certainly drink.}* Heb. *Drinking ye shall drink;* as chap. 49. 12. So, *dying thou shalt dye,* for, *thou shalt surely dye,* Gen. 2. 17.

**Verse 29.** *{For lo, I begin to bring evil upon the city that is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? ye shall not be unpunished.}* What reason have any of you, whom I own not, to expect, or hope to escape, when as I have in part already begun with my own people, and intend to go thorough with them, as well as with you, if not before some of you.

*{I begin to bring evil}* Heb. *I am beginning to do evil,* or *inflict evil:* either I am inflicting evil; by a circumlocution in Hebrew very frequent: as also in the Greek of the New Testament from thence, (See Gen. 6. 1. Deut. 3. 24. Jon. 3. 4. Acts 1. 1. & 11. 15. with 10. 44.) or in the term of *beginning,* (if any emphasis be in it) having an hint of their precedency in regard of some others, verse 18. or to what God had already begun to do in the first surprisal of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar: whereof also see there.

*{upon the city that is called by my name}* On Jerusalem, which is called and accounted in a more special and peculiar manner, my own city. Heb. *upon which my name is called:* as Chap. 7. 10. & 15, 16. & 32. 34.

*{and should ye be utterly unpunished?}* Heb. *being acquitted be acquitted;* as Chap. 38. 11. Exod. 34. 7. for if God begin so severely, and proceed too so roughly with his own people, others must look as surely and sorely to suffer at last, Luke 23. 31. 1 Pet. 4. 17, 18.

*{for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, saith the LORD of Hosts.}* Heb. *I am calling.* I am going presently about it. So Chap. 1. 19. and it cannot but come and go at his call, who, being Lord of hosts, has all creatures at command, Psal. 119. 91. & 148. 8. Esay 7. 18, 19. & 13. 3. & 40. 26. Ezek. 14. 17. Amos 5. 8. & 9. 6.

*{a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth.}* See verse 26, 27.

**Verse 30.** *{Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words}* Or, *all these things:* the subject matter of the words; as verse 1. Chap. 21. 1. & 26. 2. The manner how he was to tender the cup to them, verse 15. to wit, by way of denunciation: as Chap. 1. 10. See ver. 15, 17.

*{and say unto them}* Add these further to the former what now follows.

*{The LORD shall roar from on high, and shall utter his voice from his holy habitation;}* God is here said to roar as a lion enraged, when he is about to execute some hideous work of vengeance, or punishment, to inflict some dreadful judgment, Joel 3. 16. Amos 1. 2. & 3. 8.

*{from on high}* From heaven the place of his glorious residence, Psal. 76. 8. Esay 63. 15. Rom. 1. 18.

*{utter his voice}* Heb. *give,* or, *give out, his voice:* to call together, say some of the Jewish doctors, and others from them, those whom he purposes to employ: as Esay 13. 20, 3. but it seems rather to be here a further addition to the former: and it is used to imply the fierceness and dreadfulness of his wrath, when he comes with it unto judgment, with allusion unto loud and hideous cracks of thunder accompanied with fearful and frightful flashes of fire. See Psal. 18. 13. & 68. 33. So also, Joel 3. 16. & Amos 1. 2.

*{from his holy habitation}* Heb. *habitation of holiness;* as Psal. 68. 5. So *his Temple,* or, *Palace of holiness:* that is, heaven, Psal. 11. 4.

*{he will mightily roar upon his habitation,}* Heb. *he will roaring roar;* that is, roar exceeding loud: for these ingeminations imply, as certainty sometime, verse 28. so otherwhile a vehemency or excess: as Esay 24. 16. *upon his habitation.* So the word does commonly signify, Job 5. 3. & 18. 15. Psal. 79. 7. Esay 27. 10. & 33. 20. Chap. 10, 25. For the old Latin the word mistranslates it, rendering the word *beauty,* which those that follow descant much on to small purpose: it is applied sometime to God's sanctuary, temple or tabernacle: as Exod. 15. 2. 2 Sam. 15. 25. and so here, both Jewish, and ours, generally expound it, understanding the text, as intimating the place which God threatens, in particular, to execute judgment upon: which to me seems nothing probable; because all the following discourse is bent in general against the whole set of those, whom God intended thus to deal with: and I choose therefore to go rather with those interpreters, though very few, yet of good note, who expound this, as the former, of the place, where, or from whence; God would thus roar: and render the text, not, *upon,* but, *in his habitation,* or *dwelling.* So is the particle oft used, Neh. 9. 33, 36. Psal. 143. 4. Esay 24. 22. *in prison,* Dan. 11. 20. *in his place,* Esay 38, 20. *in the house of the Lord:* and so here, *in his habitation:* whereunto may be added, that with this particle there is oft a defect of the other particle *from:* as Psal. 81. 6. *when he came from off,* or, *out of Egypt:* and Dan. 2. 1. *his sleep was broken,* or *departed from off him,* or *from him;* as our Version renders it: and accordingly it may be here *from,* or, *out of his habitation,* or *dwelling,* for variety's sake, because this word, and the former, though in notion the same are in sound and original diverse: and though by and from his sanctuary he is said sometime, in the like case, *to roar,* and *utter his voice,* Joel 3. 16. Amos 1. 2. yet I suppose here is *heaven* rather meant, as before, because the temple then was demolished, and lay desolate, when God roared thus on some of the rest here before specified.

*{he shall give a shout as they that tread the grapes against all the inhabitants of the earth.}* Heb. *he will answer a shout:* whence some suppose it to allude to such songs as the workmen that were employed in the wine press used to answer one another withal, to make their work go the lighter and more merrily away with them: it is true, that the word here used signifies properly *to answer;* but sometime also, *to answer* one another in singing, or to sing by course; as they did, Exod. 15. 21. 1 Sam. 18. 7. & 21. 11. & 29. 5. Ezr. 3. 11. and simply also *to sing;* as Esay 27. 2. yea as *to speak* simply; which is very common in both the books of the Old and New Testament, where no question at all goes before; so more specially to make a loud noise, shout, or outcry, So Exod. 32. 17, 18. *when Joshua heard the voice,* or, *noise of the people, as they shouted he said, there is a noise of war in the camp. But* (Moses) *said, It is not the voice,* or *noise, of shouting for mastery;* (valor, or victory) *nor is it the voice of crying out* (of outcry) *for discomfiture;* (by reason of being surprised and vanquished) *a voice,* or *noise, of chanting,* (singing by course, or singing aloud simply) *do I hear:* by which place, where the word is thrice several times repeated; in the light, or single form, as here, twice; in the weighty form, wherein the middle radical is doubled, once; it appears that it is used to signify any such loud *shout,* or outcry, as either assailants in war, or persons suddenly assailed, and overpowered by an assailant enemy, are wont to make. And I conceive the *shout* here mentioned to be an *alarm,* or *shout* rather, of assailants, such as they are wont to make, either at the joining of battle in the field; or at the assault of some fort or city, Josh. 6. 16, 20. Chap. 51. 14. withal compare to that *shout* that country people are wont to make at the bringing in of their vintage and harvest; and more especially when they have their feet in the winepress, and the new liquor in their heads. See Esay 16. 9, 10. Jer. 48. 32, 33.

*{those that tread the grapes}* Heb. *treaders,* So *the treader,* Esay 6. 10. and, *he that treadeth* (to wit, grapes) *in the wine-presse,* or, *the presse,* Esay 63. 2. whereunto some allusion is here; the rather, in regard of that store of blood that should be shed by the executioners of God's wrath, to such treaders out of wine in this place compared. So Esay 63. 3. Rev. 14. 19, 20. *to tread,* for, *to tread* grapes: as, *to tread out,* for, *to tread out* corn, Hosh. 10. 11.

*{against all the inhabitants of the earth.}* Heb. *unto:* which if we retain, the meaning may be, that the shout shall be so loud, that it should be heard in all parts and places, though never so remote and distant one from another. See verse 31. the former part whereof the old Latin joins to this: but the particle is sometime also used for *against;* as Chap. 1. 19. & 13. 14, & 15. 20. of the other terms here, see ver. 26, 29. Esay 34. 1, 2.

**Verse 31.** *{A noise shall come even to the ends of the earth}* Heb. *A tumultuous noise is gone unto the lands end;* that is, say some, from the Red Sea, unto the Caspian Sea; they might as well say, from the Persian Gulf, unto the Midland Sea: but *to the lands end* is a form used indefinitely, or so far, as the lands intended reach, Psal. 72. 8. See Esay 15. 4—8. Chap. 48, 34. & 49. 21.

*{for the LORD hath a controversy with the nations:}* Heb. *for a controversie,* or *a quarrel is to the Lord with the nations.* See the same form, Hos. 4. 1. & Mich. 6. 2.

*{he will plead with all flesh}* Heb. *he will be judged,* or, *enter into judgement;* as Esay 3. 14. making it to appear, that he does most justly, what in this kind he does, *with all flesh:* all people; as before, verse 26. So Chap. 45. 5.

*{he will give them which are wicked to the sword; saith the LORD}* Heb, *the wicked,* or, as for *the wicked, he hath given them to the sword:* an elegant form of speech: the like whereunto, see Gen. 49. 19. Psal. 12. 5, 2. & Esay 65. 11, 12. and a change of the person also here, as there: *he hath designed them* thereunto, or *he hath given* them up to it, in the prophetical phrase: for, he will do it, it is as sure to be done, as if it were done already, Chap. 15. 2, 3. *the sword:* of which before, verse 16.

**Verse 32.** *{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts: Behold evil shall go forth from nation to nation.}* From one nation to another: as Psal. 105. 13. to each one, as his turn comes. See Lam. 4. 21.

*{a great whirlwind shall be raised from the coasts of the earth}* Or, *a great storm,* or, *tempest,* (as Chap. 23. 19.) *shall be raised from the uttermost parts of the earth.* Heb. *sides:* as Chap. 6. 22. from the Chaldeans, first on the one side, and from the Medes, and Persians next on the other side.

**Verse 33.** *{And the slain of the LORD shall be at that day from the one end of the earth, even to the other end of the earth:}* *The slain of the Lord:* the slain by his purpose, and at his appointment, verse 29. Zeph. 2. 12. *at that day:* that is, at that time, when he comes to take vengeance, and do justice upon the wicked (verse 31.) shall be and abound in all parts and places, from the one end of the earth to the other. Heb. *from the end of the earth, and unto the end of the earth:* as Chap. 12. 12. So Mat. 24. 31.

*{they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried: they shall be dung upon the earth}* So great shall the multitude of the corpses of the slain men be, that they shall lie without exequies or burial, without any manner of interment, unburied, until they rot upon the ground: See Chap. 8. 2.

**Verse 34.** *{Howle ye shepherds and cry}* Or, *cry out:* make an outcry, chap. 4. 6. & 6. 26. See verse 36. You rulers, and governors, kings and princes: for against them principally are these evils denounced, verse 8. 26. So is the word taken, Chap. 22. 22. & 23. 1.

*{wallow yourselves in the ashes}* Supplied from Mich. 1. 10. for in ashes they used to lay themselves down, in times of solemn mourning and humiliation, Job 42. 6. Esay 58. 5. Mat. 11. 21.

*{ye principal of the flock}* Either you master-shepherds, grandees, and chief governors; or, you the greatest and wealthiest among the people, Ezek. 34. 16, 18. for in public calamities, the meaner and poorer sort of people usually escape best: the corks swim, when the plummets sink: See 2 King. 24. 14. & 25. 12.

*{for the days of your slaughter, and of your dispersions, are accomplished;}* Heb. *your dayes for slaughter, and your dispersions:* the time designed for the slaughtering and dispersing of you is *fully come:* as Luke 2. 6. Acts 2. 1. nor past and gone: as the word in our Version might seem to import.

*{and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessell}* Or, *as a precious dish.* Heb. *as a vessel,* or, *dish, of desire,* or *delight:* So Hosh. 13. 15. Nah. 2. 9. the opposite See chap. 22. 28. *a vessell,* or *dish, unto which there is no desire,* or, *in which no delight:* Some such curious utensils, as Venice glasses, and China dishes, that by reason of their fineness are with the least fall, or casualty, soon dashed to pieces, and being once broken, cannot be cemented, or set together again, or, that are of much esteem while they are whole, but of no worth when once broken. So Psal. 31. 12. chap. 22. 28.

**Verse 35.** *{And the shepherds shall have no way to flee, nor the principal of the flock to escape.}* Heb. *Flight shall perish from the Shepherds, and escape from the principall of the flock;* as Amos 2. 14.

**Verse 36.** *{A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and an howling of the principal of the flock shall be heard}* Or, *There shall be an out-cry of the shepherds, and an howling of the principal of the flock.* Heb. *a voyce of cry,* for, *a loud,* or *clamorous voyce:* as chap. 51. 54. a grievous outcry; as we term it: See verse 34.

*{For the LORD hath spoiled their pastures}* Because the Lord has destroyed and laid waste their pastures, that is, their kingdoms and states: or, dispersed and destroyed their flocks, that is, the people that lived under their charge, chap. 13. 20. as the word is used, chap. 10. 21.

**Verse 37.** *{And the peaceable habitations are cut down,}* The stately structures, and goodly buildings, wherein formerly you lived and dwelt quietly, as in places of rest and repose, are through the fierce wrath of God ruined and demolished. Heb. *The habitations,* or *folds,* (2 Sam. 7. 8. the rather, because the allegory runs on, as taken from shepherds, and their sheep-cotes) *of peace;* as Esay 33. 20. Sion is said to be *a quiet habitation:* though I cannot accord to them, who think in the word *Shalom* here, an allusion to be unto *Salem,* or *Jerusalem,* Psal. 76. 2. because that sounds much to the same, Heb. 7. 2. for the scope and sense of this place is far more general. See on verse 30.

*{because of the fierce anger of the LORD}* Or, *through the fierce anger of the Lord.* See chap. 4. 8, 26.

**Verse 38.** *{He hath forsaken his covert, as a lion}* Or, as some not amiss, *Who* (the relative supplied; as chap. 22. 30. & 23. 29.) *hath left, as a young lion,* (as chap. 2. 16.) *his covert;* as chap. 4. 7. He is come abroad as a young lion, to range about for prey. So chap. 49. 19. & 50. 44. For I cannot assent unto that learned interpreter, who expounds these words of God's leaving his place among his people, whom he had wont to dwell with, and so exposing them, dismantled of his protection, unto ruin and destruction, chap. 12. 7. the words seem more general, than to be restrained unto God's peculiar; and the resemblance to look overfull another way.

*{for their land is desolate}* He proceeds to show the cause and ground of their howling, verse 34, 36. they are in straits unavoidable and inextricable themselves, verse 35. their states ruined, verse 36. their dwellings demolished, verse 37. and their lands laid waste and desolate, Heb. *their land is unto desolation.* See verse 11. 18.

*{because of the fierceness of the oppressor}* Heb. *heat,* or, *fervour,* (as Esay 13.) *of the oppressing* sword: as some supply it not amiss from chap. 46. 16. where it is applied to the Babylonians: and chap. 50. 16. where it is spoken of the Medes, and Persians: and so the rather, because the word here used is feminine: the sword that God threatens to send among them, to make havoc of them, verse 16, 27. a defect of the substantive: as *standing,* for, *standing* corn, Esay 17. 5. *ill-tempered,* for, *ill-tempered* mortar, Ezek. 13. 13. *beloved,* for, *beloved* friend, Hosh. 9. 16.
