**Verse 20.** *{Hear ye therefore the word of the LORD all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon.}* Or, *Hear ye also.* Unto you of the captivity I now turn my speech again, to let you know from God, what will shortly befall those your prophets, unto whom some among you give too much credit, through the just judgment of God upon them. Heb. *And hear ye* (*and,* for, *also;* as verse 24. chap. 1. 3. and 14. 6.) *all the captivity,* or *the whole captivity:* *captivity,* for, *captives;* as vers. 1, 4.

*{I have sent}* See chap. 24. 5. vers. 4, 7, 14.

**Verse 21.** *{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel,}* As verse 4.

*{of Ahab the son of Koliab,}* Or, *Achab;* as the Greek renders it: and so *Achaz.* See Esai 1. 1. Of this man and his parentage there is no mention elsewhere. Some ridiculous stories the Talmudists tell us of loose pranks played by him and his companion here mentioned, not worthy the recital.

*{and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah,}* Such another as he of the same name among Ahab's prophets, 1 King. 22. 11.

*{which prophesy a lye unto you in my name,}* See chap. 14. 14. and 27. 15. vers. 8, 9.

*{Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon,}* I will give them up into his power: as chap. 27. 6, 8. and 34. 21.

*{and he shall slay them before your eyes.}* That yourselves may be eyewitness of God's just judgment upon them, in that cruel death that the king of Babylon shall put them to, as from God's mouth I now foretell you.

**Verse 22.** *{And of them,}* Or, *From them.*

*{shall be taken up a curse}* This shall they *leave their names for a curse,* Esai 65. 15.

*{by all the captivity that are in Babylon}* Or, *captives:* as vers. 20. those of their own nation.

*{saying, The LORD make thee like Zedekiah, and like Ahab, whom the King of Babylon roasted in the fire.}* Or, *burnt with fire:* but it may seem by the use of the participle and verbals of it, applied to green corn parched with the fire. Lev. 2. 14. (for the verb itself is found only in this place) that it imports a putting of men to torment, and so to death, by a slow roasting or scorching of them with fire, so as they are not suddenly consumed, or slain with it, but endure much extremity of pain therewith ere they die: and such a kind of death, it is very probable that these two wicked wretches did by that heathen king's appointment endure; being a kind of death not unusual among the Chaldeans, Dan. 3. 6, 21. for venting such things as might cause disturbance in the state. Heb. *whom he rosted them:* an elegant redundancy very frequent in Heb. as Psalm 1. 4.

**Verse 23.** *{Because they have committed villany in Israel,}* The reason is here rendered, not so much, wherefore the king of Babylon burnt them as for which God in his secret providence, and by his just judgment so disposed of them that they should fall into his hands, and be so handled by him: *villany,* or *folly:* the form is used commonly of corporal filthiness and uncleanness. See Genes. 34. 7. Deut. 22. 21. 2 Sam. 13. 11, 12.

*{and have committed adultery with their neighbours wives,}* Or, *in committing adultery with their neighbours wives:* herein concurring with those of the same stamp with them at Jerusalem, Chap. 23. 14. where another word is used instead of that rendered *villany* here, that signifies *vileness;* whereof those vile figs; verse 17. The like syntax, see Esai 31. 5. Chap. 6. 23. and 8. 6. and 9. 18.

*{and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them,}* Chap. 14. 14. and 23. 21, 32. vers. 9, 21. Heb. *a word of falshood,* or *a false thing:* as Prov. 13. 5.

*{even, I know and am a witness, saith the LORD}* Heb. *and I am the knower, and witnesse,* to wit, of these their vile practices, how closely and covertly soever they commit them, and how smoothly soever they demean themselves in the sight of others, that know them not so inwardly. So chap. 7. 11. and 13. 27. and 23. 13, 14. See those generals, Job 24. 15. with 34. 21, 22. Prov. 5. 20, 21. and 15. 3, 11. chap. 17. 9, 10.

*{I know}* Or, *am the knower:* one that takes notice and cognizance of these things as a judge.

*{a witness}* Both judge and witness: no other shall need both to convict and condemn them for these their carriages. See Mal. 3. 5.

**Verse 24.** *{Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying,}* Or, *Say thus also.* Heb. *And thus shalt thou say;* as verse 20. Chap. 27. 4. This latter part of the chapter contains a relation of a later date than the former: in likelihood after the return of those messengers, mentioned verse 3. back from Babylon, concerning Shemaiah, who had given information by letters from thence, of that which Jeremy had written unto his countrymen at Babylon; with an heavy doom by God passed upon him for the same.

*{Shemaiah the Nehelamite}* Or, *dreamer:* for such a notion the word has in it. Which whether it have any reference to some place of his birth, or abode in time past, or to his parentage and descent, is uncertain; though it bear the name of such a kind of appellation, whereby men are usually described from their country, city, descent, parentage, kindred, and the like: but it may seem to have been a term coined of purpose to intimate his profession and practice: as if we would say, one of *dream-land:* one of the house, or lineage of *dream-wrights:* for he was one of those in likelihood that professed and practiced that special kind of imposture, whereof, see verse 8. Chap. 23. 25, 32. and 27. 9. yet seems there not to be any probability of that, which a writer of special note has, that he should be a *Nahamite,* one of the stock and lineage of that *Naham,* mentioned 1 Chronicles 4. 19. and by insertion of a letter, so termed as here, for some glance at this his practice.

**Verse 25.** *{Thus speaketh the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel,}* As verse 21.

*{saying, Because thou hast sent letters in thy name unto all the people that are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the Priest, and to all the Priests, saying,}* *Letters.* Heb. *bookes.* So verse 1. *books,* for, *letters:* and it may seem that he wrote, and sent more than one: though the sum of that one to Zephaniah be here only related, verse 26–28. which yet seems to have been directed by name indeed to him, but withal, to the rest of the priests together with him. See vers. 26.

*{in thy name}* Or, *thine own name,* (as, *thine own way,* chap. 4. 18.) of your own head; without warrant, or commission from me. So Joh. 5. 43. *if another come in his own name.*

*{Zephaniah}* The second under Serajah, who was then high priest, chap. 52. 24.

*{the son of Maaseiah}* Not the immediate son of this Maaseiah; as it is not unlikely that Zedekiah the false prophet was to one of that name verse 21. but of the issue and family of Maaseiah, and a priest of that course, whereof Maaseiah was at first the head. See chap. 21. 1.

**Verse 26.** *{The LORD hath made thee Priest in the stead of Jehoiada the Priest, that ye should be officers in the house of the LORD, for every one that is mad and maketh himself a Prophet, that thou shouldst put him in prison and in the stocks.}* Of this Jehoiada, by whose example this flattering parasite would entice Zephaniah, as one endued with his spirit of zeal for God's glory and the good of his house, to proceed with all severity and rigor against God's own minister and messenger for no other matter than the free and faithful delivery of his master's message, see 2 Kings 11. and 12. Thus there is no act so injurious, or impious, but that wicked wretches and false prophets will not only attempt it against such as out of conscience and duty to God either cross and oppose them, or refuse to comply with them in their corrupt courses and carriages; but color it also with some specious pretense of piety and zeal for God's glory. See Esai 66. 5. Joh. 16. 2. and 19. 7.

*{made thee Priest}* Heb. *given thee* to be *Priest:* as chap. 1. 5. and 6. 27.

*{instead of Jehoiada}* Hence does one of the Jewish commenters gather, that Zephaniah was high priest, as Jehoiada was: but the contrary was before showed from chap. 52. 24. So also, 2 King. 25. 18. nor was that therefore the reason why he mentions Jehoiada; but as pretending Zephaniah to be for spirit and zeal such another as he: as John Baptist is said to have had *the spirit and power of Elias;* and has his name therefore given him, Mal. 4. 5. Mat. 11. 10, 14. Luke 1. 17. and 7. 27.

*{ye shall be officers}* Or, *overseers.* See chap. 20. 1. you and the rest of the priests unto whom also together with him this letter seems to have been directed, vers. 25. So the Jewish doctor here. Howbeit, the text may rather be rendered, *that there might be officers;* for that *ye* is not in the text: you being at present the second under the chief priest, who it may be is either through infirmity of body, or some other employment, restrained from looking after these matters as he should, ought to take care that there be not a fail of such officers as may be assistant to you for the restraining and punishing of such counterfeits as this Jeremy: to which purpose he may seem also to make mention of Jehoiada, who disposed and appointed officers in several places to be assistant to him in the settling of the state, 2 King. 11. 4.

*{in the house of the LORD,}* A defect of the particle *in,* as 2 King. 18. 15.

*{that is mad and maketh himself a Prophet}* Or, *every madman* (so have God's messengers been from time to time deemed, 2 King. 9. 11. Act. 26. 24.) *that feigneth himself a Prophet;* that in a mad fit, or a frantic humor acts the part of a prophet, when as indeed he is not: for these reciprocal forms in Hebrew have oft times a notion of *counterfeiting* in them: *to make thy self sick,* for, *feign thy self to be sick,* 2 Sam. 13. 5. and, *make thy self mourn,* for, *feign thy self to be a mourner,* 2 Sam. 14. 2. and *making,* that is, *feigning her self to be a stranger,* or some other, 1 King. 14. 2. and *be made,* that is, *feigned himself mad,* 1 Sam. 21. 13. The like the captains charged Jeremy with, when he crossed them in their design, chap. 43. 2.

*{that thou shouldest put him}* Heb. *and* (as vers. 6.) *thou shalt give him;* as chap. 20. 2.

*{in Prison;}* As Pashur had before done, chap. 20. 2. of the word here also used, see there: nor was there any ground to render it *stocks* there, and *prison* here.

*{and in the stocks}* Thus this beast, not content to have God's prophet imprisoned, or so dealt with as Pashur had formerly done; but would have him yet more contumeliously abused, and further extremity to be exercised on him. That the term here used, signifies some engine used for stricter restraint, or painful torture is generally agreed: but of what kind, or in what manner, is not easily determined. One of the Jewish doctors expounds it by a word that signifies in the first place the *stock* of a tree, and from thence the *stocks:* which we commonly so term; as our Version here renders it; so used by them in that common proverb with them, *The workman sitteth in the stocks of his own making:* but another of them tells us that it is an engine of iron for the hands: whence some render it *manicles:* adding withal, that the term comes from an Arabic word, that signifies *to straiten,* or *pinch* in. A learned interpreter renders it *in the skif,* and would have it to be a word compounded of two terms; the one signifying a *skif,* or *boat;* the other having a notion of *sucking:* supposing by it to be understood such a kind of engine invented to put men to cruel pains, as Plutarch in the life of Artaxerxes reports to have been in use among the Persians: this he describes to have consisted of two hollow frames made boatwise, of equal size, between which the whole body of man being close shut up, his head, hands, and legs only extant, at places fitted and left open for that purpose: the party so enclosed, to prolong his pains, and increase his misery, through that nasty plight, and that he must of necessity be in, they enforced to eat; and instead of drink, to take in milk mixed with honey: which, says this his learned interpreter, the Hebrews termed, *the suckling-skif:* and because it might be objected, that this savage and cruel course of torment is not found to have been in use among the Jews, (though another late writer affirms, that it was at least known to them) to prevent this, he subjoins, that the Jews used this term for any the strictest and painfulest course of restraint. But to me the notation of the term seems overfar-fetched: nor is any proof brought of the word so used: it is nowhere found in Scripture save in this place: nor do I find any place produced save the Chaldee here, wherein mention is made thereof in the writings of their rabbines: nor are themselves, as you see, agreed upon the signification of it in particular; which cannot therefore, I suppose, with any certainty be determined.

**Verse 27.** *{Now therefore why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, which maketh himself a Prophet to you?}* Heb. *And now* (as chap. 27. 9.) *why hast thou not rebuked?* as it is commonly rendered; that is, taken him up, and restrained him: for the word is used most commonly, of an active, as well as of a verbal *rebuke,* Ruth 2. 16. Psal. 9. 5. and 68. 30. and 76. 6. and 105. 9.

*{Jeremiah of Anathoth}* See Chap. 1. 1.

*{maketh himself a Prophet}* See on vers. 26.

*{to you}* Or, *with you.* as Neh. 2. 12. or *among you:* as Esth. 4. 3. and 10. 3.

**Verse 28.** *{For therefore he sent to us in Babylon, saying,}* Or, *For to this purpose,* or *accordingly,* (as the like form, Chap. 5. 2.) *he hath sent,* vers. 1.

*{This captivity is long}* Heb. *long it,* for, *long is it;* that is all the Hebrew has: the word is found; 2 Sam. 3. 1. Job 11. 9. the pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive: as Psal. 25. 11. and 99. 3. So Chap. 30. 7.

*{build ye houses and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them.}* See verse 5.

**Verse 29.** *{And Zephaniah the Priest read this letter}* Or, *For* (as Esai 9. 11.) *Zephaniah had read* (as Gen. 12. 1.) *this letter.* Heb. *book:* as vers. 1. written to him by Shemaiah, vers. 25.

*{in the ears of Jeremiah the Prophet}* In his *hearing:* as Chap. 28. 7. whether out of any good affection to him, (for he was more than once employed in messages to the prophet, Chap. 21. 1. and 37. 3.) or for some other end and purpose uncertain.

**Verse 30.** *{Then came the word of the LORD unto Jeremiah, saying,}* Or, *Therefore* (as vers. 27.) *came* (Heb. *was:* as Chap. 28. 12.) *the word of the Lord unto Jeremy:* for these words have reference unto the beginning of this relation, vers. 25.

**Verse 31.** *{Send to all them of the captivity,}* Heb. *to all the captivity:* as vers. 20. send the second time to them.

*{saying, Thus saith the LORD concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite,}* See on vers. 24.

*{Because Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not; and he caused you to trust in a lye}* Or, *when I sent him not, and hath caused you to trust in a lye.* See Chap. 28. 15. vers. 9.

**Verse 32.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite}* Heb. *visit upon him:* as Chap. 25. 12.

*{and his seed}* Thus God's vengeance often pursues even the race of the wicked, Exod. 20. 6. and 34. 7. See on Lam. 5. 7.

*{he shall not have a man to dwell among this people, neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the LORD;}* Both he and his posterity shall be clean rooted out: (as Psalm 34. 16. and 109. 13, 15.) nor shall he, or any of his issue survive to see and enjoy the promised deliverance and restitution of my people. See the like judgment denounced on the like occasion, Amos 7. 17.

*{a man to dwell among}* Heb. *a man* (that is, *any* one; as Chap. 5. 1.) *dwelling,* or *remaining in the midst of;* as Chap. 39. 24. and 40. 16.

*{neither shall he see the good}* Or, or *that shall enjoy the good.* Heb. *and shall not see in the good:* the copulative for the disjunctive, as Chap. 23. 18, 34. and a defect of the relative; as Chap. 23. 29. and, *to see,* for, *to enjoy:* as Chap. 17. 8. especially with the particle here subjoined, as Psalm 27. 12. and 106. 5. and 128. 5. and I suppose that this latter branch is to be extended as well to his issue, as to himself; because it might seem but a slight matter, to tell him that he should not survive to have any share in that good that God would do for his people some seventy years hence.

*{because he hath taught rebellion against the LORD.}* Heb. *spoken revolt,* or *departure.* See the same clause, Chap. 28. 16. and of it more there.

## CHAPTER 30

**Verse 1.** *{The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,}* This inscription (the like whereunto see Chap. 18. 1.) extends itself unto that entire sermon, or prophecy laid down in this chapter and the next, consisting both mainly of gracious promises concerning the restitution of God's people.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus speaketh the LORD God of Israel, saying, Write thee all the words that I have spoken to thee in a book,}* In these words is a special charge given by God to the prophet, either to gather together those prophecies that he had formerly delivered unto him, or to enter those upon record that he should at present acquaint him with, being of the same subject, and to engross them, and make them up in a book; those of them especially which concerned the future welfare of God's people that they might not be lost, but remain to posterity, and that the faithful might have them wherewith to support their faith, and keep up their spirits in an hopeful expectation of God's goodness intended to them, during the time of their long captivity. So Habb. 2. 2.

*{Write thee}* Heb. *to thee;* an elegant redundancy: the like whereunto, see Exod. 37. 27. Ezek. 24. 2. as also, Chap. 36. 2.

*{all the words}* Or, *things;* as Chap. 26. 2. and 29. 1.

*{that I have spoken unto thee}* Or, as some, *that I shall speak unto thee:* and so the Jewish commenters understand it. See verse 4.

*{in a book}* Not in loose papers; lest some of them be lost; but made up together in a book. See the like charge; but that more specially concerning the denunciation of judgments, Chap. 36. 2. Heb. *unto a book,* for, *in a book:* as, *unto the Ark,* for, *in it,* Exod. 25. 21.

**Verse 3.** *{For lo the days come, saith the LORD, that I will bring again the captivity of Israel, and Judah, saith the LORD:}* The reason for which he would have this book written, to wit, to mind his people from time to time of his mercy intended to them: which he takes occasion also thereby at large here to relate.

*{lo the days come,}* Heb. *Behold, the dayes coming:* as chap. 23. 5. to be seen with the eye of faith, Joh. 8. 56. 2 Cor. 4. 18. Heb. 11. 13. and as sure to come, as if coming, yea, or come already, Hab. 2. 3. Heb. 10. 37, 38.

*{bring again the captivity}* So Chap. 22. 27. and 29. 10, 14. there is an elegant consonancy and vicinity of sound between the verb and the noun here used: that which occasioned a mistake in the old Latin, rendering the words as if both belonged to one root, *I will convert your conversion:* which albeit, it be a palpable mistake, and the same version elsewhere render it aright; yet divers popish, even learned interpreters admire, and descant upon, as sound and genuine. The word most commonly in its first form here used is intransitive, and signifies *to return:* but in this frame of speech seems rather to be used for *to reduce,* as here, so vers. 18. and Psal. 85. 1, 4. See on Esai 52. 9.

*{of Israel and Judah}* The remainder of his, as well among the ten tribes, as with the other two, Chap. 3. 12, 14. and 23. 6. and 31. 1–6. Ezek. 37. 21, 22.

*{and I will cause them to return to the land which I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.}* Or, *that they may possesse it:* as Chap. 29. 6, 26. See Chap. 12. 16. and 16. 15. and 24. 6.

**Verse 4.** *{And these are the words, that the LORD spake concerning Israel, and concerning Judah.}* Or, *Now* (as Chap. 29. 1.) *these* are *those things* (as vers. 1.) *that the Lord had spoken:* as Gen. 12. 1. if we suppose it to have reference to former prophecies: otherwise it seems to relate to what at present was delivered; as the Jewish doctor understands the words of the charge before related, vers. 2. which to reconcile, we may with good ground say, that what here follows is the main matter, sum, and substance of all that God had formerly revealed at several times unto Jeremy concerning the deliverance and restitution of his people: for by *words* in the charge seems to be imported, as Chap. 29. 1. not so much the precise terms themselves, as the matter therein comprised.

**Verse 5.** *{For thus saith the LORD,}* Or, *Thus* then, or, *Therefore,* (as Chap. 19. 16.) *hath the Lord said:* for there is no reason here rendered of aught foregoing, but a passage only unto the relation of that matter, that was to be recorded.

*{we have heard a voice of trembling, of fear; and not of peace.}* Or, as some render it, (which the Hebrew pauses favor, and which way the ancient Greek goes) *fear* here is, *but peace is not,* or, *there is no peace:* as Chap. 8. 11. This some of the Jewish doctors, whom not a few of ours concur with, understand of the days of the Messiah, and those of the expedition of Gog and Magog, Ezek. 38. these of the troubles raised in the world in way of opposition to Christian profession, Mat. 10. 30, 34. Luke 12. 49, 51. But the sounder sort of ours and theirs conceive the times intended of the Babylonian invasion, when the Chaldeans by their approach to Jerusalem, and the assault thereof much more, filled all places thereabout with terror and dread, Chap. 4. 9. and 6. 4. beforehand mentioned, to show how they should then be roused up out of that sense of security, wherewith the false prophets at present by preaching and promising nothing but peace to them, had so deeply possessed them, that God's prophets could hardly wake them out of it, Chap. 14. 13. for those seem to stray farthest from the scope of the place, who expound it of the Medes and Persians invading the Babylonian state, and striking a grievous terror into the Chaldeans, Esai 13. 8.

**Verse 6.** *{Ask ye now and see whether a man doth travel with child:}* The old Latin here renders the words senselessly, *Ask and see, if a man beget:* whereas the Jewish doctor notes aright upon the place, that *the man* begets, *the woman bears,* or *brings forth:* and so the text is word for word here, *Demand,* or *Enquire now and see, if,* or *whether,* (as Chap. 2. 28.) *a male bear,* or *bring forth:* or as it may well be rendered, *Enquire now and see; doth a male bear?* or *bring forth?* make enquiry and try, whether it were ever seen, or known, that a man, or male, (so Esai 66. 7.) brought forth.

*{wherefore do I see every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travel?}* Why do men generally, even the stoutest and hardiest, seem to be affected, as if like women, they were in travail? See the like demand, chap. 46. 5.

*{every man}* The word here used, signifies according to the notation of it, *a strong,* or *mighty man.* See Esai 22. 17. chap. 31. 22. not the feeble and the fainthearted only, but the strong and stouthearted ones.

*{with their hands on their loins}* The wonted posture and gesture of women in travail, striving and straining themselves to get ease of their pains.

*{as a woman in travel}* Heb. *as one bearing,* or *bringing forth:* See chap. 4. 31. and 49. 22, 24.

*{and all faces are turned into paleness?}* As is wont to be in extremity of fear, Joel 2. 6. the word properly implies the color of *corn blasted,* Deut. 28. 22. the old Latin renders it by a word that signifies the disease commonly termed *the yellow jaundise.*

**Verse 7.** *{Alas, for that day is great, so that none is like it:}* Or, *Surely,* (as chap. 22. 22. and 24. 8.) *that day* will be so *great* a day, (to wit, for calamity and misery: as Joel 2. 31.) *as none* has been *like unto it;* or *as the like unto it hath not been.* Heb. *from not* being *as it:* as ch. 10. 6. See the like expressions, Joel 2. 11. Amos 5. 18. Zeph. 1. 14, 15. *day,* for, *time;* as it is expounded in the next clause.

*{it is even the time of Jacobs trouble;}* Or, *even* (Heb. *and:* as chap. 29. 16.) a *time it is* (as chap. 29. 28.) *of straits,* or *distresse,* (as Esai 29. 2.) *to Jacob;* God's people, Jacob's posterity: as chap. 10. 16, 25. which some extend unto the whole time, not of the siege only, or sack of the city, but of their captivity also that ensued thereupon: the rather to be admitted in regard of what follows.

*{but he shall be saved out of it.}* Or, *yet.* Heb. *and* (as chap. 27. 15.) *he shall be saved:* not *saved,* by way of prevention, from it, but *saved,* by way of deliverance, by bringing them in safety *out of it.* See vers. 10.

**Verse 8.** *{For it shall come to passe in that day, saith the LORD of hosts,}* Heb. *it shall be,* as chap. 3. 16. *in that day,* for, *at that time:* as Esai 26. 1. so, *day,* for, *time,* vers. 7. to wit, when I shall visit Babylon, chap. 27. 7.

*{that I will break his yoke from off thy neck,}* This confirms the former exposition concerning the extent of the time of distress, mentioned verse 7. for from yokes and bonds they could not be loosed and freed, unless they were first under and in them: the particle *that,* is here wanting; as Esai 7. 21.

*{his yoke}* The king of Babylon's; which God would break and loose them from: not when the false prophets told them he would, but at the time that God had himself set and assigned. See chap. 27. 26. and 28. 4, 11. Many interpret it of Christ's freeing the faithful from the bondage of legal rites, and the servitude of sin and Satan, John 8. 32, 34, 36. Act. 15. 10. Rom. 6. 16, 22. and 8. 2. Gal. 5. 1. 2 Tim. 2. 26. and that was indeed by this temporal deliverance typified: but the former seems here the literal sense.

*{and will burst thy bonds;}* Either those thongs, wherewith the yoke was fastened to, or upon your neck, (see chap. 27. 2.) or bands, wherewith captives, prisoners and bondmen are wont to be bound, Psal. 107. 14. 2 Chr. 36. 6. chap. 40. 4. See chap. 2. 20.

*{and strangers shall no more serve themselves of him.}* Or, *serve him,* as some render it; that is, the king of Babylon, chap. 27. 7. but rather, as our Version, *serve themselves of him,* or *on him;* to wit, Jacob vers. 7. the Chaldeans and other people among whom they were captives, shall no longer make servants of them, detain them in servitude and slavery under them, as formerly they had done. See the use of the word on chap. 25. 14. and 27. 7. a passage from one person to another: as chap. 29. 19.

**Verse 9.** *{But they shall serve the LORD their God,}* More freely and more cheerfully than formerly, they did, or could, when such strange lords and masters domineered over them, under whom they were captives. See Deut. 28. 47, 48. Psalm 137. 4. Esai 26. 13. a blessed alteration; whereby they should make such an exchange, instead of harsh and cruel masters, Esai 19. 4. to serve a most mild, merciful, kind, bountiful, Lord, in a most free, holy, honest, and honorable service. See 2 Chr. 12. 8. Hos. 3. 5. Luke 1. 74, 75. Rom. 6. 19, 23. 1 Cor. 7. 22. *But.* Heb. *And.* as chap. 28. 12.

*{and David their King, whom I will raise up to them.}* Such of David's lineage as I shall from time to time set over them: the name of David, say some, used of such as succeeded him in the government of Judah, called *the Throne of David,* chap. 22. 2. and 29. 16. as the title of Pharaoh of the Egyptian kings anciently, of Ptolemy in later times: fulfilled in Zorobabel and others after the captivity, Hag. 2. 23. but most absolutely accomplished in the Messiah, of whom they were types, who came of the stock of David, Esai 11. 1, 10. Math. 1. 1. Rom. 1. 3. and was forever to sit on the throne of David, Luke 1. 32, 33. See Ezek. 34. 23. and 37. 24. And of him both the Chaldee and Jewish doctors expound it. See Hosea 3. 5.

*{raise up}* The term used, as of the judges and deliverers of that people after Joshua's days, Judg. 2. 16. and 3. 9. so of Christ more specially, Luke 1. 69. Act. 2. 30. and 13. 23, 33.

**Verse 10.** *{Therefore fear thou not, O my servant Jacob, saith the LORD; neither be dismayed, O Israel.}* Be not utterly discouraged and disheartened in regard of your present dejected and distressed estate: for he speaks unto them now as under captivity. See the like speeches of encouragement, Esai 41. 8, 10, 13. and 43. 5. and 44. 2. chap. 46. 27. *Jacob* and *Israel* here, one and the same; as in the places cited.

*{for lo, I will save thee from afar, and thy seed from the land of their captivity;}* Heb. *lo I am saving thee;* I intend and promise in due time *to save thee;* that is, *to bring thee safe from afar:* out of the farthest parts whereunto you have been, or shall be driven and dispersed. So Zach. 8. 7. *I will save my people* (that is, *bring them safe) from the East lands, and from the West:* and Act. 24. 44. *they were all saved* (that is, *came all safe) to land.*

*{thee and thy seed}* Them and their children; or you, Jacob, (as if he spoke to him as one yet surviving) and your seed, or posterity: which in effect will be one and the same. See the like, Esai 44. 2, 3.

*{from the land of their captivity}* From Chaldea, where most of them remained captives, said to be *a far country,* Esai 39. 3. or *land,* put collectively, for, *lands;* wheresoever they should be in captivity: *the land of ones captivity;* as 2 Chr. 6. 36, 38. chap. 46. 27. wherein one is captive: as, *the land of his nativity;* where he was born, Gen. 11. 28. and 24. 7. and 31. 13.

*{and Jacob shall return, and shall rest and be quiet}* The posterity of Jacob, as before, shall return to their own land again: as verse 3. and enjoy it quietly; or *shall again rest and be quiet:* *to return and rest,* for, *to rest again:* as, *to return and dig,* for, *to dig again,* Genes. 26. 18. *to return and tempt,* for, *to tempt again,* Psalm 78. 41.

*{and none shall make him afraid}* Heb. *and there shall be no frightner:* as Lev. 26. 6. Ezek. 34. 18. none that shall invade them, or disturb their quiet and peaceable possession.

**Verse 11.** *{For I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee:}* As Chap. 15. 20. to preserve and support you in your present difficulties, and to give a good issue to them, and deliver you out of them in due time. So Esai 41. 10, 12. and 43. 1, 2. Ezek. 11. 16, 17.

*{though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee; yet will I not make a full end of thee:}* See on Chap. 5. 10, 18. So Amos 9. 8.

*{but I will correct thee in measure,}* Heb. *and:* (as verse 9.) *I will chastise thee to judgement,* or *according to judgement:* with discretion and moderation. So is the word used, Psalm 6. 1. and 112. 5. chap. 10. 24. I will deal by way of chastisement, in another sort, in a milder and more temperate manner with you, than with others; so far for measure beneath that, which I intend to do unto your enemies. See Esai 26. 14, 19. and 27. 7, 8.

*{and will not leave thee altogether unpunished.}* Heb. *acquitting acquit thee:* as Exod. 34. 7. Num. 14. 18. Nah. 1. 3. Chap. 25. 29. The old Latin renders it, *that thou mayest not deem thy self guiltlesse;* but I see not how the words can yield it. And whereas a learned writer would have it rendered, *I will not cutting off cut thee off,* I suppose the word is nowhere found so used; though he affirm it: but producing no clear place for such use of it: for that Zach. 5. 3. elsewhere produced by him, is questionable, and by divers of good note otherwise rendered. One of the Jewish critics would have it here taken in a notion of *sweeping away,* and *destroying;* because by sweeping away and casting out of dust and dirt, a house is said to be cleansed and purged: of which use of the word, see on Esai 3. 26. But this also seems too far fetched; the use of the form so oft used elsewhere, carrying it strongly the other and plainer way. See this whole passage again repeated, chap. 46. 28.

**Verse 12.** *{For thus saith the LORD, Thy bruise is incurable}* Heb. *Mortal,* or *desperate to thy breach,* or *rupture;* but the particle seems vacant here; as chap. 18. 19. and 40. 2. *deadly,* or *desperate.* See Chap. 15. 18. in regard of human hopes, or helps; such as God alone is able to help and heal, Hos. 5. 13. and 6. 1. Mic. 1. 9. Their condition by reason of their long captivity, Chap. 29. 18. seemed desperate and past all hope of cure, Ezek. 37. 11.

*{and thy wound is grievous.}* Heb. *thy stroke* (wherewith I have stricken you) *grievous.* See chap. 14. 17. and yet nothing like so grievous as that wherewith he had struck, or intended to strike those, by whom he had stricken them, Esai 27. 7.

**Verse 13.** *{There is none to plead thy cause,}* Heb. *There is none judging,* or *deciding, thy judgement,* or *controversie:* that offers to debate, and decide your cause aright, that justice may be done you, and reparations made for the wrong that has been offered you. See Esai 40. 27. vers. 15.

*{that thou mayest be bound up;}* Or, *for binding up:* as the margin renders it: so it should be a term borrowed from the binding up of wounds, for the closing of them: as the like is Esai 1. 6. and 3. 7. but the word rather may seem to signify *unto compression,* or *crushing out:* and so it should be a metaphor, taken from the crushing out of such corrupt matter, as festered sores are pestered with, and must be voided, ere any sound cure can be had; whereunto therefore way is wont to be made by the crushing of it out: that which seems alluded unto in another word used also, Esai 1. 6. and because either of these actions tend to cure, most so render it, *unto cure,* or *healing.* Howbeit, because the word seems elsewhere used for an *ulcer,* or *sore,* that needs and requires such *compression,* or *crushing,* Hosea 5. 13. Obad. 7. some render the text, there is none that *judgeth thy cause, concerning thy sore.* And one of the Jewish doctors seems to go somewhat this way, though rendering the word rather for *healing,* or *cure,* yet thus expounding the text, *There is none that can give any judgement, or passe any doom, concerning help, or healing that may be had for thine hurt; they say all, there is no cure, no help for it:* for he supposes the words following to be conceived as the speech of those that had considered of her estate, as not unwilling to have freed her, and recovered her, if they could; not unlike that of Babel's friends and assistants, chap. 51. 9. But for the word itself, I incline still to the former sense of *compression,* or *crushing.* But because there is a twofold *crushing;* there is *a crushing* of the flesh, to put to pain, and to vex; and there is a *crushing* of it, to get out somewhat that annoys, and hinders healing: I suppose that in the other places produced, the word may signify rather *a bruise,* that comes by an excessive *pressure,* or overhard *compression* of the flesh, rather than *a wound,* or *ulcer,* as most inconstantly render it, sometime the one, and sometime the other; but here *a crushing* in the latter notion, as tending to help an healing. Howsoever we take it, There is in the text, a passage from one sort of cure, or help to another; from a judiciary to a chirurgical course; some kind of cure being intended in either, of a man's body in the one, of his state in the other. Yet an interpreter of prime note here distinguishes the terms, as containing several notions, thus distinctly delivered; *There is none that decideth the cause; there is no medicine, or cure unto healing for thee:* which might be admitted, if the pauses in the original were not directly against it. I rather accord with another learned writer, who thus paraphrases this passage; Your wound is so great, and your sore so grievous, that it passes the skill of any physician to tell what may be done to it, or to prescribe any course for the managing and handling of it, whereby any hope of cure may be had: one way of dealing with an hurt being put for all; *closing up,* as he supposes; *crushing out,* as I conceive.

*{thou hast no healing medicines}* For the sense of this place in general, there is no great disagreement, to wit, that there is in this passage an intimation of some incurable hurt, of an irrecoverable condition: But about both the right construction of the text, and the genuine notion of the words here used, there is no small difference, not without some difficulty; the former word coming from a root that signifies *to cut,* or *heal;* (whence also one that comes very near to it; *for healing,* or *health,* Prov. 3. 8.) is by some rendered *medicines,* as here, so chap. 46. 11. though by others there also, *curing, courses of cure;* for the word is plural: yea some so render it, Ezek. 30. 21. who yet render it the other way here; and as I conceive, should rather have so done there: for the words are, speaking of *a broken arm, it shall not be bound up to give curings,* or *healings;* that is, any degree, or help, of cure, or healing at all; as those plurals are also in an extenuating notion used; whereof see on Esai 27. 11. for to render it, as they there do, *it shall not be bound up with medicines* put in, to me seems a version of those words overharsh. But the old Latin (for the Greek runs here at random, and the Chaldee is as ambiguous as the Hebrew) renders it *curings* or *courses of cure:* which though it may seem not to differ much from *medicines;* yet it is of a larger extent than that term, as we commonly use it: and I suppose this to be the proper sense. But the latter word has more difficulty in it; it comes of a word that signifies *to ascend,* or *go up:* and it is used sometime for *a trench,* or *a watercourse;* whereof see on Esai 7. 3. but being applied, as here, and chap. 46. 11. to matter of cure, what it should signify is questionable. Some render it *a plaister,* both here and there; which should be so called, because it *goeth up* upon, and is applied unto, the hurt, or ill-affected place for its ease, or cure: but other render it much after the same manner with the former term, *health,* or *healing;* supposing it, some of them, to be so termed from a word that signifies *to profit,* or *avail;* because where cure is efficacious, it is available for healing: but the form of the word will hardly admit that deduction; though one of the Jewish masters there seem to allow of it. But others rather therefore from the root before mentioned, because in curing, or healing of a wound, or sore, where the course used takes effect, the flesh *groweth up,* and either the skin, or some scar is *drawn over* the place, where the wound, or sore, before was: whence that phrase frequently used in cases of that kind, *cure,* or *healing, is gone up:* as Chap. 8. 22. *and I will make cure,* or *healing, to go up,* or *to come unto thee,* vers. 17. and chap. 33. 6. whereof more hereafter: though *cure,* or *healing* may be so termed, either in regard of the *imposition* of plasters, or the like upon the place ill affected; or from the *procuration* and bringing of ease and recovery thereunto: and this latter more general sense the word seems to have. But concerning the construction of the two words here used, a new controversy arises; for some join them in regiment together, as the one governing the other; and they render them *curings,* or *curing courses, of ascension,* to wit, of flesh, or skin; that is, say they, *courses of cure contracting a skar.* Others, *curings,* or *curing courses of utility;* that is, available for recovery: and so after one of the Jewish critics, the old Latin renders it. But others render the words apart; some in way of apposition, *courses of cure, plaister there is none at all for thee:* or *none at all shall avail thee:* some in way of conjunction supplying the copulative, oft wanting as Esai 32. 13. Hab. 3. 11. rendering the words, *curings* (that is, courses of cure) and *healing* (or, means used for recovery) *there is none for thee.* So one of the Jewish commenters, who also affirms both words in effect to signify the same; and that the same thing is in divers terms expressed to make the sentence the more vigorous: whom the rather I concur with; because I find the very like, in some sort the same, the copulative being there supplied, in a parallel place, where God promises to do that for his people, which by human help is here intimated not to have been feasible, *I will cause to ascend,* or, *bring, to her* (this city and state) *healing,* or *health,* (a word answering to the latter here) *and cure:* a word from the same root with the former; and the verb, or participle rather, that, from whence the latter here arises.

**Verse 14.** *{All thy lovers have forgotten thee, they seek thee not:}* Your pretended friends and confederates, the Assyrians and Egyptians, whom you had wont to entertain with presents, 2 Chron. 28. 21. Chap. 2. 18. Hos. 12. 1. are now fallen off from you, and fail you in your present affliction, Chap. 4. 30. Lam. 1. 2, 17, 19.

*{thy lovers}* So Hos. 2. 7, 8, 12.

*{have forgotten thee:}* Neglect you; regard you no more, than as if they had clean forgotten you. So is the word used, Psal. 31. 12. & 45. 10. & 105. 21.

*{they seek thee not}* *They seek not to thee;* or, *enquire not after thee:* as in times past they had wont to do. See Chapter 15. 5.

*{for I have wounded thee with the wound of an enemy}* Or, *because;* (as Eth. 64. 5. as rendering a reason, and showing the cause why they had withdrawn themselves from her; to wit, because they saw in what case she was by reason of God's heavy hand upon her, Lam. 1. 19, 21.) or, *when* (as chap. 10. 2.) *God shall have stricken,* or *smitten thee* (So is the Hebrew; as Esay 1. 5. & 27. 7. 1 King. 20. 37.) *with the stroke,* or, *blow,* (as chap. 10. 19. & 14. 17. verse 12.) *of an enemy:* a sore and grievous one; not such as friends sometime in displeasure and anger give to those whom they yet love and affect dearly, Prov. 27. 6. but such as enemies are wont to strike enemies with, Job 13. 24. & 16. 9. & 19. 11. Esay 63. 10. For the phrase, see the like, but in a divers subject, Esay 62. 5. and if we take the particle here for an adverb of time, then the former branch is to be rendered in the future; *All thy lovers will forget thee, they will seek,* or, *look,* no more *after thee, when I have* thus *smitten thee.*

*{with the chastisement of a cruell one;}* Such stripes, as cruel and hardhearted persons are wont to inflict. So Job complains, that God was become cruel to him, Job 30. 21.

*{for the multitude of thine iniquities; because thy sins are increased}* Or, *are many:* See of the word on chap. 5. 6. & 15. 8. It is sin alone that enforces God to these harsh and enemy-like carriages toward his people; chap. 4. 18. the causal is wanting: so verse 15. see the like defect of it, chap. 36. 29.

**Verse 15.** *{Why cryest thou for thine affliction? thy sorrow is incurable, for the multitude of thine iniquity; because thy sins were increased, I have done these things unto thee}* Or, *Why dost thou cry out of thine hurt* (the *breach,* or *rupture,* as verse 12.) *and* (a defect of the copulative; as verse 13.) *of thy deadly,* or, *desperate grief;* or, *that thy grief,* or, *disease, is deadly,* or, *desperate:* a defect of the particle *that:* as chap. 27. 8. See chap. 15. 18. verse 12. what reason have you so much to complain of your present pressures, and desperate condition when as you suffer nothing, but what by your manifold sins and excesses you have procured to yourself, chap. 2. 17. & 4. 18. See ver. 14. and the like argument, Lam. 3. 39.

**Verse 16.** *{Therefore all they that devour thee shall be devoured}* Those that thus render the compound particle here used, are compelled to give the words thereafter following a reference unto what went before, ver. 10, 11. and to enclose all that lies between that and this within the compass of a parenthesis: and yet with all their contrivance the context cannot easily be brought to hang handsomely together. And one of the rabbines would have it taken in the nature of an oath. But it would rather be rendered, *Notwithstanding;* or, *Neverthelesse;* or, *Yet:* as taken, not in an illative, as most commonly it is, but in a discretive notion, as in many places of necessity it must: that which having not been by any, that I can hitherto find, observed, has in divers passages of Scripture produced very uncouth connections, and needless hyperbatons, to the puzzling of the reader, and disjoining of the context: whereas, being duly regarded, it would much conduce to the clearing of it in places not a few, See Esay 7. 14. & 30. 18. & 51. 21. a place not unlike to this: as also, chap. 16. 14. Ezek. 39. 15. Hos. 2. 14. let the places be well weighed: and this here admitted, the coherence of this passage with the very next before-going will be clear: to wit, that albeit, they had no just cause to complain of what they had suffered; sustaining nothing but what they had brought upon themselves by their sins, and deserved therefore to be left still in that calamitous condition: yet notwithstanding all this, God would out of his mere mercy take a course for their delivery, and for the effecting thereof, inflict the like heavy and harsh things upon those, at whose hands they had sustained the same. Those, says he, that have *devoured* you, or, eaten upon you (see chap. 50. 17.) *shall be devoured.* Heb. *eaten on,* or, *eaten up.* That shall be renewed, and made good again that formerly had been, when Israel was a thing consecrated to God at his first fruits, when all that did eat upon him contracted guilt, and some evil or other befell them for it, chap. 2. 3. See Esay 41. 11. & 49. 26.

*{And all thine adversaries shall every one of them go into captivity,}* They that captived you, shall themselves be captived. Thus will God show himself to be an enemy unto those that have been adversaries to his people, Exod. 23. 22. See Esay 14. 2.

*{And they that spoil thee, shall be a spoil,}* Some render it, *they that tread on thee shall be for a treading on* to others: as Esay 42. 22. & 51. 22. but the general use of the word confirms the received Version. See Zach. 2. 9.

*{and all that prey upon thee will I give for a prey.}* See Esay 33. 1.

**Verse 17.** *{For I will restore health unto thee}* Heb. *I will cause health,* or, *healing to come up to thee,* or, *come unto thee.* The word here used some render *a plaister;* and, say some of them, properly *a long plaister,* so called from the *length* of it; because the word originally has a notion of *length,* or, *prolongation,* rendered *long* chap. 29. 28. and *lengthening,* Dan. 4. 27. and so the form should have reference to the putting of a plaster on or over the hurt, or pained part, fully proportionable to the wound or sore. Some other would have it to signify *a skar:* and so should it have relation to the *skinning* of a wound, or ulcer, which, where it has been deep, is seldom done without some scar. So they say it is used in the Chaldee tongue, and in the writings of the rabbines: for which yet I see no clear place produced out of either: for that of the Chaldee, Psal. 147. 3. to this purpose alleged by more than one of them, is altogether as ambiguous, as the word itself is in the Hebrew. Thus taken here, it should be as if he had said, *I will bring a skar upon,* or, *over thy wound:* and such a notion of it here would rather blemish, than commend God's works, who in healing is not wont to leave scars behind, but to make a full and fair cure of what he undertakes to heal, and in that tenor his promises of restitution are wont to run. See Esay 54. 4.—14. & 60. Besides that, in Esay 58. 8. to render the word either of these ways, *thy plaister,* or, *thy skar, shall speedily spring forth,* were palpably to wrong the text. I see no reason, therefore, why we should recede from the signification of the word, as having a notion of *health,* and *healing,* in it, and being so commonly received: which if it be supposed to arise from that root, as it signifies *to lengthen* or, *to be long:* *health;* or, *healing,* may be so termed; because it is oftentimes long in coming, and long looked for, before it come. We have a proverb, that *sicknesse comes on horseback, but goes away on foot;* intimating the suddenness of falling into maladies, together with the slowness of recovery out of them: but it may rather have its ground from another notion, that the same root has in the Chaldee, to wit, *of expectation,* and *hope;* Psal. 147. 11. Lam. 3. 18. *health* being a usual subject matter as well of *hope,* as of *expectation* and desire, chap. 8. 15. now this *health,* or, *healing,* is said *to come up,* chap. 8. 22. or, *to be made to come up,* as here, and chap. 33. 6. as I conceive, not so much in regard of the coming up, or bringing up of flesh and skin to cover the parts, that were bare of either before: as Ezek. 37. 6. as of *accrewing,* or *coming unto* the part or party healed: for the word that properly signifies *to go up,* is very commonly also used in a larger notion, for *to passe* from place to place, *to come to,* or, *to go from,* without any special reference unto ascent, or descent: as Numb. 16. 24, 27. chap. 4. 7. Joel 1. 6. and so I conceive it to be taken in these and the like forms, wherein *health,* or *healing,* is laid *to come,* or *to be brought unto one:* as *diseases* are said to come and go at God's command, Mat. 8. 8, 9. and *health* consequently being the removal of them, as in the same place is implied. So that the meaning is no more than this, *I will bring health,* or, *healing to thee;* or, *cause it to come home unto thee:* and it is not unworthy our observation, that the same form is used also of *walls,* that *healing is brought,* or *caused to come* to them, when they are repaired, Neh. 4. 7. and *healing,* or, *health,* is said *to come to a businesse,* when it is brought to a good issue, or to a full end, 2 Chron. 24. 13.

*{and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the LORD;}* Or, *of thy hurts,* Heb. *from thy strokes,* or, *blowes;* as verse 12. a word of larger extent than *wounds.* God's restitution of his people, being as a recovery of life and health unto them, is very fitly called an healing of them. See Esay 6. 10. & 19. 22. & 57. 18, 19. chapter 3. 22. & 17. 14.

*{because they called thee an out-cast,}* The particle thus rendered, the words should import a reason, why God would the rather be induced to help and heal his Sion, to wit, thereby really to check and control that conceit, that her adversaries had of her, that she was a mean, abject and outcast, one that God had utterly cast off and abandoned, one that neither God, nor man, regarded. And it is true, indeed, that the insolent insultations of profane wretches over God's people in times of their dejection and distress, is a motive sometime to induce God the rather to show mercy unto them: in delivering and raising them up again. But I suppose the particle has rather here a discretive, or adversative notion, and would be rendered *although:* as Gen. 8. 21. Josh. 17. 18. Psal. 23. 4. chap. 12. 1. & 30. 11. though they so deem of you, yet I will, by the delivery and restitution of you, show it to be otherwise with you, than they imagine. Heb. *they called an out-cast to thee;* that is, you have been called and accounted (as Mal. 1. 4.) an *out-cast,* Mic. 4. 6. Zeph. 3. 19. So Esay 62. 4. *Forsaken shall not be said any more to thee:* that is you shall no longer be so accounted. See the like form, Esay 1. 26. & 64. 12.

*{saying}* Supplied: as Psal. 105. 15. Chap. 4. 31. and 11. 19.

*{This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after}* Heb. *Zion is,* or, *it is:* the pronoun demonstrative, for the verb substantive: as chap. 29. 28. verse 7. and they seem in way of derision to have played upon her name: the term *Tsija,* signifying originally a *dry,* or, *waste place,* Psal. 63. 1. & 107. 35. chap. 2. 6. & 50. 12. as if it were in regard of its desolation, for *drynesse,* and *wastnesse,* a place not worthy the looking after. Heb. *Seeker,* or, *seeking to her none is:* she is utterly disregarded both of God and man: for the speech is of her, as of some goodly and beautiful person, that in time past, living in a rich and honorable estate, had been much sought unto by many, but now fallen into misery, was utterly abandoned by those that had sought unto her before. See ver. 14.

**Verse 18.** *{Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will bring away the captivity of Jacobs tents, and have mercy on his dwelling places;}* A further gracious promise of the restauration of their decayed and ruined cities, and dwellings, and constitution of their state.

*{Behold, I will bring again the captivity}* Heb. *Lo I am bringing again the captivity.* See ver. 3.

*{the captivity of Jacobs tents}* In these and the like forms of speech, the term *captivity* is commonly used for *captives.* See on ver. 3. but here it has reference not so much to persons, as to places, which cannot be properly said to be captived, especially in the Hebrew, where the word has a notion of transmigration and deportation. But it may be observed, that the term of *captivity* is in Scripture sometime used to denote any calamitous condition in general: as where it is said, that *the Lord turned the captivity of Job.* Job 42. 10. though Job was never in proper sense a *captive:* which may be here admitted here, because this desolation, either with, or by reason of the people's captivity, befell the places of their wonted abode.

*{Jacobs tents}* As, *Israels tents,* 2 Sam. 20. 1. 1 Kings 12. 16. and *Davids Tabernacle,* Amos 9. 12. an allusion to the ancient patriarchs dwelling in tents, Heb. 11. 9. and the Israelites in the wilderness, Num. 24. 5.

*{have mercy on his dwelling places}* Or, *dwellings,* or, *tabernacles;* as it is rendered, Numb. 24. 5. Psal. 43. 3. & 84. 1. on them for him, Esay 14. 1. See the like phrase, Psal. 102. 14.

*{and the city shall be builded upon her own heap,}* Or, *her heap;* where before was nothing but a ruinous heap of stones and rubbish, Psal. 79. 1. Esay 25. 2. & 37. 26. so is the word used, Deut. 13. 16. Josh. 8. 28. Chap. 49. 2. or: as others, *upon her little hill:* which the margin of our Bibles exhibits: as if the word signified *an hillock,* or, *a knole;* such as Jerusalem stood upon, though situate in a plain. See chap. 17. 3. But this the Jewish doctor not content with, would have it, *an high hill:* for Jerusalem, says he, is the highest ground in all the land of Israel: (though therein we need not believe him) and a participle or participial from this root has a notion of height, and is rendered *eminent,* Ezek. 17. 22. *on a mountain lofty and eminent.* Howbeit, others take it more generally, as the Chaldee, who here renders it, *upon her place;* that is, upon her *seat* or *bottom:* upon *her* former *foundation:* as the theme seems to be taken without special regard to hill, or dale: Josh. 11. 13. *the cities that stood still upon their seat,* or *soil:* and had not been ruinated in the surprisal. Though that term seem used both there and here; because cities were usually built on some rising, or the ground at least raised for the founding and rearing of them: and from hence divers towns and cities had their appellations, as *Telmilach,* Ezr. 2. 59. *Telabar,* Esay 37. 12. *Telebib,* Ezek. 3. 15. But see Zach. 22. 6. & 14. 10.

*{and the palace shall remain after the manner thereof.}* By the *palace,* here some understand the king's house, or court; others, and so the Chaldee, God's house, *the Sanctuary,* the temple which was God's palace, Psal. 11. 4. & 68. 29. Others, both: the middle seems best.

*{remain}* Heb. *sit,* that is, be founded, and seated, and settled, Esay 13. 20. Chap. 50. 39. *abide;* as Numb. 35. 28. Psal. 9. 7. & 29. 10.

*{after the manner thereof.}* Heb. *upon its right,* or, *judgement;* that is, say some, seated in its former or wonted place: or, as others, so built, so used and so frequented, as formerly it had been: the word is of a very large extent. See 1 Sam. 2. 13. & 27. 11. 2 Kings 1. 7. & 17. 26.

**Verse 19.** *{And out of them shall proceed thanksgiving, and the voice of them that make merry:}* The comfortable effect of this restitution, cheerfulness of heart, and thankfulness to God for his goodness therein towards them, Chap. 31. 12.

*{out of them}* That is, from the tents of Jacob and his dwellings, ver. 18. and the people restored to them.

*{shall proceed thanksgiving}* That is, because the noun and the verb are of different genders; *sacrifice of confession,* or, *praise,* or, *thanksgiving:* so called, Lev. 7. 12, 13. Chap. 17. 26. & 38. 13. as some; or, as others, both Jews, and ours, the voice of *praise,* or *thanksgiving,* supplied from the next branch: as 1 Chron. 1. 15. Esay 18. 7. & 30. 17. so Psal. 28. 7. & 42. 4. John 2. 10. See Esay 22. 1. & 26. 1. & 35. 10. & 51. 11.

*{the voice of them that make merry}* Heb. *that laugh.* See on chap. 15. 77. and it seems, as some not amiss deem, to allude to the wonted mirth, music, and jollity, that was exercised by God's people, at their solemn festivals, and repairs to God's house, Psal. 42. 4. & 118. 15. Esay 30. 9. Chap. 31. 12. Esay 30. 29. but it may well be taken in a larger extent: as Chap. 31. 13. & 33. 11. See there, Zach. 8. 4. & 9. 15, 17.

*{and I will multiply them, and they shall not be few}* Or, *they shall not be diminished,* as Psal. 107. 39. Prov. 13. 11. Esay 21. 17. See Chap. 31. 27. Ezek. 36. 11. & 36. 26. Zach. 10. 8, 9.

*{and I will glorify them, and they shall not be small.}* Or, *mean,* or, *of small account,* Psal. 119. 141. and so is the word also used in the Syriac Mat. 13. 57. & 22. 7. Mar. 12. for they straiten the text too much, (which yet many, both Jewish, and others do) that make this branch no other than the same, though in other terms delivered, with the former.

**Verse 20.** *{Their children also shall as aforetime,}* Their issue (Heb. *his;* to wit, Jacob's, verse 18.) shall be settled in as good and fair an estate and condition as they were before the time of their captivity, Esay 44. 3, 4. chap. 33. 11. Lam. 5. 21.

*{and their congregation shall be established before me}* There shall be a constant succession of them, either protected by me, or attending upon me, Esay 66. 22. Chap. 31. 36. and 35. 19.

*{and I will punish all that oppress them}* Heb. *visit upon* (as chapter 29. 32.) *all his oppressors:* as Judg. 2. 18. & 6. 9. see verse 16.

**Verse 21.** *{And their Nobles shall be of themselves, and their governors shall proceed from the midst of them.}* Heb. *his noble,* or, *magnificent,* or, *honourable one:* as Esay 10. 34. 2 Chron. 23. 20. *and, his ruler,* or, *governour, from the midst of him;* that is, from among them: as Num. 14. 13. Josh. 7. 12, 13. This some restrain to Christ, the king and ruler of God's church, Psal. 2. 6. Esay 11. 1. Mic. 5. 2. Acts 2. 36. and some of the Jews themselves expound them of the Messiah. Howbeit, the words seem collective; and to imply that strangers should no more rule over them, and keep them in subjection; but they should have rulers and governors of their own, Deut. 17. 15. fulfilled in Zorobabel and others in those times, Zach. 4. 4. & 6. 11. 14. but principally indeed in Christ, of whom he was a type, chap. 23. 6. & 33. 16.

*{and I will cause him draw near, and he shall approach unto me,}* This some understand of the ruler, or rulers, before mentioned, that God would take them to be near unto him, in regard of his favor toward them, and protection of them, whereupon the safety and prosperity of the people under them would very much depend, 2 Sam. 7. 14. Psal. 20. 4. & 89. 24, 28. See Hagg. 2. 23. Others, of Jacob or Israel, God's people in general; a people near unto God, and received into favor again with God as before. Exod. 19. 5. Deut. 4. 20. Psal. 148. 14. Zach. 10. 6. Others, of Christ who as a priest makes his approaches unto God for us and by whom we have also access unto God, Joh. 4. 6. Eph. 2. 13. Heb. 4. 15, 16. & 9. 11, 12. & 10. 21, 22. 1 Pet. 3. 18. in whom without question this was most consummately made good: and the order of the context is not amiss by divers observed: as implying, say those that go the first way, that no man may intrude himself into any office of government without call from God; Deut. 10. 8. & 17. 14. Prov. 8. 15. those that go the second, that come unto God, unless God convert them, and work them to himself by his Spirit, chap. 10. 23. & 31. 18. Lam. 5. 21. John 6. 44, 65. those that go the last way, that Christ was by his Father designed unto his office, before he undertook it, Psal. 2. 6. & 110. 1, 4. Joh. 6. 27. & 10. 36. Heb. 5. 4, 5, 9. 1 Pet. 1. 20.

*{for who is this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? saith the LORD.}* This clause is very difficult, and interpreters are much divided about it: those, I mean, that take notice of it; for many of them let it pass without any regard had of it. Those that take special notice of it, some of them expound it of Christ; but diversely: some in way of admiration of his dignity and excellency, *For who is this* (that is, how excellent a person is he *(that hath given his heart* (that is, his soul) *for a pawn,* or, *pledge,* or, *engagement, to procure accesse to me?* Esay 53. 7, 10. Heb. 7. 22. Others in way of appropriation and exclusion of all others; *who but he hath engaged,* or *can engage?* *who can engage his heart to approach unto God,* in that manner, as Christ did? 1 Tim. 2. 5. or, as others, *who dare* in that manner offer to approach unto God, or, take upon him the office of mediating between God and man; unless he be by God himself called and assigned thereunto? Heb. 5. 4. But others, not a few, apply it to God's people; whom I rather concur with: and these go again two ways. For some would have it spoken in way of admiration as intimating the paucity of those at present, that did apply themselves to draw near unto God; and they render the words, *For who is he that engageth his heart to approach unto me?* So it should be like that Esay 53. 1. *Who believeth our report?* that is few or none: and Esay 64. 7. *there is none that stirreth up himself to take hold on thee.* Others in way of confirmation as rendering a reason, why he had said he would make them approach, that they might come near to him: to wit, because none could do it of himself, Cant. 1. 4. John 6. 44. & 15. 3. Others again, in way of stipulation; like that, Psal. 25. 12. and that Esay 50. 10. and one of those that goes this way, gives a twofold syntax of the terms here used; the words may, says he, be rendered, either; *who is he that hath engaged,* or, *undertaken for his heart to draw near unto me?* as *thy servant hath engaged* himself *for the lad,* Gen. 44. 32. or, *that hath made a covenant,* or, *agreement with his heart* (that is, has sincerely obliged himself and made a covenant with his heart) *to approach unto me?* as he says, *Make a covenant,* or, *agreement, with my Lord;* Esay 36. 8. and as Job, *I have made a covenant with mine eyes.* Job 31. 1. though this word be not there used: and he supposes that the words may have reference either to what went before, of taking near to him, such as had any hearty desire and resolution thus to approach and come home to him, c. 24. 7. & 50. 4, 5. Joh. 6. 37. or to that which follows, that if any such were found, whosoever they were that should be so affected, *they should be his people, and he would be their God,* ver. 22. unto which one of the rabbines, going also this way, adds, that this is adjoined to intimate, that not those of that nation, whom God formerly had taken to be near him, but such Gentiles also as dwelt among them, and were in this manner affected, should be taken in together with them, to enjoy the like communion and inwardness with him. Deut. 29. 11, 12. & 31. 12, 23. Esay 56. 5, 8. And this last seems very probable, though the rabbies' additional seem a little overcurious and needless. For as for that of a learned writer, who because the word here used has sometime a notion of *sweetnesse,* chap. 6. 20. & 31. 26. Psal. 104. 34. Prov. 3. 24. & 13. 19. Hos. 9. 4. Mal. 3. 4. would have it rendered, *who is he that hath sweetened his heart to draw near to me?* beside the uncouthness of the phrase, it cannot have place here; because the word in all the places pointed to, where alone it is certainly found in that notion, is constantly used in a passive, not an active sense for, *to be sweet,* or, *pleasant;* not for to make such. Howsoever there is here either a defect of the relative, as chap. 23. 29. or the demonstrative put for it; and the other for the verb substantive: as Psal. 25. 12. & 44. 4. Esay 66. 1.

**Verse 22.** *{And ye shall be my people, and I will be your God.}* A stipulation renewed between God and his people. So chap. 24. 7. & 31. 33. & 32. 38. A passage from person to person: as chap. 29. 19. ver. 8. and from number to number: as Psal. 127. 5. & 140. 7.

*{ye}* Both Judah and Israel ver. 3. all the families of Israel, Chap. 31. 1.

**Verse 23.** *{Behold the whirlwind of the LORD goeth forth with fury}* See before on chap. 23. 19. where the same denunciation in effect is found: the only matter of doubt is here concerning the persons against whom it is denounced. It was there denounced against the wicked among God's people, and the false prophets by whom they were seduced: and so would some have it to be here; as foretelling what shall befall the obstinate wicked among them, that kept aloof from God either in heart, or in life, or in both, Chap. 12. 2. notwithstanding the gracious goodness of God exhibited and made good unto those that sincerely drew near unto him, verse 21. which they should have no share in, but should taste deeply of his wrath. So Esay 65. 20. Chap. 17. 5, 6. But others rather, the most and best, conceive it to concern here the heathen people, the enemies of God and his church, before pointed at, ver. 16. 20. the destruction of the one being usually joined with, and making way to the deliverance of the other. See Esay 14. 1.

*{a continuing whirlwind}* Because the old Latin has two several terms here, *a whirl-wind, and a tempest,* or *storm;* some popish writers stand descanting upon and distinguishing of them; but to no purpose: for the Hebrew word is in either member the same, save that it is of a masculine form in this latter, of a feminine in the former: (as the like, Esay 3. 1. Jon. 2. 1, 10.) But of the attribute given to it, there is some question; for some render it, *grievously cutting,* as with a *saw;* which from hence is deemed to have its name, 1 Kings 7. 9. which seems to receive some strength from that in the parallel place, chap. 23. 19. where the word is *grievously paining,* or, *putting to grievous pain:* for these reciprocal forms, where they have no reciprocal signification, carry a notion of aggravation and vehemency with them: and this I take to be the genuine sense of the word. Howbeit, some other, referring it to another root, render it, some, *an affrighting,* or, *terrifying,* one; because that root has sometime a notion of *terrour,* Job 19. 29. some, *a whirling,* or, *involving* one; such an one as gathering itself together, should so wheel about them, and environ them, that they should not be able any way to get out of it, because the word has sometime a notion of *gathering together,* Esay 54. 15. Hos. 7. 14. some, *a continuing* one, whom our Version follows; or, *a sojourning* one; that is, says one of them, one that shall as an unwelcome guest take up his guests and lodgings with them, and so pass in progress incessantly from place to place, until it have gone thorough their whole land, and made an utter riddance of them; because the same root has also otherwhile a notion of *sojourning,* Lam. 4. 15. and the term is used for *a sojourner,* 1 King. 17. 20. But I adhere to the first.

**Verse 24.** *{The fierce anger of the LORD shall not return until he have done it, and until he have performed the intents of his heart}* See Chap. 23. 20. the pronoun *it,* needed not here more than there.

*{in the latter days ye shall consider it.}* See likewise on chap. 23. 20. where only the phrase of *considering,* or, *understanding,* is by a gemination made more emphatic.

## CHAPTER 31

**Verse 1.** *{At the same time, saith the LORD,}* This introduction evidently shows that the foregoing chapter, and this do jointly make up one sermon or prophecy. For in it the prophet after a close of that, with a denunciation of destruction to the enemies of God's people; does in this return again to the prosecution of God's gracious promises to his people; in the reduction of them into their own land again, restitution of their state, multiplication of their issue, collation of peace and plenty upon them in abundance, ver. 1—28. renovation and amplification of his covenant with them, ver. 29—34. and the continuation of these his favors with them to their posterity forever, verse 35—40.

*{At the same time}* In the *latter* times pointed to, Chap. 30. 24. (for where that chapter ended, this begins) that is, after the return from the Babylonian captivity in part, but more completely, and principally, under the Messiah, Chap. 30. 9. of whose times the Jewish doctors themselves observe, that the prophets use to speak in those terms, Esay 20. 2. Chap. 48. 47. & 49. 39. Hos. 3. 5. Mich. 4. 1.

*{will I be the God of all the families of Israel, and they shall be my people}* Not of Judah alone, but of Israel also, of all the twelve tribes, and of all other that shall be called and adjoined unto them, Chap. 3. 18. & 30. 3, 4, 22. for to that last this has reference. See to the same purpose, Ezek. 37. 19, 22. Hos. 1. 10. & 2. 24. Acts 2. 39. Rom. 11. 26.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus saith the LORD, The people that were left of the sword found grace in the wilderness,}* God, to put them in hope of further favors, minds them here of his former mercies, So chap. 2. 2. The words most read, as we have them here, in the time past; by *the people left of the sword,* understanding, either those that escaped the sword of Pharaoh, who pursued them with a full purpose to cut them off and destroy them, Exod. 14. 9, 10. & 15. 9. or, as some, that survived the execution done by the Levites among them for their idolatry, about the golden calf, Exod. 32. 27, 28. Or, as others, the sword of the Amalekites and Amorites that sought to intercept them, and cut them off in their way, Exod. 17. 8. Numb. 21. 22, 33. Deut. 25. 17, 18. (but the former rather here intended) found favor with God, being by him supplied with all necessary accommodations, in their passage thorough the vast and waste wilderness into the land of Canaan, Deut. 2. 7, & 8. 2.—4, 15, 16. & 32. 10—12. or, as those that go the latter way, they were for all that their horrible idolatry, at Moses' intercession and entreaty for them, reconciled to God, and brought into favor again with him, Exod. 33. 17. Deut. 9. 19. But some read and render the words in the future; *The people that are left of the sword shall find favour as in the wildernesse;* that is, say they, those that have escaped the sword of the Chaldeans, shall after the dissolution of that captivity, in their return home again, find the same favor with me, for matter, both of protection and provision, that their forefathers did in their journeying thorough those dismal deserts. Now true it is, that God does oftentimes parallel the deliverance out of Babylon, with the bringing of them out of Egypt, and describes the passages of his providence concerning their return home in the latter, by those dispensations exhibited to them in the former, Esay 11. 15, 16. & 43. 19, 20. as also that the note of similitude is oft wanting, where of necessity it is to be supplied: Esay 11. 8. & 22. 18. & 66. 3. But where there is no necessity, and the sense is plain and clear of itself without it; there to force it in, and force a Scripture to farther-fetched strains, seems neither fair, safe, nor fit.

*{even Israel, when I went to bring him to rest.}* Heb. *in going to rest him,* or, *to bring him to rest Israel.* So the words lie in the text: which most, both of the Jewish writers, and others, understand of God's going to procure rest to his people: and some of the Jewish expound of God's conducting them, and going before them to seek out fit resting places for them as they traveled along, or to and fro, in the wilderness, Exod. 13. 22. Num. 10. 33. Deut. 1. 33. Others; of the bringing of them unto a settled place of constant rest in the land of Canaan, Deut. 12. 9. Psal. 95. 11. and the word may then well be rendered; *to settle him.* See Esay 51. 4. & 63. 14. So the word *Israel* must by way of apposition, be referred to *the people* before mentioned, as our Version conceives it: or if we put off *Israel* to the end of the verse, rendering the words, *to settle him,* even *Israel;* then there is a redundancy, but elegant and vehement, like that: Prov. 5. 21. *his iniquities shall take him, the wicked one;* and *the end of his mirth,* is *grief,* Prov. 14. 13. Howbeit, some refer all this to *Israel,* reading the words, some, in the future, *Israel shall go to his rest.* So the old Latin. Others, in the time present, *Israel going unto his rest.* So some of the Greeks. Others, in the time past, *when Israel went,* or *was going, to his rest:* or, *in Israels going to his rest.* So a learned writer; who to strengthen this exposition, further observes; first, that the verb infinitive is used sometime for the preter tense, wherein the Jewish doctor here concurred with him, pointing us to the like, Chapter 14. 5. Whereof see there: and as *leaving,* for *left* there; so *going,* for, *went,* here. And secondly, that the verb of resting, in the form here used, does as often signify *to rest,* as *to cause to rest:* and so indeed it seems to be taken, Deut. 28. 64. Esay 34. 14. Chapter 47. 6. and lastly, that the infinitive is in Hebrew, as well as in other languages, used frequently as a noun: as Psal. 139. 2. *my down-sittings and mine up-risings:* and, *thy sitting,* for, *thine abode,* chap. 9. 6. The words may well bear either sense; but I incline rather to the first, understood of the promised land.

**Verse 3.** *{The LORD hath appeared of old unto me;}* Heb. *from a farre:* as Psalm 139. 2. Esay 5. 26. but it is used as well of time, as of place; and so here. Howbeit, some refer it to the time to come; as if the meaning were, *it is far off that the Lord appeareth unto us.* You tell us, that God will appear for our deliverance, Esay 60. 2. and 66. 5. but his appearance to that purpose is long a coming. So it should be the speech of the people complaining of the delay of their deliverance. But this interpretation the words will not bear. Others, and so the most read them, in the time past, as the word is used, Esay 22. 11. and well rendered here, as there also, *of old,* in times long past and gone. That they are the words of the people in captivity is generally agreed; but some would have them the words of the profane party among them, as scoffing at God's prophets, when they tell them of God's acts done in former times for his people, as if they said, You tell us of things long ago done; but what is that to us, what was then done: if any such things were then done, that was in the old time: show us somewhat in our days. But the most rather of the main body of the people, acknowledging that God had indeed so appeared unto their forefathers as was before intimated verse 2. but withal implying, that he had now withdrawn himself and his gracious presence from them, and did not manifest his affection to them, or might for them, as in times past he had done. See the like complaints Judg. 6. 13. Psalm 44. 1.—3. and 74. 12.—14. Est. 49. 14. and 63. 11. 16.

*{appeared}* Heb. *been seen* in the manifestation of his providence for his people's good and safety; as Genesis 22. 14. Psalm 102. 16. Zach. 9. 14.

*{saying, yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love;}* That these are the Lord's words, is generally received: but according to our Version, inserting the word *saying* between this and the former branch of the context, it may be deemed that they should be the words of God uttered long ago, at what time he so appeared to his people. Whereas indeed they are, as most interpreters also take them, returned from God, as an answer to the people's complaint covertly included in their aforementioned speech; assuring them of the continuance of that affection to them, that in former times he had borne toward them, and manifested unto them: and instead of *saying,* therefore, *say they,* might be supplied; as Esay 58. 3. but referring to the speech foregoing and annexing it to the close of the former branch, as also the words here following, might better be rendered, *yea.* (Heb. *and* as Chapter 18. 23.) *I love thee with a perpetual* or, *everlasting love,* Heb. *love of perpetuity,* or *eternitie;* as *kindnesse of perpetuity,* Esay 54. 8. and *joy of perpetuity:* Esay 61. 7. My love and affection continues still the same to you, and so shall do forever: or, as some other, with reference to the time past, *I love thee with an ancient,* or a *love of antiquity:* I love you still with the same affection that in former ages I bore towards you: and both the terms of the text, and the drift of the context will bear it; for the word here used has oft respect to the time past, as well as to the future, Esay 58. 12. and 63. 9, 11. See Malachi 1. 3. and 3. 6. John 12. 1. Romans 11. 29.

*{therefore with loving kindness have I drawn thee.}* Or *I drew thee,* as some I wooed you to win you and bind and engage you to me with many benefits, as with cords and bands of love, Hosea 10. 4. or as others, *I will draw thee;* to wit, after me, Canticles 1. 4. John 6. 44. or unto repentance, Romans 2. 4. But others rather, both of the Jewish writers and ours conceive the term here used, to be taken in a notion, not of *attraction,* but of *extension:* and some of the Jewish doctors render the words in the time past, *therefore did I extend kindnesse to thee;* to wit, say they, at Mount Sinai, when I took you to be a people in covenant with me, Exodus 19. 5, 6. an effect of his love and affection to them, Deuteronomy 7. 7, 8. But ours rather in the future, *therefore will I extend kindnesse to thee.* So Psalm 36. 10. *extend thy kindnesse;* and *none to extend kindnesse,* Psalm 109. 12. Heb. word for word, *extend thee kindnesse,* for *extend it unto thee:* the particle swallowed up, between the verb and the pronoun affixed: as Esay 65. 5. See instances of the like there: Wherein he would extend kindness to her, see in the words next following.
