**Verse 4.** *{Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built,}* You shall be restored and settled again; a metaphor taken from architecture: for, says the rabbin, as timber and stones and other materials are dissipated and dispersed, when a building is dissolved and pulled down; so in re-edifying of it, they are gathered and brought together again, and the fabric is raised by the conjunction of them in due manner one with another: and in like manner was it with this people; who when they were dispersed by deportation had their state dissolved, which God by the collection and reduction of them unto their own land, and settling of them therein, promises as to re-edify and build up again, Psalm 51. 18. & 102. 16. & 147. 2. c. 24. 6.

*{O virgin of Israel}* Or *O Damsel,* See Esay 47. 1. and *Damsel of Israel:* as, *daughter of Sion,* Esay 1. 8. and, *the city of Jerusalem,* it is put here for the whole state of Israel v. 1.

*{thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry}* You shall return again to a comfortable and cheerful condition, such as in times of peace and plenty, people generally, the younger sort especially, are wont to enjoy, Zach. 3. 10. & 8. 5. & 9. 17.

*{be adorned with thy tabrets}* Or, *adorn,* or *furnish,* yourself with your *tabrets,* or *timbrels.* So the verb is rendered, as in a reciprocal notion, Chapter 4. 30. Ezek. 16. 13. & 23. 40. you shall make use again of your tabrets or timbrels, which they were wont to play upon in their solemn feastings; and at times of extraordinary rejoicing, Genesis 31. 27. Esay 30. 32. and these the rather he here mentions, because he had compared the state of Israel to a young damsel; and at times of solemnities such used to play on them, Exodus 15. 20. Judges 11. 34. 1 Samuel 18. 6. Psalm 68. 25. and the use of these, says the rabbin, should then be an ornament to them, because they should use them in seemly manner and seasonably; not as those that made use of them formerly, when occasion was of mourning and grief rather than of mirth, Esay 4. 12. Amos 5. 5, 6. but the meaning may be simply, you shall furnish yourself with them, and with other your ornaments, put them on about you: for some scarf or silk ribbon, it is not unlikely they hung them on, when they made use of them. Howbeit, a learned writer would rather have the words rendered, *thou shalt adorn thy tabrets:* and the word is applied, as sometime to that wherewith one is adorned, Esay 61. 10. Hosea 2. 13. so otherwhile to the party or thing adorned: as Ezekiel 16. 11. and says he, in times of public jollity, the timbrels were wont to be adorned and set out with garlands: and I suppose indeed, that the meaning may well be, (whether any such garlands were used about them, and be aimed at, or no) that they should furbish over and trim up their tabrets again, which had been cast aside and neglected before.

*{go forth in the dances of them that make merry}* As the damsels also used at such times to do, Judges 11. 34. and 21. 21. 1 Samuel 18. 6. So verse 13. Of the latter word, see on Chapter 15. 17.

**Verse 5.** *{Thou shalt yet plant Vines upon the mountains of Samaria;}* Another note of times of public peace and security, when men apply themselves unto tilling and planting, which in times of war or dread and danger they are wont to neglect: as uncertain to enjoy, reap, or receive any fruit of their labors, Judges 6. 3, 4, 11.

*{upon the mountains}* Deemed fittest for vines, as affording the best grapes, and such as yield the strongest wines. So Ezek. 36. 8, 9. Joel 3. 18.

*{of Samaria}* The head city and royal seat of the ten tribes, 1 Kings 16. 24. put sometime, as Israel, for that whole state and the land possessed by them, Chapter 23. 13. Ezekiel 16. 46. Hosea 7. 1. & 8. 5. Amos 3. 9. hence those that are here called, *the mountains of Samaria,* are called *the mountains of Israel,* Ezekiel 36. 8. and 37. 22. This is deemed to have been in part fulfilled, after the return from the Babylonian captivity; and that partly in many of the ten tribes that returned back with their brethren the Jews, repossessing some part of their land again, and partly in the Jews, who regained at sometimes much of that country; to which purpose are produced out of Josephus' *Antiquities,* lib. 13. chap. 5, 8. the letters of two Demetrii, the father and the son, unto Jonathan the then Jewish ruler, wherein upon their conquests made on those parts, they assign the land of Samaria with some other regions thereabout unto the Jews; but was to be more fully accomplished spiritually in the restauration of the church under the Messiah. See Ezekiel 37. 21, 22.

*{the planter, shall plant them, and shall eat them as common things}* Heb. *shall prophane* them: a defect of the pronoun; as Chapter 24. 6. After the time both of the uncircumcision of them, which continued three years after the first planting of them completed, and of the sanctification of them, which lasted unto the fourth year's end now expired, those that planted them, shall in the fifth year eat freely of the fruit of them. See the law to this purpose, Leviticus 19. 13, 15. and Deuteronomy 20. 6. Those that plant them, shall in due time enjoy them, not being deprived of the fruit of their labors, nor that which they had taken pains for being either destroyed or devoured by strangers, Esay 65. 21, 23. of the use of the word, see 1 Sam. 21. 5.

**Verse 6.** *{For there shall be a day}* Heb. *there is a day.* A time is set, and shall surely come; as Esay 11. 10. Zach. 14. 7.

*{that the watchmen upon the mount Ephraim}* Heb. *the watchers* or *keepers on mount Ephraim;* for there is no article in the text: and, *mount Ephraim,* sounds better with us: as also it is rendered, Judges, 19. 1. 1 Samuel 1. 1. *Ephraim;* as, *Samaria,* for that whole land or state: the reason whereof, see on Esay 7. 2. there is a defect of the particle *that,* as Chapter 25. 12.

*{watchmen}* Such, say most, as are described, Ezekiel 33. 2. persons set on purpose on work by the state, to watch as sentinels on public places, to descry and give warning of any enemies' approach, Esay 21. 6. and the word here used seems so to be taken, 2 Kings 17. 9. and 18. 8. that which therefore most apply unto the ministers of the gospel; as Esay 52. 8. and 62. 6. Howbeit, I conceive rather that the allusion is to the keepers of the vineyards, whereof mention was before made, verse 5. as such are designed and alluded to under this term, Chapter 4. 16, 17. (for of those in times of public peace and security there is not so much use) that they should be inciting and calling one to another, to go to worship God in the places of his public and solemn service. Which albeit it was to be in its chief and highest degree, and accomplished under the Messiah, when the faith of him should by those of that nation be embraced, John 4. 43, 41. Acts 8. 1, 25. Yet I suppose that conceit of a great man a little too curious, who would have the term of *Nazarens* in the term here found alluded to, sometime given by some to the Christians, Acts 24. 5. See Esay 11. 1.

*{shall cry, Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion unto the LORD our God.}* See the like invitations and compellations of people calling one upon another to go together to God's house, Esay 2. 3. Mic. 4. 2. Zach. 8. 21.

*{shall cry}* As Esay 21. 8. or *call;* in way of invitation; as Deut. 33. 19.

*{Arise ye}* See Chap. 18. 2.

*{go up}* Or *go repair;* as Psalm 122. 1, 4.

*{to Zion}* Where the temple stood: a type of the church, Psal. 84. 7. from access whereunto by Jeroboam they had been debarred, 1 Kings 12. 27, 28.

*{unto the LORD our God}* From whom they seemed to be excluded before, as having no part or portion in him among his people, Ezr. 4. 2, 3. Matthew 10. 5. Luke 9. 52, 53. John 4. 9, 22. See the like prophecy of the conjunction and reuniting of these two, Ezek. 37. 16–20.

**Verse 7.** *{For thus saith the LORD, Sing for gladness with Jacob,}* An exhortation follows, wherein the people of Israel are called upon to acknowledge and publish with much joy God's gracious goodness towards them in their deliverance. And this branch most take as directed to the church's friends, or foreign nations, as called upon to rejoice *for her,* or *with her,* (for so is the particle also used in the former way, Gen. 21. 6. & 25. 42. in the latter, Genesis 46. 25. Chapter 19. 13.) so it should be like that, Deut. 32. 43. the Gentiles being invited to rejoice with God's people, and in the next clause mentioned, as some, because they were also to be brought unto Christ, c. 16. 19. Ro. 15. 10. Es. 66. 10. Howbeit, one of the Jewish commenters, (whom the ancient Greek herein follows) taking the particle in its most usual notion, and supposing a trajection to be in these words, renders it, *Thus saith the Lord to Jacob, Sing* or *Exult ye, for,* or *with joy:* and so it is an incitement of God's people themselves to rejoice; like that, Zach. 9. 9.

*{and shout among the chief of the Nations}* Heb. *cry aloud,* or *shrill,* (as it is rendered, Esay 10. 30. the word signifies properly *to neigh,* c. 5. 8. & 50. 11. and it is used most in a notion of exultation and alacrity. Esther 8. 15. Esay 12. 6. & 24. 14. & 54. 1.) *in the head of the nations;* which our Version renders *chief:* and so the word is sometime used; as Exodus 30. 23. Esay 9. 10. Now this some expound as insulting over the nations; that being before as the head, had made them as the tail, Deut. 28. 24. and they urge the term of *neighing,* as to that purpose here used: and this way both the ancient Greek and Latin seem to go, rendering the words, *neigh against the head of the Gentiles:* and so is the particle used, Exod. 14. 25. Numbers 12. 1. But the most rather understand it, as the Chaldee renders it, *openly, in,* or *unto the face of the nations;* (the *head,* for the *face:* as Job 10. 15. Chapter 14. 3. 1 Cor. 11. 7, 10.) as implying only a free and open profession and publication of what God had done for them: as Esay 12. 4. and this also the words following confirm. One of the Jewish commenters renders it, *on the Towers:* and *Head,* for *Top* is usual: as Exodus, 17. 9, 10. Esay 22. but then something is added; the top whereof is said to be the *Head* or *Top:* otherwise *Head,* for *Tower* simply, is nowhere found.

*{publish ye, praise ye;}* Heb. *make to hear* (as Esay 48. 20.) *praise ye;* that is, with praise relate and publish it: as, *went and wept,* for, *went weeping,* Psalm 126. 6. *stand and feed,* for, *stand feeding,* Esay 61. 5.

*{and say, O LORD, save thy people, the remnant of Israel.}* This clause is in a manner generally thus rendered. But how to fit it to the present discourse, interpreters are somewhat troubled. For some would have them the words of the people remaining yet in captivity, entreating God to deliver them, such of them, as yet survived, having escaped the sword of the Chaldeans, verse 2. but remained still in thraldom; unto which their suit an answer should by God be returned, that he would grant their request and fulfill their desire, verse 8. but others conceiving aright by the words foregoing, that this whole passage is directed unto, and concerns the people as now delivered, and set free: as that Esay 12. 4. & 48. 20. understand it, as a petition presented to God by the Jewish people delivered in behalf of the other tribes a great part whereof remained still in captivity: Which yet with others seeming not satisfactory, they would have it to be a form not of prayer, but of praise, as *Hosanna* is, say they, Psalm 118. 25. Matt. 21. 9. But this suits not well with the use of the word in the Psalm, from whence that in the Gospel has it; howsoever it may there receive another exposition, from a rite used by the Jews at one of their festivals, as some learned critics have observed. Howbeit, that should be here matter of *praise,* than of *prayer,* the foregoing words imply. And the Chaldee therefore renders it in the time present, *The Lord delivers,* or *is delivering his people,* (not as some render him, *thou hast delivered:* for it is a participle of the present that he makes use of) and the ancient Greek in the time past, *The Lord hath saved his people;* and so it suits well with the parallel places, Esay 44. 23. *Sing ye Heavens,——and shout ye lower parts of the Earth——for the Lord hath redeemed Jacob:* and Esay 48. 20. *Declare ye, tell this, utter it,——say, The Lord hath redeemed his servant Jacob:* (see also verse 11.) and it may well be rendered, *Thou hast saved,* or *saving saved thy people:* for the verb seems here to be the infinitive, which is oft in this form and others the same with the imperative, and is used frequently for the indicative, whereof see on verse 2. and that as well past as there, and Eccl. 9. 10. as future, 2 Sam. 3. 18. where the indicative of this verb there wanting, as in such defective phrases, is found supplied, c. 11. 12.

*{the remnant of Israel.}* As Esay 10. 21, 22. Romans 11. 5.

**Verse 8.** *{Behold, I will bring them from the North country}* Heb. *Lo, I am bringing* (as chap. 5. 1, 5. Zach. 3. 8.) *them* (the remnant of my people, v. 7.) *from the North;* from Babylon, and the parts thereabout, c. 23. 8.

*{and gather them from the Coasts of the Earth}* Heb. *sides* Chapter 6. 22. and 25. 32. from Assyria, Media, and other parts, whither those of the ten tribes, had been transported, 2 Kings 17. 6.

*{and with the blind and the lame, the woman with child, and she that travelleth with childe together.}* Or the copulative cast out, *among them* (as Esay 65. 4. & 66. 19. Chapter 11. 9.) shall be *the blind and lame, she that goeth great,* (See Esay 7. 14.) *and she that is near her time* (Heb. *bringing forth,* as Chapter 6. 24.) *together.* Thereby intimating, that none in regard of any defect or infirmity, which usually are wont to disable persons to travel, to take long journeys especially, (Samuel 19. 26. Matt. 24. 19.) should in that regard miss or be deprived of the benefit of return into their own country: God would in his providence so dispose things, that such as were in these regards most unfit, and unable to travel, should have such means of conveyance provided them, as should with safety bring them to their journey's end: See the like in part, Esay 60. 4, 9. & 66. 20. So rather, I suppose, than as some other, implying, either the willingness and forwardness of the people to return home again, that no want or weakness would withhold from setting forward on their way, the women great with child, and near their time, refusing to stay till they were lighter: or as others, to show that none for any natural infirmity should be refused or excluded from having a part among God's people. See Esay 35. 5, 6. and 42. 16. and 56. 3, 4. Luke 14. 21. There want not that understand all these passages spiritually, the *blind* in mind, Acts 26. 18. and through feebleness disabled to walk heavenly, Hebrews 12. 12, 13. and heavy laden with their sins, Matthew 11. 28. and ready to faint for want of inward comfort, Esay 42. 3. and 50. 10. But these particularities I conceive to be overcurious, and leave them to the judgment of others.

*{a great company shall return thither}* Heb. *hither;* into this land again: See Ezr. 2. 47. 65. & 8. 1.—20. and of converts in the apostles' time. Acts 2. 41. & 4. 4. & 8. 6, 12.

**Verse 9.** *{They shall come with weeping}* There are tears of joy, as well as of grief: See Gen. 29. 11. & 43. 30. & 45. 2, 14. these might well be mixed, as well of grief for their sins whereby they had grieved God, Ezekiel 6. 9. Zach. 12. 10. as of joy for their deliverance out of those calamities, which they had brought upon themselves by their sins: So, *going, and weeping,* that is, weeping as they go along, chapter 50. 4. Nor can I assent to that learned man, who would have it rendered, *They shall go out,* or *went out, with weeping;* as Psalm 126. 6. expounding it of their going out into captivity: the current of the text goes like a strong torrent against it.

*{and with supplications will I lead them}* With supplications, for the remission of their sins; and the word is commonly used for *supplication,* Daniel 9. 3, 17, 18, 23. and *weeping* and it are joined together, chapter 2. 11. Zachary 2. 10. But some other say, that the word is more general, comprehending as well *praise* and *thanksgiving,* as *supplication* and *prayer;* as another of the like notion is observed to do; 1 Samuel 2. 1. for Hannah's devotion there recorded is rather *tehillah,* than *tephillah,* consisting of matter of *praise,* rather than of *prayer.* And some other again, which our margin exhibits, render it *favours:* and this, though the word itself be not found directly so used, yet in the original, and the notation of it, it has a notion of *grace* or *favour;* and another term rising from the same root, & being of very near affinity with it, though commonly, yea, almost generally used for *prayer,* properly to procure *grace,* yet is once or twice at least found used for *favour* or *grace* itself, Joshua 11. 20. Ezra 9. 8. and so therefore I conceive, with one of the Jewish commenters, that it is to be taken here; as being applied rather to God that led them, than to the people led by him: *with graces,* or *favours, will I lead them:* *graces,* or *favours;* as, *tender mercies,* and *loving kindnesse,* Esay 63. 7. for, great abundance, or much of either.

*{I will cause them to walk by the rivers of waters,}* Or, *I will lead them after* (for this word and the former are in notion the same; and there is in the original an elegant consonancy between them) *by the water-brookes.* Heb. *to the brookes of water:* and so it may seem to be, as some would have it taken from the manner of leading out their sheep to the water, Psalm 23. but I suppose it well rendered, as in our Version, *by,* or *beside;* (as the particle is used, Gen. 49. 29. *bury me beside my fathers:* and as it is aright rendered Job 29. 19. *my root was spread out by,* or *beside the waters,*) because the speech is here of journeying or traveling: the meaning of it being, that they should no more want water, (a principal and most necessary means of relief unto passengers traveling in those countries and thorough dry and waste places especially) than as if they went all the way by the side of some one or other river. See Esay 41. 18. and 43. 19, 20. and 49. 10.

*{in a straight way, wherein they shall not stumble:}* Or, rather, *in an even way,* (See Esay 26. 7.) *that they may not stumble therein:* as Esay 73. 14. See Esay 40. 3, 4. and 42. 16. and 62. 10.

*{for I am a father to Israel,}* Heb. *for a father;* as Gen. 17. 4. 2 Sam. 7. 14. I retain still a fatherly affection toward him as in former times I had, Deut. 8. 5. & 32. 6. Psalm 103. 13. Mal. 2. 10. & 3. 17. and we need not insert, as a learned writer would have us, the note of similitude, reading the words, *as a father;* that is, as Jacob was to Joseph's sons, whom he adopted, making him in regard of the double portion as his firstborn, Gen. 48. 5, 16, 22. 1 Chr. 5. 1.

*{and Ephraim is my first-born}* Heb. *my first-born he:* *he,* for, *is:* as *thou he,* for, *thou art,* Psalm 44. 4. Ephraim is as dear to me, as is any firstborn to his father. So the Chaldee, with whom the Jewish commenters do herein concur. See the same spoken of Israel in general, Exod. 4. 22. of David in particular, Psalm 89. 27. of all the faithful, Heb. 12. 23. See after also, verse 20. So rather than, as some, because Joseph had the birthright devolved to him from Reuben, 1 Chron. 5. 1. and Ephraim though his younger son preferred before Manasseh in the blessing by their grandfather Jacob, Genesis 48. 14, 19. or, with some others, as if the Jewish people (for Ephraim here comprehends the whole body of them) were so termed in regard of the Gentiles, that were afterward to be taken in to them, Acts 3. 26. Rom. 2. 10.

**Verse 10.** *{Hear the word of the LORD, O ye Nations, and declare it in the Isles afar off, and say;}* *Iles,* or *Lands,* or *Countries;* as Esay 41. 1. & and 66. 19. God will have his gracious promises concerning the deliverance of his people, to be beforehand published far and near, that notice may be taken of it, and it may thereby be known whose work it is, when it is done. See Esay 44. 26. & 45. 21. & 46. 10. & 48. 3, 14. So as of the thing done and effected before v. 7.

*{he that scattered Israel, will gather him}* God who formerly in his wrath, for their sins dispersed them, (for it was not so much the enemies' might as his purpose and pleasure that enabled them to prevail against them: and unto him therefore is the dispersion of them principally ascribed, c. 9. 6. & 15. 7. & 16. 17. Zach. 7. 14.) being now reconciled to them, will gather them together again, Psalm 147. 2. Esay 11. 12. & 56. 8.

*{and keep him}* Not gather them together only, and so leave them to themselves, but protect them also when he has brought them together, and keep them in safety, Esay 38. 6. & 46. 2. & 27. 3. Zach. 2. 5. called therefore *the keeper of Israel,* Psalm 121. 4. so of all the faithful, 1 Peter 1. 5. not *called* on, but *kept,* Jude 1. See John 10. 27, 28.

*{as a shepherd doth his flock.}* Who not only seeks after his sheep, when they are scattered or have strayed, Ezek. 34. 11—16. Matt. 25. 32. Luke 15. 4, 5. but keeps them also and feeds them, and tends them, and defends them when he has them together, 1 Samuel 17. 35. Ezekiel 34. 2, 3. hence David, *The Lord is my Shepherd;* Psalm 23. 1. and God is styled *the shepherd of Israel,* Psalm 80. 1. and Christ, *the good Shepherd,* John 10. 11—16. and *the chief Shepherd,* 1 Peter 5. 4. See also Esay 40. 11.

**Verse 11.** *{For the LORD hath redeemed Jacob, and ransomed him from the hand of him that is stronger than he.}* Or *the Lord hath delivered* (as Psalm 55. 18.) *Jacob and rescued him out of the hand* (as Psalm 107. 2.) *of those* (for the term is collective) *that were stronger than he,* or *too strong for him.* Heb. *strong from him;* as Psal. 18. 17. See on chap. 20. 7. of the Chaldeans and other powerful people, corporally, Esay 40. 10. of Satan and his instruments spiritually, Matth. 12. 29. Luke 11. 21, 22. Col. 1. 13. Heb. 2. 14, 15. Some render it, in the future, *will deliver, will rescue;* because it ran so, ver. 10. but of that there is no necessity: freedom was both effected and published before they either were, or could be gathered together, being so dispersed as they were.

**Verse 12.** *{Therefore they shall come and sing in the height of Zion.}* Heb. *And.* as Chap. 29. 17. Howbeit, the copulative may here be retained. Those of the ten tribes, as well as the other two shall after their return from captivity, repair to mount Sion with sacred hymns, to celebrate God's praises in his sanctuary there seated, a type of his church, Esay 2. 2. So ver. 6. the text may well be thus rendered: *And they shall go singing unto the high place of Zion.* *To* is the particle used of motion to a place, Gen. 1. 14. Lev. 16. 21. Ezr. 9. 7. Esay 9. 8. & 10. 22. *go and sing,* for *go singing:* as *go and weep,* for *go weeping,* Psalm 126. 6. and *the height of Sion,* for the high places there; as, *the height of Israel,* for the high places thereof, Ezekiel 20. 40. & 44. 14. See chap. 17. 12.

*{and shall flow together}* Flock thither by shoals, as waters come flowing in of themselves abundantly, where they find open and free passage: for the word, as the rabbin observes, seems to note as well the alacrity, as the numerosity of those that should repair thither. See Esay 2. 2. So Psalm 34. 5. Chapter 50. 44.

*{to the goodness of the LORD, for Wheat, and for Wine, and for Oil, and for the young of the flock, and of the Herd}* *to the goodnesse of the Lord;* that is, as some to his beneficence; or unto him as the fountain and wellspring, from which all these benefits and blessings do flow: or *upon the goodnesse* of God; having received these things out of his bounty bestowed on them, as Hosea 3. 5. or as others, *goodnesse,* for *good things;* as Genesis, 24. 10. and *the goodnesse of the Land,* for *the good* things of it, Genesis 45. 18. Nehemiah 9. 12. Esay 1. 19. called here *the good things of the Lord,* because he is the giver of them, Hosea 2. 8. Act. 14. 17. and promises to bestow such on them, verse 14. which *good* things what they were, is afterward more particularly expressed: and it may according to this exposition well be rendered, *for the good things of the Lord, for Corn, and for Wine,* (Heb. *new,* or *sweet* wine, as Esay 36. 17.) *and for Oyle, and for the young* or *issue* (Heb. *sons;* as Genesis 18. 7. Numbers 7. 15. Psalm 114. 4.) *of herd and flocke,* greater and lesser cattle; as Esay 7. 25. and howsoever the particle before the term of *good* in general; be not the same with that which ushers in the particulars; yet it is observed by the Jewish critics here on verse 9. that these two, *el* and *al* are oft promiscuously used: whereof see instances not a few in this prophet, Chapter 21. 11, 18. & 26. 5. & 27. 19. & 44. 1. & 46. 2. & 47. 1, 7. & 49. 19, 20, 34. & 50. 1. & 51. 12. The meaning then is, that they shall repair for these things unto Sion, not to find these things there, as Esay 55. 1. but either to seek to God for them, as Ezekiel 36. 37. or to bless and praise him for them, who has before blessed them with the same Deuteronomy 7. 13. & 8. 10. & 16. 3—15. and howsoever these temporal good things are in a generality types of better spiritual blessings, Ephes. 3. 3. Heb. 3. 5, 6. & 9. 23. Yet I suppose them somewhat overcurious, who by *Corn,* here understand the bread of life, Christ's body, John 6. 33, 35, 51. by *Wine,* his blood John 6. 53, 56. the food of our souls, Matt. 26. 26, 28. by *Oyle,* the Spirit of grace, wherewith Christian men are anointed, 2 Corinthians 1. 11. 1 John 2. 20, 27. or of consolation, wherewith the soul is refreshed, Acts 9. 31. 2 Corinthians 1. 3, 4. by the *younglings of herd and flocke,* Christ slain and sacrificed on the cross, 1 Cor. 5. 7. Heb. 9. 11, 14, 26, 28. and 10. 10, 12. But such particularities neither sort so well with the types, to which they are applied, nor agree so well among themselves.

*{and their soul shall be as a watered garden;}* Or *for* (the copulative used in a causative notion, Chap. 23. 22. rendering a reason, why they should thus bless God, Deut. 28. 11, 47.) *their soul* (that is, they themselves, as Psalm 22. 26. & 25. 13, 20. & 63. 5. So v. 14.) *shall be as a well-watered garden,* (for the word has a notion of plenty in it: as Psalm 36. 8. Prov. 5. 19. & 7. 18.) wherein everything thrives and flourishes: a lively emblem of a plentiful and prosperous estate: see Esay 58. 11.

*{and they shall not sorrow any more at all.}* Heb. *they shall not adde to sorrow further:* as, *thou shalt not adde to rejoyce further,* Esay 23. 12. they shall have no longer cause or occasion of grief. See Esay 35. 10. the ground of their repairing with singing to Sion.

**Verse 13.** *{Then shall the Virgin rejoice in the dance, both young men and old together:}* Or *then shall the Damsels* (of the word, see Esay 7. 14. it is here collective) *make merry with dancing, and the young and old together.* There shall be abundance of joy with all sorts of people of all ages and either sex. See the like, Zach. 8. 4, 5. & 9. 17. So are all of each age, and either sex incited unto the praising of God for his goodness, Psalm 148. 12, 13. Nor need we yet to restrain the mirth here mentioned to sacred employments, though of dancing in such also we find mention in Scripture, 2 Sam. 6. 14, 16. 1 Chr. 15. 29. Psalm 149. 3. & 150. 4. and of the dancing of *Damsels* in times of public and solemn rejoicing, see Judges 11. 34. and 21. 21.

*{for I will turn their mourning into joy}* Heb. *and* but so also, Chapter 23. 2. or *when I shall have turned;* as Chapter 14. 15. & 16. 6. So David, *thou hast turned my mourning into dancing,* Psalm 30. 15. and God promises to turn his people's *fasts* into *festivals,* Zach. 8. 19.

*{and make them rejoice from their sorrow}* Either, *rejoyce* and *cease from their sorrow:* as, *thou hast freed and saved my soul from the pit,* Esay 38. 17. or, *rejoyce after their grief;* as the particle is used, Esay 38. 15. Hos. 6. 3.

**Verse 14.** *{And I will satiate the soul of the Priests with fatness;}* I will make large and liberal provision for my ministers so as they shall have wherewith to maintain them and theirs in a plentiful manner to their fill. See 2 Chronicles 31. 10. Malachi 3. 10.

*{satiate}* The word used also before, v. 12. signifies more properly *to water* largely, and plentifully, Psalm 65. 10. Esay 55. 10. or *to soake,* Esay 34. 7. than *to drinke* largely, or to one's fill, Psalm 36. 8.

*{satiate the soul}* *soul* for *desire,* or *appetite;* as Deut. 12. 15, 21. Proverbs 6. 30. & 13. 25.

*{of the Priests}* God's ministers, Esay 66. 21.

*{with fatness}* Alluding to the offerings of fat beasts brought for sacrifice, whereof the priests had their share. So also Psalm 36. 8. Esay 25. 6.

*{and my people shall be satisfied with goodness, saith the LORD.}* They shall be abundantly stored with all manner of good things. See v. 12. 2 Chron. 31. 10.

**Verse 15.** *{Thus saith the LORD, a voice was heard in Ramah, Lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.}* God had before promised to turn their mourning in to mirth: Now this promised mirth is here amplified by the mourning foregoing it, which is very pathetically illustrated by a twofold rhetorical introduction of persons, Rachel the mother here, and Ephraim her grandchild by Joseph, verse 18. In this place Rachel Jacob's beloved wife, as the common mother in some sort of both people, Judah and Israel, (for Ephraim, the head of the ten tribes, Esay 7. 2. verse 9. was her grandchild by Joseph her elder son, Gen. 48. 5. and the issue of Benjamin her younger son, Genesis 35. 16, 18. continued still in conjunction and consociation with the tribe of Judah, 2 Chron. 11. 12.) is brought in, as raised up out of her sepulcher, situate between Ramath and Bethlehem, in the confines of either tribes, Genesis 35. 19. Josh. 18. 25. Judges 4. 5. 1 Sam. 10. 2. lamenting the loss of her children led away into captivity, as making account never to see them, or to have them delivered again. And this some of the Jewish doctors apply unto the Jewish and Benjamitish matrons and mothers, who with weeping and wailing accompanied their children, led away captive toward Babylon by Ramah, where Nebuzaradan seems to have mustered them, and from whence Jeremy having been so far carried away from Jerusalem, was dismissed and sent back, Chap. 40. 1. and the Talmudists tell us that Jacob buried her there foreseeing by the Spirit of prophecy, that his posterity should that way be led captive, that she might, as they passed by her, intercede for them. But these are Jewish tables. The evangelist applies it to the mothers of the young ones at or about Bethlehem, that Herod had most barbarously caused to be slaughtered, Matth. 2. 18. Both the prophet and the evangelist do hereby imply what Rachel in likelihood would have done, had she been surviving at either of those calamities, which those of her issue sustained. The words may be read; *In Ramah hath been heard a voice of lamentation,* (*a voice of lamentation,* as chap. 9. 18.) a voice (supplied as chap. 3. 21. and 4. 31.) *of most bitter weeping,* (Heb. *weeping of bitternesses.* See Esay 22. 4. chap. 6. 26.) a voice (continued, as Esay 66. 6. chap. 4. 31.) *of Rachel,* (as Matth. 2. 18.) *who weeping for her children,* (Heb. *her sons) refuseth to be comforted,* (as Jacob, Genesis 37. 35. Asaph, Psalm 77. 2. so Esay 22. 4.) *in regard of them,* (Heb. *her children;* the noun for the pronoun: as Exodus 40. 19, 21, 25, 29. 2 Timothy 1. 18. and a defect of the relative; as Chapter 30. 21.) *because they were not:* as, Jacob, Genesis 42. 36. *Joseph is not, and Simeon is not.*

*{in Ramah}* Some take it for a common word, rendering it, *in,* or *on an high place;* as Chapter 3. 21. and this way goes the Chaldee, the old Latin, some of the Jewish and ours. But the ancient Greek and the evangelist take it for the proper name of a place; as in the places above pointed to.

**Verse 16.** *{Thus saith the LORD}* After Rachel's lamentation for her sons, as lost, follows God's consolation of her, putting her in hope of their return.

*{Refrain thy voice from weeping}* Leave, or give over weeping: but he says, *Refrain thy voice;* because he said before, *a voice of weeping,* implying not a silent weeping, but such as is accompanied with wailing and loud expressions by voice; as it is said of Esau, *he lift up his voice, and wept,* Gen. 27. 38. and of Joseph, *he gave out his voyce in weeping* (of which form, see on chapter 2. 15.) so loud, that it was heard of the Egyptians and Pharaoh's courtiers, that were without the room in his house, Genesis, 45. 2.

*{and thine eyes from tears:}* Heb. *tear;* but collectively; as Chap. 9. 2.

*{for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD.}* Heb. *there is a reward for thy work;* as 2 Chron. 16. 7. This some apply unto Rachel, that God for her piety would cause her issue to fare the better at last: and the Talmudists ridiculously expound it of her patience in suffering her sister Leah to be substituted in her room, and obedience in delivering her token to her, which they tell us also that she pleaded to God in behalf of her people. See Genesis 29. 23, 25. but this is an idle fiction, as frivolous as that of Jacob before, verse 15. Others, popish especially, of the patience of the Bethlemitish women, Matth. 2. 17. The Jewish commenters understand it of the people her issue, that they should receive a reward for their constant keeping to God, during the time of their captivity, Psalm 44. 17. Our writers most of them, of that comfortable condition that God would restore them unto, and confer upon them when the time of their captivity should be accomplished. See Esay 40. 10. and 61. 7. these terms of *worke* and *reward* being used, because it should succeed their former misery and thraldom, as *wages* does *work;* and should abundantly countervail whatsoever hardship they had endured in the former. Of such spiritual compensations, see Rom. 8. 18. 2 Cor. 4. 18. ascribed here unto Rachel the mother, because as the tribulations of the children are the mother's grief; so their prosperous condition is matter of comfort and joy to her, See Matt. 15. 22.

*{and they shall come again from the land of the enemy.}* Your children of whose return you despair, as they themselves also did, Ezek. 33. 11.

**Verse 17.** *{And there is hope in the end,}* *There is hope* (and you should not therefore mourn as one that has no hope, 1 Thess. 4. 13. John 11. 18.) *in thine end,* (as Job 8. 7. Chap. 15. 11. when the time set for their exilement shall be expired, C. 29. verse 10.) or, *for thy posterity;* as the word here used signifies, Daniel 11. 4. and that seems the genuine sense of it in this place.

*{that thy children shall come again to their own border}* Your *children,* Heb. *sons;* as ver. 17. because the males most were captived, whom you now deem as lost: (a defect of the pronoun possessive; as Esay 60. 4.) shall return to their own possessions: *border* for *borders;* alluding to the limitation of the land of Canaan, and the setting out of it to the several tribes by borders and boundaries, Josh. 15. 1, 2. or to the general manner of bounding men's lands and possessions, Deuteronomy, 27. 17. Acts 17. 26.

**Verse 18.** *{I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself}* To Rachel's lamenting for her sons is here subjoined Ephraim's bewailing of his sins; God's taking notice of it, and returning an answer full of fatherly affection to it, v. 10.

*{I have surely heard}* Of Rachel was said before, *A voice was heard;* here, as speaking in the person of God, *I have heard,* Heb. *hearing, heard;* as Exodus 22. 22. I hear attentively, so as to take notice and regard, Psal. 5. 1, 2. & 77. 1.

*{Ephraim}* The ten tribes, as v. 6, 9.

*{bemoaning himself}* The word has sometime a notion of *wandring;* as Gen. 4. 12. Chap. 1. 1. and so the old Latin, and some others here take it; as if it were said, being now in captivity and exilement, and thereby brought, as Manasseh sometime, 2 Chron. 33. 12. to a sight of himself and his sins: sometime, of *mourning,* either of *condoling* with others, as Job 2. 11. Chapter 15. 5. and 16. 5. or, *bewailing* oneself; and so here the Chaldee, Greek, and most, both Jewish interpreters, and others, take it: the verb being in a reciprocal form, wherein it is in the former notion nowhere found, nor would here well fit. See Ezek. 6. 9.

*{thus}* Or, *and saying;* as Psalm 105. 15. Esay 22. 13. speaking on this wise unto God.

*{Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised; as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke.}* Or, *Thou hast chastised me and I have been chastised; I was as a bullock unaccustomed,* Heb. *untaught.* See chap. 13. 23. to draw in *the yoke.* See Hos. 10. 11. I am at length amended by your chastising hand upon me. See Chap. 7. 8. Hos. 10. 10. for before I was thus chastised, I was like an unruly bullock, that will not be brought to the yoke, nor endure to draw in it, Psalm 119. 67, 71. Howbeit, the Chaldee paraphrast, and some others (whom a late learned writer follows, and would have the ancient Greek copies to be thence corrected) render the text in the negative, *Thou hast chastised me, but I have not been corrected,* or, *I have not received instruction, as a bullock untaught,* or *untamed.* But the negative is not in the Hebrew, nor aught from whence it may be supplied: that which that learned man perceiving, and therefore casting it out again, reads the words, *I have been chastised as a bullock untamed;* that is, I remain no more the better for all your chastisements, than such an unruly and untamed beast: but this construction seems overmuch forced.

*{turn thou me, and I shall be turned.}* A prayer either for grace and power to repent and return unto God; which without his help they cannot do, Cant. 1. 4. John 6. 44. Acts 11. 18. 2 Tim. 2. 26. or that God would reduce them, and bring them back out of thraldom; which if he undertake to do, is sure to be done, Psalm 80. 3, 7, 19. Lam. 5. 21.

*{thou art the LORD my God}* Or, *thou who art the Lord my God:* a defect of the relative, as Chap. 30. 21.

**Verse 19.** *{Surely, after that I was turned, I repented;}* After that you had wrought a gracious change upon my soul by your afflicting hand, and your Spirit working together with it, Esay 48. 10. Acts 3. 26. or after I came to myself again, as Luke 15. 17. and considered seriously with myself, how it fared with me, I was touched with repentance with sorrow and shame, for my former miscarriages, Deuteronomy 30. 1, 2. So rather than as a learned late writer, *after that I return* home again, then *will I repent:* though it be true that their repentance then also continued, Ezek. 36. 31.

*{and after that I was instructed}* As well as corrected, Psalm 94. 12. unlike to those, Chap. 2. 30. & 5. 3. Heb. *it was made known to me;* as 1 Sam. 6. 3. Neh. 4. 9. the preposition between the verb and the pronoun affixed to it being lost; as Esay 28. 15. Chap. 10. 20. so rather, than as that learned scholiast, who would have the passive here taken in a reciprocal notion, rendering it, *after that I knew my self:* or than as that other annotator, *After that thou hast shewed me some kindness,* then shall I be thus affected.

*{I smote upon my thigh}* In token of remorse for, detestation of, and astonishment at my former vile and lewd courses. See Ezek. 21.12.

*{I was ashamed, yea, even confounded}* Or, *I was abashed, and ashamed also.* So Ezr. 9.6.

*{because I did bear the reproach of my youth}* That is, such miseries, as by my excesses in former times committed, I had brought upon myself. See Job 13.26. Psalm 25.7. an allusion to the state of one, that having in his youthful days by riotous and exorbitant courses wasted both his means and himself, and in his elder years now seriously considering with himself, his own folly, and the miserable condition that he has thereby brought himself unto, is in contemplation thereof, both abashed and dejected in himself and ashamed, to be seen of any. See Job 20.11. Proverbs, 16.26. & 5.11. Esay 47.1, 5. So rather, than, as that learned man, I am so full of shame and confusion, that I cannot apply myself to any serious repentance, so long as I lie under such grievous sufferings for my former excesses.

**V. 20.** *{Is Ephraim a dear son? is he a pleasant child?}* God's gracious answer unto Ephraim's lamentation and supplication. That the words are to be read by way of interrogation, the usual notes thereof in Hebrew, one prefixed before the former member, another before the latter, do evidently show. Now because the interrogative affirmative is wont more vehemently to deny the thing spoken of; as Esay 50.2. *Is my hand at all cut short, that I cannot rescue? and Is Israel a servant? is he an home-bred slave?* Chapter, 2.14. interpreters therefore are much puzzled about the true notion of this passage: and some understand it as a flat denial of what is here demanded, concerning Ephraim; as if it were said, No, he is nothing less than a precious or a pleasant child: for by his cross and crooked courses he has so carried himself, that he has even enforced me to cast him off. And others again conceive it as spoken by way of reprehension: so a learned late writer, who so carries on the whole tenor of Ephraim's speech, not as a profession of his present repentance, but as excusing himself that he did not yet, nor could repent, during his captivity; he was so full of shame and misery, that he had no list or leisure thereunto: but would do it, when God had set him at liberty, and showed mercy and goodness unto him, by settling him in his own country again: and accordingly he brings in God returning answer here to this his presumed profession: Belike Ephraim deems himself such a darling child, as I cannot be without him, when he is so nice and delicate, that he cannot repent so long as he is in misery, and till all this be done for him. But those that go either of these two ways, have few I suppose, going along therein with them; and the main course of the context seems to run with full stream against them. And another learned man of great note seems to take to as solitary a walk, who instead of an interrogative, would make it enunciative and turns the interrogation into a more vehement asseveration: For says he, the former interrogative here used, is oft found to signify, *surely* or *verily,* as Genesis, 27.36. 2 Samuel 23.19. 1 Kings 18.31, Proverbs 24.28. Chapter 7.9. and the latter is by a Jewish Critic observed so also to signify, as both joined with the former, Numbers 17.13, Job 6.13. and alone by itself, Genesis 47.18. Numbers 16.30. Job 22.20. Psalm 63.7. Proverbs 3.34. Esay 4.4. and 29.16. But as for the former, there is not any one place produced, where the interrogative may not in his proper notion well stand: and for the latter it is true that it has divers other uses, nor is it an interrogative in his first and native notion but most commonly a conditional, sometime a discretive, and one of these two in most if not all, of the places produced. Besides that for the former, the author of this conceit, is not constant to himself: for in the close of his discourse where he has this, he inclines to conceive that in all those places *ha* may be put for *he,* and rendered *behold;* and elsewhere he goes another way for divers of them; as hereafter shall be showed. It is true, indeed, that divers interpreters render some of the forementioned places in the affirmative, and sometime with a note of asseveration prefixed: but therein they have regard not to the precise signification, and grammatical construction of the terms, but to the sense and meaning of the sentence in general, in the interrogative form implied. Another learned interpreter, whom a scholiast of note concurs with, takes the words as spoken in way of admiration or doubting; thus rendering the text, *Is Ephraim my deare Sonne? Is he a child of much delight?* Yes; or He is: which they put into the context: but this seems somewhat overbold. I should rather, did I suppose the words to be so conceived, render them on this wise, *Is this Ephraim my deare Sonne? is it my darling childe?* as if it were said, Is it he that bemoans himself in this manner? as Saul to David, *Is this thy voyce, my Sonne David?* not as questioning whether David were his son or no; but as with a kind of astonishment, making a doubt whether it were he that spoke to him in that manner: And so here, God is brought in, as speaking after mortal man's usage, but not making doubt whether Ephraim were his dear darling or no; but whether it were that his darling, from whom this pitiful and passionate complaint came. And this, whether it suit not better with the course of the context than any other of those already related I shall leave to the decision and sentence of others. Howbeit, I shall subjoin, what I conceive to be the genuine syntax: For the firmer grounding whereof, I shall suggest that, which I find not any of our grammarians, or critics, either Jewish, or others, to have observed, howsoever necessity puts interpreters, of force, now and then upon it, to wit, that in such interrogative form the negative particle is oft supposed, and necessarily to be supplied. So 1 Samuel, 2.27, 28. where our Geneva version, and the note before it, as also the Tigurine and Italian, and some others well render the text, *Did not I plainly appear to the house of thy Father? and did not I chuse him?* So Job 20.4. where besides those former, divers Latin interpreters, and our latest version also renders it, *Knowest thou not this of old?* See before, Chapter 3.6. *Hast thou not seen what back-sliding Israel hath done?* So Ezekiel 20.30. *Are ye not polluted after the manner of your Fathers? and, do ye not commit whoredome, or goe on whoring, after their abominations?* and Amos 6.2. *Were they better than these Kingdomes? Was not their border larger than yours?* The very drift and current of the context does in either necessarily exact it: And for this place, that I may not be deemed to walk alone in it: so does the Tigurine version, which Oecolampadius, and Bullinger also follow, here express it, and the Chaldee Paraphrast before them in the latter branch. As also that learned late annotator that goes here another new and strange way, yet does elsewhere come home to us contradicting what he here has in affirming, that *ha,* is oft put for *halo,* especially where it is joined with *ci,* which is, says he, in that form no other than an expletive particle. So he expounds, Genesis 29.15. *Art thou not my brother, and shouldest thou serve me freely?* though in that place himself acknowledges, that others generally expound the words there, (and that as I conceive, aright) otherwise. But so he also takes it in Genesis 27.36. *Was he not justly called Jacob?* wherein the Tigurine, and our three last versions exactly agree with him. Yea so he says that it is without doubt to be taken, 2 Samuel 23.19. where our version renders it, *Was he not the most honourable of the three?* And so Tremellius, Junius and Piscator before: and these two last places are of those, which that learned writer would above turn another way. Yea on that place, 1 Samuel 2.27. after a long discourse, much debate, many turnings and windings, having striven and struggled hard to carry it some other way: at length in the close of all he concludes, and is enforced to confess, that to take *ha* for *halo,* supplying the negative, does best agree with the sense and drift of the place: adding withal, that the like is in the Arabick very frequent, as he has, he says, in many places of the *Alcoran* observed. This I have the rather insisted upon, both because I suppose it brings some light to this place, and because I find divers interpreters of great note driven to forced constructions in some places for want of this observation See the like again, Chapter 40.14.

*{Ephraim}* The people of Israel, the ten tribes, as before, verse 9.

*{my dear Son}* Heb. *a Sonne precious,* or *deare to me;* for it comes from a root that signifies to be *precious:* and another word thence springing is for *pretious* in common use, Psalm 116.15. Proverbs 17.28. but the word here used, is in a form that seems to import some eminency, or excellency of the thing thereby signified, and is nowhere else found. It is somewhat like that, Proverb 4.3.

*{a pleasant childe}* Heb. *a Childe of delight:* as *a Vine of Delights;* Esay, 5.7. and, *Delights;* for, such an one as any person takes exceeding great delight in, Proverbs, 8.30.

*{for since I spake against him, I doe earnestly remember him still}* These words are very variously both rendered and expounded.

Those that render the former branch concerning Ephraim as delivered by way of denial; do some of them thus render them, *when I have spoken with him,* (that is, further sufficiently admonished him): *I shall have throughly minded* him of this his pertinacious carriage: but this leaves the sentence abrupt and in suspense.

Others of them, *I have a long time beene talkeing with him;* I have not ceased from time to time from dealing with him, to bring him to repentance, but all to no purpose: but *yet I will thinke on him: I will:* for all that, *remember him still* in mercy. But this seems not to flow anything freely from the text. As for those that go the other way; (to pass by the Chaldee, who swerves too much from the Hebrew, paraphrasing the text to this purpose: *Since the time that he began to lay up the words of my Law in his heart to practise them, I am mindefull of him to doe him good,*) Some of them render the words, *Ever since I had speech,* or, *I communed with him, I am* still *mindefull of him;* that is, Ever since at first I spoke unto him, and entered into covenant with him. Deuteronomy 4.12. and 5.2. I have not been unmindful of him; albeit he has not so carried himself towards me, as he should, but have constantly retained my first affection to him, and so still do, yet. 3. Others, *Even since I spake against him* (threatening to chastise them, Heb. 10.20.) *I do still constantly remember,* or, *think upon him,* in mercy, Habb. 3.2. mine heart and affection is still entire toward him, notwithstanding my sharp menaces of judgment against him. And others again lastly, *So oft as I speak of him, I am mindfull still of him;* that is, So oft as I have any occasion to speak or think of him, as at present I have by this lamentable complaint, I am in mercy very mindful of him. See Esay 49.14, 16. And this last I concur with.

*{since I spake}* So is the particle rendered also; chap. 20.8. but would rather both here and there (as the Jewish Critic on either place observes) be rendered, *so oft;* as also chap. 48.27. a place parallel to this; *so oft as thou speakest of him, thou skippest for joy.* See more instances on Chap. 20.8.

*{I spake against him}* As Num. 12.1. or, *with him,* as Deut. 6.7. or, *of him;* as Deut. 13.2. Chap. 38.24. & 48.27.

*{I do earnestly remember him}* Or, I do *constantly,* or, *carefully remember him.* Heb. *remembring remember;* as Deut. 7.18.

*{therefore my bowels are troubled for him}* Heb. *sound for him;* as Cant. 5.4. or, *earn towards him,* or, *on him:* as the mother's did towards her child, 1 Kings 3.26. See Esay 63.15. Hos. 11.8. for that learned annotator seems to be very wide here, who renders it, *for this cause am I vehemently incensed against him,* or, *am very wroth with him:* the form is never found so used, but the contrary way rather.

*{I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD}* Heb. *I will having mercy have mercy on him.* or, *I will abundantly have mercy on him* or, show mercy towards him: and there is a motion or tenderness of affection in the term itself. whereof see on Esay 54.7. & 63.15. and here again that learned man seems to run counter to the text, rendering it, as in way of indignation, with an interrogative, *should I shew any mercy to him?* as if it were parallel to that, chap. 5.7, 9.

**V. 21.** *{Set thee up waymarks;}* God by the Prophet now turns his speech to his people in captivity, (as the term hereof being now expired) enticing them to think on and prepare for their return home to their own country; as was before promised, verse 27.

*{waymarks}* Heb. *signes* or, *monuments,* 2 Kings 23.17. Ezek. 39.19. such are here meant as are wont to be erected upon the highways, plains especially, where paths are not so apparent, or where many crossways meet, to direct passengers the right way to some places of note, that they may not wander by mistake.

*{make thee high heaps}* Or rather, *pillars;* as Hos. 12.4. (for so the word may there also be rendered) and as one near to it, Cant. 3.6. & Joel 2.30. and the word, as it is here used seems to be derived from a term that signifies first and properly *a palm-tree,* then *a pillar* set bolt up right and straight, like to the body of that tree. See Chap. 10.5. So it is the same in effect, though in other terms, with the former; as the Jewish commenter here observes; who yet would have this latter word derived from a verb used, Dan. 8.7. & 11.11. supposed by him to have in it a notion of *lifting up;* of which some doubt may justly be made. The same word, but rising from another root, was used for *bitternesses,* verse 15. whence the Chaldee here conceives the whole passage to be no other than as an exhortation to repentance, admonishing them to remember the practice of their religious ancestors, and to return to God pouring out prayers unto him with *bitternesse* for their sins: and this the old Latin seems to have followed, rendering the word *bitternesses.* Which howsoever the Popish writers strain their wits to make somewhat of, yet can have no place here; there is an elegant redundancy in those forms, *set thee,* and *make thee;* whereof see on chap. 5.5. and the like, Gen. 12.1,

*{set thine heart toward the highway even the way which thou wentest}* There is in the original a twofold reading; For some read it, *the way that I went;* to wit, with you, says one of the Jewish commenters. Set your heart upon the right way, the way that I directed you to, and led you in, and return to that again, chap. 2.17. But the more received reading is, *the way that thou wentest.* Think upon the road, (Heb. *the cast-way,* or, *causey,* See Esay 49.11. & 62.10.) *the way* that *thou wentest;* that is, the way you went, when you were carried captive into Assyria, some of you and others of you into Chaldea, and by which you are now to go back home again; as Esay 37.34. See chap. 50.4, 5. a defect of the relative, as chap. 30.21. and in the like manner with us, when we say, *the way they went.*

*{turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities}* *O virgin,* or, *damsel.* See on ver. 4. and the invitation to return is doubled, to make it the more vigorous; as Ezek. 33.11. Cant. 6.13. *to these thy cities,* that have lain so long waste and desolate, to repair, and to people them again. Esay 58.12.

**V. 22.** *{How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter?}* So some of the Jewish doctors render it, because of a word thence deduced, signifying *a compasse,* Cant. 7.1. *the compasse of thy thighs;* but some other both of them, and ours, *How long wilt thou:* or, *dost thou withdraw thy self?* as Cantic. 5.6. *my beloved had withdrawne himselfe;* though that be there in another form: and of this stock is no more found in Scripture. The Chaldee gives it, *How long wilt thou harden thy self from returning:* the same terms that he has, Jer. 8.5. and the Greek to the same effect, *How long wilt thou avert,* or, *turn away?* which many expound of their not returning to God by repentance, Chap. 5.3. & 8.5, 6. But the first seems the best; that which some understand of their running after idols, Chap. 2.23, 24. Others rather, of their thinking upon, and seeking after human helps and other courses, out of a diffidence and distrust of God's promises, and the performance of them. Esay 57.10. Chap. 2.17, 18, 36, 37. Howbeit, some conceive the words as spoken by way of enticement, to set themselves upon minding the way homeward to their country; as ver. 21. without fear or forecast of the length or difficulty of the way, which raises oft doubtful thoughts and debates in the minds of weak and unsettled ones, Prov. 26.13, 14. which is also not improbable. Though some of those that go this way, take their rise from an unsound ground; as also the old Latin that renders it, *How long continuest thou dissolved with delights?* I should rather render it with reference to their long and tedious captivity, *How long shouldst thou go to and fro?* as those are wont to do, who are in captivity, at the will and pleasure of those under whose command they are. See chap. 4.1. & 14.18. as if God had said, Think on your former home again, and of the way thither, v. 21. for why should you be tossed to and fro any longer, as in your present exilement you are.

*{O backsliding daughter}* Or, *revolting.* See Chap. 3.12. who by your refractory courses, have procured to yourself those evils in this kind, which at present you endure chap. 2.19. & 30.15.

*{for the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth;}* Or, *will create a new thing on earth;* as Chap. 13.5. the rather in the future, because the next clause is generally so rendered. God will do a strange thing such as is not ordinary: so both the word of *creating* is frequently used, Esay 45. & 65.17, 18. & *new,* for *strange,* Esay 42.6. & 43.19. Mar. 16.17. Acts 17.18, 19. For as for that great man's conceit, who reads it in the time past, as spoken of the people's uncouth carriages, I suppose few or none therein concur with him; and of it more anon.

*{A woman shall compass a man}* The new or strange thing that God would effect. The place is obscure; and various interpretations are therefore given of it, as well by the Jews themselves, as by others. Some conceive it, as alluding to a woman, that should woo and seek after a man: whereas men ordinarily are wont to seek after the woman. So it should be like that, Esay 4.1. Others, to a woman that having left her husband, and lived loosely with others, should at length seek to him for reconcilement. So it should be like that, Hos. 2.7, 3, 5, 1 Cor. 7.11. and either of these the words would bear: but they seem no such strange matter simply considered. And yet more probable here to be meant, than that intended, which that learned writer suggests, of this people's seeking, like a shameless and insatiable strumpet, by wanton dalliances and embracements, to procure love to her from strangers, Esay 57.8——10. Chap. 2.24, 25, 36. Ezek. 16.33, 34. Hos. 8.9. for certainly this was no work of God's creating; and it seems to me a very forced construction, to interpret the foregoing words of God's giving them up, and abandoning them thereunto; as Rom. 1.26, 27. Christian writers the most, both ancient and latter, understand it of Christ and the Virgin his mother. *A woman* (so is she termed, Gal. 4.4.) being a virgin, and so abiding (Esay 7.14. Matth. 1.18, 25.) *shall enclose* in her womb, (Luke 1.21.) *a man;* (that is, a male, a man-child, Joh. 16.21.) as the nut (says one of ours) encloses the kernel; not receiving ought from without, but conceiving and breeding of herself, by the power of the Almighty from within, Mat. 1.20. Luke 1.34, 35. And this indeed may well be termed a new and strange thing heretofore never the like heard of. See Esay 7.14. But because the one word seems not to be used of *containing,* but of *compassing,* and *besetting,* Josh. 7.3, 4, 7. 1.14, 15. Psal. 118.10——12. Eccles. 9.14. and the other, not *a man* simply, but *a man of might,* or, *a mighty man.* See on Esay 2.9. & 3.2, 25. Divers interpreters of prime note expound it, of the Jewish people some; of the Church of Christ, others; and a third sort of both, the one being subordinate to the other; as the thing typified to the type, or rather, as in part incohated in the one, but more fully to be effected and accomplished in the other; to wit, that the Jewish people then, and the Christian Church afterwards, though in regard of their low and dejected condition, compared to a weak and feeble woman, Lam. 1.16, Rev. 12.1, 2. yet should beset and prevail against her temporal enemies, the one, Esay 14.2. their spiritual adversaries also the other, such as or their power might well be compared to men of much might, Rom. 16.20. Eph. 6.10, 11. Joh. 4.4. & 5.4. Rev. 12.11. which I take to be the genuine sense of the place.

**V. 23.** *{Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel}* As Chap. 7.21.

*{As yet they shall use this speech in the land of Judah, and in the cities thereof, when I shall bring away their captivity, The LORD bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness}* A further intimation of the reformation that shall be in the lives and courses of those, whom God shall preserve for a remnant, and bring home to their wonted places of abode again. See Esay 1.25——27. & 4.3, 4. & 60.21. & 62.12.

*{As yet}* Or, *Yet again;* as verse 5. for the particle here implies not a continuation of some present act; but the restoring or renewing of somewhat formerly used, which for some space of time had been since intermitted. So also, verse 4.

*{they shall use this speech}* Or, *this speech shall be used.* Heb. *they shall say this word:* the verb used indefinitely; as Psal. 116.2. Esay 8.19. Mat. 24.26. Luke 12.10. So ver. 19.

*{in the cities thereof,}* Heb. *of him,* or, his cities: as having reference not to the land, but to the people.

*{when I shall bring again their captivity}* Or, *when I shall have brought back their captives;* as ver. 13. Psal. 14.7.

*{The LORD bless thee,}* The usual form of salutation and well-wishing; Ruth 2.4. Psal. 129.8. for the exposition is over-narrow that the Jewish doctor gives it; Never may you be destroyed again.

*{O habitation of justice}* Or of men of *justice;* as Esay 1.21. & 41.2. as some, of *righteous ones,* Esay 60.21. So 2 Pet. 3.13. See Chap. 50.7.

*{mountain of holiness}* Or, *holy mountain;* as Psal. 15.1. Esay 11.9. in reference to mount Sion, whereon the Temple was situate, the principal seat of God's solemn service; wherein he should now be worshiped, by holy men, in holy manner, Esay 96.7. Ezek. 20.40. 1 Pet. 2.5, 6.

**V. 24.** *{And there shall dwell in Judah it self, and in all the cities thereof together, husbandmen, and these that go out with flocks.}* Or, as some, *in it* (to wit, the land before spoken of, ver. 23.) *shall the people of Judah dwell,* (*Judah,* for the men of *Judah;* as chap. 23.6.) or, rather, as I conceive, *there shall dwell in it,* even (supplied, as Esay 5.9. & 33.4.) in the land of *Judah, and in* (a defect of the preposition, but supplied from the former branch) *all his,* or, *their cities* (as before, verse 13.) *together, husband-men that shall shall go out with the flock,* or, *and such as go out with the flock;* Either such as shall both till their ground, and tend their cattle; as two several employments of the same persons: or persons employed, some in tillage, others, in tendance of cattle: the copulative for the relative, according to the latter, as verse 21. Heb. word for word, *and they shall go with flock:* Whence a Jewish commenter, therefore keeping close to the text, and retaining the proper use of the verb, (which signifies, not *a going out,* but *a going,* simply, or, *journeying,* and has reference not so much to the shepherds leading out his sheep, but his shifting with them, as his occasion for their better feeding requires) expounds it, *and they shall go,* or, men shall go, (for the verb is used indefinitely, as that ver. 23.) *with their flock;* to wit, from place to place without fear. See Gen. 37.17. Howsoever the words be taken, these employments constantly followed and exercised are here mentioned, as an argument of peaceable times, and a sign of a quiet and settled estate; so Esay 37.30. Chap. 33.12. So rather, than as some of note would have it, as a note of the most simple, harmless, and beneficial course of life, which men in those times shall generally apply themselves unto: see Gen. 25.27.

**V. 25.** *{For I have satiated the weary soule, and I have replenished every sorrowful soule.}* Or, *I will abundantly refresh* (as verse 14.) *the hungry,* or, *thirsty,* as Job 22.7. Psal. 63.1. or, *faint,* or, *fainting,* as 1 Sam. 14.31. 2 Sam. 21.15. Esay 29.8. See Psal. 107.5, 9.

*{and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.}* Or, *I will replenish every mournfull soul.* (see Deut. 28.65.) I will supply them with all manner of good, and matter of comfort to their fill, to the utmost of their desire, Psal. 36.8. & 37.4. & 81.10. & 107.9. Esay 41.17, 18. & 43.20. verse 12. Mat. 5.4, 6. & 11.28.

**V. 26.** *{Upon this I awaked, and beheld, and my sleep was sweet unto me.}* The Prophet's own speech relating the great comfort and refreshing that he had received upon this vision, and these gracious promises of God therein signified unto him concerning his people; being therewith so affected, as one, who after some tedious travel, or long and wearisome watching, had taken comfortable rest, had slept safely and sweetly, and was exceedingly therewith refreshed, Psal. 3.5. Prov. 3.24. or, as some, after these things revealed unto me, as one awaked out of sleep (Zach. 4.1, 2.) I stared up mine eyes, and looked about me. and considering seriously what I had seen and heard, I was so affected with the contemplation thereof, that from that time forward, I was able quietly to compose myself to rest, which before I could not do, Chap. 4.20, 21. & 8.18. But I concur rather with the former.

**V. 27.** *{Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that}* As chapter 30.3.

*{I will sow the house of Israel, and the house of Judah, with the seed of man, and with the seed of beast}* I will multiply and replenish the land of either family (see verse 1.) both with people and cattle, as if the whole land were sowed with the seed of either, and it did multiply, as grain cast into the ground is wont to do in some rich and fat soil, Gen. 26.12. Mat. 13.8. See Esay 60.21. Hos. 2.23. Zach. 2.4. & 10.8, 9. Nor need we depart here from the received version to render the text, with the Chaldee, which some of the Jewish commenters follow. *with the seed of man, as with the seed of beast;* because the copulative is sometime so used; as Prov. 25.25. Much less to expound it with that Jewish doctor, whom some postillers follow, of multiplying and blessing the wise and the simple together; abusing to that purpose the words of the Psalmist, Psal. 36.6. or to understand with that learned scholiast, by *men* the Jews, by *beasts* the Gentiles, expounding it of spiritual regeneration.

**V. 28.** *{And it shall come to passe, that}* As chap. 25.12.

*{Like as I have watched over them; to pluck up, and to break down, and to throw down, and to destroy, and to afflict;}* Of the terms here used, see on chap. 1.10, 11. & 10.12. & 18.7, 9. & 44.27. Dan. 9.14. there are in them some elegant consonancies, which our English cannot so well express.

*{so I will watch over them, to build and to plant, saith the LORD}* I will be sedulous and assiduous (as Psal. 127.1. Prov. 8.34.) in promoting their good. See on Chap. 1.10. & 18.9. & 24.6.

**V. 29.** *{In those days they shall say no more, The Fathers have eaten a sower grape; and the children's teeth are set on edge.}* Or, *It shall no more be said,* as verse 23. This seems to have been a common byword in the mouth of profane wretches in those times, thereby implying that their parents or ancestors had committed faults; and they being faultless yet sustained the penalty of it, Ezek. 18.2. This proverb, or byword, God says in those times, shall no longer be used, an end being now put unto those grievous calamities, which had befallen them, God punishing thereby, as well their own sins, as their parents also in them jointly together, Esay 65.7. and they should not have occasion therefore to use that proverb any longer, as it is said, Ezek. 18.3. And this I conceive, with some of the best interpreters, to be both the genuine and full notion of the place: which they seem much to swerve from, who either with that learned annotator, who taking an hint of that his conceit from one of the Jewish commenters, would have the meaning to be, that howsoever God do justly punish children for their parents' defaults, Exod. 28.5. and with this people had so done, 1 Kings 24.3, 4. yet would in regard of the excellent parts and virtues, both of their ancient progenitors, and their own also, put an end now unto that severe carriage: that which is directly contrary unto that freeness of his mere mercy, which he constantly asserts, as the main ground of their restitution, Esay 43.25. & 48.9, 11. Ezek. 36.32. or, as another Jewish doctor, because there should be no such grand sins among them, for which God with plagues should pursue them unto posterity: or, as that learned man also, fetching in hither what follows, verse 30. that the magistrates should be so diligent in execution of justice in those times, that God should not need now to punish in that manner, as formerly he had done. As also those both Popish and ours; who restraining this passage unto the times of the Gospel, say some of the former, that the penalty of Adam's sins reached unto all his posterity, and notwithstanding their circumcision, yet they went down all into *Limbo* for it; until the coming of Christ, but that all penalty of that kind is in Christian baptism taken away, original sin being washed away in it: that of their *Limbo* being a mere fancy, and the other of baptism also, a groundless conceit: and some of the latter, who dream of God's dealing more favorably now than in former times with sinners, when some one man's sin brought a penalty upon others, and the sins of the fathers were required at the children's hands: for how they are able to make this good, that sins of particular persons have not an hand in procuring of general judgments, or that God does not punish parents at this day, as well in their issue, as in their persons, I see not: and a point of that weight requires clearer proof than from this place, that will well bear another sense: which those come near to, who would have the meaning to be, that both in the one time, and in the other, as well after their temporal restitution, as also in their conversion to the Messias; they should be hereafter convinced in conscience, that those their calamities had justly befallen them for their own sins, Ezek. 6.9. & 7.15. & 36.31. and this may well be added to the former, as a consequent to the same. The byword itself contains indeed a truth in it; for God himself avows it, and threatens it, Exod. 20.5. & 34.7. and the Prophet himself, in the person of God's people, does in plainer terms complain of it, Lam. 5.7. that they suffered for their fathers' sins; nor was it without ground from God's own words, who by him menaced to send them into captivity for the sins of Manasses, who had been long before deceased, Chap. 15.4. But their meaning was, that being innocent and faultless, they suffered only for their ancestors' excesses, which was most false; for they trod in the steps of their wicked forefathers, and were themselves as bad, if not worse, than they, Chap. 7.26. & 11.10. & 16.12.

**V. 30.** *{But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sower grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.}* Heb. *A man,* for, *every one;* as Chap. 22.7. So Ezek. 18.4. So that albeit, God would by putting an end to those their former calamities, take away the occasion of this misused byword: yet he would not surcease to execute vengeance upon such wicked ones as should continue still in their wickedness, or return to it in those times. See Esay 27.4. & 65.20. For as for those who would restrain this and the former to the times of the Gospel, that no man should be excluded from God's grace in Christ, upon his return unto God, either Jew for his forefathers' obstinacy, or Gentile for his ancestors' incredulity, is no other than what has been God's constant course in all ages; no iniquity of any progenitor ever debarring any from life eternal, that returned unto God by sincere conversion, 1 Chron. 28.9. 2 Chron. 15.4. Joh. 6.37.

**V. 31.** *{Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that.}* That this passage has special reference to the day of Messias, and the times of the Gospel, appears by the Apostle's application of it, Heb. 8. & 10.36. See chap. 23.5. and verse 27.

*{I will make a new covenant}* Heb. *I will cut out;* as Psal. 50.3. Esay 55.3. of the reason of the phrase see there, and on Chapter 34.8, 18.

*{a new covenant}* Not simply in regard of the substance of it: for the main matter and substance of the former was, as here verse 33. So Gen. 17.7. Deut. 26.17, 18. & 29.13. And this old covenant was ratified as well as the new, by the blood of the Messias (who was ever the same, Heb. 13.8. 2 Cor. 1.19, 20.) that blood of his being in those times as well typified by the blood of the sacrifice, as by another element it is in these days obsignated. See the same words in a manner to this effect of either, Exod. 24.8. compared with Matth. 26.28. Luke 22.20. 1 Cor. 11.25. Heb. 9.20. But is in divers respects called *a new covenant,* as the commandment of *Love,* is in some respects called *a New Commandement,* though in nature and substance the same still that it was ever. Lev. 19.18. Matth. 22.39. Luke 10.27. John 13.34. 1 John 2.7, 8. And so is it with this covenant, though in nature and essence it continue the same, to wit, of remission of sin, and eternal salvation by the Messias, upon condition of faith in him, repentance, and newness of life; yet is it in divers regards said to be *New:* First, in that it is ratified by the death of our Savior exhibited, which was but in expectation before: the faith of God's people, being then fixed on the Messias to come; and to be sacrificed for their sins, Esay 53.10, 12. Job 8.36. Acts 15.11. the faith of Christians now resting on Christ, already come in the flesh, having been sacrificed for them, and being ascended up into heaven, John 1.14. Acts 13.31——34. Rom. 10.9. 1 Cor. 5.7. 1 Tim. 3.16. Heb. 9.11——14. & 11.13, 39, 40. 1 Joh. 4.2. 2. In that the doctrine of the Gospel is now more fully, distinctly, and clearly revealed, than formerly it had been, when it was more darkly, confusedly, and in generalities only, by that dimmer candlelight which then they enjoyed, with most that then lived, apprehended and discerned. Mal. 4.2. Joh. 3.19. 2 Cor. 3.18. 2 Pet. 1.19. 3. In that the former covenant comprehended together with those spiritual promises, which yet were the principal part of it, many temporal blessings, as the possession of the land of Canaan, and multiplicity of issue, and outward prosperity, Gen. 15.5, 7, 18. & 17.2, 7, 8. Psal. 105.8, 11. Deut. 28.1–14. whereas this latter runs wholly upon the spiritual and celestial blessings, Rom. 3.24, 25. & 5.1, 2. Eph. 1.3. Heb. 8.6. 4. In regard of those manifold ceremonies and shadows, to the observation whereof they that lived under that covenant were thereby strictly obliged: whereas in this latter they are all taken away, and a service of God more spiritual substituted in the room of them, Chap. 3.16. Joh. 1.14, 17. & 4.21, 23. Gal. 3.24, 25. & 4.1——9. & 5.1, 5. Heb. 9.2——12. & 10.1——10. 5. In regard of the dilatation and enlargement of it; it being in those days confined to the Jewish nation and state, and some few proselytes that adjoined themselves thereunto, Deut. 33.4. Psal. 76.1, 2. & 147.19, 20. Rom. 3.1, 2. & 9.4. Eph. 4.12. whereas it is now propounded and extended without respect of persons or places, unto all indifferently of all people and nations that shall embrace the faith of Christ, Esay 2.2. & 11.10. & 54.1. & 56.6, 7. Jer. 3.17. Mi. 4.1, 2. Mal. 1.11. Mat. 28.19. Mar. 16.15. Luke 24.47. Rom. 10.18. & 15.8——12. Eph. 2.13——19. Col. 1.23. Rev. 7. 6. In regard of that large measure of spiritual endowments, and variety of gifts, so plentifully exhibited, after Christ's ascension, such as the like had never been known, or heard of before, Esay 11.6. Joel 2.28. Joh. 7.38, 39. Acts 2.4, 16, 17, 33. 1 Cor. 12.4——10, 28. 7. In regard of the efficacy of the Spirit accompanying the use of these gifts, whereby so many millions have been out of all places converted unto Christ, Acts 2.41. & 4.4. & 8.6, 12. & 9.35. & 10.21, 24, 26. & 19.20. & 21.20. Lastly, in regard of continuance, the government of God's Church by the Evangelical ministry succeeding in the room of the Levitical priesthood and ministry now abolished, and the worship of God settled in place of the Mosaical rites now abandoned, being to continue without change in the Church, and among the people of God, until the end of the world, and the consummation of all things at Christ's second coming, Matth. 28.18——20. 1 Cor. 11.26. Eph. 4.11——13.

*{with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah.}* As verse 27. Chap. 3.18. with the main body of my Church consisting of Jews and Gentiles Rom. 11.25, 26.

**V. 32.** *{Not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt:}* Of this covenant see Exod. 24.7, 8. Deut. 5.2. the same that was from time to time renewed with that people as God's peculiar, Deut. 9.10——13. Chron. 15.12. & 23.16. & 29.10. & 34.31. Mal. 4.4. and was a gracious covenant, as well of mercy, as of justice, with promise of pardon upon repentance, Exod. 20.5, 6. & 34.6, 7. Deut. 4.31. & 30.1——2. Psal. 103.7——18. it consisted indeed of the Law as a perfect rule for direction for matter of obedience; but had adjoined with it faith in the Messias, (who was resembled by the lid of the Ark, wherein the Law was reserved, 2 Chr. 6.11. called therefore *the propitiatory,* Ex. 26.16, 17, 21. Ro. 3.25, 26.) for pardon of sin upon sincere repentance by his blood, typified in the blood of the sin-sacrifices, Lev. 4.3–4, 13–15, 22–24. & 5.1–6. & 6.2——7. Heb. 9.11——28. By all which it appears, that this was not barely the covenant of nature, extending itself to all Adam's posterity indefinitely, nor holding out any promise of pardon to any upon any the least disobedience, Gen. 2.17. Rom. 2.12, 14, 15. but the covenant of grace and mercy in and by the Mediator the Messias. Howbeit, the Lord here promises to renew it in another manner to his people, than as he made it then with them, and that as in divers respects that have already been specified, so in something further, which hereafter ensues. For that learned man narrows the text overmuch, who would have this only to be the meaning of it, that the covenant should not now run in those terms, as then it did, *I am the Lord thy God that brought thee out of the land of Egypt;* but in some other form mentioning some greater benefit, that should drown the memory of that, Esay 43.18. chap. 16.14, 15.
