The Jewish Doctors here dote again, who as before by the roll, that Baruch wrote from Jeremies mouth, they would have to be meant *the Lamentations of Jeremy;* so here they tell us, that there were but three alphabets of it in the first roll, the rest were added in this second.

## CHAPTER 37

**Verse 1.** *{And King Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim,}* Or, *Now* (as Ezr. 7.2. chap. 29.1. verse 4. because this discourse has no connection with, or dependence upon, any foregoing relation) *Zedekiah the son of Josiah* (so styled to distinguish him from another Zedekiah, of the same time, his Nephew, (the son of Jehojakin his brother, and brother to Jeconiah, 1 Chron. 3.16.) *reigned instead of Coniah;* that is, Jehojacin or Jeconiah, in contempt so termed, Chap. 22.24.

*{whom Nebuchadnezzar King of Babylon made King in the land of Judah.}* Heb. *made to reign:* so naming him, whereas before he was called *Mattaniah,* 2 Kings 24.15. This relation of Zedekiahs entrance into the royal government, together with the disobedient carriage of himself, his servants, and subjects, verse 2. is here prefixed to make way for a message, which he was to receive by Jeremy from God, verse 7–10.

**V. 2.** *{But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land did hearken unto the words of the LORD which he spake by the Prophet Jeremiah.}* See 2 Chron. 36.12–16. Heb. *by the hand of Jeremiah* as Esay 37.24. Mal. 1.1. Chap. 50.1.

**V. 3.** *{And Zedekiah the King sent Jehucal the son of Shelamiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the Priest, to the Prophet Jeremiah saying, Pray now unto the LORD our God for us.}* This is related together with some circumstances of the time when it was done, verse 4,5. as giving occasion of the message ensuing from God. The like address from the same King by one of those here mentioned, and another, to the Prophet. See chap. 21.1,2. See there. But thus are the wicked in their distresses glad to seek unto Gods servants for their prayers, whose wholesome advice yet they refuse to follow, verse 2. Chap. 38.15. So 2 King 13.6. Acts 8.22,24.

**V. 4.** *{Now Jeremiah came in, and went out among the people}* Heb. *and* (as chap. 36.22.) was *coming and going in the midst of the people;* as chap. 40.5,10. He went at large, being yet at full liberty.

*{for they had not put him into prison.}* Or, *he was not yet put in prison:* for the verb is indefinite; as Gen. 40.15. *They have put me in prison,* for, *I was put in prison.* Heb *they had not given him* (as ver. 18.) *into the house of restraint;* as Esay 42.5. which yet shortly afterward they did, verse 15. chap 32.2.

**V. 5.** *{Then Pharaoh's Army was come out of Egypt.}* Heb. *And.* which might here well be retained, Zedekiah was made king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar, and had sworn fealty unto him verse 1. 2 Kings 24.17. 2 Chron. 36.13. but being settled in the kingdom, he entered into a secret confederacy with Pharao king of Egypt, and revolted from the king of Babylon, Ezek 17.15–18. who thereupon made war upon him and besieged him in Jerusalem, 2 Kings 25.2. Now Pharao, though he came no more in person abroad after the great overthrow given him by Nebuchadnezzar in the reign of Jehojakim chap. 46.2. 2 Kings 24.7. yet he sent some forces to relieve Zedekiah, and to raise the siege, if it might be; but all to no purpose, Ezek. 17.17.

*{and when the Chaldeans that besieged Jerusalem heard tydings of them, they departed from Jerusalem.}* Heb. *And the Chaldeans heard — and they went up* or, *departed,* (as chap. 4.7.) *from against Jerusalem;* to go to meet with the Egyptian forces: but Zedekiah it seems feared that they might return again; and therefore sends to the Prophet, verse 3. and yet how wretchedly and perfidiously they had dealt in their covenants with God, upon the approach of those aids, see chap. 34.15,16,21. The like syntax to that in this place, see chap. 35.11.

**V. 6.** *{Then came the word of the LORD unto the Prophet Jeremiah, saying,}* Heb. *And the word was to him;* as chap. 35.12. And this has reference to what was before related, concerning the message sent from the King to the Prophet, verse 3 when unto an answer is now returned; as between this and that, verse 4,5. being all enclosed in a parenthesis.

**V. 7.** *{Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel;}* As Chapter 35.13.

*{Thus shall ye say to the King of Judah;}* Or, *Thus say;* as Chap. 21.3.

*{that sent you unto me to enquire of me:}* Or, *to seek to me;* as Esay 55.6. Ezek. 36.37 for his request to the Prophet was to pray for them verse 12.

*{Behold, Pharaoh's Army which is come to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land:}* Not daring to bicker with the Chaldean forces, or not able to stand before them, and much less able to relieve you, Ezek. 17.17. thus no course nor counsel can prevail, or avail ought against God, Psal. 33.10,11,16,17. Prov. 21.30,31. Esay 14.27 & 30.1–6. & 31.1–3. But what the talmudists here fable of the Egyptian forces coming by shipping, and what strange matters God caused the sea to raise up, that did affright them, and made them turn back again, is of the same stamp with other their absurd and ridiculous figments,

**V. 8.** *{And the Chaldeans shall return}* Having either frightened them away, or worsted them in fight, and so put them to flight,

*{and fight against this city and take it, and burn it with fire.}* Chapter 32.2,29.

**Verse 9.** *{Thus saith the LORD, deceive not yourselves}* Heb. *your souls*; as Chap. 17.21. & 51.6.

*{saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us}* Heb. *Going go* (as Judg. 4.9.) *from against us,* as verse 5.

*{for they shall not depart.}* For any long time; or; so as to relinquish and give over their siege, See of the like, on Chapter 36.30.

**Verse 10.** *{For though ye had smitten the whole army of the Chaldeans that fight against you, and there remained but wounded men among them,}* Heb. *if ye had smitten:* the conditional is a discretive or adversative notion; as Chap. 5.2. & 15.1. and; *there remained wounded;* or, *thrust thorow;* as Chap. 51.4. for, none but such, or such only: a defect of the restrictive; as Job 8.9. Eccles. 4.8. or, *they were left* all *thrust thorow;* the general note supplied; as 1 Sam. 30.8.

*{yet should they rise every man in his tent, and burn this city with fire.}* Heb. *a man* (for, each one; as Chap. 36.3.) *in his tent they shall rise:* the discretive wanting; as Chap. 15.1,10. and the noun singular with a verb plural in a distributive notion; as Chap. 36.16. See before verse 8. the weakest and feeblest shall be able to prevail against those whom God will have to be destroyed, Esay 40.29. Chap. 49.20. & 50.45.

**Verse 11.** *{And it came to passe}* Or, *Now so it was;* as Chap. 36.22,23. verse 2. For here begins a new relation of a further business, having no dependence upon the former; where it is related, first, some harsh usages of Jeremy, and his imprisonment, upon his attempt to repair to Anathoth the place of his former wonted abode, ver. 11–13, and secondly, a private conference that passed between the king and him, during the time of his imprisonment, ver. 16–21.

*{that when the Army of the Chaldeans was broken up for fear of Pharaoh's Army}* Heb. *when the Army of the Chaldeans was gone up from against Jerusalem* (as verse 5.) *from the face,* or, *before,* or, *because of, Pharaoh's Army:* for howsoever the term here used be sometime not amiss rendered, *for fear of this;* or that; as Esay 21.15. & 31.8. Chap. 35.11. yet the word signifies more generally, *because of,* or, *by reason of;* as Chap. 4.4. & 21.12. & 23.10. and there is no necessity therefore so to render it here: but it may well be rendered, *by reason of,* or, *because of, Pharaoh's army:* not so much it may be, because they stood in any great fear of them, whom they had but lately shrewdly foiled, Chap. 48.2. and had forced their king to keep in person at home, 2 Kings 24.7. but rather, in likelihood, to go forth to meet them on the way, and so to prevent their nearer approach, that so they might the more quietly, and constantly, carry on the siege afterward, without any disturbance from abroad.

**Verse 12.** *{Then Jeremiah went forth, out of Jerusalem}* Or, *That, And Jeremiah went forth out of Jerusalem:* taking in here the particle *that;* from verse 11. where it has no place. So the copulative is familiarly used; as Esay 2.2. Chap. 3.9. & 4.9. & 6.19.

*{to go into the land of Benjamin}* To Anathoth his own town in that country, Chap. 1.1. & 11.21. & 12.6.

*{to separate himself thence in the midst of the people}* The verb here used is diversely expounded, according to its divers and different acceptions: it signifies sometime to divide, or, share, as Deut. 4.19. Prov. 17.2. and so some, following the Chaldee, and the old Latins here take it; he went to divide his possession among his people, or to share with the priests at Anathoth, to receive among them his portion accruing to him. Others, to buy, or get some share of bread among his countrymen: And some again, to divide, that is, to sever and withdraw himself from that people; which he did not offer to do, say some, while the Chaldeans lay in siege about them, but stayed to continue his prayers for them: This our version follows; and it consists well with that wish of his, Chap. 9.2. But the ground that those give for it is frivolous; there was still as much need of his prayers as ever; and that he himself well knew: Besides that, it is not said, from the people, but amidst them. Others, from another use of the word; in a notion of making slick, or, smooth, Esay 41.7. Chap. 23.21. render it, to slip away, that is, to get slily and secretly away, in the midst of, or, among the people; as Chapter 39.14. verse 4. in the throng of those that issued out of the city to repair to, and look after, their wonted places of abode, hoping now quickly to enjoy them again, and that they might be in safety there: and this seems most probable: But of the ground or end of this attempt of the Prophet, we have no great certainty. Some suppose with the Jewish doctors, that he did it out of fear to be clapped up in prison, as shortly after he was, for his forementioned free language to the king's messengers, verse 9,10. Others; because he knew that the city would be taken by the Chaldeans ere long. Others again, because he saw that he could do no good upon them, and grew weary therefore of his work and pains with them; as Esay 49.4. Chapter 20.8,9. But to fix ought here is unsafe, unless we had surer footing.

**Verse 13.** *{And when he was in the gate of Benjamin}* That looked that way, and by which, men passed into those parts. See Chapter 20.2. & 38.7.

*{a Captain of the ward was there,}* Heb. *a master*, or, *owner of oversight*, or, *charge*; that is, an overseer: one that had the charge to keep watch and ward there, and to look to it, that none went out to agree or join with the enemy; but such only as had occasions otherwise, whom it was not unlikely that they were content to let return unto the places of their former habitations, to ease the burden of the city, much shortened of provisions by the length of the siege, having been begirt some good space of time already, 2 Kings 25.1,2.

*{whose name was Irijah the son of Shelamiah, the son of Hananiah,}* Heb. *Jirijah:* and this Hananiah his grandfather the Rabbines tell us was that false Prophet, whose death Jeremy foretold, Chap. 28.16,17. and that upon his death-bed charging Jeremy as the procurer of his end, he gave his son Shelemah withal in charge to be avenged upon him for the same, if it lighted in his lot, and that Schelemiah accordingly gave the like charge to his son after him, who thereupon out of a spite to Jeremy, for his grandfather's quarrel, dealt with him as is here related. But these are groundless reports of no great probability; nor does the small distance of time between the decease of that Ananias, and this occurrent, afford any great likelihood of it. See Chap. 28.1.

*{and he took Jeremiah the Prophet,}* Or, *apprehended*; as Chap. 26.8. or, *laid hold on him*; as 1 Kings 13.4.

*{saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans}* Heb. *thou art falling to the Chaldeans;* to fall to them; as afterward, to go out to them, Chap. 38.2. and both together, Chap. 21.9.

**Verse 14.** *{Then said Jeremiah, it is false,}* Heb. *And,* or, *But* (as Chap. 12.2.) *Jeremy said, Falshood,* or, *A lie:* the abstract for the concrete; as Chap. 27.14.

*{I fall not away to the Chaldeans}* Heb. *I am not falling to the Chaldeans;* as before.

*{but he hearkened not to him:}* Heb. *And;* as before: He would not give credit to him, regarded not his words: being one it seems ill affected towards the Prophet.

*{So Irijah took Jeremiah, and brought him to the Princes.}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 36.14.

**Verse 15.** *{Wherefore the Princes were wroth with Jeremiah,}* Upon the captain's misinformation, ver. 14. Heb. *And;* which may well be here retained; albeit the copulative be also sometime so used: as Neh. 2.2. Esay 8.2.

*{and smote him}* Caused him to be smitten: as Chap. 39.6. & 52.20. Acts 5.40. & 16.22,27. with 23.2.

*{and put him in prison,}* Heb. *gave him into the house,* or place, (as verse 4.) of the bond; as Judg. 16.21. Eccles. 4.14. they were grown now more rough and rigorous against him, than in Jehoiakim's time they had been. See Chapter 26.16. and 36.19.

*{in the house of Jonathan the Scribe}* One of the scribes belonging to the court, and having his lodgings in some part of it, as had also Elishama under Jehoiakim, Chapter 36.12,30.

*{for they had made that the prison}* Heb. *made that* (or, *prepared and fitted it*; as Gen. 28.7.) *for an house*, or, *a place*, (for the word is very general. See on Gen. 28.22.) *of restraint*: as verse 4. a very inconvenient place it seems to have been for that purpose, verse 20. This (besides that of Pashur's, which was but for a night, Chap. 20.2,3.) seems to have been the first commitment and oversharp usage of Jeremy, which some deem might befall him through an hand of God, for attempting to withdraw himself, and relinquish that place, wherein by God's appointment his office was principally to be performed. See Chap. 26.20,21. But such censures, unless better ground were for them, are not safe.

**Verse 16.** *{When Jeremiah was entered into the dungeon, and into the cabins;}* Heb. *when Jeremy was come into the house,* or, room, or, place, of the pit, or, the hole: as Exod. 12.29. and *into the cabines,* or, cells, or, wards, or, lodges. The Jewish critics some of them tell us, that they were cells or lodges situate before the prison, for the guards, or wards, that kept the prison to abide in: but it may seem rather to signify such sorry cells or cabins, as the prisoners had to lie in, for the word is with the Talmudists said to be used commonly for an inn, or lodging, wherein travelers and passengers are wont to rest and repose themselves: for that seems not agreeable to the present relation which some other of them have, that by it should be here meant a certain room about the Temple built with hewn stone, situate without the place of judicature: whereas it seems rather to have been about some part of the king's house, about the uttermost court in likelihood. See Chapter 36.20. verse 17.

*{and Jeremiah had remained there many days.}* Heb. *sat*, or *dwelt*: as Chap. 35.11. & 40.6. had remained some good space of time there: in likelihood until the Chaldeans came back again, having repelled, if not dispelled and dispersed the Egyptian forces, that were coming to raise their siege. See on verse 10.

**Verse 17.** *{Then Zedekiah the King sent and took him out,}* Caused him to be brought unto him. So Chap. 38.14.

*{and the king asked him secretly in his house,}* In that part of the court where his own residence was. See Chap. 36.20. secretly; for fear of the princes, whom he was too much overawed with, and overmuch enslaved unto, Chap. 38.5,24,25.

*{and said, Is there any word from the LORD?}* Thus obstinate and rebellious persons would fain have some word of comfort from him, whom yet they refuse to be ruled by, and to obey, vers. 2. Heb. *a word*, for, *any word*: as, *a man*, for, *any man*, Chap. 23.24. or, *any thing*, *ought*: as Chap. 26.2.

*{and Jeremiah said, There is: for, said he,}* Heb. *and he said:* as Psal. 60.11.

*{thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the King of Babylon.}* Heb. *given:* and hand, for power. So Chap. 24.8. and 32.4. and 34.3.

**Verse 18.** *{Moreover, Jeremiah said unto King Zedekiah,}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 33.1.

*{what have I offended against thee, or against thy servants, or against this people, that ye have put me in prison?}* Heb. *to thee, and to thy servants, and to thy people;* as Psal. 51.4. and, for, or; as Chap. 35.9. and so vers. 19. and, *given me;* as vers. 4. and, house of restraint; as vers. 15.

**Verse 19.** *{Where are now your Prophets?}* As Chap. 2.27. *Where are your gods?* See the like, Judge 9.35. Heb. *And where,* for, *Where now;* as judge 6.13.

*{which prophesied unto you, saying, The King of Babylon shall not come against you, nor against this land.}* See Chap. 28.4. and it may well hence be deemed, that by this time the Chaldeans, having defeated the Egyptians, were returned unto the siege of the city again. See Chap. 38.2. Else it might have been excepted, Why you see yet, that they are gone again, and have not prevailed.

**Verse 20.** *{Therefore hear now, I pray thee, O my LORD, the King,}* Heb. *And now:* which may well be retained: Nor is it unworthy our observation, both how free and plain the Prophet is in delivering of God's errand, vers. 17. and yet withal how submiss and humble in his addresses otherwise concerning himself to his sovereign, notwithstanding the hard usages that he had through his default unjustly sustained, and did still sustain for the faithful discharge of his duty: therein directly opposite to those, of whom, Jude, vers. 8.16.

*{Let my supplication, I pray thee, be accepted before thee}* Heb. *let my supplication fall before thee;* as Chap. 36.7. and 42.2. Give me leave humbly to present my supplication in your presence; as Psal. 119.170.

*{that thou cause me not to return to the house of Jonathan the Scribe}* Heb. *and cause me not to return.* Of this place, see above verse 15.

*{lest I die there.}* The place being so vile and noisome: wherein he could not but have endured much annoyance already, having been no small space of time there. See vers. 16.

**Verse 21.** *{Then Zedekiah the King commanded}* Or, *So he commanded:* according to the Prophet's request, vers. 20. Heb. *And;* as verse 14.

*{that they should commit Jeremiah into the court of the prison}* Removing him from that hole, and those cells, in which before he was cooped up, verse 16. unto a place, where he might have fresher air and more liberty, and his friends freer access to him, Chap. 38.1. Of this place, see on Chap. 32.2. Heb. *and they committed him:* yet our English version may well stand. See the like, Josh. 24.9. Mal. 1.9.

*{and that they should give him daily a piece of bread}* Heb. *and to give him dayly a piece of bread:* as the Chaldee renders it, both, here and elsewhere: or, a morsel of bread; as our English renders it, 1 Sam. 2.36. and it may not amiss be rendered, Prov. 6.26. and 28.21. But it may rather, I suppose, be here rendered a loaf; and so the Greek after this manner for want of that variety, which our English affords, a bread, both here, and 1 Chro. 16.3. as also in divers places of the New Testament, as Matth. 14.17. Luke 11.5. Joh. 6.9. 1 Cor. 10.17. (in which place also in our English one loaf, would do better) the old Latin renders, *a wreath,* or, *roll;* and that the word does signify a loaf, and that as the notation of it seems to imply, a round one, and that of some bigness (for it has near affinity with a term that is used for a talent, or great lump of lead, or other metal, Zach. 5.7.) appears by Exod. 29.23. where Moses is willed at the consecration of Aaron to take out of the basket one *ciccar* (the word here used) that is, says the Jewish critic, one great round loaf; the quantity whereof he thence gathers, because it is distinguished from the oily cake, and the wafer, or the thinner, or broader sort of cakes, such as we call cracknels: as also by that place, 1 Chron. 16.3. for howsoever that which is called *ciccar,* a loaf there, is termed a cake of bread, 2 Sam. 6.19. yet being the king's dole, and having a fair piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine joined with it, it could not but be a loaf of some bigness: and such a loaf, though not so great, but according to the scarcity of the time and place then afforded; yet a loaf, not a piece of one, was that in likelihood, that the king willed to be assigned for the Prophet's daily allowance, so long as any remained of the public store in the city. Howbeit, if a piece of a loaf, not a whole one should be meant, it might have reference to such quarters of loaves as were in common use among the Romans, which being made of some bigness, but after the fashion of our buns, were at table usually divided into four quarters, whereof each took one: whence the byword with them, of living on another man's *quadra,* not *trencher,* as by many it is mistaken; but bread, or, quarter. But I adhere to the former.

*{out of the bakers street}* That were set on work to bake out of the public stores for the relief of those that wanted.

*{until all the bread in the city were spent.}* Thus God made the king himself, though no friend to him, an instrument to provide for him, that he might not perish for want of sustenance. See 1 King. 17.6,9,14. Job 5.20. Psal. 33.19. and 34.10.

*{Thus Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.}* Until he was by the importunity of the princes removed thence for a while into a worse place, where yet he stayed not long; but returned soon thither again, Chap. 38.6,13. Heb. *And* (as Chap. 7.34. & 25.14.) *Jeremy sate* (as vers. 16.) *in the court of the prison;* as Chap. 32.2. and 33.1. See Chap. 38.28.

## CHAPTER 38

**Verse 1.** *{Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying;}* Poor Jeremy is no sooner rid out of one strait and difficulty, but he is shortly after cast again into another, as bad, or worse than the former: Out of Jonathan's house, or hole rather, he is, at the king's command, removed to the prison court, Chap. 37.21. where he is at more liberty, and people have now freer access to him than before; and there repair to him not a few; some of kindness and goodwill to him to visit him; Others, and those many more in likelihood, either out of an itching affection to hear some novelties and strange matters; or out of a longing desire to understand what he thought, or said concerning the issue of their present troubles and distresses, as in such cases, both good and bad, are ready to inquire after the thoughts and speeches of those that are by them deemed to have any spice of a prophetical spirit. But this freedom and frequency of access was a means of bringing this our Prophet into new troubles, and grievous annoyances, even to the hazarding of his life. For he cannot forbear speaking, he must of necessity be doing his duty, 1 Cor. 9.17. chap. 20.9. acquainting those that came to him with God's mind, his messages, to wit, that if they stayed in the city, they should be sure to miscarry; if they quitted the city, and yielded themselves to the Chaldeans, they might thereby secure themselves, verse 2,3. Hence some of the princes ill affected, clamor to the king against him, and require to have him, either executed, or clapped up closer again, verse 1–4. and upon the king's delivering of him up to their wills, verse 5. they put him into a worse pit, or hole, than that of Jonathan's was, where he remains sticking in the mire, verse 6: until a religious courtier, but a stranger, by importunity wrests from the king his delivery from thence, and restitution to the place of his former restraint, verse 7–13. After which there ensues a new privy conference between the king and the Prophet, verse 14–23. and the means contrived to conceal what had passed between them in private from the princes, verse 24–28. And this is the sum of the whole chapter.

*{Then}* Or, *Now when;* as chap. 37.1.

*{Shephatiah}* Divers others of this name are mentioned in Scripture; but of this man, no mention is found, save in this place.

*{Gemariah the son of Pashur}* Of that Pashur, says one, mentioned chap. 20.1. but of that no great likelihood; for that Pashur was a priest: this Gemariah seems to have been a prince.

*{Jucal the son of Shelemiah}* Of whom, chap. 37.26. and this the more likely.

*{Pashur the son of Malchiah}* The same before mentioned; chap. 21.1.

*{heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken,}* Heard of them in likelihood by such as came to inform against him: as those, chap. 20.10.

*{unto all the people}* That either were in prison with him, or repaired unto the prison to him.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus saith the LORD, He that remaineth in this city shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence:}* Heb. *He that sitteth,* or, *stayeth;* as chap. 28.21. See the like denunciation, chap. 21.9.

*{but he that goeth forth to the Chaldeans}* *And falleth to them;* as chap. 21.9. that yields himself to them. Heb. *and he,* etc. as chap. 12.2.

*{shall have his life for a prey}* *He shall live:* he shall by so doing save his life, chap. 21.9. See the form also, chap. 39.18. and 45.5.

**Verse 3.** *{Thus saith the LORD; This city shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylons Army, which shall take it.}* Heb. *being given be given:* and, hand for, power; as chap. 34.2,20,21. and, *and he shall take it:* to wit, the king, Chap. 32.3,28.

**Verse 4.** *{Therefore the Princes said unto the king,}* Or, *These Princes then said unto the king:* for this has reference to the persons named, vers. 1. Heb. *And they heard—and they said;* for, *When they heard—then they said.* See the like, chap. 36.11,12.

*{We beseech thee, let this man be put to death.}* The poor Prophet is now in a pitiful plight, in a forlorn condition, when the princes that saved him before from the priests, are turned as eager against him, as the priests then were: nothing can satisfy them but his blood; they cry out now against him to the king, as the priests did then to them. See Chap. 26.8,11,16.

*{for thus he weakneth the hands of the men of war that remain in this city, and the hands of all the people in speaking such words unto them.}* Or, *because,* or, *for that, he weakneth.* So is the particle oft used; as Gen. 38.26. Num. 10.3. and 14.43. Heb. *to speak* (for, *in speaking*: as, *not to drink*, for, *in not drinking*, chap. 35.8,9.) *according to these words*, Gen. 39.17,19. Thus out of carnal policy is piety impugned. So 1 King. 12.27. Joh. 11.48.

*{For this man seeketh not the welfare of this people, but their hurt}* Heb. *is not seeking the peace;* as chap. 28.9. and 29.7. or, to the peace: those things that concern, and conduce to the peace and welfare of the state: as Luke 19.42. and yet none sought the true welfare of it more than he: the common plea against God's ministers, that seek to reclaim people and states, and to save them from ruin by reducing them to God, 1 King. 18.17,18. & 21.20. Act. 16.26. and 17.6.

*{but the hurt.}* Heb. *the evil*, or, *to the evil*: such things as tend thereunto, as chap. 29.11.

**Verse 5.** *{Then Zedekiah the king said}* Heb. *And.* which need not here be altered.

*{behold, he is in your hand}* In your power, to do with him, as you please; as chap. 26.14. Job 2.6.

*{for the king is not he that can do any thing against you.}* As if he had said, the king can deny you nothing: too large a condescension, ill beseeming a ruler, without all regard of right, or wrong, and tending to an unjust, cruel, and impious usage of God's Prophet. Howbeit, the text seems not so clear here for this sense. It is true, that the particle here used does sometime signify against. So is it deemed to do, Esai. 10.15. and Ezek. 21.20. Yet those places are questionable: and it is very rare, if anywhere it so do: for howsoever in those forms where it is subjoined to terms of fighting and striving; as Psalm 35.1. Esai. 49.25. Chap. 33.5. it be sometime rendered against: as Chap. 37.10. and in effect, it imports as much: yet in propriety of speech it sounds no more than with, and is so most commonly expressed. Nor has it that notion of opposition from itself, but from the *word* it is annexed unto. Some therefore would rather have the words thus rendered; *For without the king, the thing* (Heb. *word*, as Chap. 32.27.) *may be done, by you:* as Esai. 7.17. or, *with you;* among yourselves. You have power enough to dispatch this business without me; which some also apply unto the power that they had, being some of the grand consistory to try and doom a false Prophet, such an one, as they pretend Jeremy to be. But there appears here no hint of any judiciary proceeding; but a motion made, and pressed for dispatching the Prophet without more ado, and ridding their hands of him by any means whatsoever: and that not upon suggestion of any false prophecy, but upon grounds of policy, because by his prophecies he disheartened the soldiery, and discouraged the people: and according to this reading therefore the king should rather imply, that having him in their hands already, they had power enough to dispose of him as they pleased, without asking his assent. And this way I should incline to, did I anywhere find the negative particle here found, to be used for without: with another prefixed I find it so used, Chap. 33.12. and elsewhere, but never alone: and I leave it therefore to the determination of the learned: I shall only subjoin, how I conceive, it may, very near to the former notion, be rendered, *The king is not he that can prevail in ought against you:* as Psalm 13.4. *I have prevailed him,* for, I have prevailed against him; for the verb is the same there with that here used; as also, Esth. 6.13. Psalm 129.2. Chap. 20.10. vers. 22. a defect of the relative there is, as Chap. 31.24. a word, for, ought, as vers. 14.

**Verse 6.** *{Then took they Jeremiah}* Or, *So they took;* as Chap. 32.14. Heb. *And.* Having gotten the king thus far to condescend unto them, and to leave him wholly to their disposal, vers. 5.

*{and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelek, that was in the court of the prison:}* Or, as some read the words, supposing a trajection in them, *they took Jeremy who was in the court of the prison* (as yet remaining there, Chap. 37.21.) *and cast him into the pit,* or, *hole* (as Gen. 37.22. Chap. 41.7.) *of Malchiah, the son of Hammelec,* or, the king's son. See Chap. 36.26. a filthy dungeon, far worse than that of Jonathan's, Chap. 37.15,16. situate in some part, or place of Malchiah's house where being destitute of all means of relief, he might by the noisomeness of the place soon perish, and nobody know what was become of him. Thus Satan's instruments, therein like their master, are wont to be the fiercer, the shorter their time is to tyrannize. Rev. 12.12.

*{and they let down Jeremiah with cords:}* There being it seems no stairs, or ordinary passage down into it, vers. 12,13. and no means consequently of any relief likely there to come at him.

*{and in the dungeon there was no water, but mire:}* Which made it the more noisome, Zach. 9.11.

*{So Jeremiah sunk in the mire.}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 32.15. sunk, or, stuck fast; as 1 Sam. 17.49. Psalm 69.2. So verse 22. And of this pit some expound that in Lamentations 3.55. but see there.

**Verse 7.** *{Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the Eunuchs, which was in the kings house, heard that, they had put Jeremiah into the dungeon,}* The business, it seems, was not so closely kept, or covertly carried, but that it came to this godly courtier's ear; whom the Lord, according to his promise more than once to the Prophet, Chap. 1.19. and 15.20,21. made an instrument of his delivery and safety.

*{Now when}* Heb. *And. And he heard,—and he went out,* vers. 8. for, *Now when he heard,—he went out;* as vers. 1.4.

*{Ebedmelech}* Or, *a servant of the King,* a courtier, as the Chaldee, who renders it, *a servant of the King Zedekiah:* and the Jewish doctors, descanting thereupon, tell us, that by the Cushite is meant Zedekiah, that had changed his hue with the times, from good to bad, but would not change back. Again: as Chap. 13.23. and that this *servant of the King,* was Baruc the son of Neriah: but these are their fond fancies, which one sounder than his fellow Rabbines justly controls, observing that then the article would have been prefixed before the word *King,* as in the clause following it is, but is not here; and concludes therefore Ebedmelech to be his proper name, Chap. 39.16. as the like is Abimelech, Judge 8.31. and Achimelech, 1 Sam. 21.1.

*{the Ethiopian}* Heb. *Cushite*: as Num. 12.1. See Chap. 13.23. Better affected did this stranger show himself towards God's Prophet, than those that professed themselves to be, and by birth were, of the body of God's people; and well therefore deserving to be preferred before them, Rom. 2.26,27.

*{one of the Eunuchs}* Heb. *a man an Eunuch*; as Act. 8.27. whence the word may seem to be as there, so here, a name, not of office as the Chaldee takes it, but of bodily state and condition, See Esai. 56.3,4.

*{which was in the Kings house}* Or, *who was* (Heb. *and he was;* as Chap. 26.23.) *of the Kings house.* So is the particle used and rendered, 2 Sam. 12.1. In this ungodly king's family as well as in Herod's, Luk. 8.3. and in Nero's, Phil. 4.22. there were yet some well affected. See 1 King. 14.13. and 18.3,12,13.

*{in the dungeon}* As verse 6.

*{(the King then sitting in the gate of Benjamin)}* To receive petitions, hear causes, and decide controversies; and pass censures; the gates of the cities being the ordinary places of audience and judicature, Deut. 17.2,8. 2 Sam. 19.8. Prov. 21.22. Lam. 5.12. for it is but a frivolous conceit of those, who suppose that the king sat in the gate, considering how to make an escape out of the city, he had other privater ways to have done it than that, 2 King. 25.4. Of this gate, see Chap. 37.13. Heb. *and the king was sitting in the gate.*

**Verse 8.** *{Ebedmelech went out of the kings house, and spake to the king, saying;}* He stayed not till the king came in again, (the Prophet in the mean space might have perished) nor did he wait his time, to break the matter to the king in private; but though he knew beforehand, how distasteful his motion would be to the princes, who in likelihood were divers of them there attending upon him, he had the courage in open court to complain to the king sitting on the bench to their faces, of their barbarous and inhuman usage of God's priest and Prophet; and to press the king in his behalf, for his speedy delivery out of the present distress.

**Verse 9.** *{My LORD, the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the Prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon.}* These men that stand here attending upon you: he dares tell them their own to their faces; and in open court publish how they had dealt with God's Prophet in secret. Such courage and confidence, and such freedom of speech should men have in God's cause, Psalm 119.46. Thus the Prophet found more favor and aid at the hand of a stranger, than at the hands of any one of his own countrymen: as God more obedience, Chap. 3.14,15. and more repentance, Jon. 3.10. and Christ more faith, Matth. 8.10. than in God's own professed people; to their greater condemnation, Matth. 21.41,42.

*{and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is:}* And there he is like to perish for want of relief; because nobody seeks him to pity him, nor can look after him to relieve him (as formerly they might and did) where now he is. So the Rabbine; or, as the words would rather be read, *who* (Heb. *and he,* as verse 7.) *would have dyed* (Heb. *will dye;* but used here in a potential notion, as Hosea 7.1.) *for hunger in the place where he was.* Heb. *under him,* or, *in his place:* as Job 7.10. Psalm 109.16. to wit, in the prison, Chap. 37.21. and it argues therefore in them a most spiteful and inhuman disposition toward the Prophet, by so vile and base a course to seek to hasten his end, when as he could not have long subsisted, though they had let him alone, had the siege been for any considerable time lengthened; the reason is subjoined in the words following.

*{for there is no more bread in the city.}* The city stores are in a manner clean spent; from whence by the king's appointment, so long as they held out, he was to receive some daily, though but slender, allowance, Chap. 37.21.

**Verse 10.** *{Then the King commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying; Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the Prophet out of the dungeon before he die.}* The hazard the Prophet was in, required haste. And the king, better advised, presses it to be done speedily, without further delay; and orders Ebedmelech therefore to take a competent number of persons then and there present to be assistant unto him in dispatching the business; which as he readily goes about, verse 11. But why thirty men to draw up one? when as three or four at most would suffice: To this some answer; because the pit was very deep: and so in likelihood it was; the upper part of the city standing on a craggy hill, and yet mire found in the bottom of it: yet fewer might have served for such a business; nor could many in likelihood be employed about it: the Jewish doctors say, because their bodies were generally so weakened, and their strength so impaired with famine, that a few men were not able to do it; but this seems as improbable as the former: it is rather therefore not amiss conceived by others, that those men were taken along with him to be assistant unto him, not in the drawing up of the Prophet only, but in withstanding and keeping off of any that should offer to oppose, or disturb them in the execution of the king's command.

*{Then}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 37.6.

*{take from hence}* take and lead from hence. So ver. 11.

*{with thee}* Heb. *in thy hand;* as Chap. 4.19. So ver. 11.

**Verse 11.** *{So Ebedmelech took the men with him,}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 6. and, *in his hand;* took and led them along with him; as vers. 10.

*{and went into the house of the King under the treasury,}* Or, *storehouse*, (as the word in a generality signifies, 1 Chro. 27.22. Neh. 12.44. and 13.12.) under which, into some cell, cellar, or vault, were cast-clothes and such trumpery wont to be cast. Heb. *to under*, for, *to a place under*: as, *to a place that I know not*, 1 King. 18.12.

*{and took thence}* took, and brought, or, carried from thence, a complexive form of speech; as Chap. 36.14.

*{old cast clouts, and old rotten rags,}* Heb. *old*, or, *worn*, clouts, *of cast*, or, *torn things*; (for the one word comes of a term that signifies to be old, and worn out with long wearing, Deut. 9.5. the other of a root that signifies to drag, and tear, chap. 15.3.) and old, or, *worn* clouts (for the subject wants, as Esai. 28.4. Ezek. 13.4.) of salts; that is, rotted, as with salt; or wasted with wearing, as salt does when it melts. See Esai. 51.6. and 64.6.

*{and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.}* To make use of in the drawing of him up: being softer and fitter for that purpose than clothes of better worth.

*{by cords}* Partly, because the pit in likelihood was deeper, than that they could by hand be reached to him; and partly, lest they should in casting down be scattered, or falling into the mire be made unserviceable unto him.

**Verse 12.** *{And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah; Put now these cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords.}* That is, between your armholes and the cords, to keep the cords from fretting and galling the skin and flesh of those parts, which the weight of his body was to rest and hang upon in the pulling of him up. Heb. *under the hollow places of thine hands;* that which some render, *put them under thine arm holes with thine hands:* and such a defect of the instrumental particle is not unfrequently found; as Psalm 17.13,14. but I suppose we need not have recourse to that defect here: the hollow places of the hands, are no other than the armholes: so likewise termed, Ezek. 13.18. the hands put for the arms; as Esai. 25.11. See there; as also chap. 48.57.

*{and Jeremiah did so.}*

**Verse 13.** *{So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him out of the dungeon; and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.}* Where before he abode, and whither now he was remitted. See Chap. 37.21.

**Verse 14.** *{Then Zedekiah the King sent, and took Jeremiah the Prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the LORD.}* Hence follows the narrative of another personal conference had in private between the king and the Prophet, during the time of his restraint. A former, see Chap. 37.17. that but short, this more large.

*{Then}* Or, *Afterward.* Heb. *And,* as Exod. 32.6.

*{took}* Caused him to be taken and brought; as vers. 10.11.

*{into the third entry}* Of this third entry, or, as some would have it rendered, principal entry; (as coming from a term that signifies a prince. Exod. 15.4. 2 King. 7.2.) being nowhere else read; neither our writers, nor the Jewish themselves, have any great certainty: the most suppose it to be that on the south side of the Temple, by which the king entered, when he came thither from his palace; called therefore the king's entry, 2 King. 16.18. yet it seems by Ezek. 46.1,8. that the king used to enter, not by the south, but by the east gate.

*{that is in the house of the LORD}* Or, *that went to it.* See 1 King. 10.5,12. 1 Chro. 26.16,18. 2 Chr. 9.11. Esai. 6.13. and it may as well be meant of an entry in the king's house, as of an entry in the Temple: and to the former rather I incline, supposing this prison, wherein the Prophet now abode, to have been in some part of the king's house. See Chap. 37.15,22. and conceive that the words may well be rendered, *into the third entry* (to wit, of the king's house that, consisted of three several courts, or parts, 2 King. 20.4. Chap. 36.12,20.) *which is by the house of the Lord;* near unto it, or of all the entries, or passages about the king's house next to it. See the very like, Chap. 2.20.

*{and the King said to Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me.}* Heb. *I am asking thee a word; conceal not a word from me:* a word, for, a thing, or, ought; as Chap. 26.2. and 32.27. So ver. 14. Thus wicked men will seem desirous to know, what they are not willing to hear.

**Verse 15.** *{Then Jeremiah said unto Zedekiah}* Heb. *And;* as before, verse 14.

*{If I declare it unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death?}* Heb. *slaying slay;* as Chap. 26.19. as if he had said; will you not put me to death, if I deal plainly and freely with you; if I tell you the truth.

*{and if I give thee counsel wilt thou not hearken unto me?}* This latter branch would rather be read enunciatively; on this wise, *and though* (as Psal. 23.4.) *I advise thee, thou wilt not hearken to me:* as if he should say, it is to small purpose for me to speak ought to you; for if I tell you the truth of things, you will but slay me for it: (for negative interrogatives do more vigorously affirm) and though I give you never so good counsel, (as formerly I have done) yet you will not follow mine advice.

**Verse 16.** *{So the King Zedekiah sware secretly unto Jeremiah, saying,}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 13. in secret; as Chap. 37.17. being overawed by his princes, verse 25.

*{As the LORD liveth}* The usual form of an oath, Chap. 4.2. and 5.2.

*{that made us this soul}* That gave unto either of us that soul, or that life, whereby we live, Gen. 2.7. Psalm 33.15. Eccles. 12.7. Esai. 57.16.

*{I will not put thee to death}* Heb. *if I slay thee;* and so in the next branch, *If I give thee,* etc. of which manner of speech, usual in oaths, see on Esai. 5.9. and 22.14. and 62.8.

*{neither will I give thee into the hand of those that seek thy life.}* Heb. *and.* and, hand, for, power; as chap. 34.20.

**Verse 17.** *{Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah,}* Heb. *And,* as before, verse 15.

*{Thus saith the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel:}* As Chap. 35.17.

*{If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylons Princes,}* Heb. *going forth, go forth;* as 2 King. 4.11. and yield yourself to them, vers. 21. as Jehoiachin did, 2 King. 24.12. *unto his Princes:* for the king himself was not in person then before Jerusalem, nor at the surprisal of the city. See Chap. 39.3,5.

*{then thy soul shall live;}* Heb. *and thy soul shall live;* (as Gen. 19.20. and my soul shall live) thou shalt live; you shall be in safety. So Psal. 119.175. *Let my soul live,* for, *Let me live.*

*{and this city shall not be burnt with fire,}* As otherwise it will, chap. 37.8. vers. 18.

*{and thou shalt live, and thine house.}* Your family, wives, children, and servants. See vers. 23.

**Verse 18.** *{But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylons Princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand.}* Heb. *And.* and, And, for, But, and, Then; as verse 2.5. See Chap. 32.3,4.

**Verse 19.** *{And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid of the Jews that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me.}* He feared more the mocking of men, than the disobeying of God. Thus a man's fear casts him into a snare, Prov. 29.25. See the like, 1 Sam. 31.4. 1 Chro. 10.4. Judge 9.54.

**Verse 20.** *{But Jeremiah said, They shall not deliver thee:}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 18. and give thee, as vers. 19. God knows the affections of all men, and sways them as he pleases. See 1 Sam. 23.14. Psal. 105.25. and 106.46.

*{obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the LORD, which I speak unto thee;}* Heb. *hear* (as Chap. 7.23.) not my word, but God's; who is able to secure you against all these groundless and false fears.

*{so it shall be well unto thee,}* or, *it shall go well with thee,* as Deut. 28.63. Job 22.21.

*{and thy soul shall live.}* As vers. 17.

**Verse 21.** *{But if thou refuse to go forth; this is the word that the LORD hath shewed me;}* Heb. *And.* as verse 18. and, the word, for, the thing, or, that, simply; as verse 14. and, made me see; does as certainly assure me of it, as if I saw it. See Esai. 2.1.

**Verse 22.** *{And behold,}* Or, *That behold;* as Chap. 35.11. or, *Then behold;* as vers. 17.18. otherwise the words following will have no good coherence with the former.

*{all the women that are left in the King of Judahs house,}* Either those that were left in the king's palace, when Jeconiah and his mother, and others with them were carried away, 2 King. 24.12. or that Zedekiah should leave there, when he should seek to save himself by flight, chap. 39.4. 2 King. 25.4. and then the noun is put for the pronoun: as Esai. 2.1. But the former seems more probable, that such court-ladies that were left behind, when Jeconiah went away, a crew of wanton creatures, would be insulting over Zedekiah, and asking him why he could not do as Jeconiah did before.

*{shall be brought forth to the King of Babylons Princes,}* To be disposed of at their pleasure.

*{and those women shall say,}* Heb. *and they will be saying;* these twitting terms, or the like, will be rife in their mouths.

*{Thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee;}* Heb. *The men of thy peace,* or, *thy men of peace;* as Psalm 41.9. Chap. 20.10. Obad. 7. Either your false Prophets and priests, and princes; or the Egyptians your confederates have enticed, and encouraged to revolt from, and rebel against the king of Babylon, and to stand out stiffly and unadvisedly against his forces, and have contrary to that wholesome advice that has been from time to time given you, and your own inclination at some times to hearken thereunto, persuaded you, and prevailed with you to hold on in that desperate course to your own ruin, and now leave you in the lurch, Chap. 2.36,37. and 30.14. 37.19.

*{thy feet are sunk in the mire;}* Or, *stick fast*, or, *are set fast*: as the word is used, Job 38.6. Prov. 8.25. So vers. 6. a proverbial speech used of such, as are brought into grievous difficulties, out of which they are unable to unwind themselves, Psalm 69.2. And some of the Jewish doctors suppose, that there is in these terms an allusion to some quagmire, wherein Zedekiah should be taken, when the enemy overtook him, Chap. 39.5. But howsoever, thus that befell him from women, which from men he so much feared. See Prov. 10.24.

*{and they are turned away backward.}* This the Jewish commenters, and most others, understood of Zedekiah, and apply to his feet before mentioned, *thy feet are turned backward:* and this some expound of his revolt from the king of Babylon; as the word is used of the like, Psal. 44.18. and 80.18. Others of his being constrained at length to turn back, and betake himself to flight, not being able now to go on, or hold out any longer. So is the word used, Psal. 35.4. and 70.3. Esai. 42.17. chap. 46.5. and this seems most probable. Howbeit, some understand it, of his friends before spoken of: that they were turned back, and had deserted him in his straits. See chap. 37.7. But the former seems the better. Some learned interpreters mince this passage into parcels, reading the words, that *thy friends have incited thee,—and that thy feet are fast in the mire,* and that *they are turned backward.* But such supplies I suppose here needless.

**Verse 23.** *{So they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children to the Chaldeans}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 11. or, *For;* as chap. 36.9. as rendering a reason of the foregoing predictions; or subjoining the means, whereby this should come about, and be effected: *For they shall bring out all thy women,* (the word is the same with that, ver. 22. and may well comprehend concubines, and such like court-creatures, as well as his wives) *and thy sons;* (for so the word here is) who were taken and carried away by the Chaldeans, and slain before their father's face, and in his sight. chap. 39.6. for as for his daughters, it seems that, being less regarded, they were left behind. See Chap. 41.10. and 43.6. These he mentions the rather, to move him to hearken to the advice given him, if not for himself, yet out of fatherly regard and tender affection unto them: See the like, Deut. 28.32,41. Chap. 5.17. and 16.3.

*{and thou shalt not escape out of their hand}* As verse 18. though you attempt so to do, 2 King. 25.4–6.

*{but shalt be taken by the hand of the King of Babylon.}* That is, by such power and force, as he shall raise and send to take you, and your city. See vers. 17.

*{and thou shalt cause this city to be burnt with fire}* Heb. *thou shalt burn this citie with fire;* as Num. 4.18. cut not off, for, cause not to be cut off: you by your obstinacy will be the means to procure the burning of the city, which by rendition of yourself you might save. Yet some render the words, *and this citie shall be burnt with fire:* And in our English indeed, it might run well enough, were it said; *And this citie shall burn with fire.* But I find not where the Hebrew verb here used is in this form ever found in a passive sense.

**Verse 24.** *{Then said Zedekiah unto Jeremiah}* Heb. *And;* as verse 17.

*{Let no man know of these words}* These matters that have passed between you and me in private. Heb. *Let not a man know:* a man, for, any man; as chap. 5.1. and, words, for, things, or, matters; as chap. 26.10. Esth. 9.31.

*{and thou shalt not die.}* You shall not suffer death for ought that you have now spoken; according to his solemn oath and promise, vers. 16. or, as the words may well be rendered, *that thou die not:* so is the copulative oft used, Josh. 24.9. Mal. 1.9. lest the princes put you to death, as it is to be feared they will do, if they come to understand what you have spoken to me.

**Verse 25.** *{But if the Princes hear that I have talked with thee}* Heb. *And* (as vers. 21.) *when;* as Jer. 12.5. the princes that overawed the king, and whom he was afraid to displease, vers. 5.

*{and they come unto thee, and say unto thee; Declare unto us now what thou hast said unto the King: hide it not from us and we will not put thee to death; also what the King said unto thee.}* In such a vassalage was this poor king to his princes, that he might not have any communication in private with any, but they would be diving into it, and dealing with him for it beyond duty, if they liked it not.

**Verse 26.** *{Then shalt thou say unto them,}* *And;* as before, verse 17.

*{I presented my supplication before the King, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathans house to die there.}* Heb. *I made my supplication to fall before the King,* or, to his face, or, in his presence; Chap. 36.7. and 42.2. that is, in humble and submiss manner falling down before him, I preferred my suit to him; and this indeed he had formerly made suit to the king for, Chap. 37.20. and it is not unlikely but that he now renewed it again; the rather, some hint being given him by the king to that purpose, that so he should do.

**Verse 27.** *{Then came all the Princes unto Jeremiah, and asked him;}* What the king suspected, accordingly fell out, Heb. *And;* as verse 24.

*{and he told them according to all these words, that the King had commanded:}* Words, again, for, things; as vers. 24.

*{so they left off speaking with him:}* Heb. *and* (as vers. 23.) *they were silent* or, *ceased, from him;* as Job 13.13.

*{for the matter was not perceived.}* Or, *while* (as Prov. 19.18.) *the matter* (Heb. *word;* as vers. 14. chap. 52.34.) *was not perceived;* as chap. 5.15. as if he had said, *the matter* remained the while undiscovered, according to the king's desire.

**Verse 28.** *{So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison}* Heb. *And;* as ver. 27. and, sat in the court of custody, chap. 37.21.

*{until the day wherein Jerusalem was taken;}* As he still told them it would be, vers. 3. chap. 37.8. being now no more shifted from place to place, as formerly he had been.

*{and he was there when Jerusalem was taken.}* Being then there found, and from thence taken, and not long after set free by the king of Babylon's officers, at their master's command. chap. 39.12–14. and 40.1–4. a defect of the local particle; as Job 3.18.

## CHAPTER 39

**Verse 1.** *{In the ninth year of Zedekiah King of Judah,}* This relation of the siege, and surrender of Jerusalem, ver. 1–3. Zedekiah's attempt to escape by flight, apprehension and captivity, together with the slaughter of his sons and his nobility, and loss of his sight, ver. 4–7. the burning of the city, vers. 8. the deportation of the people, ver. 9,10. and the Prophet's delivery out of prison, ver. 11–14. is here inserted, partly, to declare the complement of the Prophet's foregoing predictions; and partly, to make way for, and give light unto some occurrents afterward reported in the chapters ensuing.

*{In the ninth year of Zedekiah}* For in that year the siege began, 2 King. 25.1.

*{in the tenth month}* The month Tebeth, Esther 2.16. containing part of our December, and part of our January, Chap. 52.4.

*{came Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon, and all his army against Jerusalem and they besieged it.}* Or, *with all his army:* for so is the copulative oft used: as chap. 26.21. and 27.2. the occasion of this his expedition and invasion was, because Zedekiah, whom he had made king of Judah, was revolted from him, and rebelled against him, 2 King. 24.17,20. He came thither with them, but having settled the siege, withdrew himself to take his ease and pleasure elsewhere, leaving the business to be pursued and carried on by his princes. See chap. 38.17.

**Verse 2.** *{And in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month,}* The month Tamuz consisting partly of our June, and partly of our July.

*{the ninth day of the month the city was broken up:}* Stormed and taken: some of the gates being first broken open, and part of the city surprised, ver. 3. the rest thereupon given up, 2 King. 25.3. Chap. 52.6. So that the siege continued about a twelvemonth, and an half. Hence the fast of the fourth month, Zach. 8.19. for the surprisal of the city.

**Verse 3.** *{And all the Princes of the King of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate:}* Called the second gate, Zeph. 1.10. situate in the mid-wall that divided the one part of the city from the other; So the most. Yet some of the Jewish doctors say, it was the eastern gate: of which, Chap. 19.2. so called; because it stood between two other gates on one side of the city: And others again, because it stood between the city and the Temple. But howsoever about the particular gate they jar; herein they agree, that Jeremy's prophecy was hereby fulfilled, of the king of Babylon's commanders setting their thrones in the gates of Jerusalem, Chap. 1.15. But of that place, see there. Why they made a stay at this gate is some question made: and some suppose it done out of wariness, it being not safe to pierce suddenly overfar into a strong and large city, wherein trains and ambushments may be, until all be well cleared; which is not unlikely.

*{even Nergal-sharezer}* The Jewish doctor tells us, that these are two several names of several parties: but the most rather (as does our version) take them for one name: the latter part of the name, one of Sennacherib's sons bare, Esai. 37.38. whence it may seem to have been an Assyrian name.

*{Samgar Nebo}* This most take also for the proper name of a party distinct from the former. But a learned interpreter deems it to be a name of office belonging to the fore-named party; and to signify the keeper, or treasurer of the temple of Nebo, a principal idol among the Babylonians, Esai. 46.1. and the Hebrew points and pauses, both in this, and the following, incline this way.

*{Sarsechim, Rabsaris,}* The former seems the name of the man; the latter is clearly the name of his office; and signifies the captain of the guard.

*{Nergal Sharezer, Rabmag,}* One of the same name with the first; (whereby it appears, that it was an usual name with them) from whom to distinguish him, his office is added: and the title given him is by some deemed to signify the camp-master: though a learned late writer would have it to be, the master of the magicians. But the former seems more probable.

*{with all the residue of the Princes of the King of Babylon.}* Heb. *and all;* as ver. 1. for three only of them are here named.

**Verse 4.** *{And it came to passe, that when Zedekiah the King of Judah saw them, and all the men of war, then they fled,}* Or, *And so it was* (as chap. 36.16.) *when Zedekiah and all the men of war saw them;* (for there is a trajection in the words) *that they fled.* Heb. *And they fled;* as chap. 35.11. as despairing now, and not daring, either to hold out any further, or to stay any longer by it; considering how far they had pierced into the city.

*{and went forth out of the city by night}* The more secretly to escape in the dark: which secret flight of his, see described, Ezek. 12.12.

*{by the way of the Kings garden, by the gate betwixt two walls;}* By some postern gate on the south side of the city, (for on that side the king's gardens seem to have been situate) by some supposed to have another wall before it, besides that wherein it stood: but it seems rather to have been situate at the end of some private passage, having on either side a wall to make it the more private. The Jewish doctors tell us of a cave, or vault, underground, reaching from the king's house to the plains of Jericho, by which the king should attempt to escape: but this seems one of their wonted figments. See 2 King. 25.4. Chap. 52.7.

*{and he went out the way of the plain.}* Intending, it may be, for Egypt.

**Verse 5.** *{But the Chaldeans pursued after them,}* Heb. *And;* as chap. 38.15. See Lam. 4.19.

*{and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho:}* This is the sandy ground on which the Talmudists build their fabulous vault: whereof, on vers. 4. But this is not amiss observed to be the net that God threatened to catch him in, for the breach of his oath, Ezek. 17.10.

*{and when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar King of Babylon.}* Heb. *and they took him, and made him ascend,* or, *brought him,* simply; as 1 Sam. 7.1. So 2 King. 25.6. chap. 52.9. See this foretold him by Jeremy. chap. 32.4. and 34.3.

*{to Riblah in the land of Hamath}* Of this Riblah, see Num. 34.11. It is supposed to be that which was afterward called Antiochia in Syria: a very pleasant place, where Nebuchadnezzar lay, and kept his court, to repose, and solace himself, during the siege: which it may be also proved longer than he looked for.

*{where he gave judgment upon him.}* For his perfidious treachery and perjury joined with it. Heb. *spake judgements with him;* as chap. 4.12. and 12.1. and 21.9.

**Verse 6.** *{Then the King of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah in Riblah before his eyes,}* He caused them to be slain, (as chap. 37.15. and 52.10. 1 Sam. 15.33.) being brought thither to him, (as was foretold they should be, chap. 38.23.) in his sight, before he put out his eyes: to aggravate his grief, see Deut. 28.32. Heb. *And;* as Chap. 38.24.

*{also the King of Babylon slew all the nobles of Judah}* That had encouraged, yea, in some sort, enforced Zedekiah to stand out against him, Chap. 38.4,22. Heb. *and;* as Chap. 29.20. and white ones, as Chap. 27.20.

**Verse 7.** *{Moreover he put out Zedekiahs eyes:}* Heb. *And* (as chap. 38.12.) *he blinded* (as Deut. 16.19.) *Zedekiahs eyes:* and so abandoned him to a perpetual darkness: hence that Ezek. 12.13. that he should not see Babylon, though he should be brought thither. Howbeit, he slew him not, as Jeremy had also foretold, ch. 34.4.

*{and bound him with chains}* Heb. *with two brasses;* or, *of brasse:* to wit, chains, or fetters; as Judge 16.21.

*{to carry him to Babylon.}* So bound; as also he did, Chap. 32.5. and 34.3. and 52.11. Ezek. 12.13. 2 King. 25.7. See the like, 2 Chron. 36.6.

**Verse 8.** *{And the Chaldeans burnt the kings house, and the houses of the people with fire:}* Chap. 21.10. and 37.8. and 38.18,23. and 52.13. Lam. 2.5. 2 King. 25.9. Heb. *the house of the people*: which some of the Jewish doctors expound of synagogues, or other places of public convention: and some of ours, a place near to the king's court, whither people used to resort for exercise of shooting, sporting, walking and feasting: But others, and most of both, take it in an ordinary, but collective notion, for the dwellings of the inferior people; confirmed by that, 2 King. 25.9. and Chap. 52.13. *and all the houses of Jerusalem.*

*{and brake down the walls of Jerusalem.}* Chap. 52.14. 2 King. 25.10. Lam. 2.2,8,18. Neh. 1.3.

**Verse 9.** *{Then Nebuzaradan the Captain of the Guard.}* Or, *Provost Marshall.* Heb. *chief*, or, *master of the executioners*, or, *slaughter-men*: as Gen. 39.1. So also, vers. 10.11. the old Greek renders it, *the master of the cooks:* because the word is sometime used for a cook, that kills and dresses flesh, 1 Sam. 8.13. and 9.23. And some other again, *the master of the butchers;* because the Greek term includes either: but neither of these here seems suitable. Heb. *And;* as vers. 6.

*{carried captive into Babylon the remnant of the city, and those that fell away, that fell to him, with the rest of the people that remained.}* Heb. *and the rest:* Whence some interpreters supposing three sorts of persons here prescribed, would have the first, such as were found in the city, when it was taken: the second, such as had gone out to the Chaldeans during the time of the siege: the third, such as had left the city, when the siege was intermitted, Chap. 37.12. Others would have the first to be those that were left in the city formerly, when Jeconiah was carried captive: the last, those that were now remaining there. But I conceive only two sorts mentioned that were led away; those left in the city, and those that had gone out to the Chaldeans together with them: as our version well renders it. Nor is that use of the copulative unusual. So vers. 1,3. Chap. 22.7,14. and 26.2. Neh. 12.42. Even those also that turned to them, as well as those that stayed in the city, they took along with them to Babylon, though better entreating, it may be, the one than the other.

**Verse 10.** *{But Nebuzaradan the Captain of the Guard}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 5. See vers. 9.

*{left of the poor of the people, which had nothing in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields, at the same time.}* That they might till and husband the land, and it might not wholly run to ruin, and become utterly waste, 2 King. 25.12. Chap. 52.19. but might yield some revenue to the king of Babylon, and such rulers, as he should set over it, Neh. 9.36,37. But thus the rich and mighty, that trusted most to their shifts and means, were through God's just judgment most rigorously handled, when the meaner sort fared better than either they now did, or themselves formerly had done: And by this means, God in all likelihood providentially so disposed it, that many poor, who had by the greater and wealthier sort, been formerly oppressed and forced out of their possessions, came both to recover their own again, and to be owners also of their lands, who had in former times so oppressed them. See Esai. 5.15,17. and 7.21,22. and 28.15,18. Ezek. 34.17–22.

*{at the same time}* Heb. *in that day:* As Esai. 26.1. vers. 17.

**Verse 11.** *{Now Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon gave charge concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, saying:}* Or, by Nebuzaradan. Heb. *by the hand of Nebuzaradan:* as Chap. 37.2. God not unmindful of his Prophet, and his promise to secure him, Chap. 15.11,21. inclined the heart of this great monarch, and conqueror, to provide for the Prophet's safety: that which he the rather, in likelihood, was also inclinable unto, having been informed by those who during the time of the siege had got out of the city, of the Prophet's preaching and pressing both king and people to submit and yield themselves up unto him: and what hard measure he had sustained for so doing. See chap. 21.9. and 38.2–6. *Now.* Heb. *And;* as Chapter 27.4. So verse 15.

**Verse 12.** *{take him, and look well to him;}* *Set thine eyes upon him;* as Psal. 34.15. So Chap. 38.4.

*{and do him no harm}* Heb. *evil*; as Chap. 38.4.

*{but do unto him, even as he shall say unto thee.}* Let him have whatsoever he shall require. Thus God used him as an instrument to deliver and preserve his Prophet, whom he made a scourge to punish his adversaries.

**Verse 13.** *{So Nebuzaradan the Captain of the guard sent, and Nebushasban, Rabsaris, and Nergal Sharezer Rabmag, and all the King of Babylons Princes}* Heb. *great ones*; as Chap. 41.1. and 52.13. Of these names, see before, vers. 3. He that was called Sarsechim there, is called Nebushasban here: it may seem he had two names; or there were two of them that bare that office: all the princes, for, the rest of them; as Chap. 36.12. and as, all the captains, Chap. 40.13.

**Verse 14.** *{Even they sent and took Jeremiah out of the court of the prison,}* Where as yet he remained, chap. 38.28. Heb. *And.* as chap. 33.24. *they sent and took,* that is, they sent to take: and so after, to commit: as, rose and warred, for, rose to war, Joh. 24.9. They give order to have him taken out of prison, and set at liberty, and recommended to Gedaliah: which yet seems not to have been presently put in execution. See chap. 40.1–4.

*{and committed him}* Or, *and to commit him*; as before. Heb. *and they gave him;* as 2 Chron. 24.12. Esay 22.21.

*{unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan}* Whom the king of Babylon had set over those that were left in the land, 2 Kings 25.22. chap. 40.5. he seems to have been the son of that Ahikam, that rescued the Prophet out of the hands of the priests in Jehoiakim's reign, chap. 26.24.

*{That he should carry him home}* That he might either take him home to him; or convey him home to his own house at Anathoth, chap. 1.1.

*{so he dwelt among the people}* Heb. *and.* as verse 13. and, in the midst of the people; as chap. 29.32. & 37. Howbeit, the words would rather be rendered; *Yet* (as chap. 37.15. and 35.14.) *he abode* still, or, *staid,* (as the word is used, Deut. 9.9. Chap. 38.13,28.) *among the people;* with whom, through the negligence of those, to whom the charge of him was committed, though let out of prison, with such others as were found there, yet was he not loosed from his bonds, but carried among the rest in chains unto Riblah. See chap. 40.1.

**Verse 15.** *{Now the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah, while he was shut up in the court of the prison saying;}* Here begins a new relation of a business that fell out in the time of his latter commitment to the prison court, after he had been drawn up out of Malchiah's dungeon, chap. 38.13,28. and it concerning a gracious message sent by him from God to Ebedmelech, who had been a chief instrument of helping him out of that dungeon, chap. 38.7–13. Heb. *And the word of the Lord was,* etc. as Chap. 32.1. & 33.1.

**Verse 16.** *{Go and speak unto Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying,}* Heb. *Going go, and thou shalt say;* as chap. 28.13. of this Ebedmelech, see Chap. 38.7. Yet we are not hence to gather, that the Prophet was then at liberty; because God bids him go, and deliver him this message: it is a familiar term of incitement to the doing of ought, requiring nothing of the Prophet, but that he should sometime acquaint him with it, either by sending to him, or by word of mouth when he should come to visit him.

*{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts; the God of Israel;}* As Chapter 33.13.

*{Behold, I will bring my words upon this city for evil, and not for good}* See chap. 21.16. & 44.27.

*{and they shall be accomplished in that day before thee.}* At that time, as verse 12. You surviving to see it; as chap. 16.9. & 20.4.

**Verse 17.** *{But I will deliver thee in that day, and thou shalt not be delivered into the hand of those men of whom thou art afraid.}* This reward had he for his piety showed to God's Prophet, Chap. 37.7–13. Heb. *And.* as verse 20. and, before whose face you are afraid; as Chap. 22.25.

**Verse 18.** *{For I will surely deliver thee,}* Or, *But,* as chap. 14.2. and, Heb. *delivering deliver;* as the like, Esay 36.15.

*{and thou shalt not fall by the sword,}* That is, be slain; because men slain fall to the ground. So Psalm 63.10. Luke 21.24.

*{but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee,}* Heb. *and thy soul shall be for a prey unto thee.* See chap. 21.9. So chap. 45.5.

*{because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.}* *He will deliver them—and save them, because they trust in him,* Psal. 37.40.

## CHAPTER 40

**Verse 1.** *{The word of the LORD, which came to Jeremiah,}* These words are the title or inscription, of a word or message sent from God, and delivered by the Prophet unto the captains, or heads of those people, that were left in the land, under the government of Gedaliah, recorded, chap. 42.7. for all between this and that, is but matter of story, relating the time and occasion of it, to clear the way to it, and to procure the better understanding of it. See of the form, chap. 42.4.

*{after that Nebuzaradan the Captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah,}* Heb. *had sent*, or, *dismissed him* (as 1 King. 20.42.) *from Ramah*, whither he had by oversight, contrary to the king's charge given concerning him, been brought, so soon as he understood who he was, Verse 4. See chap. 31.15. & 39.11,14.

*{when he had taken him being bound in chains among all that were carried away captive of Jerusalem and Judah, which were carried away captive unto Babylon.}* Heb. *when he had taken him, and he was bound,* etc. or, *for he was bound;* and being found in bonds, was brought along to Ramah among the rest of the captives intended for Babylon; no notice being taken of him before he came thither, *in chains,* or manicles, Verse 4. See Job 36.8. Psal. 149.8. Esay 45.14. Heb. *in the midst* (as chap. 39.14.) *of all the captivity;* as chap. 29.1.

**Verse 2.** *{And the captain of the guard took Jeremiah,}* Or, as some render it, *For* (as chap. 36.9.) *the captain of the guard took him.* I should rather take the former copulative, verse 1. in a causative notion; and this in a discretive: *for he was bound,—but the captain of the guard,* so soon as he had notice of him, took him, and loosed him from his bonds, and set him at liberty.

*{saying, The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place.}* The infidel prince is caused to utter and aver that, which out of obstinacy God's own people would not see and acknowledge: and it is not unlikely, but that by those that fled to the Chaldean camp, he had heard of the substance and subject matter of Jeremy's sermons.

**Verse 3.** *{Now the LORD hath brought it, and done according as he hath said:}* Heb. *And the Lord hath brought and done according to what he said.*

*{because ye have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing is come upon you.}* See chap. 50.7. or, *for ye have sinned against the Lord,* (Heb. *unto the Lord*, as chap. 8.14.) *and have not hearkned to his voyce;* (as chap. 9.12.) *and this thing* (Heb. *word*; as chap. 38.14.) *is come upon you,*

**Verse 4.** *{And now}* Here seems to have been a twofold reading, the one most commonly received; which our version follows: another, some interpreters exhibit, who render the words, *And thou,* O, as for you; put absolutely: as, *and I,* or, as for me, 1 Chron. 28.2.

*{behold, I loose thee this day from the chains which were upon thine hand:}* Or, *that are upon thine hands;* as it is said of Peter, Acts 12.7. *his chains fell off from his hands:* for the word hand, is collective: and it appears that he came in chains manacled to Ramah Verse 1.

*{if it seem good unto thee to come with me into Babylon, come, and I will look well unto thee:}* Heb. *if it be good in thine eyes* (as Gen. 20.15.) *to go with me to Babylon,* (a defect of the local particle; as Chap. 32.5.) *come,* as 1 Kings 13.7.) *and I will set mine eye upon thee;* as chap. 39.12.

*{but if it seem evil unto thee to come with me into Babylon, forbear:}* O, or (Heb. *and*, as chap. 2.18. & 5.12.) *if it like thee not* (Heb. *be evil in thine eyes;* as Josh. 24.15.) *to go with me unto Babylon.*

*{behold, all the land is before thee, whither it seemeth good and convenient for thee to go, thither go.}* Heb. *unto good, and unto the right in thine eyes to go;* as chap. 26.14. A free and a large offer. Pharaoh could say no more to Joseph concerning his father and his family, Gen. 47.6. See the like speech of Abraham to Lot, Gen. 13.9.

**Verse 1.** *{Now while he was not yet gone back,}* he said, *{Go back unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan,}* These words are very diversely rendered and resolved. Who the person should be that is here spoken of, said not to have returned or gone back, is by some questioned; and the generality goes for Jeremy: but these among themselves much divided: for some make all these the words of Nebuzaradan. So the Chaldee, thus rendering them, *And if thou like not to dwell, then return to Gedaliah.* Which our old English seeming to follow, renders it: *And if thou canst not be content to dwell alone, then dwell with Gedaliah.* The old Latin, *And come not with me but dwell with Gedaliah;* as joining them to the words foregoing, *forbear,* Verse 4. But how the Hebrew will bear any of these versions, I see not. The most rather conceive them as a relation inserted of something concerning, or occasioning, the speech ensuing. And one of the Jewish doctors renders them, *And when he had no mind to go back* he said, that is, the blessed Lord God said, *Go back to Gedaliah.* God suggested that to him, that made him willing to go, when as of himself he had no inclination thereunto: another of them, *And when he had not yet said, that he would return,* Nebuzaradan perceiving yet by his silence, that his mind was rather to go back; than to go along with him, said to him, *Go back to Gedaliah.* And others again, as the Tigurine, whom our Geneva, and the next version before it, concur with, render them, as by way of parenthesis, (*for as yet he was not returned,* or, *come back,*) and then carrying on the sentence, *and go back,* or, *or go back to Gedaliah.* Take your choice, either to go along with me, or to seat yourself elsewhere, wheresoever you please, or to repair to Gedaliah, that he may provide for you. Others, as our last version, *And when,* or, *while he was not yet gone back,* he said, *Go back to Gedaliah.* Either make your abode where you please in any part of the land elsewhere, or repair to Gedaliah and abide with him. And this seems the most probable of any of those, that understand the words of Jeremy. But some others expound them of Gedaliah, and render the words thus, *And because he is not to come back, repair to Gedaliah.* Since that Gedaliah is not to come hither to me, but to stay at Mizpah to settle things in his new charge, repair thither to him, who will be careful both to protect you, and to provide for you: the copulative in a causative notion is not infrequent; as chap. 36.9. & 38.23. The Italian to remove the ambiguity, renders it, *And because Gedaliah—returneth not hither, return thou to him.*

*{Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan,}* To whose care he was to be commended, chap. 39.14.

*{whom the King of Babylon hath made governor over the cities of Judah,}* So 2 Kings 25.22. being in likelihood one of those, and a principal man among them, who had joined themselves to the Chaldeans before the surprisal of the city.

*{and dwell with him among the people.}* Or, *abide with him among* the rest of *the people,* that are with him, Heb. *sit*; as Genesis 24.55. 2 Samuel 7.18. Chapter 39.14. and *in the midst of*, as chap. 36.12.

*{or go whithersoever it seemeth convenient unto thee to go}* Heb. *or to all* (all, for any; as Job 1.11. & 8.12.) place (a defect of the subject; as c. 38.11.) *that is right in thine eyes to go to,* (as verse 4.) *go.* A full freedom.

*{So the Captain of the guard gave him victuals, and a reward, and let him go}* Heb. *and.* as c. 39.13.

*{victuals}* The word arising from a root, that has a notion of journeying, signifies properly, that which the Greeks call *ἤια,* the Latins, *viaticum,* victuals, or provisions for a journey: and so it seems to be here intended. Howbeit, because it is used sometime for a meal, Prov. 13.17. for a dinner, there is too scant; and a feast too large: some here render it, *he feasted him;* and so some Greek versions, *he made him a feast;* or he entertained him: and again, because it is used of a constant allowance, or diet, 2 Kings 24.30.
