*{ye will surely accomplish your vows, and surely perform your vows.}* Heb. *establishing establish:* and, *doing do;* as before: a passage from person to person, as chap. 29.19. and the same thing repeated, with vigorous ingeminations again and again, as to express their extreme obstinacy, stiff resolution, and full account to carry things as themselves lusted; so withal to intimate the fierceness of God's wrath incensed against them, for such their presumptuous and scornful carriage toward him. See verse 28.

**Verse 26.** *{Therefore hear ye the word of the LORD, all Judah that dwell in the land of Egypt;}* As verse 24. So Esay 28.14,23. *dwell,* or, *abide;* as chap. 40.10,13.

*{Behold, I have sworn by my great name, saith the LORD,}* That is, by myself; as Gen. 22.16. So, *by his soul,* Chap. 71.14.

*{that my name shall no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah, in all the land of Egypt, saying, The Lord GOD liveth.}* The usual form of an oath. See chap. 4.2. & 5.2. & 38.16. I so exceedingly hate and abhor these abominable wretches, who thus demean themselves, that I cannot endure to have my name come in their mouths. See Psal. 50.16. Ezek. 20.39. Mal. 1.9,10. Luke 6.46. and I will therefore utterly destroy them, that I may no more be once named by them, verse 14.

**Verse 27.** *{Behold I will watch over them for evil, and not for good,}* Heb. *I am watching.* As one that purposely watches, and lies in wait to do a man a shrewd turn, or to mischief him, Psal. 56.6. Chap. 1.12. & 20.10. & 21.10. & 31.28. & 39.16.

*{and all the men of Judah that are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword, and by the famine, until there be an end of them.}* See chap. 42.22. verse 12.

**Verse 28.** *{Yet a small number that escape the sword shall return out of the land of Egypt into the land of Judah,}* Heb. *And* (as verse 4.) *the escaped of the sword* (So Ezek. 6.8. as, *the left of the sword,* chap. 31.2. to wit, of the Chaldeans invading Egypt) *men of number:* such as may be soon numbered; as Deut. 4.27. Esay 10.19. a small reserve God had yet among them, whom he was careful to protect wheresoever they were, Ezek. 11.16. and in his due time, to bring back again, Esay 27.13.

*{and all the remnant of Judah that are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall know whose word shall stand, mine or theirs.}* Heb. *from me,* and *from them;* that is, that which came *from me,* or that which comes *from them:* the copulative in a disjunctive notion as chap. 42.6. whether shall stand; *firm,* as Numb. 30.4. that is, be fulfilled and made good. So, *The counsell of the Lord shall stand,* Psal. 33.11. and, *It shall not stand,* Esay 7.7. See verse 29.

**Verse 29.** *{And this shall be a sign unto you, saith the LORD:}* As Esay 37.30. & 38.7. Luke 2.12.

*{that I will punish you in this place,}* Heb. *am visiting on you;* as chap. 23.2. & 29.32. am resolved so to do, and am about to do it. See verse 13. and I will do it in this very place, which you presumed and made full account would be a place of the surest security and safeguard to you, Chap. 42.14.

*{that ye may know that my words shall surely stand against you for evil.}* Heb. *shall standing stand.* It is again repeated with a more vehement ingemination, to control their peremptory resolutions, and resolute presumptions, so speaking, as if it had been in their power to cross God's counsels, and accomplish their own purposes and designs, as themselves pleased, verse 25. to assure them by a sign which should now be given them, that they should find shortly to their smart by woeful experience, the truth and stability of God's Word, which should undoubtedly and unavoidably take effect, and be fulfilled; and the folly and vanity of their own presumptions, which should be frustrated and annulled, Psal. 33.10,11. Esay 14.24,26,27.

**Verse 30.** *{Thus saith the LORD, Behold I will give Pharaoh Hophra King of Egypt into the hand of his enemies: and into the hand of them that seek his life;}* God in these words, as he pointed them before unto the instruments, and the persons of those, by whom the judgment denounced should be put into execution upon them, Chap. 43.10. so here he foretells them of somewhat that should forego and make way for it. There is a twofold question here moved; the one who this *Hophra,* or, *Chophra* should be? the other; who it should be into whose hands, he was given. For the former, some of the Jewish masters suppose, that there is no proper name at all here of any Egyptian king, but that *Hophra,* or, *Chophra* is by change of a letter (*Chet,* or, *Het,* put for *He*) *Pharaoh* inverted; to note the overturning or overthrow of him; and the Chaldee seems to go much the same way, rendering it, *I will give,* or, *make Pharaoh broken;* that is, *a confusion,* or, *broken.* But this seems of the same stamp with other their Talmudical toys; it is rather to be deemed, that this *Hophra,* is that king of Egypt, whom the Greeks call *Apries,* being nephew, or son's son to Nechoh; in fight with whom Josias was slain, 2 Kings 23.29. and herein most concur. But concerning the party unto whose power he was delivered, there is more difficulty and diversity of opinion. For some conceive that this *Hophra* or *Apries,* was, by sedition, moved among his people deposed, and one Amasis set up in his room; who for a time kept him alive under restraint, but for his own better security afterward slew him. So Herodote reports it, lib. 2. and this, say some, made way for Nebuchadnezzar to seize the easier upon Egypt, the Egyptians having been divided among themselves, and not well cemented yet again. But others rather conceive it to be meant of Nebuchadnezzar, and the Chaldean forces, who under this *Hophra,* or, *Apries,* invaded Egypt: Howsoever that Greek authors make no mention of any such their expedition into those parts, either under Apries or any his successors, following only such relations of those times, as he had from the Egyptian priests, who would tell him no stories, but such as might stand with the honor and reputation of their own nation. But to this purpose Joseph the Jew tells us in his *Antiquities,* lib. 10. cap. 12. that Nebuchadnezzar in the twenty and third of his reign, about five years after the destruction of Jerusalem, having subdued the Moabites, and the Ammonites, invaded Egypt: slew their king, spoiled their country, and carried away the Jews that he found there captive to Babylon. For my part, I doubt not but this Hophra was then king of Egypt, when that Chaldean king invaded that country, as was foretold he should do, Chap. 43.10. & 46.13.26. a place parallel to this, Ezek. 29.19. & 30.10,17. Howbeit, as concerning Joseph's relation, to let pass his computation of times, which is nothing exact here, (See 2 Kings 24.12. & 25.8.) that he says concerning this deportation of the Jews out of Egypt to Babylon, seems not true; God threatens the contrary, that they should die in Egypt, where at present they were, Chap. 42.16. verse 12. See the like; Hos. 9.6. and it is not improbable that Nebuchadnezzar would rather do execution there upon them, being enraged against the nation, as well for the murder of Gedaliah and his officers with him, though acted by others, Chapter 41.3. as for their repairing for shelter against the Chaldeans to Egypt, unto whom he had a quarrel before for the like office, Chap. 37.5. and unto his sword they were now exposed, having gone out of the verge of God's protection. See Chap. 42.10—16. Howsoever, the slaughter of this Hophra (under whose wing they supposed themselves safe and secure) by some hostile force, which they should survive to see, was to be unto them an undoubted sign and forerunner of their ensuing ruin and destruction.

*{as I gave Zedekiah King of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar King of Babylon his enemy, and that sought his life}* See this before menaced, Chap. 34.3,19,20,21. & 37.17. & 38.18,23. and accordingly accomplished, Chap. 39.5. *hand* for *power;* and, *soul,* for *life;* as chap. 34.20. and so also in the former branch.

## CHAPTER 45

**Verse 1.** *{The word that Jeremiah the Prophet spake unto Baruch the son of Neriah, when he had written these words in a book at the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah King of Judah, saying,}* Unto the former prophecies concerning either whole nations, Chap. 25. & 43.10. & 44.30. or public persons, as Jehoaz, Jehojachim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, Chap. 22.11,18,24. & 34.2. & 36.29. & 37.17. & 38.17. or whole companies of people, Chap. 42—44. is subjoined in this chapter a prophecy concerning a private man, Baruch the prophet's scribe; not unlike Paul's epistle unto Philemon concerning his servant Onesimus subjoined unto the main body of his epistles concerning public affairs, directed either unto whole churches, or to some chief ministers in them, as were Timothy and Titus. And, as by the date in the title, prefixed here before it, appears, delivered many years before, either the matters related, or the sermons and prophecies recited in the chapters next before-going.

*{The word}* Or, *thing;* that which he spoke: as Chap. 37.13. & 42.4.

*{unto Baruch,}* His scribe, Chap. 36.4,26.

*{when he had written these words,}* Or, *these things;* as chap. 26.2. & 36.13. not the things next before related, (for they were of a far later date) but those that God had long before commanded Jeremy to gather together, and make up in one volume, chap. 36.2. unto which chapter therefore this, if we regard either the subject matter of it, or the term demonstrative here used, it ought to have been annexed.

*{in a book}* Heb. *on a book;* as c. 36.4,18.

*{at his mouth}* Heb. *from his mouth:* as c. 36.17.

*{in the fourth year of Jehoiakim:}* See c. 36.1.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, unto thee O Baruch,}* As chap. 44.25.

**Verse 3.** *{Thou didst say, Woe is me now:}* Or, *Thou sayest.* You begin to be distracted and discouraged, considering with yourself, what troubles are like to befall you, and what difficulties you may have procured yourself by the writing and publishing of this roll, for which the king has given out order to apprehend you. ch. 36.26. The words contain an usual form of lamentation. See c. 4.31.

*{for the LORD hath added grief to my sorrow;}* Heb. *upon my sorrow:* has given me grief upon grief: as Psalm 69.27.

*{I fainted in my sighing,}* Or, *I am faint with my sighing,* Psalm 6.6.

*{and I find no rest}* I see no hope of rest or relief. So Lamentations 1.3.

**Verse 4.** *{Thus shalt thou say unto him}* Or, *Say thus unto him;* or, *tell him;* as c. 34.2.

*{The LORD saith thus, Behold, that which I have built, will I break down; and that which I have planted, I will pluck up even this whole land:}* Heb. *I am pulling down,* and *plucking up.* I am about to demolish mine own special buildings, and to pluck up mine own peculiar plantations, the Jewish state and people. Psalm 44.2. & 80.8—15. Esay 5.5—8. & 37.26. whereof you are but a limb, and one of the smallest and meanest. Of the forms of speech, see c. 1.10. and 18.7,9.

**Verse 5.** *{And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not:}* Have you any thoughts of honor and credit? or of a peaceable and prosperous estate? do you require or desire to live quietly, and at ease, when all is going to wreck and ruin? never dream once of any such matter.

*{for behold I will bring evil upon all flesh, saith the LORD;}* Heb. *I am bringing evill* (as Chapter 19.3.) *upon all flesh:* either upon all the nations in the world, (as the word *flesh* is more generally taken Psalm 143.2. Rom. 3.20. c. 32.27. See c. 25.15,31.) or upon this whole nation, v. 4. c. 11.12. as the word is to be taken Matth. 24.22.

*{but thy life will I give to thee for a prey in all places whither thou goest.}* Heb. *and;* as Chapter 43.17.18. Suffice you it well may that you escape with your life. (Heb. *thy soul:* as Chapter 43.30.) See Chapter 21.9. & 39.18. I will protect you and secure you, whatsoever shall become of these, and wheresoever you shall be hurried. See the like of other the faithful, Psalm 125.1,12. Ezek. 11.16.

## CHAPTER 46

**Verse 1.** *{The word of the LORD which came to Jeremiah the Prophet against the Gentiles,}* From this place, ensues a recital of divers prophecies against several nations; the most, such as were to be subdued and subjugated by the Babylonian monarchy; as Egypt, Chap. 46. Palestine, Chap. 47. Moab, Chapter 48. Ammon, Chap. 49.1. Edom, Chap. 49.7. Damascus Chap. 49.23. Kedar, Chap. 49.28. and Elam, Chap. 49.34. And lastly, against the Babylonian Empire itself, Chap. 50. & 51. And this verse seems to contain a common title or inscription, belonging in general to them all. See the like, Esay, 1.1. Chapter, 1.1.

**Verse 2.** *{Against Egypt}* Or, *Concerning Egypt.* Heb. *unto Egypt:* but the particle is used sometime for, *concerning;* as chapter 44.1. and sometime for, *against:* as Chapter 34.7. with the Egyptians the rather he seems to begin, because God's people were too prone to rely upon them, Esay, 30.1. and 31.1. and 36.6. Chapter 2.18,36. and 37.5. and 41.17,18. and 42.14. Ezekiel 29.6,7,16.

*{against the Army of Pharaoh-Nechoh King of Egypt,}* Or, *concerning;* as Esay 1.1. c. 23.2. & 49.1. This Pharao-Nechoh was the son of Psammetichus, and was king of Egypt in Josias' time, who was also slain by him in fight; 2 Kings 23.29.

*{which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah King of Judah.}* Of this *Carchemish* see on Esay 10.9. whence it appears, that the Assyrian king had subdued it, and held it about Ezekiah's time. But the Egyptian king in Josiah's days, went with an army towards those parts; to recover it from them; which whether he did at that time, is not certain; yet is not unlikely but that he might. Howbeit whether making a second attempt to the same purpose in Jehoiakim's reign, or the Chaldeans, now masters of the Assyrian monarchy, seeking then to regain it back from him; he and his forces opposing them, were then foiled, as by this place appears; yea his strength so impaired, and he so stripped of all that before he held between Euphrates and Egypt, that he never dared in person stir abroad again out of Egypt, 2 Kings 24.7. And this great overthrow was by Jeremy foretold some space of time before the same, in this prophecy, though after it was entered into, and recorded in this latter volume with the rest. The former part of this chapter, is concerning this foil given to Pharao, Verse 3—13. the latter part concerning the conquest of his country, Verse 14—26. with a close of comfort and encouragement to God's faithful people, containing a promise of protection and restitution, Verse 27,28.

**Verse 3.** *{Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle,}* Or, *Prepare,* or, *Weld;* the word is used sometime of *preparing* and *furnishing* of the table; as Prov. 9.2. Esay 21.1. sometime, of fitting armor for fight, or *welding* it in fight, 1 Chron. 12.8. The prophet makes entrance into the prediction of this overthrow that should be given to Egypt, with an ironical incitement of them, to make all the warlike preparations that they could, to encounter the Chaldeans and their forces, with whom they were to join battle, verse 3,4. but withal implying that all would be in vain, they should not dare, or be able to stand to it, verse 5,6. of the defensive warlike implements here mentioned, See also Psal. 35.2,3. Esay 22.6.

**Verse 4.** *{Harness the horses,}* Heb. *Bind;* either, saddle and girt them, as some; or rather, make them fast to the chariots, which they are to draw in. So 1 Kings 18.44. See 2 Kings 9.21. Mich. 1.13. where the *charet* is said to be *bound* in the one place; the *beasts* that draw in it to *the charet* in the other.

*{and get up ye horsemen;}* To wit, into the chariots; in those times much used in war. See Esay 21.7,9.

*{and stand forth with your helmets:}* Heb. *set your selves,* or, *present your selves;* as it is rendered, 1 Sam. 10.19.

*{furbish the spears,}* Or, *polish;* as 2 Chron. 4.16. great care there was anciently among the soldiery, commanders and officers especially, to have their arms glitter.

*{and put on the brigandines.}* Or, *corslets,* or, *coats of maile:* the term here used is more commonly found written with another letter, to wit, with *shin;* as Esay 59.17. with, *samec;* here only, and chap. 51.3.

**Verse 5.** *{Wherefore have I seen them dismayed, and turned away back?}* Or, *wherefore do I see* (as if he beheld in vision what he relates, as chap. 4.23. to wit, their affrightment, flight, and shameful discomfiture) *that they* (to wit the Egyptian soldiery for all their gallant preparations) *are dismaid, and recoil;* turn back upon the enemy. See the like chap. 30.6.

*{and their mighty ones are beaten down,}* Or, *and that their mighty men* (such as should support and stay the rest) *are beaten down;* to carry it on in the same tenor with the former. Heb. *are broken to pieces:* as Mich. 1.7.

*{and are fled apace,}* Or, *{and fled apace}* Heb. *fled a flight;* or, *fled with flight.*

*{and looked not back;}* Or, *look not back.* So chap. 47.3.

*{for fear was round about, saith the LORD,}* Or, *fear* being *round about:* or, by reason of *fear on every side:* a defect of the particle *for;* as Mal. 2.5. of this proverbial form, see chap. 6.25. & 20.3,10.

**Verse 6.** *{Let not the swift flee away nor the mighty man escape}* Or, *The swift shall not flee away:* (that is, escape by flight; as chap. 25.35. See Esay 30.16.) *nor shall the mighty man escape,* Psal. 33.16,17. neither shall be able to save himself, nor the one by flight, nor the other by his might, Amos 2.14,15. for the particle here used is not always an inhibitive, but sometime a bare negative. See on Esay 2.9.

*{they stumble and fall}* As Psal. 27.2. Esay 8.15. being discomfited by the Chaldean forces, Verse 12,13.

*{toward the North}* Or, *in the North;* in the northern parts: for *Carchemish* where this overthrow was given, verse 2. lay northward from Egypt; and the paragogical addition does sometime denote not a motion to the place, whereunto it is affixed, but a stay, or abode in it, as, *on the ground.* Gen. 28.12. and *on the altar,* Exod. 29.13,18. and, *in Babel,* chap. 29.15. and so it is expounded here, verse 10.

*{by the river Euphrates}* Heb. *upon the hand;* that is, place, or region, near Euphrates, on the banks whereof Carchemish was situate: *hand,* for, *place:* as chap. 6.3. or, *side,* as 1 Sam. 19.3. and *by the hand of Jordan,* Numb. 13.29. that is, beside it, on the *bank,* or the coast of it. So also Josh. 15.46.

**Verse 7.** *{Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers?}* Or, *stir themselves,* as the waters of rivers: of many joined together, more than one. See Esay 11.15, the word *waters* supplied from the former member: as Psalm 91.10. chap. 6.23. and the verb imports a vehement concussion, either through fear from without, Psal. 18.7. or force and violence from within, as Chap. 5.22. and so here so rather, than as that learned annotator, *her flouds are troubled or, muddy;* as alluding to the sliminess of Nilus' waters. See chap. 2.18. Esay 23.3. The prophet in this passage describes the great preparations that the Egyptian king had made for this expedition, and with what multitudes of men, and show of valor and vigorousness, they set forward to the place of encounter, as if the waters of their river Nilus, or of Euphrates had broken through their sea walls, or got over their banks, and with a stream irresistibly bore down all before them. See the like, Esay 8.7. & 59.19. chap. 49.19. And he speaks it, as if he beheld Pharaoh Nechoh marching out of his own land with a vast army, overspreading the face of the country, and proceeding without resistance. See the like, Esay 63.1.

**Verse 8.** *{Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and cover the earth; I will destroy the city, and the inhabitants thereof.}* The Egyptian forces they are that rise and swell and surround their banks, as their river is wont to do, and make full account to cover the face of the country, and to carry all away before them, and with their impetuous assaults to beat either the city of Carchemish, as that against which their expedition was principally intended, Verse 2. down to the ground, and destroy her inhabitants, see on verse 7. or *city,* that is *cities,* (for the article is not in the text, *city* put collectively for *cities,* as Esay 25.2.) *and their inhabitants;* whatsoever cities or people shall come or stand in my way. See chap. 47.2. the like: and see this his peremptory Egyptian vaunts in confidence of his forces, yet all blown away with a blast of God's breath, Exo. 15.9,10.

**Verse 9.** *{Come up ye horses, and rage, ye chariots: and let the mighty men come forth;}* Before the prophet had by way of derision incited them to make what preparations they were able to make for their expedition then in hand; Verse 3,4. now in like manner he calls upon them, as being come near to the place of encounter, and ready to join battle with the adverse party, to come on gallantly, and in fierce and furious manner set upon fight.

*{rage:}* Bestir themselves, as if they were wood or mad; so the word properly signifies, 1 Sam. 21.14. Psal. 102.8. Eccl. 2.2. So it is used also, chap. 25.17. & 50.38. & 51.7. Nah. 2.4. where it is applied to *charets,* or *cavallery,* as here: the verb is plural; because the noun, though singular, yet is collective, and might not amiss be rendered *cavallery;* both here, and Exod. 14.7. *all the cavallery of Egypt.*

*{the Ethiopians,}* Heb. *Cush,* or, *the Cushites,* the Egyptians' kinsmen and allies coming both of Cham, Gen. 10.6. near neighbors and confederates, Esay 18.1. & 20.4. Ezek. 30.9. See more of them, chap. 13.23.

*{and the Libyans that handle the shield,}* Heb. *Phut,* or, *Put,* or, *Phuta:* people of the same race with the former, Gen. 10.6. 1 Chron. 1.6. situated in Africa to the west of Egypt; in which parts was sometimes a city of the same name mentioned by Ptolemy, and a river likewise, that in later times retained the same appellation. See Pliny, l. 5. c. 1. Joseph in his *Antiquities,* l. 1. c. 7.

*{and the Lydians that handle and bend the bow.}* Heb. *handlers,* and *treaders, of the bow;* as chap. 50.14,29. and two regents to one subject; as the like, Deut. 33.19. Job 20.17. Esay 19.11. Of this name are two found in Moses his antiquities, one the son of Sem, of whom came the Lydians in Asia, Gen. 10.22. another the son of Mitsraim, from whom descended the Lydians in Africa, Gen. 10.13. and of these latter a learned writer would have to be the Lydians here mentioned, and to be no other than those who are now termed Ethiopians; the rather for that they are here brought in as auxiliaries to the Egyptians, and have a peculiar mark set upon them, as noted for skill in archery. See Esay 66.19.

**Verse 10.** *{For this is the day of the Lord GOD of Hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries:}* Or, as some rather render the copulative particle, taking it in a discretive, or adversative notion, *But.* They mind one thing, but God intends another; as chap. 33.5. Mic. 4.12. They make account to carry away all hand-smooth before them; but it will prove far otherwise, God in this expedition has a purpose to take vengeance upon them to the purpose, which to this time, as a day of assize or execution, he has hitherto deferred. So Esay 61.2. & 63.4. chap. 51.6.

*{and the sword shall devour, it shall be satiate, and made drunk with their blood:}* It shall be glutted with their flesh, and drenched with their blood. See Esay 34.6.

*{for the Lord GOD of hosts hath a sacrifice in the North country by the river Euphrates.}* Or, *a slaughter:* as Esay 34.6. and of the place before, verse 2.6.

**Verse 11.** *{Go up into Gilead, and take balm;}* Or, *Go* (as Gen. 13.1. & 19.30. & 26.23.) *to Gilead;* where the best balm was to be had for the cure of wounds. chap. 8.22. implying that the hurt that Egypt should receive by the blow that should now be given to that state, should prove incurable, and irrecoverable, Ezek. 30.21—25. See the like of Babylon, chap. 51.8,9.

*{O Virgin, the daughter of Egypt:}* Or, *O damsel, daughter of Egypt:* not, as some, *Virgin;* because unconquered: it is a term usually given to great and goodly states, compared to some fair and beautiful damsel, the daughter of some great person, living deliciously, faring delicately, sumptuously & gorgeously attired, brought up suitable to his state, whose daughter she is, and, as is with such usual, priding herself in her bravery & her beauty. See Esai 47.1. So verse 20.

*{in vain shalt thou use many medicines:}* Heb. *multiply medicines:* as, *multiply washing,* Ps. 51.2. and *multiply sope,* chap. 2.22. no medicine will heal, or help against the stroke of God's hand, Hos. 5.13.

*{for thou shalt not be cured.}* Or, without the *for,* which is not in the text, *thou canst not be cured;* the verb in a potential notion: as chap. 22.32. Heb. *no cure shall be to thee.* See chap. 30.13.

**Verse 12.** *{The Nations have heard of thy shame;}* Of your shameful discomfiture, vers. 5.

*{and thy cry hath filled the land}* The outcries and lamentations for their defeat and loss of their men, is gone over the whole country. See the like of Moab, Esay 15.5,8. Chap. 48.34. and the same term used, Psal. 144.14. Chap. 14.2.

*{for the mighty man hath stumbled against the mighty, and they are fallen both together}* That is, says a learned late writer, the Egyptians against the Chaldeans, against whom they come forth, but fell before them in fight, vers. 6. and those that go this way, render the latter clause, *and they shall both fall alike;* as the Egyptians by the Chaldeans now, so the Chaldeans hereafter by the Medes and Persians, Chap. 50.32. Others, not altering the received version, understand it of the Chaldeans and Egyptians falling one upon another, and making much slaughter of men on either side: and so many of either party falling together as did those, 2 Sam. 2.16. But the generality of interpreters, both Jewish and others, expound it all of the Egyptians, their mighty men, that stumble one upon another, as in a confused flight is wont to be; those that first fled, some of them stumbling at somewhat in the way, and those that come after them, before they are able to recover themselves, stumbling at, and upon them, & so both coming to the ground together.

**Verse 13.** *{The word that the LORD spake to Jeremiah the Prophet, how Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon should come, and smite the land of Egypt}* Heb. *concerning* (as Psalm 91.11.) *his coming to smite the land of Egypt.* Here begins a new prophecy; but this also, as the former against Egypt; that only of a discomfiture that the Chaldean forces should give Pharao-Nechoh's army in a foreign land, in the time of Jehoiakim's reign, verse 2. this of their invasion of the Egyptians' own country, and the subduing of it; which was done divers years after that overthrow, yea, sometime after both Zedekiah's reign, and the dissolution of the Jewish state, in another Egyptian king's reign. See Chap. 43.10—15. and 44.30. of this expedition, see also Ezek. 29. and 30.

**Verse 14.** *{Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph, and in Tahpanhes:}* Of these places, see before on chap. 44.1. that is, in all parts of Egypt; say some, *in Migdol,* toward the east; in *Tahpanhes,* toward the north; in *Noph,* toward the south: for as for the western part, it lay out of the Chaldeans' way. But not to stand scanning of this chorography; these places seem rather here mentioned, because the Jewish fugitives had in these places most of them settled themselves, to let them know what was like to befall them, being by the Chaldeans found there.

*{publish}* Heb. *make to hear,* as chap. 4.5,16.

*{Say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee:}* Make preparation against an invasion: as vers. 3,4.

*{for the sword shall devour round about thee.}* Heb. *hath devoured round about thee,* and so the ancient both Greek and Latin render it; has already destroyed all your neighboring countries, and so cleared the passage to you. See 2 Kings 24.7.

**Verse 15.** *{Why are thy valiant men swept away?}* Put to flight and cut off; or overthrown and beaten down to the ground. The word here used is nowhere else found, save here and Prov. 28.3. which must give light therefore to this place: from thence it appears, that it is borrowed term, taken from some vehement and violent shower of rain, or hail, that either *breaketh* the boughs and branches of trees, and the stems and stalks of lesser plants, like that in Egypt, Exod. 9.25. So a Jewish doctor supposing it to be of affinity with another term used, Esai 10.33. or *beateth down* to the ground. So a learned late writer, because in the Syriac the word is sometime so found used, Mat. 21.12. Luke 19.44. or that *sweepeth* all away, and so say the Jewish commenters is the word commonly used in the Talmudic language. So it should be not unlike that *the river Kishon swept them away,* Judge 5.21. The verb is singular, the noun plural; and it would therefore be rendered, *Why are thy strong men* each of them *beaten down,* or, *swept away;* as the like, Esay 2.20. and 26.19. Howbeit, the Latin here renders it, *Thy strong one is rotted;* Which Popish writers labor in vain to make some good sense of: hither forcing that, Esay 19.3. and the Greek, *Why is Apis, thy choice cattel,* or, *ox, fled?* because the term is used sometime for a fat ox, or, *bull,* Psal. 22.12. See chap. 50.11. to which purpose some fetch hither that, chap. 43.12,13. But these both stray overfar from the text.

*{they stood not, because the LORD did drive them.}* Or, *they can none of them stand* (for the verb is again singular and in a potential notion; as Psalm 76.7. *Who shall stand* (for, *who can stand*) *before thee when thou art wroth?* and Joshua 21.44. *not a man hath stood,* (for, *could stand*) *before you; because the Lord driveth them.* It is an answer to the former question, no marvel if they cannot stand to it, or stay by it (so the word also is used, Deut. 5.31.) because the Lord pursues them: it is he that by the Chaldeans drives them before him. It may seem an allusion to that speech of theirs at the Red Sea, recorded by Moses. Exod. 14.25. See verse 21.

**Verse 16.** *{He made many to fall, yea, one fell upon another,}* Heb. *He multiplied the faller* (as before, ver. 11.) *and a man fell upon his neighbour,* or, *friend,* or *fellow,* that is, *each one* (as chap. 34.9.) *upon another;* as Lev. 26.37. chap. 19.9. and 36.16. See on ver. 12.

*{and they said, Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our nativity from the oppressing sword.}* The speeches of hired soldiers of other nations, that assisted, or served under the Egyptians, repenting them of their undertakings when they began to perceive what the issue of them would be. See the like of those that were assistants to Babylon, chap. 51.9. See also, vers. 21. Of the last clause, see before on chap. 25.38. the meaning is plain, from the sword, or force of the Chaldeans that destroys all before it, ver. 14. For as for that which the Chaldee here exhibits, and some of the Jewish doctors admit, rendering it, *the winy sword,* or, *the sword drunk as with wine,* vers. 10. It is both too far fetched, and has no good analogy. And for that which the ancient Greek has *from the Grecian sword;* as if it came from *Javan:* it swerves from analogy as well as the former, and is directly against the story; as also what the old Latin yields, *from the face of the Dove:* though the word sometime so signify; as Hosea 7.11. yet has no place here: However Popish writers to maintain that vicious version, some of them tell us, that the Chaldeans and Assyrians had a *dove* in their ensigns, in memory of Queen Semiramis, who was either nursed and fed by a dove, or turned into a dove: and other of them, because that is a groundless relation, and they find the same used of the Persian sword, Chap. 50.16. would have the Chaldean forces so termed for their swiftness, Chap. 4.13. and 48.40. as winged like a *dove,* Psalm 55.6. But the collation of places, where the same term is used, refells all these fancies.

*{land of nativity}* As Gen. 31.13. and 32.9.

**Verse 17.** *{They did cry there, Pharaoh King of Egypt is but a noise;}* The continued speech of Pharaoh's foreign auxiliaries, uttered in contempt of Pharaoh, as if he were nothing but a sound of words, or, *a noise,* like one of those tinkling cymbals, or jingles, so rife in his country. See Esay 18.1. which may seem here alluded to; as the like, 1 Cor. 13.1. one that vaunted and bragged, promised and menaced much; made a great bluster and bustling, but performed nothing; so is the word commonly used for *noise* and *tumult,* or, *a tumultuous noise,* Psalm 74.23. Esay 24.8. and 25.5. Chap. 40.45. and 51.55. The restrictive particle is supplied: as Job 8.9. Chap. 37.10. yet some retaining this notion of the term, would have it, the speech of Pharaoh's parasites, flattering their king, and persuading him that the prophet Jeremy's words, concerning the overthrow that should be given him, were but empty words, were but wind; as they, chap. 5.13. Others, because the root whence it comes has a notion of *devastation,* and *wastenesse,* would have the word here so to signify, and to be the speech of the people complaining of their king, that he is one of a tumultuous and restless disposition (taking in withal the former notion) and one that thereby is like to bring nothing but *devastation* and destruction upon this whole country and himself. But I find not where the word here used has the notion here assigned it. As for the Greek that renders it, *Call ye the name of Pharao Necho King of Egypt, Saon Esbie Moed:* which the Syriac is said to render, *One that disturbeth and translateth the times:* and the old Latin treading somewhat in the same track, *Call ye the name of Pharao, Time hath brought tumult:* which so parallel with that. Esai 8.3. they wrong the text, both by corrupting it, and confounding one member with another. I adhere to the first, as the most familiar, and most generally received. I shall add only, that I conceive the words may well be rendered, *Pharao the King of Egypt,* is a king *of noise.* See of the like supply, vers. 7.8.

*{there}* So has the text *sham;* which these last turn into *shem,* a name: *there,* at Carchemish, say some, where the fight was, vers. 2. and then Nechoh should be the king here intended, as the Greek would have it, inserting overboldly his name into the text: or in Egypt his own country; as others rather: for this latter concerns not a foregoing fight abroad, but the conquest of it: and so Hophra should rather be the party here implied, Chap. 44.30.

*{he hath passed the time appointed.}* So both the Jewish doctors, and some Greek versions, and most of our interpreters. He has let slip his opportunities, or the fit season for action, and warlike employments: not unlike that, Chap. 8.20. where they complain in like manner, that the times of year for such affairs were over; and yet they were not relieved by such succors, in likelihood, as from Egypt they then expected. And the most conceive this to be the speech of the foreign soldiery, as before. Howbeit, because the word here used does sometime signify *solemn meetings* and *festivals,* Esay 1.14. a learned late writer would therefore have it to here to signify, and to be the voice of the people, complaining, that by reason of their king's tumultuous and turbulent courses, and the troubles and devastations, which thereby he had brought upon the state, they had not opportunity to observe their solemn festivals, as in times past they had wont to do. But this I leave to the judgment of others.

**Verse 18.** *{As I live;}* The usual form of an oath (chap. 44.26.) God himself here uses, as Chap. 22.24.

*{saith the King}* The sovereign Lord of heaven and earth, Psal. 103.19. Mal. 1.14. Mat. 11.25.

*{whose name is the LORD of Hosts}* See Esai 47.4. and 48.2. Chap. 48.15.

*{Surely, as Tabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, so shall he come.}* Or, *it shall come: Tabor,* a mountain of the tribe of Issachar, Josh. 19.22. Judge 4.6,14. called in the Greek version, *Itabyrium,* supposed commonly, but groundlessly, to have been the place of our Savior's transfiguration, Mat. 17.1. *Carmel* another mountain situate in the confines of Asher and Issachar, not far from the Midland Sea coast, and extending itself into the land near to mount Tabor, Josh. 19.26. 1 King. 18.42,43. Amos 9.3. The meaning is, as some of the Jewish commenters, and others, As sure as these two mountains keep their several settled situations, and fixed seats; so assuredly shall that which I now foretell and threaten, come to pass and be effected. Whereunto some add, that there is here an allusion to two ancient stories; the one of Barac, going down against Sisera from mount Tabor, Judge 4.14. the other, of that storm of rain, the approach whereof Elias described from mount Carmel, 1 King. 18.41,42. as if it were said, the king of Babel shall as surely come upon Egypt, as Barack did with his forces upon Sisera from Tabor, and the storm of rain, that Elias foresaw and foretold, from Carmel. But this seems overnice and needless. Others thus understand and open it, As Tabor advances itself above, and overlooks, and commands the lesser hills, and lower grounds, round about it, and Carmel the sea near unto it; So shall Nebuchadnezzar come into Egypt to subdue, and bring under the whole country, both before, and on every side of him. And lastly, some later interpreters, *Though* (as Josh. 17.18. Psalm 23.4.) the Egyptians be *as Tabor among the hills, and as Carmel that goeth,* (or, *reacheth*) *unto the sea;* that is, albeit, they seem as well secured, both by sea and land, as Tabor that is encompassed with hills, and Carmel that has the sea near to it; yet shall these things befall them. So should there be a defect of the reddition, or latter part of the sentence, and application of it to the present purpose: not unlike that, Psalm 48.7. Matth. 25.14. Marc. 13.34. And this seems not improbable; more probable sure, than that far-fetched conceit of a great Jewish master, who would have *Tabor* and *Carmel* here mentioned, to intimate, that the Chaldean forces should hunt the Egyptians, as men used to hunt deer, or other wild beasts on mount Tabor, Hosea 5.1. and that they should carry them away captive, as merchandise used to be transported in shipping, built of the timber trees growing on mount Carmel: though the words next following imply this latter.

**Verse 19.** *{O thou daughter}* Of this title, see on vers. 11.

*{dwelling in Egypt,}* That seems to have there a sure seat of constant abode; as chap. 10.17. and 21.13.

*{furnish thyself to go into captivity;}* Heb. *make thee instruments,* or, *implements of captivity;* or, *captivity furniture.* So Ezek. 12.1.

*{for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant}* Or, *Memphis.* See Chap. 44.1. verse 14. and of the like condition, Chap. 9.10.

**Verse 20.** *{Egypt is like a very fair heifer;}* Or, *calf.* So the word is rendered, Psal. 106.19. Chap. 34.18. A rich and goodly kingdom, and not inured to the yoke of subjection; as Hosea 10.11. Though in the word *heifer,* some suppose an allusion to *Apis the Bull,* and *Mnevis the Cow,* adored with them, as deities. See Herodote, lib. 2. and verse 5. And the epithet here given her, arising from a root that has a notion of *beauty,* some make but one word, but in a doubled form; as the verb it comes of is found, Psalm 45.2. Others divide it into two words, and render it, *fair of face:* as, *fair of visage,* Genes. 12.11. and, *fair of shape,* Deut. 21.11. Heb. *of mouth:* and the latter word here used, though nowhere found in the singular form, as here, yet in the plural it is found, Judge 3.16. Prov. 5.4. But others go a step further, and deem it a compound of three simple terms, *fair face,* or *mouth* and *God,* and to signify *fair of face to God;* as it is said of Moses, that he was *pretty,* or, *comely to God,* Act. 7.20. as being of the same form with those emphatical words, *a flame of God,* for, *a most intense flame,* Cant. 8.6. and, *a mist of God,* for, a most thick mist, Chap. 2.31. Howsoever it be not the genuine frame of the word; (for a twofold exception may be taken to these latter: one, that the term of *mouth* is hardly found used in Hebrew for *face,* though in Latin nothing is more common; another that in those forms a point is usually in the belly of the last letter, which is wanting in this) yet certain it is, and generally acknowledged, that the word imports an eminency of goodliness and beauty.

*{but destruction cometh; it cometh out of the north.}* Heb. *cutting out,* or, *cutting up, from the north cometh cometh,* or, *coming cometh:* for I suppose the former to be a participle, the latter a verb; as Heb. 10.37. though for the participle the verb infinitive be found, Habb. 2.3. howsoever, the gemination argues the certainty of it, as in that of Habbakuk, and in that of Ezekiel 7.6. *An end is come, the end is come, it is come:* and the word rendered *destruction,* nowhere else found, save in the writings of the Talmudists, where it is said to be used for the *killing,* and *cutting up* of a beast: (only the word whence it springs in that notion Job 33.6. where man is said to have been cut out of clay) may well be deemed to have some respect to the former similitude of an heifer; as if it were said, *from the North* (that is, from Chaldea, lying north from those parts, chap. 1.14. and 4.6. and 6.1.) shall *slaughter-men* come (so the Chaldee renders it) that is, sacrificers, or butchers that shall kill and *cut up* this *fair heifer,* or fat calf.

**Verse 21.** *{Also her hired men are in the midst of her, like fatted bullocks:}* Her soldiery likewise of foreign forces, hired from abroad, (see ver. 16.) that are with her, or within her, in her country (see ver. 17. Heb. *in the midst of her,* as Esay 5.18.) are like *fatted,* or, *stalled bullocks,* (Heb. *bullocks of the stall;* as *calves* or, *heifers of the stall,* Mal. 4.3. and, *calves out of the midst of the stall,* for, *out of the stall,* Amos 6.4.) they are fat & lusty, and in appearance likely to perform, and go through with whatsoever they undertake: the prophet persists in the same similitude that he used before, v. 19. Egypt like a goodly fair calf, or heifer, and her soldiery like stalled oxen, or bullocks. See Chap. 50.11. the note of similitude wanting there, as Psal. 11.1. Esay 21.8. is here expressed.

*{for they also are turned back, and are fled away together;}* Or, rather, *but:* for the particle here is in no causal, but in a discretive notion; as Chap. 43.3. as strong, and stout, as they seem to be, *they turn* their backs, or *necks* (as the Hebrew phrase is, and the word here to be supplied; as Josh. 7.8. Psal. 18.40.) to the enemy, and instead of fighting, betake themselves to flight. See ver. 5. and the like, Esay 22.2,3.

*{they did not stand}* Or, *could not stand.* See ver. 15.

*{because the day of their calamity was come upon them, and the time of their visitation.}* See ver. 10. So chap. 50.27.

**Verse 22.** *{The voice thereof shall go like a Serpent,}* Or, *Her voice,* that is, Egypt's shall be low and submiss, not loud and lofty, as formerly. She shall not now bellow, like an heifer, Esay 15.5. or like a bull, or bullock, chap. 50.11. as most there render it: but she shall now, as being utterly daunted and damped, whisper softly and submissly, like a snake out of some hole in the ground, scarce able to mutter, or utter ought for fear, Esay 29.4. For as for the old Latin version that renders it, *a voice of brasse;* that is, say your Popish writers, *the sound of trumpets,* or, *of cymbals,* and *jingles,* 1 Cor. 13.1. See Esay 18.1. some writhing it this way, and some that way, some applying it to the Chaldeans, and some to the Egyptians; it is grounded on a palpable mistake, and we shall leave it therefore to them, to make what they please of it. Nor do those Jewish commenters stray less from the notion of the text, who expound it of the noise and sound of the Chaldean arms and army, that should come creeping toward Egypt, like a serpent, Gen. 3.14. And as for their Talmudists, they dote here prodigiously, when they would have it meant, that the cry of Egypt should be so loud, that it should pass through the whole world; like that hideous cry that the serpent made, what time, God having passed that doom on him, that he should go upon his belly, the angels came down from heaven, and cut off his legs, Gen. 3.14.

*{for they shall march with an army,}* Or, *when* (as chap. 11.23. and 10.2.) *they,* to wit, her enemies, the Chaldeans *shall come* marching *with an army* into her country.

*{and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood.}* The prophet here passes to another comparison, wherein Egypt is compared to a wood, or a forest, bethwacked with trees; either in regard of her numberless towns and cities, or of the multitude of her people. Howbeit, there want not those, who conceive some respect to be had here to the former resemblance, supposing the state of Egypt to be compared to a wanton heifer running at large; and the country to a large wood, grove, or coppice, wherein she ran so at large, grazing, browsing, and sporting herself at pleasure. See somewhat the like to this, Chap. 22.7. Heb. *hewers of trees;* as Josh. 9.21. Judge 9.8.

**Verse 23.** *{They shall cut down her forest, saith the LORD;}* Or, *That shall fell,* (a defect of the relative, as Chap. 31.21,24.) or, (as some of the rabbins would have it read in the imperative; which though others of them justly control, yet some of ours retain) *Fell ye,* (as spoken in the person of God enjoining it) the trees (supplied from verse 22.) *of her forest.* See Esay 10.18,33,34. Chap. 22.7.

*{though it cannot be searched:}* Heb. *though* (as Josh. 17.18.) *it shall not be searched:* but the verb is in a potential notion, as some other in this chapter before ver. 11,15,21. It is a proverbial form of speech, intimating such a number, or quantity of ought, as it is vain to endeavor to take any reckoning, or tale of it. See 1 King. 4.47. 2 Chron. 4.18. of the almost incredible number of their towns of note, and cities anciently, and the populousness of the country. See Herodote, l. 2. & Diodore, l. 1. c. 31. Howbeit, some expound the form here used, as implying not so much the number of the places, or people, as the difficulty of passage and access to them, the land lying low, and full of streams, and watercourses, either branching out of Nilus, or derived from it. See Esai 19.5—10. Ezek. 29.3,4. But the former seems the right. Howbeit, the Jewish commenters expound this clause of the Chaldean army that was to come against Egypt, and render the words, *for* (as chap. 10.21.) *it* (that is, their army, verse 22.) *is unsearchable.* But it seems rather to have relation to Egypt.

*{because they are more than the grasshoppers, and are innumerable.}* This last clause is likewise variously expounded; some conceiving it to be spoken of the Chaldean forces: as rendering a reason how they should be able to do such execution, as was formerly intimated, to wit, fell down a whole forest so large, as seemed scarce possible to pierce through it, or find an end of it. To which answer is returned, that their multitude should be answerable to the largeness of that forest; for they should come, as *locusts* that are wont to come flying, in such swarms, or clouds rather, that they overspread a whole country, and seize on all the trees and shrubs, and whatsoever else is green that grows in it, and make havoc of all before them. See Exod. 10.5,15. Esai 7.19,20. Joel 1.6,7. and 2.2—10. And this exposition seems most probable. Yet some others understand it, as spoken of the Egyptians; and either as rendering a reason of the branch next foregoing, why *her forest could not be searched;* to wit, *because* the trees thereof *are more than locusts;* (Heb. *locust;* taken collectively: as judg. 6.5,10.) *and there is no number of them,* as Psal. 104.34,35. or, as further preoccupating and meeting with what might be suggested to make the matter here foretold unlikely ever to be effected: and of these, some render the particle, as before; *though* (as it is repeated also in the like speech, Josh. 17.18.) they be so many: as if it were said, their numberless number shall not hinder the doing of this execution upon them.

**Verse 24.** *{The daughter of Egypt shall be confounded}* See verse 11.19.

*{she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the North.}* *hand,* for, *power;* as chap. 44.30. *North;* as vers. 20.

**Verse 25.** *{The LORD of hosts the God of Israel, saith;}* Or, *hath said it;* as chap. 48.8. and it shall surely therefore be effected; for, *shall he say, and not do?* Num. 23.19. The Jewish doctor supposes *the God of Israel,* to be here added, to intimate that the ground of God's proceeding against Egypt, was for the wrong done to Israel in the death of Josiah, 2 Kings 23.29. but this seems somewhat too nice and narrow. See the same title with this here, chap. 35.13,17.

*{Behold, I will punish the multitude of No.}* Heb. *Lo, I am visiting,* (or, coming to visit) *to,* or, *on,* (as chap. 44.13. and 50.18.) *Amon Minno,* or, *from No.* The Chaldee by *Amon* understands the *company,* or, promiscuous *multitude,* which our version follows, taking *Amon* for the same with *Hamon;* and so is the word used, chap. 52.15. as also many take it, Nah. 3.8. rendering *No Amon* there, *populous No:* whereunto would fit well that of a late learned annotator, could it be made good, who affirms *Amon* here to be a dialect, for *Ommin,* or *Ummim;* that is, *people.* But I see little ground for this his conceit. The learned scholiast, who alone seems to have taken notice of the particle *min,* renders it, *the multitude* born *at,* or issuing *from No:* as, *the boar from the wood,* for, *the wilde boar,* Psal. 80.13. But others both there and here render it *nourisher,* or *nourishing, No:* and so *Amon* here should be the same with *Omen,* Num. 11.12. and these would have *No,* or *Alexandria,* (for that both Jews and ours most generally agree to be meant) to be so called, as a city that by its trade and traffic being the principal seaport town and mart for merchants from foreign parts, fed and furnished the whole country with wares and commodities of all sorts from abroad. The same term is found, Prov. 8.30. but there somewhat ambiguous, whether one *nourishing,* or *nourished,* as some Greeks here render it: and the ancient Greek here, *Ammon her son;* as if it were rather *nurse-childe,* than *nurse:* whereunto also they seem to incline that render it, *the foster-childe of No;* to wit, *Pharao,* and *Egypt:* for they go too far wide here, that render it, *the cunning workman,* or *artificer, of No;* because the term *Amon* is so found used, Cant. 7.1. The Jewish doctors affirm it to be the name of the king of Alexandria that then was. But for that they give no great ground, or proof. A learned late writer here departing from the common stream of former authors, would have this *Amon* to be *Jupiter,* whom the Egyptians should term *Amoun:* the Africans (and the Greeks and Latins after them) *Ammon,* and *Hammon,* not from a Greek word that signifies *sand,* because a famous temple of his was situate amidst the sandy wastes of Cyrene; but from *Ham,* or *Cham,* one of Noah's sons; whom another in part complying with, would have *Amon* to be *Jupiter Altor,* that is, *the nourisher;* as before: or *Jupiter Stator,* that is, *the confirmer,* or, *establisher:* because the word, *Amen,* has sometime a note of *stability* and *firmnesse,* Esai 65.16. that former learned writer would likewise have *No,* not to be *Alexandria,* a city built, long after the times of those prophets that mention it by Alexander, whose name it yet bears, but to be *Diospolis,* as the Greeks render it, Ezek. 30.16. which *Amon No,* or, *No Amon,* does, as he conceives, exactly express. Howbeit, because there are two cities of the name in Egypt, the one famous, called also *Thebe,* but an inland city, and not so furnished with water, as the description of *No* in Nahum imports, the other situate in the lower part of Egypt, with much water about it, but of less note, whereas Nahum's *No* seems to come in competition with Nineveh itself: this learned author seems somewhat uncertain in his judgment concerning this *No,* sometime hanging it upon the one, sometime fixing it upon the other. I shall leave the controversy to be decided by others better seen, and versed therein than myself. Hence it appears, as also by those other places, that it was a principal city in the land of Egypt, and of great repute, and renown also in foreign parts.

*{and Pharaoh, and Egypt:}* See chap. 44.30.

*{with their gods;}* Heb. *and,* as chap. 39.1,3. See chap. 43.12,13.

*{and their Kings}* Petty kings, or princes; for Egypt was divided into divers principalities. See Herodote, lib. 2.

*{and Pharaoh,}* *Hophra;* the sovereign of them, chap. 44.30.

*{and all them that trust in him.}* Those of the Jewish people that make full account to sit safe under his shadow. See chap. 42.14,16. and 43.11. and 44.27,29,30.

**Verse 26.** *{And I will deliver them into the hand of those that seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon, and into the hand of his Servants:}* See chap. 44.30. and the like, chap. 34.20,21.

*{and afterward it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old, saith the LORD.}* After the space of forty years expired from this time of its conquest, and spoil made of it by the Chaldeans. See Ezek. 29.13. Heb. *shall sit,* or, *dwell,* or, *inhabit:* as Esay 13.20. Chap. 17.6. and 50.39. and, *dayes of antiquity:* as Lam. 1.7. and 5.21. yet the meaning is not that Egypt should at that time be raised to its former luster again but that it should then be peopled again, whereas by this conquest, there had been much of it dispeopled, and the residue much impaired. See Ezek. 29.13—15.

**Verse 27.** *{But fear not thou, O my Servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for behold, I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and be in rest, and at ease, and none shall make him afraid.}* A consolatory clause for the comfort and support of God's faithful ones, though dispersed abroad, and abiding in captivity at present. See the very same in the very same terms, chap. 30.10. Thus God yet never forgets, or forsakes those that continue constant and loyal to him, Ps. 9.10. and 94.14. Ezek. 11.16.

**Verse 28.** *{Fear thou not, O Jacob, my servant, saith the LORD;}* The same exhortation inculcated and repeated again and again, to cause it to make the deeper impression upon their drooping and dejected spirits. So Esay 41.10,13,14. and 43.1,5. and 44.2,8.

*{for I am with thee: for I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee, but I will not make a full end of thee; but correct thee in measure: yet will I not leave thee wholly unpunished.}* See chap. 30.11. where the very same words are.

## CHAPTER 47

**Verse 1.** *{The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the Prophet against the Philistines,}* Or, *Concerning the Philistines;* as chap. 44.1. The foregoing two prophecies, chap. 46.1,13. were concerning the Egyptians, the wonted stay that God's people were too prone to rely upon: the present in this chapter, is concerning the Philistines the bad neighbors, and both ancient and constant vexers and annoyers of them. See Esai 9.12. Chap. 25.20. and the like prophecies concerning them, Esai 14.29. Ezek. 25.15. Amos 1.6. Zeph. 2.4,5. Of the phrase, see Chap. 1.2,4.

*{before that Pharaoh smote Gaza.}* Before *that Pharaoh* Nechoh, as most suppose, either by the way, in his expedition against Carchemish, as some would have it, 2 Chro. 35.20. or, as others, rather, in his return from thence, after he had slain Josiah in Megiddo, 2 King 23.29. and was now on his way homeward, had *smote,* that is, by force stormed and taken, (as Ezek. 40.1.) *Gaza.* Heb. *Azzah;* a strong town of the Philistines, Judge 16.1. See on chap. 25.20. And this seems more probable, than that which the rabbins out of their *Seder Olam,* or, *Chronicles,* relate, that the Egyptians coming to relieve Jerusalem, besieged by the Chaldeans, in the tenth of Zedekiah's reign, when they found them risen, should in their return home overrun Palestine, and surprise Gaza. See chap. 34.22. and 37.9,11. This is here mentioned, to show that this prophecy was then delivered, when the Philistines were in a present quiet and flourishing condition, and had no fear of ought, either from Egypt, or from the Assyrians; much less, with whom they were at peace and amity: as also, as some suppose, to let the Philistines know, that they were to receive a far greater, and more general hurt from the Chaldeans, than that blow that the Egyptians were shortly to give them in the surprisal of Gaza.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus saith the LORD, Behold, waters rise up out of the North, and shall be an overflowing flood, and shall overflow the land, and all that is therein, the city, and them that dwell therein}* A far greater deluge will come upon the Philistines' land, from the north (that is, from Chaldea, Esai 14.31. chap. 6.1.) than that tempest from the south, from Egypt, Esai 30.6. that lighted upon Gaza: such an one as should overflow and drown, not some one city alone, but the whole land city, and country. As the Egyptians' excursions are resembled by the inundations of Nilus, chap. 44.7,8. So the Assyrian and Chaldean invasion by the overflowings of Euphrates, Esai 8.7. See the like, Esai 28.18. and 59.19. ch. 51.42. Heb. *the land, and the fulnesse thereof;* as Psalm 24.1. and *the city:* not this, or that particular, but collectively, *the cities,* in general; as Esai 19.2. and 27.10. See chap. 46.8. This, in all likelihood, came to pass, not long after the destruction of Jerusalem. See Joseph's *Antiquities,* lib. 13. cap. 7.

*{then the men shall cry, and all the inhabitants of the land shall howl.}* Heb. *and;* as chap. 44.15. and *man,* for *men; the man shall cry,* for, *they shall cry each one:* the noun singular, the verb plural; as chap. 4.3. & 44.16. there shall be nothing but crying and howling everywhere with them. See Esai 14.32.

**Verse 3.** *{At the noise of the stamping of the hoof of his strong horses;}* A description of such a dreadful approach of the enemy, as should so affright men, that it should make them, forgetting all natural affection, to seek only how to shift for themselves, with an utter neglect of those that are wont to be naturally dearest unto persons of all degrees. Instead of *strong horses,* which our version exhibits, some both here, and Judge 5.21. a place parallel to this, understand *strong men:* among whom the old Latin: the word is used of the prime, or principal, eminent, or excellent in any kind, whereof it is used. See Esai 10.13. and is most attributed unto *beeves,* or, *bulls,* Psal. 22.12. Esai 34.7. and *horses,* or *steeds,* chap. 8.16. and 50.11. and so here: and might well be rendered, without further addition, *of his steeds:* the word rendered *stamping,* is nowhere else found, but of the like notion another. Judges 5.22. by which some of the rabbins here expound it: Yet the Chaldee renders it, by a word that signifies *to go, passe,* or *pace,* in sound near to these our latter: and a learned late writer the rather inclines this way, because in the Syriac it is so commonly used.

*{at the rushing of his chariots,}* Or, *rustling,* Esai 17.12. or *ratling,* Nah. 3.2. the word signifies such a sound or noise, as is raised by the violent *concussion,* or *shaking* of ought, chap. 10.22. Heb. *chariot,* for, *cavalry;* as chap. 46.9. See there.

*{and at the rumbling of his wheels}* Of their chariot wheels, Esai 5.28. Ezek. 23.24. Nah. 3.2.

*{the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands.}* Extremity of fear, joined with feebleness as well of hand as of heart, shall so oversway natural affection with them, that they shall cast and seek everyone only how to shift for, and save himself, not once looking after their children, as unable to rescue them, though never so fain they would, and being in vain for them therefore to hazard their own lives, by looking after those, whom they were not able to relieve: they will trust to their heels rather than to their hands. See Chap. 16.6,7. and 46.5. and 49.5. See also, Deut. 28.31,32.

**Verse 4.** *{Because of the day that cometh to spoil all the Philistines}* The time by God designed for their destruction; as Chap. 46.10.

*{and to cut off from Tyrus, and Sidon, every helper that remaineth;}* For these being the issue and posterity of Cham by Canaan, and seated not far from the Philistines' quarters, who likewise were descended from him by Cush, were on all occasions ready to be assistant unto them. See Gen. 10.14,15,19. Joel 3.4.

*{for the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor.}* That the *Caphtorim* were of the same lineage and race with the Philistines being both of them descended from Mitsraim, appears Gen. 10.13,14. that before Moses his time, they dwelt near unto them, possessing the land that bordered upon them, even unto *Gaza,* from whence they had expelled the Avites, appears Deut. 2.23. and it may seem that they had sometime subdued the Philistines, and carried of them captive into their own country, from whence God had yet by some means rescued and reduced them again, Amos 9.7. Howbeit, in Jeremy's time it may hence be gathered, that they and the Philistines were confederate together, and in regard both of vicinity and confederacy, were likely to fare alike the one with the other. By *the remnant* of them some would have meant the Philistines, in general, because descended from the Caphtorim; but that is not so: for the *Philistines* are said not to have descended from the *Caphtorim,* but from the *Casluchim,* Gen. 10.14. Others, those of them, whom the Caphtorim should leave, when they did overrun Palestine. But they seem rather to be distinguished here from the Philistines, as well as the *Tyrians,* and *Sidonians,* before mentioned, and to be called *the remnant* of that country, either because the Egyptians had made spoil of them before, when they invaded Palestine, and Gaza, near unto which their ancient abode was: or because the Chaldeans were to begin with them, before they fell upon the Philistine country. See the like, chap. 25.20. What country this *Caphtor* should be, much doubt is made. The Chaldee paraphrast both here and elsewhere renders it, *Cappadocia:* and with him most, both Greeks and Latins, concur: and a learned late writer, though assigning Cappadocia to others, yet would seat these Caphtorim in Colchis, a country, if not coming within the compass of some part of it, yet confining at least upon it: and that the rather, because he finds a region in those parts, called *Sidene* from a city therein situate termed *Side,* which in Greek signifies a *pomegranate,* as does *Caphtor* also in Hebrew, Exod. 39.24—26. But as well Colchis, as Cappadocia, seems too far remote from the habitation of these Caphtorim. One of the Jewish commenters on this place, with whom the Arabic interpreter, and one, or two other Jewish writers are said to agree, would have *Caphtor* to be *Damiata,* which the later Greeks call *Tamiathis,* a city in Egypt: which though it may seem the more probable because they were of Mitsraim's race, yet the sacred records seem still to seat them not far from the Philistines, and more into the land, and not likely therefore in Egypt. I should rather suppose their place of abode to have been between Palestina, and Idumea, by conjecture from a city in Idumea, or its confines, called anciently from this *Caphtor Caparorsa;* as out of Ptolemy a learned annotator here observes. But why is their country then termed an *ile?* may some say; for that term in Hebrew, though it do not always denote an *Iland,* properly so termed; yet it implies, at least, *a sea-coast,* or a country bordering upon the sea: whereunto some answer, that all remote, or transmarine parts, such as passage was to by sea, are in Scripture so termed: but the word is used more generally for any foreign country, one, or other indefinitely. See Esai 20.6. and 41.1. and so the Caphtorims' country, though an inland one, may well come within the compass of that term.

**Verse 5.** *{Baldness is come upon Gaza:}* Either she is shaved and stripped of all her wealth by the enemies' pillage of it: as Esai 7.20. or rather they have made themselves bald by shaving and cutting, or pulling and tearing of their hair; which upon occasions of great grief was a thing usual among them, Job 1.20. Esai 15.2. chap. 16.6,7. and 41.5. and 46.37. Ezek. 29.18. Mic. 1.16. Of *Gaza,* see vers. 1. Heb. *Baldnesse is come unto Gaza:* and so the ancient Greek renders it sometime: but *el* is oft used for *al,* or *upon;* as chap. 36.23. and so the old Latin.

*{Ashkelon is cut off with the remnant of their valley.}* A chief city in Palestine: whereof see 1 Sam. 6.17. 2 Sam. 1.20. instead of, *is cut off;* as the word commonly signifies, Esai 15.1. Hosea 10.15. Zeph. 1.11. the old Latin here reads, *is silenced:* and the two roots in Hebrew are somewhat near, but divers. By the *remnant of their valley,* some of the Jewish doctors following the Chaldee, understand their *wealth:* for the word of *depth,* say they, from whence the word comes, has a notion of *abundance,* or *muchnesse,* Esai 7.11. Hosea 9.9. But other of them take the term in its ordinary sense, and understand it of such Askelonites, as lived not within the city, but in the vale near unto it. Some others more generally of the rest of the Philistines' country, that lay most of it low, and is termed thereof a *vale.* See Joseph the Jew his *Antiquities,* lib. 5. cap. 1. the ancient Greeks following some corrupt copy, render it, *the remnant of the Enakim;* as if it had some reference to the sons of *Anak,* Num. 13.22,29. Deut. 1.18,21. which yet a learned annotator seems to approve.

*{how long wilt thou cut thyself?}* Spoken to Askelon, or to Palestine in general, or the inhabitants of either; demanding of them how long they will be taking on in that manner, cutting & maiming themselves, as in extremity of grief and vexation, out of impotency and impatience of spirit, heathen people were wont to do. See Lev. 19.28. chap. 16.6. The speech implies, as a grievous, so a long and tedious calamity, and lamentation thereunto correspondent. The Greeks join this clause to the words following, rendering it, *how long wilt thou cut, O sword of the Lord?* but the word is in a reciprocal form: nor is it ever found in any other notion elsewhere. Howbeit, those reciprocal forms are not in notion perpetually such: and if any instance of this therein varying from the ordinary use could be produced, I should incline to this version: the rather, for that the text would go very smoothly away with it.

**Verse 6.** *{O thou sword of the LORD, how long will it be ere thou be quiet?}* The words, as some would have them, of the Philistine people cutting themselves, verse 5. But it sounds not after their profane strain; little dreamed they in likelihood of any hand of God in those things that now befell them. And the most therefore rather conceive them to be the prophet's own words, lamenting the havoc that the sword made among them, ranging up and down so long together from place to place with them, and humbly preferring his supplication to God for a stay of it. For God's prophets are sensible of, and affected with the calamities not of their own alone, but of other people also, though their enemies. See Esai 15.5. and 16.9. chap. 48.31.

*{O sword of the LORD?}* The *sword* he speaks of is the sword of the Chaldeans; but it is called *the Lords sword,* because sent by him; because it comes by command, and with commission from him, chap. 25.29. vers. 7. So, *the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon,* Judge 7.18,20.

*{put up thyself into thy scabbard:}* Not, *gather thy self,* or, *be gathered;* as some render it: though the word have usually a notion of gathering: but *retire*, or *betake thy self unto thy scabbard*; as the word is used, Exod. 9.19. Num. 11.30. 2 Sam. 17.13. Psalm 104.22.

*{rest, and be still.}* *Rest*; Of this term, see on chap. 31.2. the Latin renders it *be cooled*, or *cool thyself*: and that Popish Expositors descant upon to no purpose; for the word has no such notion in it; *and be still*. Heb. *be silent*; as Psal. 4.4. Esai 23.2.

**Verse 7.** *{How can it be quiet?}* An answer to the Prophet's request: or his own reply to himself, as recalling himself, and demanding of himself, how it could be that it should so do, when as God had given it a charge and command to the contrary. Heb. *How shalt thou be quiet?* or, *shouldest thou*; as in a potential notion: a change of the person; as Ezek. 31.10.

*{seeing the LORD hath given it a charge}* Heb. *and* (as chap. 10.26.) *the Lord hath commanded it*, and it cannot stay till his Command be executed, till his work be done, till his will and word be fulfilled. See chap. 23.20. and 30.24.

*{against Askelon, and against the sea shore? there hath he appointed it.}* Heb. *unto Askelon, and unto the sea-port*, or, *coast*, Gen. 49.13. Deut. 1.7. but *el*, may be for *al*; as before, vers. 5. *the sea-coast*; that is, Palestine in general, which coasted much on the midland Sea, Esai 9.12.

## CHAPTER 48

**Verse 1.** *{Against Moab}* Heb. *Unto Moab*; or, *Concerning Moab*: as Gen. 20.13. Psal. 91.11. chap. 14.10. See the like Prophecies against Moab, Esai 15. and 16. Amos 2.1. but those to be executed for the greatest part of them by the Assyrians; this, as that also, Ezek. 25.9. by the Chaldeans. See Joseph's *Antiquities*, lib. 7. cap. 11. on chap. 44.30.

*{thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel,}* As chap. 46.25. but here the rather so styled, because he is coming to be avenged upon Moab, for his Israel, and the wrongs by Moab done them; as the like, Esai 34.8.

*{Woe unto Nebo; for it is spoiled:}* *Nebo*, a city of Moab; whereof, see Esai 15.2. It seems to have its name from some idols' oracle there seated: and the Prophet is by some deemed the rather to begin with it: because thence they had their oracles of prosperity and peace, such as themselves desired, and their idol Interpreters were wont to coin for them, and to furnish them with.

*{Kiriathaim is confounded and taken:}* Another City of Moab, sometime belonging to the Reubenites, Josh. 13.19. it is of a dual form, whereby the city seems to have consisted, as divers others, and so Jerusalem itself, of two parts.

*{Misgab is confounded and dismayed.}* Whether the word here used be a noun of common notion, signifying *an high place*, as Psal. 9.9. and 46.7,11. but taken collectively for the high & strong forts of Moab in general, or the proper name of a place, is questionable: and it may well seem to be, either the peculiar name of some place usually so termed, though from a word of more general notion; as *Bostrah*, both in Moab, vers. 24. and in Edom, Esai 34.6. and 63.1. or, as some think, an attribute of it, rendering the Text, the city *of the high place*; thereby understanding a city in Moab from its situation called *Bamoth*, Num. 21.20. and *Sela*, Esai 16.1. because situate *aloft* upon a *rock*.

**Verse 2.** *{There shall be no more praise of Moab: in Heshbon they have devised evil against it;}* This passage is variously both divided and rendered. This of our Version will not well stand; for who in Heshbon should consult, or conspire against Moab? *Heshbon* itself being a city, and that a chief one in Moab's country, Esai 15.4. & 16.8. and no better will that of the old Latin hold, *There shall be no more exultation of Moab against Heshbon.* For there is as little reason, why Moab should exult against Heshbon, as why Heshbon should conspire against Moab. Others therefore render it, *There shall be no more vaunting of Moab in Heshbon*; that is, Heshbon shall no more vaunt itself of the strength of their State, of the Kingdom of Moab its wealth and power. Others, *There shall be no more vaunting in Moab concerning Heshbon*; that is, the Moabites shall no more vaunt of Heshbon as a place impregnable; esteemed one of the greatest strength in those parts, verse 45. Others lastly, *No more praise of Moab shall there be*; (there shall be no more talking abroad of Moab, as of a goodly, famous, rich, flourishing State) *as concerning Heshbon*, (so is the particle used, chap. 38.24. vers. 27.) *they* (that is, the Chaldeans) *have devised evil against it*. There is in the words an elegant allusion to the name of the city; as if it were said with us, *There is mischief devised against Devises*: a Town of that name with us, that suffered in the late civil wars; and for notion answers precisely to the Hebrew *Heshbon*.

*{come, and let us cut it off from being a nation.}* The Chaldeans' words expressing their purpose against Moab, and egging one another on to the execution of it, as c. 6.4,5. See the like of other nations, among which Moab is one, now paid in his own coin, against Israel, Psal. 83.4. The like form, see vers. 42. Esai 17.1. and 23.1. and 24.10. 1 Sam. 15.22. Hos. 4.6. and 9.12.

*{also thou shalt be cut down, O mad-men;}* Another city of Moab called *Madiama* by Ptolemy; *Madeba*, (which some suppose should be *Medema*) in Joseph's *Antiquities*, lib. 13. cap. 17.) thereof see Esai 25.10. Heb. *thou shalt be silenced*, or, *brought to silence*; as Psal. 31.17,18. you shall be brought so low, that you shall not dare so much as to mutter for fear and dejection of spirit, much less vaunt yourself as formerly. See Esai 29.4. chap. 46.22. There is again in the terms here used an affinity of sound, as if it were said, *Silly* (the name of an Island with us) *shall be silenced*.

*{the sword shall pursue thee.}* Heb. *Go after thee*, as chap. 42.16. and 49.37.

**Verse 3.** *{A voice of crying shall be from Horonaim:}* A city of Moab, where Sanballat was born; or whereof he was sometime Governor, Neh. 2.10. See Esai 15.5. vers. 5. And it is of a dual form, says the Rabbine, because there were two *Horons*, the upper and the lower. See Josh. 10.10,11. and 16.15. and 18.13.

*{spoiling, and great destruction.}* Heb. *a great breach*; as chap. 4.20. So chap. 50.22. and 51.54.

**Verse 4.** *{Moab is destroyed:}* Heb. *is broken*; as chap. 22.20.

*{her little ones have caused a cry to be heard.}* While the great ones leave them to save themselves; as chap. 47.3. and there is an elegant consonancy in the words of *little ones*, and *cry*, which our English cannot express. See the like, Esai 5.7. For the Chaldee seems to stray here, rendering it *Sultans*, or *Princes*; which yet the Jewish Commenters retaining, say, some of them, that they are so called here, because less than Kings, lower than Sovereigns. Other of them, that they are so termed in way of derision and contempt. But these are like herein to the Popish Expositors, torturing the Text, and their wits withal, to make somewhat of a vicious Version.

**Verse 5.** *{For in the going up of Luhith, continual weeping shall go up:}* Up, and down all the way along, that the Moabites flee from, or before the Chaldeans pursuing them, ver. 2. shall be nothing but continual weeping and wailing. See Esai 15.5. Heb. *weeping with weeping shall go up*; as Esai 16.9.

*{for in the going down of Horonaim the enemies have a cry of destruction.}* Heb. *of breaking*; as vers. 3. which some expound *a broken cry*; as having reference not so much to the occasion, or subject of it, as the Jewish Commenters, and others of ours take it; as to the manner, or quality, and affection of their cry: and because the word *enemies* is in a form of regiment, they render it, *the enemies of breaking*, or, broken noise, *have heard a broken cry*, to wit, from the Moabites, crying so loud, that they drown the enemies' shouts with their outcries. But the Jewish Critic well observes, that the form regent, or the contracted form, is not infrequently found used for the absolute and entire; as Num. 5.18. 1 King. 4.6. and 17.13. and our Version therefore may well stand. As for that which a learned Writer has, that they wept indeed as they went up to Luhith, but more abundantly and vehemently when they went down from Horonaim, because that was the utter limit of their land; and they were then going into captivity to leave their country, seems not so probable, because of that which follows, ver. 6. Whereby it appears, that they fled rather from them, than were yet led away by them. It seems rather to argue the impotency of their spirits, and excessiveness of their griefs; that whereas it had been their wisest course to have made away, with as much silence and secrecy as they could; yet they were not able to contain themselves, but must needs cry out, and that so loud, that the enemies themselves might hear them. See somewhat the like, but in another case, Gen. 45.2.

**Verse 6.** *{Flee, save your lives, and be like the heath in the wilderness.}* These are by the most Interpreters conceived to be the words of the Moabites, calling one upon another to flee with all speed for their lives, and betaking themselves to the deserts, there to live; as Psal. 55.7. The word *Aroer* here used, the Chaldee takes for the proper name of a place, as it is afterward, vers. 19. as if it were said, *Be like the tower of Aroer* that stands in the waste; but therein few follow him: the word signifies *a bare naked tree*: whereof see on chap. 17.6. and one of the Jewish Doctors seems to expound it of their cities, leave them as bare as such trees on the waste. See vers. 9. Some would have them to be the speech of the Prophet himself in a prophetical way, foretelling what should befall them, to wit, that they should be compelled to flee for their lives, and be as bare and vile as the heath that grows on the waste; or as some naked tree, standing by itself alone on the waste, stripped of all graceful furniture of fruit, or leaf, and exposed to all winds and weathers. And a learned Writer conceives it to be mixed with an Irony, as if he should say, Flee, you may save your lives, and so do; but when you have done all you can, and escaped the sword, your life will be such, that it had been better for you to have died by it; your life will prove more miserable and bitter to you than death. See Lam. 4.9. I adhere to what was propounded at first: or, if ought further be deemed to lie hid in this last clause, I should rather conceive it to be spoken out of a regard had, above all besides it, to life; as Job 2.4. Matth. 16.26. as if it were said, *Flee, and save your selves*, or *your lives*, (Heb. *soul*, as chap. 51.6.
