Job 2.6.) whatsoever we do else, though you leave yourselves as bare as the nakedest shrub that grows on the wild waste: the looking after ought else may cost you your life. It seems to me not unlike that advice of our Savior, Mat. 24.16–18. Luke 17.31,33.

**Verse 7.** *{For because thou hast trusted in thy works, and in thy treasures, thou shalt also be taken,}* Your self-confidence shall prove your ruin. *Thy works*; some understand their idols, Psal. 115.3. Chap. 32.30. Others, their possessions, 1 Sam. 25.2. Others again, their fortifications, verse 18.41. It may seem to comprehend all those means, whereby they had endeavored to strengthen themselves.

*{and Chemosh shall go forth into captivity with his Priests, and his Princes together.}* *Chemosh*, your chief idol, Numb. 11.29. 1 Kings 11.7,23. whom in vain therefore you shall seek unto, Esay 15.2. verse 13.46. *shall go into captivity*, (as Chap. 15.1,2. See Esay 46.2. Chap. 43.12.) and all his abettors together with him, the *Priests* that attend on him, and *Princes* that maintain both them, and him, Chap. 49.3.

**Verse 8.** *{And the spoiler shall come upon every city, and none shall escape}* The King of Babylon. chap. 6.26.

*{the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed,}* The cities situate in the vale and in the plain, together with those that stand on the hills, and higher grounds, verse 1. See chap. 47.5.

*{as the LORD hath spoken.}* *Asher*, for, *caasher*, as the Jewish Critic here observes; and so the ancient Greek here renders it *as*; so also, Exod. 34.18. Chap. 9.14. & 23.32. or, as others, and so the old Latin; *because the Lord hath spoken*; as 1 Kings 15.13. Neh. 2.3,10. Chap. 1.15. & 13.25. or, *surely*; as a learned late Writer; and so says he, 1 Sam. 15.20. Neh. 4.12. Psal. 10.6. & 9.11. & 44.11. Esay 8.20. Habb. 3.16. I suppose it may as fitly be rendered, *for the Lord hath said it*: as 1 Sam. 15.15. Chap. 3.23. a defect of the pronoun, as Esay 1.20. See chap. 46.25.

**Verse 9.** *{Give wings unto Moab,}* Implying, that there would be no possibility for him to escape, unless he could get wings and fly. So Psal. 55.6. Heb. *Give ye feather*, or, *wing to Moab*: the word here used, does with the Hebrews, in the first place, signify *a flower*, Job 14.2. Esay 40.6. in the next place, *a feather*; so termed, says the Jewish Critic, because feathers sprout out from the bodies of Fowls, as flowers do from the stems and branches of trees and plants: and from a word therefore of that notion have the young of Birds and Fowls their name, Deut. 22.6. Job 39.30. Psal. 84.3. *feather* therefore for *feathers*, or for *wing*, consisting of *feathers*: either taken collectively. Howbeit, some of our Jewish Masters fetch it another way about; the word, say they, in Chaldee, signifies the fins of fish. So used, Lev. 11.5. and in the next place the *wings* of Fowl: so they use it, Psal. 139.9. because *wings* are to the one, as *fins* to the other; the one to fly, the other to swim with. The word in this notion is nowhere else found in the Hebrew. But the old Latin taking the word in his first and proper sense, as also some Greek Versions before it, renders it, *Give Moab a flower*, or, *flowers; for he shall go out flourishing*: Which though it be here so senseless a notion, that it can be no way fitted to the context; yet Popish Expositors waste ink and paper in discoursing at large of it, and descanting upon it; forcing in hither the fading nature of flowers, and the sticking of corpses with them, and adding a forged fiction withal of a ceremony used in the land of Moab, of setting garlands on the heads of those that were to be executed: and all this, because their vicious Version must be maintained, though it be never so absurd. What the ancient Greeks read here is uncertain: for they render it, *Give Moab a sign; for with a touch he shall be touched*. And the Chaldee roves here as wide as the rest, rendering it, *Take away the crown from Moab, he is going into captivity*: and it seems that hence the Paraphrast took his rise for this Version; because the word here used does sometime signify *a plate of gold*, Exod. 28.36. Lev. 8.9. such as *crowns* are wont to be adorned with, or consist of: whence also some expound that, Psal. 132.17. *I will adorn his crown, with golden plates*. But the text speaks of somewhat to be given to him, not taken from him: and the very next words sufficiently refell all these figments and fancies: whereof thus much only, that none may trip or stick at them.

*{that it may flee, and get away,}* Heb. *that* (as Job 11. Psal. 25.15.) *she may flying, fly*; as the word is used, Job 4.15. and thence a word for *a feather*, wherewith Fowl fly, Lev. 1.16. Ezek. 17.3,7. and for the *Estrich*, a Fowl of goodly, large, and fair feathers, Job 39.15. an irregularity which the Jewish give notice of, not observed in the word here used, has caused a mistake both in our Version, and some others: which yet for the meaning in general are sound, though they fail in the genuine notion of the terms, supposing them to come from two several roots: and the latter to signify *to go out*, not *to fly*.

*{for the cities thereof shall be desolate without any to dwell therein.}* Heb. *desolation*: as Chap. 44.2,22.

**Verse 10.** *{Cursed be he that doth the work of the LORD deceitfully,}* Or, *negligently*: (and so the Greek renders it) or *slackly*: as, *a bow of slackness*, or, *a slack bow*, Psal. 78.57. and *an hand of slackness*, or, *a slack hand*: opposed to a *diligent* one, Prov. 10.4. & 12.24. The work of the Lord in destroying the Moabites, and doing execution upon them: which God has now given in charge to the Chaldeans, by a secret instinct concerning the Moabites: as by an express word to Saul concerning the Amalekites, 1 Sam. 15. and would have done to the purpose. See chap. 47.6,7. & 50.25.

*{and cursed be he that keepeth back his sword from blood.}* A curse there is as well on such as shed not blood, when they have Commission and charge from God so to do, as on those that do the like without either: Numbers 34.31,33. 1 Kings 20.42. Proverbs 17.15.

**Verse 11.** *{Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity:}* Moab has lived a long time at ease, he has not been disturbed much in his land, or removed out of it, and hurried from place to place, as Israel has been: illustrated by a resemblance taken from wines that have not been drawn from lees, as those whereof Esay 25.6. Heb. *to his lees*: *el*, for, *al*; as chap. 36.23. & 47.5,7.

*{therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed,}* Or, *remaineth*. Heb. *standeth*, or *stayeth*: Deuteronomy 5.31. Eccles. 1.4. He retains still his state, his dignity, his strength, his wealth; and withal (as with such wicked ones especially is wont to be) his pride, his presumption, his impiety, his impurity, his iniquity. See Psalm 55.19. Esay 26.10. Hos. 4.7. Zeph. 1.12. verse 26,29.

**Verse 12.** *{Therefore behold the days come, saith the LORD;}* Heb. *The days coming*; c. 31.27.

*{that I will send unto him wanderers that shall cause him to wander;}* Heb. *and* (as chap. 41.15.) *I will send him wanderers*; (such as come from a far country, from Chaldea Esay 39.3. chapter 6.22. and 8.19.) or *transporters*; as the Jewish Commenters would have it: so rendering it also, Esay 63.1. such as make others to wander: but the word seems rather to be in a consistent, than a transient notion, both here and there; and to signify in his first and single form *to wander*, or travel from place to place; in his second or double form, *to make to wander*, or *to remove*: and there is an elegant *antanaclasis*, or variety of notion in the terms; as if it were said, the Chaldeans shall come far from their own place of abode into the Moabites' country, as if they were some *vagrants*, or *wanderers*; but they shall make the Moabites in good earnest to wander, by leading them away captives, v. 46.

*{and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles.}* Alluding to the former resemblance of Wine, either in casks, or in bottles. They shall depopulate his Cities (as Chapter 51.34. and break them as earthen bottles, Psalm 2.9. Esay 30.14. Chapter 19.10,11.

**Verse 13.** *{And Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel their confidence}* Because he shall be no more able to deliver, them from the Chaldeans, v. 7.46. Esay 15.2. and 16.12. than the golden calf at Bethel, 1 Kings 12.39. was able to save the Israelites from the Assyrians, 2 Kings 17.6,12. Hos. 8.4,5. & 10.15.

**Verse 14.** *{How say yee, we are mighty and strong men for the war?}* Or, *How can yee say?* As Chapter 2.23. with what face can you brag of your valor, when you carry yourselves as cowards? vers. 39.41. See the like in another kind: Esay 19.11. and of Moab's vaunts, 2.29,30.

**Verse 15.** *{Moab is spoiled and gone up out of her Cities}* There is no small variety of Versions and Interpretations of the latter clause here; for the former is the same in effect with what he had before, v. 1.8. and has after again, ver. 18,20. The Hebrew has no more than this, *and her Cities it*, or *he, is gone up*. Some render it *her Cities*, or the multitude of her *Cities are gone up*, to wit, into smoke; that is they are burnt: as Judges 20.40. Esay 9.18. Others, *her Cities are gone*; they are lost, fallen down. So the old Latin: Or *are gone up* say some, that is, are perished and *destroyed* as the Chaldee has it: taken from vapors, that as they ascend, vanish away, James 4.14. so they suppose the word to be taken, Amos 8.8. Nah. 2.1. but these places are as dubious, if not more than this. Others, *he* (that is, the inhabitant of Moab) *is deported* from, or *gone out of his*, or *her Cities*, or *he shall depart* from *his Cities*; as the word is used, Numbers 16.26. 1 Samuel 14.46. Chapter 37.57. but the Verb is here masculine, the Pronoun affixed to the Noun feminine. Others, *he* (to wit, the enemy) *hath made the Cities to ascend*; that is he has destroyed and taken them away; as Psalm 102.24. but the forms are not the same. Others, *the stirrer up of her is come up*; that is, one is come, or coming up to her that will rouse her from her security, verse 11. from a word that signifies *to raise*, or *rouse up*, Joel 3.9. but no instance of such use of the word is produced. A learned late Annotator coming after all these, renders it, *her enemies are got up*, over her: *to ascend*, or *get up*, or *over one*, for to overmaster him, or to be advanced to greater honor and dignity than he: and *to descend*, for to be overmastered by another, and depressed to more disgrace and misery. Deut. 28.42. So here in this branch, and the next: and the word *ar*, is by a Chaldaism put sometime for *tsar*; that is, *an enemy*, or *adversary*; as 1 Samuel 28.16. Neh. 4.12. Psalm 10.6. & 95.11. & 144.12. Esay 8.20. Dan. 4.16. and for the diversity of the number between the Verb and the Noun, it is not unusual in a distributive notion; *her enemies each of them hath got up*, or *shall get up*; as the like, Exodus 17.12. Job 12.7. Proverbs 14.1. Joel 1.20. But this learned man does elsewhere go himself another way, one of those before specified. I shall add in the last place mine own opinion, yet mine alone; for I find it backed by a Jewish Master, I light hitherto on none that take notice of it, and his son, though he relate him, seems not to adhere to him: I render the words with him, *Moab is*, or, *shall be spoiled*; *he* (to wit, the spoiler) *is come up*, or, *shall come up on her cities*; as verse 18. *the spoiler is come upon thee*: and of Babylon, Chap. 51.48,56. and, *her cities*, as *her young men*, in the next branch: the noun or participle is supplied from the foregoing verb; as Gen. 50.2,26. the preposition included in the verb present.

*{and his chosen young men are gone down to the slaughter,}* Or, *shall go down*; that is, be struck down, and slain, as an ox, or other the like beast, by the sacrificer, or the butcher; as Esay 34.6. chap. 50.27. & 51.40. So rather than as that learned Annotator, who would have it parallel to that, Deut. 28.42. and an *antithesis* herein between this and that of *ascending* in the former branch: which though some may well be granted; yet that which he would have, the very words of the text refuse to admit. Heb. *the choice of her young men*; as Exod. 15.4. and there is an elegant consonancy of the two terms in the text, not in sound of letters only, but in notion also, and notation; as if it were said, *The choice of her choice ones.*

*{saith the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts.}* As chap. 46.18.

**Verse 16.** *{The calamity of Moab is near to come, and his affliction hasteth fast.}* So Esay 13.22. Mal. 3.5. 2 Pet. 2.13.

**Verse 17.** *{All ye that are about him bemoan him, and all ye that know his name;}* Condole with him, both you that are his near neighbors, and have been formerly acquainted with him, and you also that are further off, and have known him only by hearsay.

*{Say ye, how is the strong staff broken, and the beautiful rod?}* Heb. *staffe of strength*; and, *rod of beauty*, or, *bravery*; as it is rendered, Esay 3.18. See Ezek. 19.11,14. How is Moab destroyed, notwithstanding the greatness of his strength and state, that he so much gloried in, and trusted unto? Ezek. 19.12. *staffe and rod*, are emblems of power and authority Psal. 110.2. Zach. 11.7. Yet because the same terms import oft-times an afflicting and chastising or punishing power, Esay 10.5. Lam. 3.1. in regard hereof some conceive here to be an intimation withal of Moab's having been over-troublesome and burdensome to others in the height of her former strength and state; and this way the Chaldee Paraphrast seems to incline. See the like of some other, Esay 14.4,10,12. Chap. 50.23. & 51.41. Lam. 1.1.

**Verse 18.** *{Thou daughter that dost inhabit Dibon,}* You goodly fair city, like some beautiful and gorgeous damsel, See chap. 46.11,19. and of Dibon, see Num. 21.30. Esay 15.2,9.

*{Come down from thy glory,}* As Esay 47.1. Chap. 13.18. the pronoun is wanting, as chap. 31.17.

*{and sit in thirst}* Not in your fat soil, and well-watered plains, where formerly you did reside, Numb. 21.13,14,20. & 22.1. but in some dry and thirsty place: *thirst*, for a place *of thirst*; as Psal. 107.33. Esay 35.7. or, *a thirsty place*; as Esay 44.3. a defect of the subject, see verse 6.

*{for the spoiler of Moab shall come upon thee and he shall destroy thy strong holds.}* See verse 8.15. & verse 1.

**Verse 19.** *{O Inhabitant}* Heb. *Inhabitress*; as chap. 10.17. & 22,23. & 44.19. & 51.35. So verse 18.

*{of Aroer}* A city of Moab situate on the banks of the river Arnon, Deut. 2.36. & 3.12.

*{stand by the way, and espy, ask him that fleeth, and her that escapeth, and Say, what is done?}* Ask of every one that passes by you, whether man or woman, What is the cause of their flight; as chap. 46.5. or inquire of them how things go abroad; as people full of fears are wont to do, 1 Sam. 4.13.

**Verse 20.** *{Moab is confounded; for it is broken down:}* The answer of those that either flee, or pass by, returned to the former inquiry: that all is lost, verse 4.

*{howl and cry,}* Esay 16.7. So chap. 47.2.

*{tell it in Arnon}* Of this river, see Num. 21.13. and it may seem that some city of special note had its name also from it: otherwise, by *Arnon* must be understood the region near about it, or on the other side of it.

*{that Moab is spoiled.}* Verse 15.

**Verse 21.** *{And judgment is come upon the plain country,}* As well as upon the higher land: or upon Moab's land in general, being most of it such. See the like, chap. 47.5. Heb. *land of plainness*, or, *evenness*; as Psal. 143.10. Esay 26.10.

*{upon Holon,}* A city of Moab. verse 24. We find one of that name in Judah's lot, Josh. 15.51. assigned the Levites. Josh. 21.15.

*{and upon Jahazah,}* Mentioned in Reuben's lot, Josh. 13.18.

*{and upon Mephaath,}* Out of Reuben's lot, Josh. 13.18. assigned the Levites, Josh. 21.37.

**Verse 22.** *{And upon Dibon,}* In Reuben's lot, Josh. 13.17. See verse 18.

*{and upon Nebo,}* See Num. 32.3. from whence it appears that most of the Towns here mentioned, were sometime part of the possessions of those Kings of the Amorites, whom the Israelites subdued beyond Jordan. See also verse 1.

*{and upon Beth diblathaim,}* One of the Israelites' stations in their passage to Canaan, Num. 33.46,47. called there *Aimon-Diblathaim*, and *Dibla*, Ezek. 6.14. whence it appears, that it stood toward the wilderness. The ancient Greek renders it, *the house of Dethlathaim*; and the old Latin accordingly, though less corruptly, *the house of Deblathaim*; as if it were the name of some person, as is *Diblaim*, Hos. 1.3. but *Beth* is part of the name of the city, as in *Bethlehem*, and *Bethshemesh*, and *Bethoron*, and the like: and it may in them signify, not so much an *house*, as *a city*. So *Beth-gamul*, and *Bethmeon*, verse 23.

**Verse 23.** *{And upon Kiriathaim,}* Of it, see Num. 32.37. Josh. 13.19.

*{and upon Bethgamul,}* This city I find not elsewhere named in Scripture: A learned late Writer supposes it to signify in notion and notation, the same with *Gag-gamal*, or *Gaugamela*, the place of Darius his last defeat by Alexander; and to signify *the Town of Camels*: (as Strabo also, lib. 16. observes of that other, that it signifies, *the house of a Camel*) and to be that which for *Gamala* is written *Malala* in Ptolemy.

*{and upon Beth meon.}* See Esay 15.2.

**Verse 24.** *{And upon Kerioth,}* Josh. 15.25. Amos 2.2.

*{and upon Bozrah,}* Not that in the land of Edom, Esay 63.1. but another of the same name in the land of Moab, called also Bezer, Josh. 22.36. the word signifies a strong fort, or hold, Esay 25.2. & 26.10. See on verse 1. and thence came the Punic pronunciation, *Bursa*, and by Inversion of letters in the Greek and Latin, *Byrsa*, the name of the Fort that Dido built in Africa; of which they give another fabulous notation. See Virgil. *Eneides*, l. 1.

*{and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near.}* *And*, for, *the rest of*; as Chap. 43.2.

**Verse 25.** *{The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, saith the LORD.}* His might and majesty is utterly abandoned; set out by a twofold expression and resemblance: the one taken from beasts, whose force and grace is in their horns, Psal. 74.4,5,10. & 89.17. & 92.10. & 148.14. Lam. 2.3. the other from man, whose strength, for action, consists most in his arms Job 22.9. Psal. 10.15. & 18.30. & 37.17. & 89.13,21. Ezek. 30.21,22. A learned late Writer supposes in the terms of *horn* and *arm*, the names of two cities in that country alluded to, called by Ptolemy, the one *Karna* the other, *Zoara*; which come very near to those words in the Hebrew. And by *horn*, and *arm*; some, after the Chaldee, understand *Sultans* or *Princes*, Num. 22.14,15.

**Verse 26.** *{Make ye him drunk,}* Make Moab drunk, you Chaldeans; not with wine, but with the wine cup of God's wrath, cause him to drink of it, till he stagger and fall. Esay 51.17–23. Psal. 60.3. & 75.8. Chap. 21.17,21,28. Ezek. 23.32–34. as drunken men use to do, Psal. 107.27.

*{for he magnified himself against the LORD:}* So Lam. 1.9. Zeph. 2.10. and those that so do, God will expose to shame and contempt, Prov. 3.34,35. & 11.2. Luke 14.11. & 18.14. *against the Lord's people*, says the Chaldee. So verse 27. & Zeph. 2.4,10. See Psal. 89.50,51. Ezek. 36.20.

*{Moab also shall wallow in his vomit,}* As men in drink are wont to do, Esay 19.14. Heb. *and*; as chap. 1.3. or, as some render it, *then*: as Chap. 44.10. The old Latin renders the verb here used, *shall clap his hands*; and though the word *hand*, be not in the text, yet the word here found, is so used: sometime with it, as Numb. 24.10. Job 27.23. Lam. 2.15. sometime without it, as Job 34.37. but this seems not to fit so well here: the word is used for *to smite*, or, *beat*. So, *to smite on the thigh* Chap. 31.18. Ezek. 21.12. and, *to beat down*, or, *beat one against another*, Job 34.26. and might therefore not amiss be rendered, *beateth himself* (as he tumbles and rolls to and fro) *in his vomit*. I shall add only a conjecture, and shall leave it to the Learned. Why may not the verb be taken here indefinitely? and then might the word well be rendered in its most usual acception, as the old Latin takes it, but making Moab, not the agent, but the object of the action: *he shall clap the hands at Moab* lying *in his vomit*: he that is, any one, or, every one; as in such indefinite forms, the words are commonly expressed: as Gen. 11.9. Some such thing the Chaldee gives an hint of: who paraphrasing the place, says *jidreshun*: that is, in the common acception of the word, *they shall seek out the Moabites in their holes*; but peradventure it is a term, by corruption drawn from the Latin *irrideo*: as divers terms in Chaldee both from the Latin and Greek are, See Dan. 3.5. and then it is, *they shall deride them*. But this I propound only: yet hence observing that the Chaldee took the word *Moab* here for a noun, not preceding, but following the verb.

*{and he also shall be in derision.}* As men in such case are wont to be exposed, while they so lie along, to scorn and derision, Gen. 9.21.

**Verse 27.** *{For was not Israel a derision unto thee?}* Heb. *And*. as Chap. 44.13,17. Did not you deride him in his misery, and rejoice at his fall, Job 31.29. when the ten tribes were spoiled and captivated by Salmanesar? 2 Kings 17. and is it not just then, that the like now befall you? See Judg. 1.7. Prov. 24.17,18. See the like charge against the Ammonites, Ezek. 25.6. and of the insolences of them both against God's People, Zephan. 2.8,10.

*{was he found among thieves?}* That you should so deride him, insult over him, and make a laughingstock of him, as men are wont to do with thieves, when they are taken in the manner? a proverbial form of speech. See Chap. 2.26. and Job 30.5. and the like expostulation, chap. 2.14. & 49.1. Some require here a supply of somewhat, whereof they conceive a defect, to make the sentence more complete: and they supply therefore both the negative particle from the former branch, as Psal. 9.18. Ezek. 20.30. and the note of similitude, as Psal. 11.1. Esay 21.8. and whereas in the copies there is here some variety; the word *found*; being in a masculine form, in some of them, in a feminine in others; some following the former: which is the more commonly received, render the words, *was he not to thee as one found among thieves?* Others, taking to the latter, render it, *Was he not with thee a thing found among thieves?* for the Hebrews use ordinarily the feminine in a neutral notion: and the theft or thing stolen being found about a thief, is wont to be much matter, as of shame and disgrace to him, so of merriment and laughter to others. But I see no necessity of departing from the received, either reading or version.

*{for since thou spakest of him, thou skippedst for joy.}* Or, *that* (as Verse 20.) *so oft as thou speakest of him*, (so is the particle here found used, 1 Sam. 18.30. 1 Kings 14.28. 2 Kings 4.8. 2 Chron. 12.11. Esay 28.19.) Heb. *from thy words of him*; as Chap. 20.8. & 31.20. So oft as you have any words concerning him, or his calamity, or captivity, *thou shakest thyself*, or, *movest thyself*, for joy, or, with laughter; as is implied from the former branch: or, as some, *thou shakest* the head at him, in way of insultation, and derision, Psal. 22.7. Lam. 1.8. and so also some would have the word here, used; Psal. 64.8. Howbeit, a learned late Writer following the old Latin, would have this clause rendered; *but* (as Gen. 45.8. Chap. 46.21.) *for those words* (or, because of that which you have spoken) *against him; thou shalt wander*, or, *be led captive*; and the verb indeed in his first form signifies *to remove*, or *wander*, from place to place: whence the land of *Nod* Gen. 4.14,16. But the reciprocal form will not so well here admit it.

**Verse 28.** *{O ye that dwell in Moab; leave the cities, and dwell in the rock:}* Leave your wonted places of abode, verse 6. and betake yourselves for surety and safety to the ragged rocks, if you can find any succor or shelter there, Judg. 20.45. and 21.23. Esay 2.19,21.

*{and be like the dove, that maketh her nest in the sides of the holes mouth,}* That for fear of birds of prey is wont to build in some cleft on the side of a rock, Cant. 2.14. Chap. 49.16. Heb. *in the passages of the mouth of the pit*. Whence the Chaldee understands it of a dove that is come down from her turret, or locker, to hide herself in some hole on the ground: but the former seems the genuine sense and more agreeable to that fowl's wont.

**Verse 29.** *{We have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart.}* God's words, manifesting his taking notice of Moab's proud and arrogant carriages. See Esay 16.6. where a great part is found of that which follows. Yet somewhat is added here to Esay's words, and so after again; to show, says a learned Writer, that the Moabites not only persisted in the same sins, but grew worse rather than better; as those, Chap. 9.3.

**Verse 30.** *{I know his wrath, saith the LORD, but it shall not be so, his lies shall not so effect it.}* His vain vaunts and menaces against me and my people, Verse 26. Zeph. 2.8. which I take notice of, (as Hos. 5.3. Amos 5.12.) shall not take effect, Psal. 1.4. & 33.10,11. or, as some render the latter words, *those on whom he stayeth*, or, relies, (Heb. *his bars*) *do not right*. See Chap. 50.36. A late learned Annotator gives here a twofold reading diverse from others before him; either thus, *I know his rage, and that not to be right*, just and equal; I know also that *they do* each of them *his lies*, and not that which is right: or thus. *I know his rage*, is it *not so?* (is he not exceedingly outrageous? and *his lies*, (I know also) *do they not do so?*) Is it not true, that he is in either kind very faulty? the words read interrogatively; as 1 Sam. 20.14. But of this passage, see more on Esay 16.6.

**Verse 31.** *{Therefore will I howl for Moab, and I will cry out for all Moab:}* Esay 16.7. *Moab shall howl for Moab.* But what was there said of the Moabites howling one for, or over, another, the Prophet applies unto himself here. So verse 32.

*{mine heart shall mourn for the men of Kirheres}* *mine heart*, is supplied from Esay 15.5. Yet some render it without any supply, *he shall mourn*, that is, *Moab shall mourn*: or, taking the verb indefinitely, *men shall mourn*; or, *mourning there shall be*: as Esay 32.12. *for the men of Kirheres*. Esay 16.7. *for the foundations of Kirhareseth*; for the city there, for the people here: for the city is the same.

**Verse 32.** *{O vine of Sibmah, I will weep with thee for the weeping of Jazer:}* Or, as some render it, or, *above more than, the weeping of Jazer*. So is this form taken; Psal. 45.7. & 130.6. Chap. 49.19. I will bewail you more largely and lamentably than Esay bewailed Jazer: whose words and forms of lamentation Jeremy here entertains and enlarges, the rather for that this devastation of Moab by the Chaldeans was to be much more grievous, than that Esay foretold by the Assyrians, Esay 16.14. See of Sibmah, and this passage there, Esay 16.8,9.

*{thy plants are gone over the sea, they reach even to the sea of Jazer:}* See Esay 16.8.

*{the spoiler is fallen upon thy summer-fruit, and upon thy vintage.}* See Verse 8,18. & Esay 16.9.

**Verse 33.** *{And joy and gladness is taken from the plentiful field, and from the land of Moab, and I have caused wine to fail from the winepresses; none shall tread with shouting,}* See Esay 16.10. *tread*, for, *tread grapes*. as Esay 63.2. Chap. 29.30. and in Esay, *to tread wine*, for, to tread grapes, to make *wine*.

*{their shouting shall be no shouting}* The shout of the enemies assailing them, and breaking in upon them, Chap. 25.30. or the shout and outcry that themselves shall make at the enemies' irruption after storming of them, shall be another manner of shout and cry, than that which they were wont to use in the Vintage or harvest times, at the bringing in of the wine and corn; a shout, not of joy and mirth, but of terror and dread, vers. 34. chap. 51. See Exodus 32.18.

**Verse 34.** *{From Heshbon, even unto Elealeh, and even unto Jahaz have they uttered their voice}* See Esay 15.4.

*{from Zoar even unto Horonaim, as an heifer of three years old,}* Thus begins to low after the bull. See Esay 15.5. Verse 3.

*{for the waters also of Nimrim shall be desolate.}* Heb. *desolations*; as Chap. 51.62. See Esay 15.9.

**Verse 35.** *{Moreover, I will cause to cease in Moab, saith the LORD, him that offereth in the high places, and him that burneth incense to his gods.}* Heb. *And*. as Chap. 44.24. that which was before threatened, Ver. 7. See Num. 21.28.

**Verse 36.** *{Therefore mine heart shall sound for Moab like pipes, and mine heart shall sound like pipes for the men of Kirheres:}* Alluding to the custom of playing with flutes and pipes certain sad and doleful tunes or funerals and solemn mournings. Mat. 6.23. See Esay 15.5. & 16.11.

*{the riches that he hath gotten is perished.}* See Esay 15.7.

**Verse 37.** *{For every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped}* Heb. *diminished*, or, *cut short*. Ezek. 51.11. See Esay 15.2. Chap. 47.5.

*{upon all the hands shall be cuttings, and upon the loins sackcloth.}* See chap. 27.5. Esay 15.3. *hands*, for, *arms*, as chap. 38.12. for their arms they used to cut and slash in such cases. So also, *wounds in their hands*, for, *upon their arms*. Zack. 13.6.

**Verse 38.** *{There shall be lamentation generally upon all the house tops of Moab, and in the streets thereof:}* See Esay 15.3.

*{for I have broken Moab,}* Or, *for I will break*; or, *when I shall break, Moab*; as Chap. 13.21.

*{like a vessell wherein is no pleasure, saith the LORD.}* See Chapter 22.28.

**Verse 39.** *{They shall howl, saying}* Or, *Men shall howl*; or, *There shall be howling*, and, saying; for the verb is indefinite, as verse 31. Esay 32.12.

*{How is it broken down?}* See the like, verse 17.

*{How hath Moab turned thee back with shame?}* As those that dare not show their face for shame; say some: but rather, as those, that dare not look the enemy in the face, but turn their back to them; and in shameful manner instead of fighting betake themselves to flight: as Chap. 46.5. Heb. *neck*; or, hinder part of the *neck*; as Chap. 2.27. So Josh. 7.9,12.

*{So shall Moab be a derision, and a dismaying to all those about him.}* Or, *thus*. Heb. *and*, as Chap. 25.14. and, *for laughter*, or, *unto a derision*; as Israel was before to him, verse 27. and, *for a dismaying*, or, *affrightment*. as Esay 19.16,17. & 23.5. as fearing yet, lest the like might also befall them.

**Verse 40.** *{For thus saith the LORD; Behold, he shall flye as an Eagle and shall spread his wings over Moab.}* Nebuchadnezzar shall come swiftly, like an Eagle, flying at, and spreading his wings over his prey. Deut. 28.49. Chap. 4.13. & 49.22. Dan. 7.4. Hos. 8.1. Habb. 1.6. and in the term of *wings*, may an allusion be to the *wings* (as they are termed also) of an army: wherewith the Chaldean Kings' forces should overspread his whole land. See Esay 8.8.

**Verse 41.** *{Kerioth is taken, and the strong holds are surprised:}* Or, *The Cities are taken*, for it may be, either the proper name of a city, as verse 24. or, a common term of *cities* in general: as Hab. 2.5,12. and it sorts well here with what follows, *cities* and *forts* are all surprised; no place so strong, that is able to hold out, See Verse 15,24.

*{and the mighty mens hearts in Moab at that day shall be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.}* The hearts of the strongest and stoutest of them shall quail; and it shall be with them, as with a woman that has grievous hard labor. So Esay 21.3. Chap. 30.6. & 49.22,24. Mich. 4.9,10.

**Verse 42.** *{And Moab shall be destroyed from being a people.}* See verse 2. Esay 7.8.

*{because he hath magnified himself against the LORD.}* See Verse 16.

**Verse 43.** *{Fear, and the pit, and the snare shall be upon thee, O Inhabitant of Moab, saith the LORD.}* See Esay 24.17.

**Verse 44.** *{And he that fleeth from the fear, shall fall into the pit; and he that getteth up out of the pit, shall be taken in the snare:}* He that escapes one danger, shall be surprised with another; and if that miss also, with a third. So 1 Kings 19.17. & 20.30. Amos 5.19. See Esay 24.18.

*{for I will bring upon it, even upon Moab, the year of their visitation, saith the LORD.}* So chap. 11.23. & 29.22. & 46.21. There is an elegant redundancy of the noun subjoined to the pronoun; that makes the sentence more vigorous; as the like, Prov. 5.21. Esay 8.13. & 48.6. Chap. 9.15.

**Verse 45.** *{They that fled, stood under the shadow of Heshbon, because of the force:}* Those that fled out of the villages, *for want of strength*, (as some render it; like that, *from fat*, that is, *for want of fat*, Psalm 109.24. See Lamentations 4.9.) or *from* the enemies' forces pursuing them, betook themselves to Heshbon, as being a place of chief strength; hoping to find succor and shelter there, as it is the shade of some great tree against the scorching heat of the Sun, or under the shroud of it against a storm: *shadow*, for, *protection*: as Judges 9.15,20. Eccles. 7.12. Esay 32.2. Daniel 4.12.

*{but a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon}* But their expectations shall be frustrate: for both Heshbon shall be surprised by the Chaldeans, who from thence shall surround, and with fire and sword waste the rest of the Country unto the utmost bounds of it. This whole passage with little variation, is taken out of Moses, in whose writing is recorded a proverbial kind of speech in those days very common in men's mouths, concerning the mischief that from Heshbon King Sihon's city the Amorites had done to the Moabites, Numb. 21.28,29. but by the Prophet here applied to the Chaldeans. See v. 2.

*{a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon}* So Judges 9.15,20.

*{and a flame from the midst of Sihon}* Heb. *from between Sihon*, that is, simply, *from Sihon*, or *from out of Sihon*: and *Sihon*, for *the city of Sihon*; as it is in Moses, that is, *from Heshbon*: for Heshbon was the City and seat of Sihon a King of the Amorites Numbers 21.26.

*{and shall devour,}* Or, *which shall devour*; the copulative for the relative: as c. 4.18.

*{the corner of Moab}* Or as some render it, *the side* from Exodus 27.9. Numbers 35.5. but it may here better be rendered *coast*, than either *side*, or *corner*: as it is Numbers, 34.3. As also Nehemiah 9.22. *coasts*, rather than *corners*, or *the end*: as it is rendered, Ezekiel 41.12. it shall spoil all Moab's land from the one end to the other.

*{and the crown of the head of the tumultuous ones}* Or, *revellers*; Heb. *children of noise*; as chapter 46.17. not so much the rude and promiscuous multitude, Esay 16.14. & 17.12. as the gallants those revelling and roaring ones; as Esay 5.14. & 24.8. So rather, than as some of those *tumultuous ones*, that could not be quiet, but would needs be shaking off the Chaldean yoke. See Chapter 27.3,8. and, *the crown of the head*: Either the King and his Princes; as Esay 1.5,6. so the most, because they find *Lords*, Numb. 21.28. though the word be no more than *owners* and *masters*, there: or, *the chief and principal*, among those revelling gallants; as the like Esay 28.1,3. or the principal of the wealthy and fat soil, that maintains them, and their riot: as Esay 28.1,4. Chapter 2.16. or simply, which I take to be the genuine sense. It shall destroy these gallants, it shall break their heads; as Psal. 68.21.

**Verse 46.** *{Woe be unto thee, O Moab,}* See Num. 21.29.

*{the people of Chemosh perisheth,}* Or *is perished, the people of Chemosh*, their chief Idol whom they served, v. 7.13.

*{for thy sons are taken captives, and thy daughters captives.}* Heb. *they have taken them in captivity*; as vers. 7. but the verb is indefinite: and is best therefore rendered by the passive: As Nehemiah 2.7. Job 7.3.

**Verse 47.** *{Yet will I bring again the captivity of Moab; in the latter days saith the LORD.}* Heb. *And*; as chap. 44.4. Either *I will bring back his captives*; as Psalm 126.1. Chap. 30.3. or *I will restore him again* to his former state; as Job 42.10. Heb. *in the posteritie of dayes*, or *the after-times*, chap. 23.20. After a long time of desolation; by a spiritual restitution principally in the days of the Messias. So the Jewish Commenters themselves here, and c. 49.6,39. Zeph. 2.11. See Esay 49. v. 6.

*{Thus far is the judgment of Moab.}* The conclusion of this long prophecy concerning Moab; as the like of the whole volume of his prophecies, c. 51.64. So rather than as some, following the Chaldee, would have it, as setting a limit to Moab's desolation: *Thus long* shall *the judgement of Moab* continue:

## CHAPTER 49

**Verse 1.** *{Concerning the Ammonites, thus saith the LORD}* Into this Chapter are cast divers several Prophecies, against several people, most of them the Jews, their near but bad neighbors. The first that he begins with are the Ammonites, the Moabites' brethren, Lot's issue, Psalm 83.8. the former by his elder daughter, the latter by his younger, Genesis 19.37,38. they dwelt near together, and banded both with the Chaldeans and others against God's people, 2 Kings 24.2. Psalm 83.6,7. and therefore joined together, Zeph. 2.8. Heb. *sons of Ammon*: as chapter 43.10. they are so constantly termed from the root of their stock, whom his mother named *Benammi*, Gen. 19.38. Heb. *unto them*, and so some render it: but the particle is sometime also so used, as our Version renders it, Genesis 20.13. Psalm 91.11. Chapter 14.10. & 28.8. Others, *against*; as it is rendered, Job 7.20. & 8.4. chap. 3.25. See the like denunciation with this against them, Ezekiel 1.28. & 25.2. Amos 1.13.

*{Hath Israel no sons? hath he no heir?}* He begins this discourse about the Ammonites, with an expostulation concerning their wrong offered God's people, in seizing on their Land, as if they wanted issue of their own, or other nearer of kin, that might more justly lay claim thereunto; continues it with a denunciation of judgment against them for their so dealing, verse 2–5. and concludes it with a gracious promise of restitution, verse 6. See the like expostulation, or demand at least, Chapter 2.14.

*{Why then doth their King inherit Gad, and his people dwell in his Cities?}* What reason is there, that their King or Idol should as by right of Inheritance seize upon, and hold any part of that Land, that God has by lot assigned to his people, as escheated to him for want of Heirs? See Judges, 11.23,24. and Zeph. 2.8.

*{their King}* Or, *Melcom*, their Idol, 1 Kings 11.5. whom in place of the true God, they set up in those places which they seize upon. See Verse 3. and the like ambiguity, Zephaniah, 1.5.

*{Gad.}* The Tribe of Gad, that which God had by Moses assigned unto it, the one half of Gilead (for the other half of it, the Tribe of Manasses held, Numbers 32.39. Joshua 13.29,31.) even so much, or all of it, as coasted upon half of the Ammonites' country, Joshua 13.24,25. (for so I should rather choose to expound that place, than as some other, of Lands taken by Sihon from the Ammonites, and so possessed by the Amorites, Numbers 21.26. for there is no mention at all of the Ammonites' country in that place) and that the Ammonites had by their vicinity, when the Israelites were sometime in a weak and low condition, either by distractions at home, or disturbances from abroad, taken occasion to encroach upon the possessions of that Tribe, that part of it especially, that lay so near to them, to wit, Gilead, appears plainly by Amos, 1.13. howsoever the Text (in one word there ambiguous, whereof see on Esay 7.14.) be rendered: and this seems to have been about Jeroboam the second's reign, for under him Amos prophesied, Amos 1.1. and at that time was that State in a very dejected and forlorn condition, 2 Kings 14.26. Howbeit, some suppose this to have more special reference to Pekah's reign, under whom the Ammonites, joining with Tiglath Pileser King of Assyria, should seize upon the Gadites' inheritance: and that Tiglath Pileser indeed then seized among other places in that kingdom, upon Gilead, we find 2 Kings 15.29. and that both Pul and he carried the Gadites away captives, 1 Chronicles 5.26. but of the Ammonites joining therein with either of them, nothing is said in the Holy Story. Yet is it not unlikely, that those parts being by this means much dispeopled, they took occasion thereby to seize upon some part of that Tribe's inheritance lying so near to them, and so fit for them: as also that after the dissolution of that State by Salmanesar, 2 Kings 17. they continued their possession of it; while the Assyrian Kings having disposed much of it, did not look much after it. To which purpose Zephany also long after gives us an hint, that both the Ammonites and Moabites in Josias his reign had encroached upon the borders of Israel, Zeph. 2.8. and we find them both further in Jehoiakim's reign joined with the Chaldeans against Judah, 2 Kings 24.2. And that at the time of this prophecy they held some good part of that territory, does from God's expostulation with them by the Prophet here appear: God withal intimating, that they could have no right thereunto; since that, albeit those ten tribes had had no issue of their own, yet they wanted not an Heir; Judah by right of consanguinity might well come in before the Ammonites, and lay claim to that Land, which his brethren of the other Tribes had formerly held, 1 Kings, 12.24.

**Verse 2.** *{Therefore behold the days come, saith the LORD,}* The wrong was before, v. 1. the righting by judgment to be executed upon the Ammonites now follows. Heb. *the dayes coming*; as c. 48.12.

*{that I will cause an alarm of war to be heard in Rabbah of the Ammonites,}* Heb. *and* (for, *that*; as c. 48.12.) *I will cause to be heard a shout*, or *sounding of war*, (that is, a warlike, or military shout; as Chapter 4.19. & 20.16. So Amos 1.14. & 2.2.) *in Rabbah*: the chief City in the Ammonites' country, 2 Sam. 11.1. & 12.26. Amos 1.14.

*{and it shall be a desolate heap,}* Heb. *an heap*, or *hillock of desolation*: as Deut. 13.16. See Ezekiel 25.5.

*{and her daughters shall be burnt with fire:}* The Towns and Villages belonging to her, as a mother city to them. See ch. 15.18. So are the inferior Towns usually termed in Scripture, Num. 21.20,33. Lam. 3.51.

*{then shall Israel be heir unto them that were his heirs, saith the LORD.}* The Israelites shall then inherit the Ammonites' land, who had before, as if he had been rightful heir to them, possessed himself of theirs, v. 1. See the like, Esay 14.1.

**Verse 3.** *{Howl O Heshbon}* A City which had been sometime King Sihon's chief seat, Numbers 21.20. re-edified by the Reubenites, Numbers 32.37. but whether parted afterward between them and the Gadites, or whether by lot it fell afterward to the latter, does not so clearly appear; for it is mentioned as one of their boundaries, Joshua 13.15,16. and as a City out of their inheritance assigned to the Levites, Joshua 21.38,39. but seemed to have been about these times possessed by the Moabites. See Chapter 48.2,34,45. And hence some gather that the Ammonites were overrun, and ruined before the Moabites; because Heshbon is willed to howl upon the taking and sacking of Rabba, and some other place between Heshbon and it, as expecting to fare as Rabba, and those others had done.

*{for Ai is spoiled:}* Not that Ai, whereof mention is made, Josh. 7.1. & 9.3. but another of that name, on the other side of Jordan, situate between Heshbon and Rabbah; by Ptolemy deemed to be called *Gaia*; as *Gaza*, for *Azzah*, Chap. 47.1. and *Gomorra*, for *Amorah*, Esay 1.9.

*{cry ye daughters of Rabbah,}* Either you towns belonging to it; as verse 2. but then *towns*, for *inhabitants*; as Esay 1.27. and so the Jewish Commenters: Or, *ye women of Rabbah*; as *Daughters of Israel*, 2 Samuel 1.24. and *Daughters of Sion*, Isaiah 3.16. and, *Daughters of Jerusalem* Luke 23.28.

*{gird ye with sackcloth:}* Heb. *gird sackes*: the usual mourning weed in those times, c. 4.8. & 6.20.

*{and run to and fro by the hedges:}* To hide yourselves behind them in the fields amidst the bushes and the thickets, for fear of the enemy ranging up and down; seeing you have no towns or cities left for you to repair unto, they being all surprised, sacked and burnt down to the ground, vers. 2. For the Jewish Masters seem to stray, who expound it of such mounds or fences as their villages had about them, that had not walls and gates, as their great cities had, 1 Sam. 23.7.

*{for their King shall go into captivity, and his Priests, and his Princes together.}* Heb. *Malcam*. Either the King of the Ammonites that resided at Rabba, verse 2. or their idol, as verse 1. *shall go into captivity*, or *shall goe among the captives*; as Ezekiel 12.1. the very same is said of *Camosh*, Chapter 48.7. of *Malcam*, Amos 1.15. but there their King seems to be intended, because he speaks only of his *Princes*: here the idol rather, as *Camosh* before; *Priests* are also in both places mentioned; of idols carried captive, See also, c. 43.12.

**Verse 4.** *{Wherefore gloriest thou in the valleys}* In your rich and fertile soil, in your well-watered plains that therefore fear no drought, c. 17.8. and that by their constant fertility make you so wealthy. So the Jewish Commenters, whom most others concur: yet a learned Interpreter of ours would have it rather rendered *in thy profundities*, as in a notion of fortification, see v. 8,30. because though low, yet environed with hills. But the former notion seems the natural, and is the more familiar notion. The Greek here has, *the fields of Enacim*: whence I know not. See c. 47.5. & 48.8.

*{thy flowing valley,}* Your vale that flows with abundance of all revenues, as well for delight and pleasure, as necessity and wealth; as the land of Canaan is said *to flow with milke and honey*, Chapter 11.15. and 32.22. But the most, both Jews and others read it, *thy vale floweth*: which they expound diversely. Some, *it fainteth*, and is grown weak; as a woman in her infirmity, or man and woman by an immoderate flux, Leviticus 15.2,3,10,23. Others, *it shall flow*, with blood of those that shall be slain in you: As Esay 15.9. and 34.7. Others with such a storm of rain or land-floods, as shall wash away all that is in you, or grows on you, your inhabitants and all their wealth: As Chapter 48.8. Others, lastly, It shall *flow away*, waste, vanish away, and be gone or destroyed; as Lamentations 4.9. See Job 20.28. It is an allusion, says one of ours, to the site of Valleys, that shoot along between the Hills, as Rivers, or, Brooks, or, Land-floods run down, till they empty themselves into the Sea, Psalm 104.10. Either Version has good probability; of this latter, the last, most of any. But I incline rather to the former reading, because the menace comes after, verse 5.

*{O backsliding daughter}* Or, *that turnest away*; to wit, from God; as Isaiah, 57.17. Chapter, 31.22. But I should rather here render it *untoward*, or *refractory*: because spoken of a people, that never had been joined in Covenant with God. Of the term Daughter: See on Chapter, 46.11,19.

*{that trusted in her treasures,}* Or *trusteth in thy treasure*: a change of the person, as Job 18.4. *O thou that tearest himself in his wrath*: Of such vain confidence. See Psalm 49.6. & 52.7. Prov. 11.28. Mark 10.20. 1 Tim. 6.17.

*{saying}* Supplied; as Psalm 105.15. Acts 7.32.

*{who shall come unto me?}* or *who can come at me?* in a potential notion; as supposing themselves impregnable, and sufficiently able to keep out any foreign force, that might offer to invade them. See the like, c. 21.13.

**Verse 5.** *{Behold, I will bring a fear upon thee, saith the Lord GOD of Hosts, from all those that be about thee:}* Heb. *I am bringing*; as c. 42.17. & 45.5. *fear upon thee from all thy circuits*, or *from all* (places, rather than persons here) *round about thee*; as c. 46.14. I will rouse you out of this your self-confidence and security, by surrounding you with terrors on every side of you; as Chap. 46.5. So v. 29,32. See Ezek. 32.32.

*{and ye shall be driven out every man right forth,}* As Amos 4.3. not daring either to stand still or to look back, Genesis 9.17. Chapter 46.5. and 47.3. Matthew 24.16–18. Mark 10.14. Luke 16.31,32. and 21.21. Heb. *a man*, for *each one*; as chapter 44.6.

*{and none shall gather up him that wandereth.}* None shall entertain them, or take them in, when they flee and wander from place to place, seeking for refuge and relief; as Psalm 27.10. Mic. 4.6. or none shall be able to rally them, or bring them together again, to make head against the enemy; as Judges 3.13. or none shall look after any other to succor them, or to take them along with them in their flight, but as in great consternation and affrightment is wont to fall out, every one shall seek only how to shift for himself; as c. 47.3.

**Verse 6.** *{And afterward I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon, saith the LORD.}* or *yet afterward*; as c. 44.4,28. A gracious close with promise of restitution: the like whereunto, see c. 48.47. So v. 39.

**Verse 7.** *{Concerning Edom, thus saith the LORD of Hosts;}* Heb. *unto Edome*. See ver. 1. The second Prophecy is of the Edomites, the posterity of Esau, Genesis, 36.8,9. See other the like concerning them, Esay 21.11. & 34.6. & 63.1. Ezekiel 25.12. Amos 1.11. Obad. 1.

*{Is wisdom no where in Teman?}* The Arabians, or those of the East, were anciently famous for wisdom, 1 Kings 4.30. Mat. 2.1. those of Esau's posterity especially, and among them the Temanites, a race descended from *Teman*, the son of Eliphaz, whom Esau had by Adah his first wife, Gen. 36.10,11. of which family was Eliphaz one of Job's friends Job 2.11. God therefore demands, whether all their wisdom that they had wont to be so much cried up, and renowned for, were utterly lost, that they seem to be at their wits' end, like those at sea, Psalm 107.27. See the like of Egypt, Esay 9.11–13. and of this concerning Edom; Obad. 8.

*{is counsel perished from the prudent?}* Heb. *from the understanding ones*. Howbeit, some of the Jewish Masters render it, *sons*; which the word also may well signify: and one of them taking it to have reference to *Teman*, expounds it from those of this generation; as if it were said, *from the children of Teman*, from those of his race that now live: the old Latin also going this way renders it: *from the sons*, which some referring to *wisdom*, expound it, *from the sons of wisedom*; as Matt. 11.19.

*{is their wisdom vanished?}* Some render the word here used, *is it become superfluous, unprofitable*, or *useless*, *naught worth*. So the old Latin, and the Tigurine, because the term has sometime a notion of superfluity, Exodus 26.12,13. The Jewish Doctor after the Chaldee, *It is corrupted and spoiled*, from a term that very commonly in the Talmudic tongue signifies, *to be corrupt, rotten, stinking, vile*, and *abominable*. A learned late Writer, *Is it tired out?* from an Ethiopic term, that signifies to be wearied or tired, Matth. 11.28. An Interpreter of note, *Is it worn out?* and consequently, become useless: which may seem to come home to the first, nor to swerve from the second; for that things worn out, are usually such, as that Rabbinical term imports c. 38.11. and to suit also with our Version, since that things waxen old and worn out, are ready *to vanish*, Heb. 8.13.

**Verse 8.** *{Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O Inhabitants of Dedan.}* These words are diversely read, and diversely rendered. Some read the words all in one notion; as imperative, or hortative. *Flee, turn back, dwell deep*: as this our present Version exhibits them: and to the same effect our former; as also the old Latin, the Tigurine, and some other Interpreters of note. But against this a Jewish Critic excepts, and says, the two latter terms cannot have that notion; because there is no such mood in that form of the one, and the vowel is divers in that mood with the other: and a learned Scholiast therefore to establish this Version, requires some change in the points. But to help this without any such alteration, a late learned Annotator well observes, that there may be, as oft there is, an interchange of the person, the third for the second, as was before, Verse 4. and the Tense past or present, for the Imperative; which is also not unusual: *Flee yee, they turne, they dwell deepe*, for *Flee yee, and turne yee backe, and dwell deepe, O yee Inhabitants of Dedan*. See the like change of person, Genesis 18.21,22. Esay 2.29. and 61.7. Chapter 5.21. and 6.17. and 16.12. and 29.19. and 44.10. and the Tense past or present with the Copulative here understood, Exodus 3.16. and 4.22. and 12.22. and 25.13. 2 Kings 9.3. Chapter 2.2. and 3.12. and 5.20. Howbeit, other of both the Jewish Commenters and ours, render the two latter Verbs as in an enunciative form; one of the Rabbines, *Flee yee Inhabitants of Dedan*; they, (that is, the Enemies) *are turned against you, and have pierced deep*, or, *farre* into your Land *to dwell* in it, and to expel and drive you out of it: and other, when they said, *Flee*; (such a defect and supply; as Psalm 27.8. no sooner was such a word cast out, but presently) *the Inhabitants of Dedan turned their backe, and dwelt deep*; sought to get into Caves and Holes as deep as they could, where they might be most safe, and secure from the Enemy, for fear of whom they fled. A late learned Interpreter including the two latter in a parenthesis; *Flee* *ye (it shall come to pass that they shall turn themselves away, and retire to deep dwellings) O Inhabitants of Dedan.* If any change in the vowel points might be admitted, I should rather choose to attempt it in the first word, reading *Nasu*, for *Nusu*, rather than with that learned Scholiast, *haphnu*, for *hophnu*: but I see not why *nasu* may not be here a Verb of the indicative past or present; since that form is in divers particles of Verbs of the same stamp and rank found, as in *Cushim, besetting*, Numbers 32.17. *surah sitting*, Esay 49.21. *shube, returning*, Mic. 2.8. and other the like. Thus they might run all in the indicative, *The Inhabitants of Dedan are fled*, or *flee, they have turned the backe*, or *are turned backe, they dwell deep*, or *abide in deep places*. But since that I find the same in effect, yea, for the first and last in terms the same, again afterward, v. 30. I adhere to that which our Version exhibits, and with the change of the person only allowed, the irregularity, found in the last, is not great, nor such as need force it from being an imperative form.

*{turn backe,}* Or, *they turn backe*: a term used sometime of turning, or looking back, either to make head against the enemy in pursuit, or to save and rescue somewhat from them: So c. 46.3. & 47.3. See v. 5. sometime of turning the back to the enemy, to make an escape by flight, chap. 46.21. and 48.39. So here, and again v. 24. One of the Jewish Masters renders is, *they have removed themselves*, as says he, the word is used, Leviticus 14.36. where it is rendered, *they shall empty the house*; that is, remove all the household stuff out of it: but the forms are not here and there the same.

*{dwell deep}* Or *they dwell*, or *abide deep*. Heb. *they make deep*, or *make deep to sit*: that is, *to dwell*, or *to abide*; as 2 Kings 6.2. Chapter 43.4. So Psalm 113.5. *that maketh high*, or *aloft, to dwell*: that is, *who dwelleth aloft*, or *on high*; as our Version well renders it. So, *make deep demand*, for ask somewhat below, or in the deep, Esay 7.11. and, *that make deep to consult*, for, devise profound projects, Esay 29.15. and, *they corrupt, they make deep*, for they are deeply corrupted, Hos. 9.9. and that which comes nearest home to this, *he digged and made deep*, for *he digged deep*, Luke 6.48. the meaning is, not *dwell*, or *abide in the vale*, as a learned Interpreter would have it, because the word for *a vale*, v. 4. comes from this root: but retire, pierce as deep as you can into the clefts of the Rocks, or Grots and Caves in the ground where you may lie hid, by most out of sight, and so safest and securest from the enemy, and there make your abode. See Judges 6.2. 1 Samuel 13.6. & 14.11. Esay 2.19,21. c. 48.27. The very form is verse 30.

*{Dedan}* A city in Arabia, joining upon Idumea, Esay 21.13. inhabited by the people descended from Abraham by Keturah, Genesis 25.3. who it seems had been subdued by the Edomites, and their city with its territory annexed to the Land and State of Idumea. See Ezek. 25.13.

*{for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him.}* Heb. *for I have brought*. As Chapter 32.42. and 44.2. but the time past here for the future, as Esay 30.19. Micah 7.8. yet it may be rendered, *when I bring*, as Chapter 10.2. and 13.21. And, *in the time of his visitation*: a defect of the Particle *in*; as Chapter 11.23. that is, what time I come to visit them: as Chapter 10.15. & 46.21. *Esau*, that is, *Edom*; for *Esau* and *Edom* are one and the same, Genesis 36.1,8,9. as *Jacob* and *Israel*, Genesis 32.28.

**Verse 9.** *{If grapegatherers come to thee, will they not leave some gleaning grapes?}* Heb. *clusters*: but the word seems peculiarly to signify such clusters as are wont to be left, either by oversight, or wittingly, according to the Law, Leviticus 19.10. Deut. 24.21. in the cutting and gathering of the grapes in Vintage: alluded to, Judges 8.2. & 20.45. Esay 17.6. & 24.12. chap. 6.9. Mic. 7.1. The same thing is found Obadiah 5. and thereby is implied, that the Chaldeans when they came, should strip the Edomites utterly of all their wealth, leaving nothing of worth behind them. The old Latin, not regarding the interrogation, makes the sense directly contrary to what is intended, while he renders the words, *they would not have left a cluster*: it is intimated indeed, that the Chaldeans would do no less; but that illustrate by an agreement of dissimilitude. Which howsoever the Greek not unfitly expresses, rendering it, *There are grape-gatherers come, that will leave thee no remnant*; yet they mangle the Text, and do not faithfully exhibit it, but instead of the *Protasis*, or former part of the collation, give us there the *Apodosis*, or application of it, which comes after, as being the latter part: v. 10.

*{if thieves}* To wit, had come unto you: supplied from the former branch: as the like, Gen. 1.16. 2 Chron. 10.11. compared with 1 Kings 12.11.

*{by night}* As thieves usually do, Job 24.16. 1 Thessalonians 5.2. 2 Pet. 3.10.

*{they will destroy, till they have enough.}* Or, *they would have destroyed*. Heb. *their sufficiency*; as Exod. 36.7. Prov. 25.16. they would have taken so much as would serve their turn, and left the rest behind, not have swept all away, as the Chaldeans will do, when they come.

**Verse 10.** *{But I have made Esau bare:}* Or, *I have stript*, (as Joel, 1.7.) or *will strip Esau*: that is, the Edomites descended of Esau Gen. 36.1. as v. 8. I will by the Chaldeans strip them of all that ever they have.

*{I have uncovered his secret places}* Heb. *his coverts*, or *hiding places*, or *places of covert*; as Chapter 23.24. either their forts and strong holds, Esay 4.6. or the holes that they creep into to hide themselves in, v. 8. or the secret places where they hide their treasure, Esay 45.3. See Esay 15.7. or both the one and the other: implying that nothing should be concealed or kept from the enemy. See v. 20.

*{and he shall not be able to hide himself,}* Or, *so that* (as Chapter 29.6,26.) *he shall not be able to hide himself*. Heb. *to be hid*; as chap. 36.19.

*{his seed is spoiled}* Either the Edomites themselves; as *the seed of Jacob*, the Israelites, Chap. 33.26. or their children: as Chap. 36.31. for whom they shall find no place, wherein to conceal, or secure them, nor friend or neighbor to commit them unto, verse 11.

*{and his brethren}* The Moabites and Ammonites descended from Lot Abraham's nephew, Genesis 11.31. and 19.37,38. undergoing the same calamity with the Edomites, Chapter 48. verse 1.

*{and his neighbours,}* The Philistines, Psalm 83.7. spoiled as well as himself, chap. 47.

*{and he is not}* Edom is no more a Kingdom, or a State; as, Psalm 37.36. c. 31.15. or as some of the Jewish Masters, who join this clause to the next verse; *there is none to him*; or *there is none left him*: he has none, either brother or neighbor to take charge of his children, that, they may say, as it is there, or *there is not he*, that may say, *Leave thy orphans with me*, v. 11. But of this further there.

**Verse 11.** *{Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive, and let thy widows trust in me.}* These words most Interpreters conceive to be the words of God himself to the Edomites, as advising them to commit their children and their widows to him. And our ancient English Versions render them: *Thou shalt leave thy fatherless children with me, and I will keep them*: for it is no small comfort, say some of them that go this way, when men die, or when they see they must perish themselves, yet if they have some friends, that will take care for their widows and their orphans: or say others, when men are compelled to flee, or withdraw themselves, being constrained to shift from place to place, if they have some friend with whom they may leave wife and children, as David did his parents with the King of Moab, 1 Sam. 22.3. that which God, as some suppose, should put the Edomites in hope that he would do for them, when all others should fail them; and so it should be not unlike that, Psalm 27.10. But others conceive that God speaks it, not as promising any such thing, but implying only that they should have none left to leave them to, but God, their friends, alliance, and neighbors being in the same case with themselves, verse 10. Others, that they should have no such to leave to any their wives and children being slain as well as themselves. Whence it is said, that there should be no *remainder* of them, Obad. 18. and that of Babylon say they, includes also the Edomites, Psalm 137.7,9. Others, that God speaks it by way of irony or derision, as if he should say, you may do well to command and commend your wives and children to me, as hoping that I should undertake the securing of them; but little favor or mercy are either they or yourselves like to find with me, who have carried yourselves so insolently towards me and my people. But these seem all of them somewhat strange and strained Interpretations. Which the Chaldee perceiving, makes it God's speech to the Israelites, rendering the Text, *O house of Israel, ye shall not leave, or leave not your orphans, I will secure them: and let your widowes rely on my word*; as encouraging them, not the Edomites, to depend upon him; as one that would take care of them, and provide for them, Psalm 68.5. But others, as was in part before hinted, suppose them to be conceived as the speech of some friends, if any such were, that would offer such kindness to the Edomites in this their distress, as to undertake such an office of love and amity in their behalf: to which purpose some, not of the Jewish Doctors only, but of ours also following them, tear off the last clause from the former verse, and affix it to this. But howsoever in some places, there may seem some necessity of so doing; whereof, see on Esay, 64.1. yet seems not so here. That may well stand still, as in our Version it does; and this, with that supply, which a learned Scholiast suggests, follow as a Sentence distinct from what went before: No man is there that may say, *Leave me thine Orphans*, &c. Or, as I should rather supply it, to make some coherence of this with the former: *He is not*: (Edom himself is lost, is gone:) Nor is there any to say, *Leave thine Orphans, I will keep them alive*. See the like supply of the negative, from the Verse foregoing, Esay 28.28.

*{fatherless children}* Not at death bequeathed to them; but committed to them at departure by flight: called *Orphans* or *fatherless*; because bereft of their father, though living, yet leaving them, and living apart from them; in regard whereof they are as without a father, their father neither being with them, nor able to do ought for them,

*{I will preserve them alive:}* *Leave* them to me, and I will secure them. Heb. *make them live*, or *quicken them*; but the word is used also, for *to preserve in life*, or *keep alive*, Exod. 1.18. Numb. 31.15,18. Psalm 22.29. and so it would also be rendered, Psalm 119.25,37,40.50.88,93.

*{thy widows}* Or, *wives*, in no better condition than widows; because bereft of their Husbands, being either fled from them, or carried away captive, and uncertain whether ever to see them again.

*{trust in me.}* Or *trust to me*: rely upon me; as undertaking the charge of them.

**Verse 12.** *{For thus saith the LORD, Behold, They whose judgment was not to drink of the cup, have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shalt altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished; but thou shalt surely drink of it;}* I have not spared mine own peculiar people, who might rather have expected this favor at my hands than you; and what reason have you then, who have no such relation to me, to expect to be spared? See this very message of the cup here intimated, Chapter 25.29. See also, Obad. 19. Heb. *drinking drinke*; as Chapter 25.28. and *acquitting be acquitted*; as Chap. 46.28.

**Verse 13.** *{For I have sworn by myself, saith the LORD,}* As Gen. 22.16. See c. 44.26.

*{that Bozrah}* Not that of Moab, Chapter 48.24. but that of Edom, and their principal City of strength, Esay 63.1.

*{shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse.}* As chap. 42.18. So v. 17.

*{and all the Cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes.}* The inferior Towns and Cities belonging to it, or near about it: As Chapter 48.24. verse 2. Heb. *shall be wastes of perpetuitie*: As Esay 61.4.

**Verse 14.** *{I have heard a rumour from the LORD:}* I have heard it in a Spiritual rapture, wherein this has been by God revealed to me. So Esay 13.4. Chapter 4.19,21. See the same, Obadiah 1. for with this Relation he begins his Prophecy.

*{and an Ambassador is sent unto the Heathen}* Either from God to the Chaldeans by a secret instinct, inciting them to war upon Edom; as Chap. 34.22. or from the Chaldeans calling upon their confederates, and inferior potentates that held from them, to be assistant unto them, or attendants upon them, in this expedition, c. 1.15. & 25.9.

*{saying}* Supplied, as ver. 4.

*{Gather ye together and come against her, and rise up to the battle.}* Against Edom, v. 17.

**Verse 15.** *{For loe I will make thee small among the Heathen,}* So Obad. 2. Heb. *I have given thee* to be *small*. As Chapter 1.5. and 6.27.

*{and despised among men}* As Psalm 22.6.

**Verse 16.** *{Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart.}* The word rendered *terribleness* is nowhere else found; and is therefore by divers diversely both rendered and expounded. The root from whence it rises has a notion of *terror* and *trembling* in it; and it is but once found, Job 9.6. but another word thence springing is found oft used for *dread* or *terror*, Job 21.7. Psal. 55.5. Esay 21.4. Ezekiel 7.18. Some render it, *thine idoll*, because a word from the same root, differing only in a ministerial letter, is used for an *idoll*, so termed, because the worshippers of such dread them, 1 Kings 15.13. 2 Chron. 15.16. Others, *pride* or *arrogancy*; so some of the Jewish Masters, whom the old Latin follows, and they say, *pride* is so termed, either by a contrariety of speech, because proud persons are furthest from fear, or because they affect to be frightful to others, Job 40.10–12. The Chaldee renders it *fatness*, or *fatuity, folly*; for the word he uses may signify either: and they go frequently together, as the Greek Proverb informs us. See Esay 6.10. nor are *pride* and *fatness*, far asunder, Psalm 73.6,7. and 119.69,70. the Greek gives it, *sport*, or *mockery*: whence I know not. A learned Interpreter, *horror* or *roughness*; as having reference to the roughness of those mountains, on which, having expelled the Horites, Edom seated himself, called from their roughness, says he, *the mountains of Seir*, Deut. 2.12. But of these scarce any seem very probable. The plainest, and that wherein most both Jewish and ours agree, is of those that take the word, as its fellow, in a notion of *terror*; thereby understanding not the *terror* wherewith Edom was affected himself, but the *terror* that he struck into, and wherewith he was wont to affright others: as the like is said of other great States, Esay 14.16. Ezekiel 32.23–27. and it is therefore in our Version very fitly and exactly rendered *terribleness*. And *pride of heart*, or *a proud heart*, (Heb. *thy pride of heart*, for *thy proud heart*; as *his greatness of heart*, for *his great stomacke*, Esay 10.12.) is well adjoined to this terribleness: for that is one principal thing that puffs up persons with pride, when they perceive that others stand in awe of them, and dare not stir, or do anything to cross or oppose them in ought, Esay 10.12–14. and this *terribleness* is here said to have deceived the Edomites, or to have *seduced*, and led them aside as the Chaldee renders it; and as Babel's *wisdom* is said to have *perverted* her, Esay 47.10. because it made them secure and presumptuous, as if none dared attempt ought against them and and their State, as their ensuing vaunts show. But herein a learned late writer controls all the former versions; for says he, the word of *terror*, or *terribleness*, cannot here be joined with the Verb *deceived*, or *deceiveth*: for the Noun is feminine, and the Verb masculine, and agrees therefore not with *terror* but with *pride*: and he would therefore have the Text thus to be rendered; *Oh thy terror!* (as spoken by way of admiration; as, *O their perverseness!* Esay 29.16.) *the pride of thine heart hath deceived thee*; and this Syntax the place in Obadiah, whence this passage is taken, may seem to second: for there this first term is not found, but the text runs there, *The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee*: Obad. 4. But to let pass that place of Esay, wherein I conceive that this notion will not so well fit, it seems not to carry any plain or smooth sense here: and for the diversity of the gender, it is frequently found, and there is an instance of it in the verse next beforegoing, where the word *widowes* is feminine, the Verb of *trusting* joined with it, masculine. Howbeit because the words are so conceived in Obadiah, I suppose that they may well here be thus rendered; Through *thy terribleness*, or Because of, or by reason of *thy terribleness, the pride of thy heart*, or, *thy proud heart hath deceived thee*, The particle Beth, taken in such a procuring, or, producing notion, is frequently wanting: As Psalm 56.4. and 167.8,15,21.

*{O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill:}* The land of Idumea, was much of it hilly and rocky, in regard whereof they deemed it inaccessible and impregnable, Gen. 36.8,9. supposing themselves as safe there; (See Obad. 3.) as the Dove when she has made her nest within some cleft of a rock, where the Fowl of prey being bigger of body, cannot get in to her, or her young: for that seems here alluded to. See c. 48.28. and of the cony, Prov. 30.26.

*{though thou shouldst make thy nest, as high as the Eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the LORD.}* So Obadiah 4. of the Eagle, see Job 39.27,28. *nest*, for, *habitation*: As Numbers 24.21. Job 29.18. As *house*, for *nest*, or *harbor*, as Psalm 104.17.

**Verse 17.** *{Also Edom shall be a desolation}* Heb. *And Edom shall be for*, or, *unto desolation*. As verse 13. that is, utterly desolate.

*{every one that goeth by it shall be astonished; and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof.}* A Proverbial form of speech; intimating a strange alteration, and extreme desolation. So 1 Kings 9.8. chapter 52.13.

**Verse 18.** *{As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah:}* Or, *According to the overthrow* (as Amos 4.11.) *of Sodome and Gomorrah.* Whereof, see Genesis 19.24,25. So Esay 1.9. Chapter 50.40.

*{and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the LORD:}* Admah and Zeboim, Deut. 29.23. Hos. 11.8. the subject concealed; as Esay 5.4. and 17.5,10. and 28.4. Ezek. 13.11.

*{no man shall abide there; neither shall a son of man dwell in it.}* So v. 33. c. 50.40.

**Verse 19.** *{Behold, he shall come up like a Lion from the swelling of Jordan.}* This passage is very variously by Interpreters expounded. Some expound it of the Edomites in fierce and furious manner invading Judea God's people, 2 Macab. 10.15. Others, of some enemy that should in like manner break in upon the Edomites: and this enemy some would have to be the Israelites according to that, Obadiah 18.21. which they understand of Hircanus and Judas the Jews' victories against them; whereof Joseph's *Antiquities*, l. 13. c. 17. 1 Maccab. 5.3. 1 Maccab. 10.16–23. but the most understand it of Nebuchadnezzar, and the Chaldean forces; of whom chap. 46.20. v. 28. resembled by a *Lion*, as here, so chapter 4.7. this *Lion* is said *to come up* as some conceive it, *from the swelling of Jordan*; as noting the place from whence he should go up against the Edomites, whether the Jews' army under their conductors, that were to pass Jordan, ere they could invade Idumea, or the Chaldean forces under Nebuchadnezzar, who having first conquered Judea, fell afterward upon Idumea, marching up thither from the fertile soil that Jordan waters, Zach. 11.3. where the word seems to be so taken. Others, as designing the violent manner of irruption, whether of the Edomites into Judea, or of foreign forces; Jews or Chaldeans, breaking into Idumea, and these render the words, *he shall come up above*, or *beyond the swelling of Jordan*; (Heb. *the excellency*, as Esay 2.10. or *pride of Jordan*: as it is rendered, Zeph. 2.10. and so Zach. 11.3.) that is, more forcibly and violently, than Jordan is wont to break in upon the plains near to it, when it gets over its banks: and such hostile irruptions are indeed compared to such inundations, Esay 8.7,8. chap. 46.7,8. & 51.42. and the particle is in comparisons commonly so used, Genesis 19.9. Esay 2.6. and 48.4. and 53.5. But others rather, as pointing to the place where Lions used to harbor, to wit, in the woods and groves near to the banks of that river, from whence they were wont to prey upon cattle that feed thereabout, Zach. 11.3. and of these some more particularly to the manner of those Lions that harbored thereabout who at that time of the year, when Jordan used to rise and swell above his banks, were fain to quit the plain, being then all overflown, and to make up to the higher grounds. And the learned Scholiast's supply does very well here; *as a Lion*, or *Lions* (the word taken collectively) *cometh up*, or, *are wont to come up* (as Genesis 44.5. *drinketh*, that is, *is wont to drink*) *from the over-flowing of Jordan*, *so shall he come up.* See the like, Chapter 46.18. Or Jordan's over-flowings: See Joshua 3.15. 1 Chronicles 12.15. Chapter 12.5. of the Lions leaving his covert, Chap. 25.38. and this whole passage again repeated, chap. 50.44.

*{against the habitation of the strong:}* Heb. *of Ethan*; which some take for the proper name of a place in the land of Edom, which they conceive to be that, which was one of the Israelites stations, in their journey from Egypt, Exod. 13.20. Numb. 33.6,8. but they are herein much mistaken: for that place is termed not *Ethan*, but *Etham*; and so the ancient Greek, but corruptly, reads the word here: but the word, as most take it, signifies *strong*; as Numb. 24.21. chap. 5.15. Psalm 74.15. Or as some, *strength*: and so it is clearly taken, Genesis 49.24. and Seir or Idumea is here termed, as Babylon also, chap. 50.44.) *the dwelling of the strong* or *a dwelling of strength*, that is, *a strong dwelling*: in regard of that supposed strength of their land, which the Edomites so much boasted of, and whereunto they so much trusted. See Obadiah 4. for as for those, who interpret it, *the habitation of the mighty*, to wit, God; understanding it of Judea, by the Edomites invaded; I suppose to be out of the way here, as well in that as in this. A late learned Writer would have it rendered, *a rough*, or *rocky habitation*: from hint of Moses before cited: Supposing also a city in Sicily so situate, to have its name *Neeton* in Greek, and the inhabitants thereof *Netini* in Latin, from the very terms here used: and true it is, both that Edom's land was such, as also that such a site confers much to the strength of a place; but the word seems to be much larger.

*{but I will suddenly make him run away from her}* This branch is exceedingly tortured with multiplicity of Versions and Interpretations. And whereas the root, whence the former word here used does arise, has a threefold notion, sometime of *feeding* and *breathing*; sometime of *short* and *sudden acting*; sometime of *resting* and *being quiet*. Some take the word here in the first notion, rendering the Text; *I will break* or *rent them* (to wit, the Edomites) *asunder*, as the word is used Job 7.5. and chap. 31.15.) *and I will make them run out of their Land.* I will carry them out of their Land into captivity. Others take the word in a notion of *sudden*, *quick*, *momentary* motion, or action. And of them some, whom our Version may seem to follow, take it for an adverbial, as they suppose it also to be, Prov. 12.19. and they apply it to the Edomites invading Israel, whom God would suddenly drive out again, See Esay 59.20. The same way go the ancient Greek and old Latin, though in exposition of the sentence they depart both from those, and each from other: for the Latin renders it, *I will cause him to come suddenly into the land.* I will cause the enemy suddenly to invade it: the Greek, *I will make them suddenly to run out of their Land*; being by the enemy thence expelled. Others taking it for a Verb, but in the same notion, thus render it, *I will in a moment appoint to her* or *bring him to her, and I will make him run from her*; that is, depart again and retire as speedily, having had good success, and obtained in a short time, what he came for. Those lastly, that take it in a notion of *rest*, render it; some, *when I shall have rested a while*, as Esay 18.4. Others, *when I shall make to rest*: when my purpose is, and I shall come to give rest to my people Israel, chap. 31.2. *I will make him* (to wit, Israel) *to run out of her*; that is, out of Edom's land, where they had been in captivity.
