Others, *when I have caused him to rest, I will make him run out of it*: after that I have suffered the Edomites to enjoy rest for a while, I will compel them to quit their Country, and disperse themselves into foreign parts. Of all these the old Latin seems to have come nearest home to the true notion of the Text; the terms whereof yet require some clearing. The initial particle would be rendered *for*; as chap. 47.4. the next word, whether it be an Adverbial or a Verb, is to the sense not much material; it comes from a root, that signifies *a moment*; and is used for *speedily*, *suddenly*. Esay 26.20. & 47.9. & 54.7,8. chap. 18.8. I suppose it to be here a Verb; so taken it should signify *to cause ought to be done in a moment suddenly*: and after the Hebrew Idiom to say, *I will cause to be done in a moment*, or *suddenly, will cause him to run* (for in such transitive forms both the Verbs are) is no more than, *I will cause him suddenly*, or *in a moment to run*: as *wilt thou not return wilt quicken us?* for *wilt thou not quicken us again?* Psalm 85.6. and, *they made haste forgot*; for *soon*, or *hastily they forgot*, Psalm 106.13. and, *they have made deep they have corrupted*, for *they have deeply corrupted*, for *they deeply corrupted*, Hos. 9.9. which by the Adverb, whether it be an adverbial or a verb, is to be alike expressed here; as the like, though Verbs, in all those other places you see it: thus the sense is thus far plain: *I will cause him in a moment*, or *suddenly to run*: about the last particle is most doubt, and it has contrary senses given it: that the words may signify *from off her*, or *it*; cannot be doubted, much less denied: as 2 Chron. 33.8. chap. 24.10. and 28.16. Ezekiel 1.19,21. & 10.16. but one of the Jewish Critics observes on the place, that the term *meal*, is sometime as much as *mimmaal*, *above* or *over*: as says he, Gen. 1.7. *the waters above the firmament*: and Ezekiel 1.26. *above the firmament that was over their heads*: and besides these instances, a learned late Annotator supplies us with some other, Gen. 27.39. *the dew of Heaven from above*: and Gen. 49.25. *the blessings of Heaven above*: and Psalm 50.4. *He shall call the Heaven from above*; or *above*: but those of the Rabbine fit here better than these; because in these the term is absolute and consistent, whereas in those is transitive; as it is also in this place. Thus then conceived, the Text runs smoothly. The Destroyer, Nebuchadnezzar shall come up with his forces against Edom's strong dwellings, like a Lion, or as Lions use to do from their covert about Jordan, when by that River overflowing the plains near unto it, they are forced to make up into the higher grounds; and shall suddenly, or in an instant, overrun his whole Country, get above it, and become master of it: that which is after set forth by another resemblance of an Eagle, the chief of Fowls of prey, as the Lion of beasts, Verse 22. See further there.

*{and who is a chosen man, that I may appoint over her?}* This branch is as many ways tentered and tortured, as the former. Some understand it of the Jewish people, whose land the Edomites had invaded; I will drive them again out of it: and *I will set over it, him, whom I have made*, or *shall make choice of*: not him to whom they design it, as Esay 7.6,7. Others of the Edomites, and those diversely: Some, *whatsoever choice young man there is with her*; to wit, with Edom, *him will I visit*; that is, I will destroy all the flower and choice of her youth: as of Moab, Chap. 48.15. Others, *what choice of young men is there that I may set up for her?* to oppose the Chaldean forces that came against her? implying that she had none at all left. Others, apply it to those that were either to afflict or to destroy Edom; and of them some more generally; *what choice ones* (as Rev. 17.14.) *are there that I may muster against her?* as if he had said, I will pick and cull out Warriors as many as can be found fit for such a service, to be employed in this expedition against Edom, as 1 Chron. 19.10. Other of them restraining it to one chief Commander, *and him that is chosen*, (that is, whom I have designed to that service) *will I set up against her.* Others again, *what choice one is there, that I may set over* those forces that are to go *against her?* and others, *what choice one* is there *for me to set over her?* as implying, that he would find out one such to set over the Edomites as should not mildly and moderately rule, but tyrannize over them, and grievously oppress them: like that of Egypt, Esay 19.4. I concur with those, who understand it of one that he intended to employ in that service, to wit, Nebuchadnezzar, the *Lion*, or *spoiler*, before spoken of; and render the words, *for* (the copulative in a causal notion; as chap. 44.13,17.) *I will give charge to* (as Ezr. 1.2.) *him* that is (the interrogative for the demonstrative; as Eccles. 9.4. and a defect of the relative, as chapter 50.5.) *a choice one*, (as Psalm 89.19.) *against her*: *el*, for *al*; as cha. 48.11. that shall do this service effectually for me; as Esay 44.28. See Esay 10.6.

*{for who is like me?}* Who can do as I can? Who am able to enable whomsoever I commit any charge unto, to go thorough with whatsoever I give him in charge to do. See the same. Exod. 15.11. 1 Kings 8.23. Psal. 35.10. & 88.6,8. Chap. 10.6. & 50.44.

*{and who will appoint me the time?}* Or, *or*, (as Chap. 23.18.) *will*, or, *dare*, (as Chap. 2.23.) *set me a time?* either to join issue with me in judgment, as some; from Job 9.19. or, as the most rather, to join issue with me in battle. See Chap. 46.17.

*{who is that shepherd that will stand before me?}* Or, *or*, (Heb. *and*; as before; which ought not to be omitted) *who is* (the pronoun demonstrative, for the verb substantive; as Psal. 25.12.) *the shepherd*, (that Prince, or Potentate; as Esay 44.28. Chap. 6.3. & 12.10. but the term here used the rather; as alluding to a shepherd into whose flock a fierce lion is broken, and makes havoc of his sheep, Esay 31.4. Joel 2.1. Mich. 5.8.) *that can*, or, *dare to stand before me*, Psal. 76.7. Nah. 1.7. or, before any one, that shall come with commission from me? as he Esay 36.9. *shall stand*; for, *can stand*; as Prov. 27.4. or, *dare stand*; as Job 41.10. See Chapter 46.21. and the same again, Chap. 50.44.

**Verse 20.** *{Therefore hear the counsel of the LORD that he hath taken against Edom, and his purposes that he hath purposed against Teman:}* Heb. *the counsel that he hath consulted*; as Esay 8.1. verse 30. or, *the course that he is resolved upon*, as it were upon due deliberation: not that God consults as men use to do about ought; but to show the seriousness and settledness of God's actions and executions; that he has good ground for the doing of them, as men for those things usually, which they do not rashly, but considerately and advisedly undertake; and he is peremptory in them, when he has once resolved upon them, and will be sure to effect them; as men are wont to proceed constantly in those things, that they have advisedly undertaken. See Esay 19.17. & 44.25. & 46.10. *and the thoughts that he hath thought*, or, *the devices*, or, *the contrivements, that he hath devised*, or *contrived*; as 1 Sam. 14.14. Verse 30. a form of speech taken likewise from men, who having cunningly contrived, and prudently plotted things beforehand, are the more likely to go thorough with their designs, and to bring them to good effect. See Esay 14.24,26,27. Heb. *unto Edom*; or, *concerning*, as Chapter 44.1. Of *Teman*, see on Verse 7. and the same again, Chapter 50.45.

*{surely the least of the flock shall draw them out}* Heb. *if the little ones* (for, *least*; as 1 Sam. 9.21.) *shall not draw*, or, *drag, them out*; as dogs do a carcass, Chap. 15.3. or wolves a sheep, when they worry it: it is conceived as in the form of an oath; as Psalm 95.11. chap. 44.26. and it is as if he had said; What speak I of Nebuchadnezzar as a fierce lion, that I shall bring in upon the Edomites, the very weakest and feeblest of all his retinue, of those that follow his camp, going under my conduct as their shepherd and leader, (alluding to the title of a shepherd before mentioned, v. 19.) shall fetch out the strongest and valiantest of the Edomites: nor shall they be able to stand before, and make head against, or by skulking into caves and corners to conceal themselves from the meanest of his followers. See Rabshakeh's vaunt of his master's followers, Esay 36.9. and see v. 10. As for those Jewish Doctors, who by little ones here mentioned would have understood, either the Persians, because they came of one of Japhet's younger sons; or the Jews that were of small esteem at present, but were still God's flock, Ezekiel 34.30,31. The posterity of Jacob, younger brother to Esau, to fulfill that Prophecy, *The elder shall serve the younger*, Genesis 25.23. and some again of them more particularly of the issue of Rachel, Benjamin and Joseph, who were Jacob's youngest children: they are many miles from the Prophet's meaning in either.

*{surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them}* Heb. *if he make not* (as before) *their dwellings desolate upon*, or, *together with them*: As Exodus 35.22. Esay 7.2. Chapter 3.18. *he*; that is, the Lord, says the Rabbine; the enemy, says the Scholiast: but there is no necessity of either: the Verb is indefinite; and it may well be rendered, *their dwelling together with themselves shall be destroyed*: as Chap. 51.30. See the same again, Chapter 50.45.

**Verse 21.** *{The earth is moved at the noise of their fall}* Either the earth itself shall shake with that hideous noise, that the fall of their State, as of a vast structure, shall make: or the people of the lands and countries round about them shall tremble and be dismayed at the report of this their downfall. So Ezekiel 26.18. and 32.10. See Chapter 38.39. and the same with this, c. 50.46. *voice*, for *report*: as c. 4.15.

*{at the cry, the noise thereof was heard in the red sea.}* Heb. *a cry by*, or, *in the sea of weed*, or, *reit, shall be heard her voice*, or, *its voice*; not, *their voice*: as, *their fall*, before; though some here so render it. Where the interpreters suppose a defect, and make assay of sundry supplies, some one, some another: some prefix a preposition, so ours, *at the cry*; others, by reason *of the cry*. Others supply a verb, *a cry* is heard: but neither is needful. The old Latin, and divers others, render it not altogether amiss, without either, *the clamor of his*, or, *its voice is heard in the red sea*: but more agreeably to the syntax and prophecy of the original thus, *the noise of the out-cry is heard to the red sea*: for the pronoun feminine affixed to the word *voice*, or, *noise*, has reference to *cry*, or, *out-cry*, by an elegant redundancy so rife in that language as nothing more, Gen. 2.14. 1 Sam. 9.13. Job 3.8. Psal. 18.30. & 104.17. Eccl. 2.18. Esay 8.13. & 45.9. & 48.6.

*{in the red sea}* Or, as some render the particle, *beside the red sea*: in the coasts, and places adjacent: and so it is used, Chap. 32.7. & 36.10. I should rather render it *unto*: as Esay 8.8. & 9.8. & 30.28. Heb. *the sea of weed*, or, *sedge*, or, *flag*, or *rush*, (as some render it, Exod. 2.3,5.) or; *reed*, (as others, because they find it joined with the *cane*, Esay 19.6.) or, *reit*; for, so, I take it, we call that sea-weed, which the Latins term *alga*; and which seems to be the Hebrew *suph* that Jonas says was *wrapped about his head*, Jon. 2.6. and whereof store is said to be found in the bellies of whales: this *sea* is that which is by Geographers called *the Arabian Gulf*, because it shoots in from the main sea between Arabia and Africa; and is by the Hebrews termed the *weedy*, or, *sedgy*, or *flaggy*, or, *rushy*, or *reedy*, or *reity, sea*, in regard of the great abundance of such kind of weeds that grow in it, being but shoaly, and especially about the banks of it: it coasts in the inwardest parts of it, on Egypt on the other side, and on Idumea sited in some part of Arabia, the stony, on the other side; as appears by Solomon's shipping there built, 1 King 9.26. from whence it came at first to be termed *the Edomean* or *Idumean sea*; and because *Edom* has a notion of *redness* in it, Gen. 25.30. it came therefore to be termed by the Greeks, and the Latins from them, *mare Erithræum* that is, *the red sea*; not as some have thought from the color of the sands, or the water of it, or of the coral growing in it; and much less as the Greeks, who have thence forged a fable, from one Erithræus, or Rufus, a King, that should be either drowned in it, or buried near to it: the meaning is, that the cry of the Edomites should be so loud, and so great, that it should run thorough the whole country, and be heard as far as the red sea, See the like of Moab, Esay 15.4,9,8. Chap. 48.34.

**Verse 22.** *{Behold, he shall come up and fly as the Eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah.}* Nebuchadnezzar compared before to *a lion*, for his fierceness, verse 19. here to *an eagle* for his swiftness, and sudden access, Job 9.26. & 39.29. Hos. 8.1. See the like before, Chap. 48.40. where of Moab the same is said; only the word of *coming up* is here added, being a military term, whereof see on Esay 7.1. and of this *Bozrah* before, verse 13.

*{and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom, as the heart of a woman in her pangs,}* See the same of Moab, chap. 48.41.

**Verse 23.** *{Concerning Damascus:}* The third Prophecy in this Chapter contained, has reference to *Damascus*, the head city of Syria, Esay 7.8. put here for the whole country; as Esay 17.1. Amos 1.3. Heb. *unto*: which the old Latin here retains. See on verse 1,7.

*{Hamath is confounded, and Arpad:}* Two other cities giving denomination to two other parts of that country: concerning which, see on Esay 10.9.

*{for they have heard evil tidings:}* To wit, of the Chaldeans breaking into their country, as the Assyrian had formerly done, Esay 10.9. & 36.19. & 37.13. Heb. *an evil hearing*; as v. 14.

*{they are fainthearted.}* As Esay 14.31. Ezek. 21.15.

*{there is sorrow on the sea, it cannot be quiet.}* Or, *as us upon the sea, which cannot rest*: a defect of the note of similitude; as Psalm 11.1. Esay 21.8. and of the relative; as chap. 31.21,24. they are like persons tossed up and down, to and fro at sea in a storm, Psalm 107.25–27. Jon. 1.4,13. or, as others, with those that inhabit near the sea-coast; as Esay 23.4. Heb. *in the sea*, for, *beside it*; as Chap. 13.5. See on verse 21. whether way it be taken, an allusion there seems to be in it to the unquietness and restlessness of the neighboring sea, Esay 57.20.

**Verse 24.** *{Damascus is waxen feeble.}* Heb. *is grown remiss*, or, *faint*: her spirits are abated; as Judg. 8.3. or her hands hang down: as 2 Sam. 4.1. Chap. 6.24. & 50.43.

*{and turneth her self to flee}* Or, *or, she turneth her self to flee.* See on verse 8,

*{and fear hath seized on her,}* Or, *for*, or *because*, (as rendering a reason of her faintness and flight: the copulative in a causal notion: as Chap. 74.34. 13,17.) *terror* (the word is almost the same) or, *trembling, hath taken hold on her*: as Chap. 6.24. & 50.43. the term rendered, *fear*, is nowhere else found in Scripture: but in the Chaldee it is found, Job 7.5. and the verb it comes of in a notion of *trembling*. Esth. 5.4. Psalm 39.7. and that which our Version here exhibits concerning this branch, agrees with the Chaldee, ancient Greek; and the Latin, and the most Interpreters, one and another: yet an Interpreter of prime note, and a learned Scholiast following him, render it, *she shall get*, the one, *she hath gotten*, the other, *a feverish trembling*, she is fallen into a shaking fit of a fever: that, I suppose, that induced them to swerve from the foregoing Versions: was because they found no point in the body of the last letter; and took it therefore not for a pronoun affix, which has usually that point in it, but for a feminine form of the verb, which yet they needed not to have scrupled; for that point in the affix is sometime wanting; and that in the very next clause, where yet themselves take it for a pronoun.

*{anguish and sorrows have taken her as a woman in travail.}* So Psalm 48.8. Chap. 6.24. & 22.23. & 31.21. & 50.43. Mic. 4.9. verse 22.

**Verse 25.** *{How is the city of praise, not left, the city of my joy?}* A lamentation for the ruin and destruction of Damascus, not unlike those, Chap. 48.17,39. & 50.23. & 51.41. Lam. 1.1. *a city of praise*; for a renowned city; as *praise*, for matter of *praise*, Esay 62.7. spoken of Jerusalem, and of Babylon. Chap. 51.41. and *a city of joy*, for, *a joyous city*; as, *a name of joy*, for, *a joyous name*, Chap. 33.9. so Jerusalem is said to be *the joy of the whole land*, Psal. 48.2. for the joy affixed in the end is by some learned deemed, not to be a pronoun, as it is commonly taken; (whence many Interpreters make it the speech of the King of that State) but a mere termination only, taken from the Syriack idiom; like whereunto is in many places found, as Esay 20.4. & 19.9. Ezek. 13.9. Nah. 1.9. Zach. 14.5. Damascus is meant, said, *not to be left*: to wit, standing by the enemy: as some cities in Canaan were left by the Israelites when they burnt down others, Josh. 11.12,13. as if they should say, what meant the Chaldeans to destroy so goodly a city; *and not leave it* standing, though they had razed and ruined others that were not of the like note? Howbeit, some of the Jewish Doctors would have the word taken in a notion of *fortification*; as if it were said, *why was not so famous a city* better *fortified?* Why was she not so fortified with walls and bulwarks, that she might have been impregnable? and they allege to that purpose a place in Nehemy, in which the word seems so used, where it is said, *and they fortified Jerusalem*, Neh. 3.8. to which may a second be added, Neh. 4.2. where the same word again is found, as it cuts off all those farfetched and forced interpretations that some of the greatest note give of that other place; and from thence a term in the Talmud, which some expound *a pavement*: some *a parapet*, (to which purpose also one of the Commenters on Nehemy, expounds the word in the former place there used, *they filled it up with earth unto the wall*) Others, *the plaistering*, some more generally, *the structure*: hither also is that use of the same term referred in that place, Exod. 23.5. of the helping up of a beast, that lies under his burden: where the words would be rendered, *shouldest thou forbear to lift him up? thou shalt in any wise lift him up together with him*: that is, be assistant to the owner, though your enemy, in helping to *lift*, or *set* him up again: a metaphor from the erecting and setting up again of an edifice or building, when it is fallen. And this interpretation of the word in this place, seems to me not altogether improbable: Though I cannot come home to that learned Annotator, who would have it rendered, *How is that so much commended city not paved?* that is, has not now so much as *a pavement*: because the word forementioned is said sometime so to signify: if instead of pavement he had said *terrace*, or *parapet*, it might more easily have passed: this of *pavement* seems no way to suit well here.

**Verse 26.** *{Therefore her young men shall fall in her streets, and all the men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the LORD.}* How this *Therefore* suits well here, I see not. I rather accord with what one of the Jewish Masters suggests, that the particle is here a note of asseveration, as it is also, and so acknowledged, Chap. 5.2. and I should therefore render it, *Surely, her young men shall fall* (that is, be slain, as chap. 6.15. & 8.12. *in her streets*, as chap. 9.21.) *and all the men of war shall be cut off* (as Chap. 51.3.) *in that day*: at that time: as verse 22. See the same, Chap. 51.30.

**Verse 27.** *{And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Benhadad.}* See the same in effect, Amos 1.4. and like, Amos 1.7,10,12,14. as also, chap. 17.27. Of *Benhadad* sometime King of Syria, see 1 Kings 20.1. by whom those palaces might at first be built: but it may well be understood simply of the King of Syria: the name of *Benhadad* importing *the son of Hadad*, their idol, whereof see on Esay 66.17. being a title given commonly to the Kings of Syria; as Pharaoh and Ptolomy to those of Egypt. See 2 Kings 13.3,24.

**Verse 28.** *{Concerning Kedar,}* A people living in Arabia descended from *Kedar*, the son of Ishmael, Gen. 25.13. of whom, see Esay 21.13. Heb. *unto Kedar*; as before, verse 17,23. and so in the next member.

*{and concerning the Kingdoms of Hazor,}* The Provinces of *Hazor*, whereof that was the head city, Josh. 11.10,11. the royal seat of Jabin, Judg. 4.2. but this Hazor seems to be another from that there mentioned, situate in the land of Canaan, whereas this seems to have been seated in Arabia either stony or desert, and to have been built by such as having fled out of Canaan from that part of the country, where the former stood, into those parts of Arabia, and there seated themselves, named this their city by the name of that from whence they came.

*{which Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon shall smite;}* Heb. *smote*: as Chap. 46.2, for, *was to smite*; speaking in the Prophetical strain of a thing to be done, as already past and done. So verse 23,24. though, *smote*, may be retained: this prophecy being after the accomplishment of it by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, (God's chief instrument in taking vengeance on most of the nations here menaced, Chap. 46.13,26. & 47.2. verse 30.) for the use of posterity inserted into this volume, or book of prophecies. See on ch. 46.4.

*{Thus saith the LORD, Arise ye,}* You Chaldeans: God's speech to them, as inciting and setting them on work to invade the Kedarens: Of which form of speech, see on chap. 1.17. & 13.6. So verse 31.

*{go up to Kedar,}* Or, *go up* (in hostile manner; a military term, as verse 22. Esay 7.1.) *against Kedar*; as chap. 28.8,16. & 34.7.

*{and spoil the men of the East}* Heb. *the sons of the East*; as Job 1.3. Judg. 6.3. Esay 11.14. the inhabitants of Arabia, that lay to the East from Judea, as did also Idumea and Syria. See Gen. 10.30. & 25.6,18. 1 Kings 4.30. (See on verse 7.) Esay 2.6. & 9.12.

**Verse 29.** *{Their tents,}* For the Kedarens lived most in tents, called therefore by the Greeks *Scenitæ*, Psal. 120.5. Cant. 1.5.

*{and their flocks:}* For they lived most upon the feeding of sheep, whereof they had great store, and for their accommodation therein used to remove their tents from place to place, to have fresh pasture for them. Esay 13.20. Hence they were also called *Nomades*, See Esay 60.7. Ezek. 27.21. So verse 32.

*{shall they take away:}* That is, their tents and flocks shall be taken away: for the verb is indefinite: as, *this night shall they take away thy soul*; that is, shall your soul be taken away, Luke 12.20.

*{and they shall take to themselves}* Those that take them the Chaldeans (the nominative case included in the verb; as Gen. 50.26, See on chap. 48.15.) shall take them, to their own proper use, having now seized on them, and become masters of them, as their own; as Psal. 44.10. or it is an elegant redundancy, common also in their language; as Gen. 12.1. Exod. 32.2. See on Chap. 13.2.

*{their curtains}* Whereof their tents consisted. See Esay 54.2. Chap. 10.20. Habb. 3.7.

*{and all their vessels,}* Or, *with* (as Chap. 44.26.) *all their vessels, furniture, stuff*, or *utensils*; for the word is of a large extent. See on Esay 22.24. & 39.2. Chap. 22.28.

*{and their camels}* Of much use in those parts, because able to travel and endure long without water, Job 1.3. Esay 60.6. verse 32.

*{and they shall cry unto them, fear is on every side.}* Some read the words, as two distinct sentences, as our version does: which some thus paraphrase, *they shall* but cry *to them, Terror terror, on every side*: and the very cry of it alone shall so dismay them, that they shall have no heart or lust to fight, but leave all to be taken, and carried away by the enemy without resistance. But some again make them but one joint sentence; so the old Latin, and divers others, *They shall cry*, or, *proclaim fear upon them*, or, *against them, on every side*: they shall by their hideous cries put them on every side in fear. So rather than as a learned Writer, Who would have *fear* here put for *arms*, the matter of fear: as *praise*, for matter of *praise*, verse 25. and so expounds it, *They shall beset them with arms on every side.* Of the form of speech being proverbial; see ch. 6.25. & 46.5.

**Verse 30.** *{Flee, get you far off, dwell deep, O ye inhabitants of Hazor, saith the LORD:}* The like advice was given before to the Edomites, verse 8. See there. Heb. *Flee, flit greatly, make deep to dwell*: which last branch, yet a learned interpreter reading enunciatively, incloses it in a parenthesis, and thus renders, (although *the inhabitants of Hazor dwell deep*) that is, seem to have a seat firm and safe. But I suppose that few herein concur with him, and it seems to mangle the context.

*{for Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon hath taken counsel against you, and hath conceived a purpose against you.}* See the same terms, verse 20. and of them there.

**Verse 31.** *{Arise, get you up into the wealthy nation that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates, nor bars, which dwell alone.}* Against the Kedarens; a people not *wealthy* (as some amiss render it) but *quiet*, that lives quietly, or at ease, as 1 Chron. 4.40. Zach. 7.7. and securely without fear of invasion. Heb. *in confidence*, or *confidently*; as Ezek. 38.11. like those of Laish, Judg. 18.10,27, that keep not in fenced cities, 2 Chron. 14.6. but scattered here and there in tents, (see on verse 29.) apart one from another, or apart from others in the wilderness, Mic. 7.14. aloof from any that may aid them against any that shall come to invade them, the case of Laish, Judg. 18.28. and all these things being laid together, such as may without any great difficulty be surprised.

**Verse 32.** *{And their camels shall be a booty, and the multitude of their cattle a spoil;}* As before, verse 29.

*{and I will scatter into all winds,}* Into all parts of the wide world. So verse 36. See the like form of speech, Dan. 11.4. Zach. 2.6. and the like judgment menaced, Ezek. 5.12.

*{them that are in the uttermost corners;}* Or; *cut off into corners*, or *that have the corners of their hair cut*. See on chap. 9.26. & 25.23.

*{and I will bring their calamity from all sides thereof, saith the LORD.}* See verse 5.8. and of the words rendered *sides* here on Chap. 22.20. So it is used, 1 Kings 4.24. *he had peace on all sides.*

**Verse 33.** *{And Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons, and a desolation for ever.}* See of Hazor before; verse 28. and of the like menaces, Chap. 9.11. & 12.22. & 51.37.

*{there shall no man abide there, nor any son of man dwell in it.}* As before, verse 18.

**Verse 34.** *{The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah, the Prophet, against Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, King of Judah, saying,}* This last Prophecy concerning *Elam*, has the usual introduction prefixed before it: such as Chap. 14.1. & 25.1. & 33.1. & 46.1. & 47.1. and a date withal annexed to it; as Chap. 27.1. & 28.1. In the first words of the inscription, or introduction, there is a trajection.

*{against Elam,}* Or, *touching*; as Chap. 21.11. or *concerning Elam*; as Chap. 27.19. & 44.1. the *Elamites*; that is, the Persians, a people more remote than any of the former in this Chapter mentioned; descended from *Elam* the son of Sem, Gen. 10.22. Of them, see on chap. 25.25. as also on Esay 26.6. whence it appears, that they served under Sennacherib in his expedition against Jerusalem; nor is it unlikely, that they served under Nebuchadnezzar also, having made himself master of the Assyrian Monarchy, in his invasion of Judea, which the Jewish Masters therefore say was the main ground and cause of this prophecy against them,

*{in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, King of Judah, saying,}* A long time before the execution and accomplishment of it, much about that time, when the Prophet was by God commanded to make those yokes, and send them to the neighboring Kings, implying their subjection to the Babylonian King, Chap. 27.2,3. and when the false Prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke, that the Prophet himself by God's appointment wore, withal promising a dissolution of the Babylonian dominion, and the return of the Jews abiding at captivity in Babylon, Chap. 28.1–3. to control that vain conceit, that he endeavored thereby to work into the minds of Zedekiah and his people, as being able to shake off the Chaldean yoke: when as Nebuchadnezzar should carry all away, as well farther off, as nearer at hand before him, Chap. 25.9. & 27.8.

**Verse 35.** *{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts, Behold I will break the bow of Elam, and the chief of their might.}* Instead of that yoke, which Hananiah broke, implying a dissolution of the Chaldean power, God threatens by that Chaldean power to *break the bow of Elam*, that is, their main might and principal strength, and that which the Elamites most trusted unto, being noted for expert archers; as Esay 22.6. See Psal. 18.34. & 37.15. & & 46.9. Chap. 51.56. Hos. 1.5. the latter expression may be joined by way of apposition to the former; and so most here take it. Yet it may be a distinct notion, and imply as the former their *arms*, so the latter their men of arms, the chief of their soldiery. Heb. *the beginning*, or *the principal* (as the word is used, 1 Sam. 15.21. Amos 6.6. *of their strength*, for, *their strong ones*; as Esay 2.25. the like term is used of the first-born, Gen. 49.3. Deut. 21.17. Psal. 78.51. & 105.37. thus taking it, the copulative is to be supplied; as Exod. 1.2. Habb. 3.11.

**Verse 36.** *{And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and I will scatter them towards all those winds, and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come.}* See the like before, verse 32. and the like menaces, Deut. 28.64. Chap. 24.9. and of the *four winds*; blowing one against another, Dan. 7.2. here intimating a violent driving of the Elamites to and fro, as either ships at sea, or, light matter on land, by contrary blasts and gusts, driven one while one way, and soon back again another.

**Verse 37.** *{For I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies and before them that seek their life:}* Heb. *And*, as chap. 48.27. and and *soul*, for *life*; as chap. 44.30, See the like threatening of consternation and terror, verse 5.14,29.

*{and I will bring evil upon them, even my fierce anger, saith the LORD}* Or, *I will bring evil* as Chap. 2.6. & 11.12. & 36.21.) *upon them in my wrath*, or, *with my fierce wrath*. Heb. *the fervor of my nose*, or *face*. See Esay 13.9,13. Chap. 25.37,38. The like defect of the particle, see Esay 51.19. Chap. 46. verse 21.

*{and I will send the sword after them,}* See the like menaces, Lev. 26.33. Chap. 48.2. Ezek. 5.2.

*{till I have consumed them.}* As chap. 9.16.

**Verse 38.** *{And I will set my throne in Elam,}* I will place Nebuchadnezzar there; as Chap. 43.10. whose throne is termed God's throne, because he received his royal power from God assigned to him by a peculiar providence to do God special service, Chap. 27.6. or I will execute judgment upon them, as having erected a tribunal, or seat of judicature among them; as Dan. 7.9–11. yet there want not, that refer this to Cyrus, and some to his conquest of Media, which, say they, marching out of Persia, he made entrance unto by breaking first into Elymais a part of it. Others, of Cyrus, his throne in those parts by God settled, to do him service against Babylon, termed therefore by him, *his Anointed*, Esay 45.1. But the received opinion of the Babylonian King seems the better.

*{and will destroy from thence the King and the Princes, saith the LORD.}* To seat the Chaldean King and his Princes in their stead; and by so doing to execute judgment upon them: as Dan. 7.11,12.

**Verse 39.** *{But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD.}* Or, *Yet it shall be.* Heb. *in posterity of days*: in after times, either when the term of the Chaldean Monarchy shall be expired, chap. 25.12–14. or, and that principally, in the days of the Messias, Acts 2.9. The like gracious closes, see before, Chap. 48.47. verse 6.

## CHAPTER 50

**Verse 1.** *{The word that the LORD spake against Babylon, and against the land of the Chaldeans by Jeremiah the Prophet.}* In this Chapter, and the next, is a very prolix prophecy against Babylon, which comes last here, because that State was to drink last of the wine-cup of God's wrath, after that it had gone round, and that the rest had drunk deep thereof by it, chap. 25.9. and it is therefore the larger, because the comfort of God's people depended much upon the expected downfall of that State. The whole prophecy is intermingled, partly, with dreadful menaces against Babylon, describing the manner of her overthrow, the persons by whom it should be effected, their proceedings in it, and successes against it, as if the design had been already accomplished, and the Prophet present himself at the accomplishing of it; together with the procuring causes of this her calamity, among which, their cruelty exercised on the people of God, one of the chief; and partly with gracious promises of protection and deliverance to God's people, together with encouragements of them, not to doubt or despair, though they see not things so soon, or so suddenly effected, as they desire, but to bear up their spirits with a hopeful expectation of assured freedom from captivity, and return to their own country in the time by God prefixed: and these are so closely interwoven, and so variously intertwined thorough out the whole body of it, the one with the other, and that also accompanied with so many interchanges of persons speaking, spoken of, and spoken to, as that it may well challenge any the strongest and clearest brain, to make out an exact and accurate analysis of it, which also when all were done, it may be, would not prove so useful neither. The inscription of the whole prophecy is in this first verse, wherein is declared the person, from whom it comes, *the Lord*; as chap. 46.13. against whom it is directed; *Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans* (Heb. *unto*; but *el*, for *al*: *concerning*, or *against*; as Chap. 49.19,20,34. and so chap. 51.12.) and by whom denounced, *Jeremy*. Heb. *by the hand of Jeremiah*; as, *by the hand of Malachy*, Mal. 1.1. See the like prophecies concerning Babylon, Esay 13. & 14. & 21. & 46. & 47. whence also some things are transferred into this prophecy.

**Verse 2.** *{Declare ye among the nations}* The entrance is made into it, with a commandment to publish in all places the downfall of Babylon, as a business already accomplished, *among the nations.* Because it concerned them, as well as God's people, who were to be freed from the Chaldean tyranny by the fall of Babylon: as well as they, Esay 14.6,7.

*{and publish}* Heb. *make it to be heard*; as Esay 48.20. See the like, Psal. 96.20. Esay 12.4,5. Chap. 31.10.

*{and set up a standard,}* Heb. *lift up an ensign*: not, as some to gather God's people together, to acquaint them with this prophecy; nor, as others, to get people together to be employed in service against Babylon; as Esay 14.2. for the work is here described and delivered, as already done; but to call people together, to impart unto them the glad tiding of Babylon's ruin and downfall; as the manner was on such occasions for those that came with good tidings of victory, delivery, good success, or the like public affairs: to get up into some eminent place, and from thence by some signal given to gather people together, to declare it unto them, and acquaint them therewith. See Esay 40.9. & 52.7. Nah. 1.15. the words following confirm it.

*{publish, and conceal not,}* Heb. *cause it to be heard*; as before: the copulative here is needless, See Psal. 50.9,10.

*{Say, Babylon is taken,}* So, *Babylon is fallen*, Esay 21.9.

*{Bel is confounded,}* The Babylonians chief idol, Chap. 51.44. Of it, see at large on Esay 46.1.

*{Merodach is broken in pieces,}* Another of their Idols; from which some of their Kings had their names: and was, it may be, at first, the name of some King who after his decease was idolized: such as were many of the Pagan deities. And this Merodach is by some learned supposed to be the same with him, whom Africanus calls Mardocentes, one far more ancient than Bel. See Esay 39.1. & 46.1.

*{her idols are confounded.}* Being neither able to save their people nor themselves, Esay 46.1. where also see of the term here used.

*{her images are broken in pieces.}* Esay 21.9. the term here used comes from a word that signifies *dung*. Ezekiel 4.12. Zeph. 1.17. and imports consequently *dungy*, *dirty idols*; idols, as vile, base, loathsome, abominable, as dung and dirt.

**Verse 3.** *{For out of the North, there cometh up a nation against her,}* or, *there is come up* (a military term, as Chap. 49.22.) or, simply *is come* (as Exod. 16.13. and he speaks of it, as of a thing already done) *against her, a nation* (the Medes and Persians accounted as one nation, because belonging to one crown. See Esay 13.17.) *from the North*: from Media, lying North from Chaldea; and from Assyria, through which Cyrus marched unto Babylon, verse 9.21.41.

*{which shall make her land desolate; and none shall dwell therein:}* Or, *so that none shall dwell therein*: the copulative for the infinitive: as Chap. 9.6,26. Heb. *shall put it unto desolation*; as chap. 2.15. See 13.20. verse 40.

*{they shall depart both man and beast}* Heb. *from man to beast*; as chap. 9.10. Esay 10.18. See chap. 51.61. and the like, chap. 4.25. & 33.10,12. Zeph. 1.3.

**Verse 4.** *{In those days, and in that time, saith the LORD,}* As chap. 33.15. When Babylon shall be taken by Cyrus, verse 2.

*{the children of Israel shall come, they, and the children of Judah together,}* The Jews being set at liberty by Cyrus, Ezr. 1.1,2. and many of the other ten tribes joining themselves to them. See ch. 30.3. & 31.5,6.

*{going and weeping:}* Or, *weeping as they go*; as chapter 41.6. as with grief for their sins whereby they had grieved God, and provoked him to wrath, and procured those forepassed calamities to themselves: so for joy also in the apprehensions of God's present gracious goodness toward them in remitting their sins, removing his wrath, reconciling them to himself, reducing them from their long captivity again: for tears there are of joy, as well as of grief, and some mixed ones of either. See Gen. 29.11. & 42.24. & 43.30. & 45.2,14,15. & 46.29. Nor need we therefore to understand these words, as a learned Writer therein following the Chaldee, of their weeping what time they went out into captivity, Psalm 126.6. and while they continued there, Psalm 137.1. but of tears shed in their return, as before, and after it also. See ch. 31.9. Ez. 3.12,13.

*{they shall go and seek the LORD their God.}* Or, *go to seek*; as, *arose and warred*, for, *rose to war*, Josh. 24.9. or, *go seeking*: as, *stand and feed*, for, *stand feeding*, Esay 61.5. to seek after him who had showed so much mercy, goodness, and kindness to them: to acknowledge their thankfulness for the same. See Psal. 24.6. & 105.4.

**Verse 5.** *{They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward,}* Heb. *They shall ask after Sion, the way thither* shall their faces be: they shall inquire the way to Jerusalem, (see Ezr. 8.21,23,31.) and that more specially in regard of Sion, the ancient seat of God's residence among them, and principal place of his solemn service, Psalm 84.7. See chap. 37.21.12. Zach. 8.21,22. and *their faces* shall be set *that way*. Of which form of speech, see on chapter 42.15.

*{saying, Come and let us join ourselves to the LORD, in a perpetual covenant, that shall not be forgotten.}* Let us renew our covenant with God again, let us enter into a firmer and more constant covenant with him than ever: (Heb. *a covenant of perpetuity*; such as God promised to make with them, chap. 32.42. Ezek. 16.60. & 37.26.) such as we will never start from again, Psal. 80.18. Chap. 32.42. See the like form of expression in another kind, chap. 23.40. there is in the Text a defect of the relative; as chap. 31.21,24. and the word *saying* is supplied; as chap. 48.39. Howbeit, the Chaldee acknowledges no such supply, but renders the words in an enunciative form; *they shall come and join themselves to the Lord's people*: which some of the Jewish Doctors following, expound the Text of those strangers that should adjoin themselves to God's people, either upon their return from captivity, Esay 14.1. or in the days of the Messias, Zach. 2.11. because the same word is there used: and of such it is used indeed also, Esay 56.3,6. But neither is the word *people*, here, which the Chaldee crams into the Text: nor is there any necessity that the word should here be taken, since that the current of the context runs clearly for Judah and Israel: it may rather imply, that they had so broken their conjugal Covenant with God, and God so cast them off thereupon, chap. 3.1,8. and 31.32. that they were in a manner become as mere strangers to God, chap. 2.5,15. Hosea 9.10. Amos 9.7. and may seem as such to be now new joined again to God, from whom they had severed themselves before by their sins, Esay 59.2. And of them a learned late Writer aright understanding it, but for the notion of the words concurring with the Chaldee, renders the text; *They shall come and adjoin themselves to the Lord*: and the same way go both the ancient Greek and old Latin: nor is this Version improbable, though some difficulties there seem in it: for as concerning the former word of *coming*, the form here used is generally an imperative, nowhere found in an enunciative notion: but to remove this scruple, that learned man produces two of the same stamp with it in an enunciative notion, the one in these words, *they were abashed*. Chapter 14.3. the other in those, *they are pleasant*, Canticles 4.10. for the latter, the Jewish Critics, whom most of our Grammarians concur with go another way: they take it for an Imperative and render the words therefore as the former *Come ye*; so this, *be ye adjoined*, or *adjoin yourselves*: the passive form in a reciprocal notion; as Chapter 4.4. & 23.4. & 36.19. and some Interpreters of prime note, whom the learned Scholiast also follows, do herein agree with them: an irregularity indeed, they acknowledge in it so taken: but they suppose one other Imperative, just of the same making, to be found in those words, *and be gathered together*, Joel 3.11. But this place produced by them, is as questionable as the present; and I incline therefore to the former, which is neither pestered with much irregularity and does very smoothly and evenly, without any supply, carry on the context: conceiving the words do contain a prediction, what the faithful party of God's people, being set free from their forementioned captivity, should do. Though some Interpreters of prime note read and render this whole passage concerning God's people, as spoken by way of adhortation or advice. *Let them come—let them seek—let them ask—let them say*, verse 4,5. But I leave that to the consideration of others.

**Verse 6.** *{My people have been lost sheep:}* God's Word speaking of the Jewish people, as still owning them; *My people*; as chap. 33.24. *hath been lost sheep*, or *as lost sheep*: a defect of the note of similitude: as Psalm 141.2. Esay 21.8. chap. 26.18. straying from God, Esay 53.6. Matt. 18.11,12. 1 Peter 2.25. and chased out of their own country into foreign parts, Psalm 119.176. v. 17. Heb. *perishing*, or, *perished*; and so Psalm 119.176. that is ready to perish: as Esay 27.13. and because the Noun subject is singular, the attribute plural: some render it, *a flock of perishing sheep*: as if there were a defect of some other subject to be supplied: as Ezekiel 13.11. but neither does the word signify *a flock* properly; and yet being here in a collective notion, the Syntax is not unusual; yea with the very same Syntax is the word found used, 1 Samuel 25.18.

*{their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away on the mountains:}* Their Rulers, Princes and Pastors, Magistrates and Ministers (for the word comprehends Governors as well Ecclesiastical as Civil Esay 56.11. chap. 3.15. & 3.1. & 25.34. Ezekiel 34.2.) have by their bad example, and false Doctrine, led them out of the way and made them to go astray from God, Esay 3.12. & 9.16. chap. 23.13,14,15. & 28.16. & 29.32. and by means thereof they caused them to be turned out of their own land, as sheep out of their pasture, and driven into strange countries, as sheep to graze on barren hills and bare mountains, Nah. 3.18. See chap. 27.10. Lamentations 2.14. and it seems an allusion to those mountains which they were forced to pass when they were carried away in captivity to Babylon, chap. 13.16. Yet want there not, both of the Jewish and others, who understand this of the mountains on which they worshiped their idols, Esay 65.7. Ezekiel 18.6,11. and they render the words some, *they have broken them upon the mountains*: as they suppose the word to be used, Ezekiel 38.4. & 39.2. Others, *they have made them to rebel upon the mountains*: as the word is used, Esay 47.10. chap. 8.5. the latter whereof seems the more probable: but neither to suit so well with the Prophet's purpose, and the resemblance used by him in this place.

*{they have gone from mountain to hill}* That is, as some, they have run up and down from one idol to another, chap. 2.23,24. or as others, they have been hurried up and down from place to place, during the time of their captivity; as scattered sheep are wont to be, Ezek. 34.4,6.

*{they have forgotten their resting place.}* Heb. *place to lie down in*; as Prov. 24.15. that is, as some they have forgotten God their only true rest, chap. 6.16. while they run thus after idols, chap. 2.31–33. & 23.27. Hos. 8.14, or rather, as others, they have been so long absent from their own country the place of their rest, Deut. 12.9. Psalm 95.11. chap. 31.2. that they may seem to have forgotten it: as in continuance of time, by long discontinuance, folk are wont to forget persons or places, that they formerly either conversed with or abode in.

**Verse 7.** *{All that found them have devoured them:}* As silly sheep when they stray, without any to look after them, and secure them, become a prey to every Wolf, or other ravenous wild beast that lights on them, Ezekiel 34.8. Thus the most: only one learned Interpreter renders it, *All that lead them out devour them*; as chap. 23.1. Zach. 11.15. and so it should be much the same with that before, v. 6. But the vowel points in the text will not admit this reading.

*{and their adversaries said; We offend not, because they have sinned against the LORD,}* Those that prey upon them, pretend that they deal but justly with them, no otherwise than as they have deserved for their sins against their God, chap. 40.5. Zach. 11.2. and we are therefore faultless. But see the contrary, chap. 2.3. nor indeed did those wicked wretches intend or regard any such thing, whatsoever they pretended, Esay 36.7,10. but the satisfying of their own ambitious dispositions, and the enlargement of their Dominions, Esay 10.6,7. Heb. *they have sinned to the Lord*: as Psalm 51.4. and so both the ancient Greek, and old Latin renders it: but the Particle is frequently used also for *against*; as Job 7.20. & 8.4. chap. 3.25.

*{the habitation of Justice:}* This our present Version, as others before it do, as by way of apposition, adjoin to the former; and make an attribute of God, and so the Jewish Doctor expounds it, *a just habitation, a sure dwelling*: according to that, *Lord, thou hast been our dwelling*, Psalm 90.1. & 91.1. The Chaldee renders it, *they have gone far*, or *kept aloof from the habitation of his holiness*, seeming to understand it of their leaving his Temple to go after their idols. The old Latin goes the same way herein with ours, but renders it *the beauty*, or *goodliness* of righteousness. But I find not where the word here used has any such notion, though one near to it has. Other Interpreters of good note, conceive a defect of the particle *in*, oft suppressed; as Job 1.13. Esay 26.8,18. chap. 5.7. and the place here designed, *in which they so sinned*, which did much aggravate their offense; and they render the words, some, *in the fold of righteousness*; because they find the word so used 2 Samuel 7.8: 1 Chron. 17.7. See Ezekiel 34.14. Some *in the habitation of righteousness*; that is in the Church of God, in the land of Judah and the city of Jerusalem; the place where righteousness should dwell. See chap. 31.23. or *righteousness*, as some for men of *righteousness*; *righteous ones*; as Esay 1.21. See Esay 60.21.

*{even the LORD the hope of their fathers.}* Heb. *and the hope*, or, *expectation of their fathers the Lord.* That which divers diversely render and expound: the old Latin retaining the copulative; *and the expectation of their fathers the Lord*: nor does our English Versions much swerve from this; only they make the copulative, nor so much a note of conjunction as of amplification, or exaggeration; as chap. 15.13. & 23.9. But others make the copulative a note of similitude: as it is Prov. 17.3. & 20.25. rendering the text, Who would have been a sure habitation to them, if they had not sinned against him, *as* he had been *the hope of their fathers*. Others take it in a relative notion *Whose fathers expectation he was*, and of them, for *whose*; the copulative with the Pronoun demonstrative, for the relative: as chap. 15.19. & 17.7. Some lastly, with whom I close, take the copulative in a discretive notion, as it is frequently used, Psal. 78.3. Esay 35.9. chap. 31.33. and make it an entire sentence. So a learned Scholiast renders it, *albeit the Lord was the expectation of their fathers*, that is, he, on whom their Ancestors depended and from whom they expected relief, succor, safety, and all manner of good. See c. 17.13.

**Verse 8.** *{Remove out of the midst of Babylon, and go forth out of the land of the Chaldeans:}* Or, *Remove out of her*; as Esay 5.8. & 7.23. See Esay 48.20. & c. 51.6. Rev. 18.4.

*{and be as the he goats before the flocks.}* O, *as the great he-goats*, that are as ringleaders to the rest of the flock. See Esay 14.9. and *goats* he mentions rather than sheep; though God's people are more usually compared to sheep, Matt. 25.32,33. because they are the nimbler and the swifter of the two, strive to go one before another, in making haste to your own country again. See Esay 60.8.

**Verse 9.** *{For lo, I will raise, and cause to come up against Babylon, an assembly of great nations from the North country;}* Heb. *I am raising* (as Esay 13.17.) *and making to come up*, or *march* (as v. 2.) *against Babylon, an assembly* (a company, as called together; as Zeph. 1.7.) *of great nations* (as c. 27.7. the *Medes and Persians*, Esay 13.17.) *from the land of the North.* See v. 3.

*{and they shall set themselves in array against her,}* Or, *set the battle in array*; as 1 Chr. 12.33. & 19.9. the like defect is, 2 Sam. 10.17. Heb *to her*, for *against her*; as v. 3.

*{from thence she shall be taken:}* *From thence*; that is, by people and forces coming from those parts, So rather, than as a learned late Writer, *from thence*; that is, out of hand, suddenly, unexpectedly: or, as one of the Rabbines, from the place; where they sit down, and set their forces in array against her, not needing to remove to any other place from thence: *shall she be taken*, verse 2.

*{their arrows shall be as of a mighty expert man.}* Heb. *their arrows* shall be *as a mighty man*, for, *as* the arrows of *a mighty man*: as, *he maketh my feet like hinds*, or, *harts*: that is, like the feet of *hinds*, or *harts*: Psal. 18.33. and Esay 63.2. *garments like one that treadeth the wine-fat*, for; like the garments of *one that treadeth the wine-fat*. In the latter term here used, there is some variety of reading: as in the pronunciation of *Sibboleth*, and *Shibboleth*, Judg. 12.6. according to the diverse placing of a point upon the right or left corner of the initial letter. The Chaldee, and the Jewish Doctors, with whom the old Latin concurs, place it on the right hand, and then it signifies one *that destroyeth*, that bereaves wives of their husbands, children of their parents, and parents of their children; as the word intimates, Hos. 9.14. Others turn the point over to the left side, and then it signifies one *expert*, or *skillful*; and so the ancient Greek here renders it, which our Versions follow: unto which I shall add a third Interpretation, from the root, which the word comes from in the latter form; wherein it signifies, not to deal *prudently*, and *skillfully*, only, but to *prosper* also and *be successful*. See Esay 52.13. & Jer. 23.5. and so it may be rendered of one *successful*, whose shafts never miss, like those Benjamites, Judg. 20.16. hence it follows.

*{none shall return in vain.}* But shall hit and speed, 2 Sam. 1.12. effect what it was shot and sent for; as Esay 55.11. understood of their arrows; because like the arrows of a man both of strength to draw the bow, and of skill to guide the shaft, and that directs it to the speeding places, and is successful in his shot. But the words in the text rather are, *it shall not return empty*; as the term is used, Chap. 14.3. that is, as some other expound it, *the assembly of nations*, before mentioned, *shall not return empty*; but furnished and laden with store of rich spoils; as Exod. 3.21. the contrary whereunto, see Ruth 1.21. See verse 18. those that go the former way are fain to render it; *there shall not* any of them, to wit, of their arrows, *return empty*, or *in vain*: Either may stand with the terms of the text.

**Verse 10.** *{And Chaldea shall be a spoil, all that spoil her shall be satisfied, saith the LORD.}* They shall find wealth enough in her to satisfy them to the full: the state of Chaldea, and city of Babylon being the richest place at that time in the world. See Esay 13.19. & 14.4. & 45.3. Chap. 51.13,44.

**Verse 11.** *{Because ye were glad, because ye rejoiced,}* Because you have rejoiced at, and sported yourselves in the miseries and calamities of my people; as of Moab, Chap. 48.27. or, as some read it, *When* (as Chap. 10.2.) *ye shall be merry and revel it*; as alluding to the festival, at which Babylon was surprised, Chapter 51.39,17.

*{O ye destroyers of mine heritage,}* You Chaldeans, that have made such spoil and havoc of my land, Lev. 25.23. chap. 2.7. & 16.18. or of my people, chap. 12.7–9. as dear to me, as any man's inheritance is to him, 1 Kings 21.3.

*{because ye are grown fat,}* Or, *big*, or *corpulent*; as some: or; *when* (as before) *ye abound*: or, as others, *are grown fat*, or, *lascivious*, as, fullness and fatness is wont to produce wantonness, Deut. 32.15. chap. 5.8. Ezek. 16.39. the same word is found, Mal. 4.2. but in no evil notion there: and from thence a word for *abundance*, Job 35.15. Others again, *Ye are diffused*, and skip up and down; as alluding to beasts that grow skittish, when they are full fed, and run at large, because the word is found in a notion, of *diffusion* and *dispersion*, Habb. 1.8. Nah. 3.18.

*{as the heifer at grass,}* Or, *like an heifer*, or *calf*, (the same word with that, chap. 48.34.) *feeding on*, or *fed with tender grass*: for it is an adjective derived from a term that signifies such herbage as does first sprout out, and is not grown over rank, or exhausted, but is full of moisture and sweetness, and does therefore suddenly fill and fat. See Esay 15.11. & 66.14. as also, Deut. 32.2. 1 Sam. 23.4. instead whereof to the same purpose, is *calves*, or, *heifers of the stall*; that is, *stalled* ones, Mal. 4.2.

*{and bellow as bulls.}* The word here used signifies properly *to neigh*; the peculiar note of *horses* Chap. 5.8. & 13.27. Job 6.5. Psal. 23.2. and because not without cause it may be questioned how *bulls* should be said *to neigh*: some suggest from a Jewish Master, that the word is used for *any shrill*, or: *loud voice*, or, *cry*, of what kind soever. See chap. 31.7. but we need not flee to any such metaphorical use of the word: or, to Oxen used for treading out of corn, Hos. 10.11. to which employment, the strongest of them should be designed, (which seems nothing probable; and that of Hosea implies the contrary) and used to grow yet fatter and lustier by that employment, having by the Law liberty to feed the more freely, Deut. 25.4. for the latter word here used signifies as well *horses* as *beeves*, as well *steeds* as *bulls*. See on chap. 46.15. & 47.3. and it would therefore be rendered, *ye neigh as steeds*, or, *lusty steeds*: for the word has a note of eminency in it, as has been before showed: and this Version the Prophet leads us unto from Chap. 5.16. where both the terms here used are the same found joined together; save that the noun of the one is there, the verb whereof is here, in those words, *the neighing of his steeds.*

**Verse 12.** *{Your mother shall be sore confounded, she that bare you}* (shall *{be ashamed:}* Your former routing and reviling, insulting over and deriding of others shall be seconded with shame and confusion; as Chap. 48.26,27. for your mother-city Babylon, or your native country Chaldea: as Esay 23.4. & 51.18. Chap. 15.8,9. shall be ashamed of you, that could defend her no better: as they of their idols, chap. 48.14.

*{behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.}* Or rather, as most both Jewish and others, *the last of Kingdoms* shall it be, &c. she that was the foremost of nations before, shall become the hindermost, the last, the lowest: she that was before so rich and wealthy, shall become a wild waste; as of Judah the like, Lam. 1.1. and of Egypt the same, Ezek. 29.12,15. See Esay 13.20.

**Verse 13.** *{Because of the wrath of the LORD}* This clause would rather have been annexed to the words foregoing; as the like, chap. 41.18. Heb. *bubbling*, or, *boiling wrath*, Esay 34.2. Chap. 10.10. & 21.5.

*{It shall not be inhabited, but shall be wholly desolate.}* Heb. *It shall not sit*, or *dwell*; See Esay 13.20. Chap. 17.6. So ver. 3.39.

*{every one that goeth by Babylon shall be astonished, and hiss at all her plagues.}* In disdain and derision; as chap. 49.17.

**Verse 14.** *{Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about:}* Or, *Set the battle in array round about against Babylon*. See verse 9.29. God's speech to the Medes and Persians, and their assistants. Of whom verse 9. and chap. 51.1.

*{all ye that bend the bow shoot at her;}* Heb. *tread the bow*: as chap. 46.9. So verse 29. and *throw*, or, *cast*, or *cast out* (as Lam. 3.53. Joel 3.3. Zach. 12.4.) to wit, arrows, or shafts: a defective speech: the like whereunto see chap. 4.29,

*{spare no arrows,}* Heb. *have no pity on arrows*: for so the word properly signifies, having in it a notion of *pity*, and *sparing* out of pity, Exod. 2.6. 2 Sam. 21.6. 2 Chron. 36.15. *arrows*, collectively, for, *arrow*: as Psal. 9.5. and *el*, for, *al*: as also, chap. 51.3. this latter particle being of more frequent, almost general, use in this form. See chap. 48.11. and one of the Jewish Doctors supposes that there might be in the words a close preoccupation of a secret suggestion, which the Persian soldiery might think, when they should be called upon to spend their arrows apace, that it would be great pity to have so many arrows cast away and lost: to which answer should be returned here, that no such pity should need, for none should be lost: they should every one do execution, as had been before said, verse 9. But this I conceive to be somewhat overnice.

*{for she hath sinned against the LORD}* That which they pretended to be their ground for afflicting God's people, verse 7. and it is, *to the Lord*, here also, as there: though it may be understood, *they have sinned exceedingly*: as it is said of the Sodomites, *They were sinners unto God*, or, *of God*; that is, exceedingly great, or grievous sinners, Gen. 13.13. the words are in either place the same. See verse 29,

**Verse 15.** *{Shout against her round about:}* Assault her on every side with a warlike shout, such as assailants are wont to make, therewith partly, to incite, and set on one another, and partly to affright those whom they assail, Chap. 4.19. & 49.2. So rather, than as some, who would have it understood of shouts used in a triumphant manner after victory obtained, and conquest of a place made: though of such also the word be used, as Psal. 47.5.

*{she hath given her hand:}* That is, says a learned late Writer, she has entered into confederacy with the Lydians, our adversaries, (for which he cites Herodote) and therefore we must not spare her: and these words he would have to be uttered by the assailants in the shout enjoined: for *to give the hand*, is used for to enter into society and confederacy, Ezek. 17.18. 1 Maccab. 11.50. Gal. 2.9. and so, *to put hand*, Lev. 6.2. and *to strike hands*, Job 17.2. But the most and best go rather another way, understanding it, as it is in other languages also, as well as in Hebrew, very frequent, in the Latin especially, for *to yield up* one's self into the power of another. So 2 Chron. 30.8. Lam. 5.6. it implies, as a learned Writer supposes, a holding up of one's hand to be bound and manacled, as slaves, prisoners, and captives were wont to be. See chap. 40.4. But I conceive rather, as showing them quitted of arms, making no opposition, but suing for mercy: as Psal. 68.31. used also as a signal of submission and allegiance 1 Chron. 29.24.

*{her foundations are fallen, her walls are thrown down:}* So, ch. 51.58. *the broad walls of Babylon shall be razed*: but here speaking of it in a prophetical strain, as of a thing already done, Howsoever a learned Writer would have it taken, as spoken by the enemy, in way of incitement at the time of the assault: *Let her foundations be razed, let her walls be thrown down*: like that, Psal. 137.7. Strabo lib. 16. reports that a great part of her walls were razed by the Persians, and the rest ruined by neglect and continuance of time; so that it might well be said of it, *the great city* (the greatest, says Pausanias, in his *Arcadiacks*, that the sun had seen) *was become a great waste.*

*{for it is the vengeance of the LORD:}* Against whom she had sinned, ver. 14. as that execution done upon Moab, is called *the work of the Lord*. Chap. 48.10. the pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive; as Psal. 25.11. So also ver. 25.

*{take vengeance upon her; as she hath done, do unto her.}* Pay her in her own coin, deal with Babylon, as she dealt with Jerusalem, Ps. 137.8. no juster Law than that of retaliation, Exod. 21.23,25. Deut. 19.19,21. acknowledged so to be, even by those that have themselves suffered it, Judge 1.5. So ver. 29. Rev. 18.6.

**Verse 16.** *{Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him that handleth the sickle in the time of harvest:}* *Sickle*, or, *Sithe*: so Joel 3.13. Destroy her so that none of hers be left, either to till the ground, or to take the crop of it, if any come up of itself; which yet God caused the Chaldeans to leave, when they carried the Jews away captive, 2 King. 25.12. The Chaldee renders it, *cut off the King from Babylon, and whet the sword for the time of slaughter*. But that departs too far from the Text.

*{for fear of the oppressing sword, they shall turn every one to his people, and they shall flee every one to his own land.}* Her hired soldiers and assistants. See the same before of Egypt, Chap. 46.16. See also, Chap. 51.9.

**Verse 17.** *{Israel is a scattered sheep:}* Or, *as a scattered sheep*; as ver. 6. he is scattered among the nations, Joel 3.2.

*{the lions have driven him away:}* That is, as the Chaldee, fierce and mighty Kings compared to lions the King of beasts; have driven him out of his country. See Chap. 4.7. yet the term may be more general, and comprehend any potent adversaries, Psal. 57.6. Chap. 2.15.

*{first the King of Assyria hath devoured him}* Or, *first the King of Assyria did eat upon him.* See Chap. 10.25. most understand it of the Assyrian Kings vexation of the ten Tribes by Pul and Tiglath-Pileser, 2 King. 15.19,20,29. 1 Chr. 5.26. and the deportation of them by Salmaneser, 2 Kings 16.7. and 17.3,4. Yet I conceive that it may have more special respect to the people of Judah invaded and much spoiled by the hostile incursions of Sennacherib, 2 King. 18.13–17. and Esarhaddon, 2 Chr. 33.11.

*{and last this Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon hath broken his bones.}* Heb. *hath boned him*; that is, as the most, has utterly ruined him by carrying away captive Judah and Benjamin, 2 King. 24.14–16. and 25.7,11,19,20. as the other had done the ten Tribes: or referring both to those two Tribes; making up jointly the State and Kingdom of Judah, he has utterly deprived him of all strength and support, which lie in the *bones*. See Esay 38.13. Lam. 3.4. the other tore his fleece and his flesh off him; but this latter has even broken his bones too: *to bone*, for, *to break bones*, or, *to unbone*: as, *to neck*, for, *to break the neck*, or, *cut off by the neck*, Exod. 13.13. Deut. 21.4. Esay 66.3. and, *to tail*, for, *to curtail*, or, *cut off the tail*, Deut. 25.18. Josh. 10.19.

**Verse 18.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel,}* As Chap. 48.1.

*{Behold, I will punish the King of Babylon, and his land, as I have punished the King of Assyria.}* I will pull down the one, as I have already done the other: and the one produced the rather to give assurance of the other: as Esay 14.25. Heb. *visit upon*, as Esay 10.12. So Chap. 51.44.

**Verse 19.** *{And I will bring Israel again to his habitation;}* Or, *to his fold*; as 2 Sam. 7.8. or, *his pasture*: as Ezek. 34.14. See on Chap. 9.9. (for he continues still the former metaphor taken from sheep, verse 6.17.) to their wonted places of feeding and lodging.

*{and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan,}* Which were of the richest and fertilest parts of that country, Numb. 32.4. Psalm 18.12. See Esay 33.9. and 35.2.

*{and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead.}* Or, *he shall be satisfied*, or, *satiated*; as Esay 58.10. Psal. 63.5. he shall feed as largely as he can desire to his fill: of *Gilead*, see chap. 22.6. and of mount Ephraim, chap. 31.5,6. that these places were after the return from the captivity, by such Kings as prevailed in those parts adjoined to the State of Judea, Some Writers observe here from Joseph's *Antiquities*, lib. 13. cap. 5.8.

**Verse 20.** *{In those days, and in that time, saith the LORD:}* As before, ver. 4.

*{the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none;}* Or, *it shall not be*; as Psal. 39.13. Chap. 31.15. it shall no more be, than as if it never had been, God forgiving and forgetting it, Chap. 31.34. Zech. 10.6.

*{and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found:}* The same thing in divers terms: *not to be found*, for, *not to be*; as Psal. 10.15. with 7.9. and 37.36. Dan. 2.35.

*{for I will pardon them whom I reserve.}* And God where he forgives sin, forgets it, and utterly abolishes the guilt of it, Esay 45.23. Mic. 7.19. Heb. *I will be propitious to them*; as Chap. 5.7. and 33.8. in Christ, the only true propitiatory, Rom. 3.25. 1 Joh. 2.2.

**Verse 21.** *{Go up against the land of Merathaim, even against it, and against the Inhabitants of Pekod.}* God's speech to Cyrus. The words *Merathaim* and *Pekod*, as some Interpreters of the best note deem, are here the names of two countries, through which Cyrus was to pass unto Babylon. The former is conceived to be that of the people called *Mardi*, so termed from their head City *Marde*; and the word seems to bear a dual form, in regard that the country was divided into two parts by the river Tigris that ran through it; that nation inhabiting part of the one side of it, which stood in Assyria, and part on the other side, within the circuit of Armenia. See Ptolomy, lib. 5. cap. 13. Strabo, lib. 11. and 12. and Stephen the Byzantine, place them either within Hyrcania, or in the confines thereof; in whose works also they are called diversely, sometime *Mardi*, and sometime *Amardi*: the latter, to wit, Pekod, is found mentioned, Ezek. 23.23. whence some conceive it to have been a city, or region of Chaldea; others rather of Assyria, situate in the lower part of it; and so termed as some suppose, because it was invested with the *prefecture* and command of the parts thereabout; Nineveh has sometime had the preeminence, being then ruined: that it belonged to one of those Provinces, that place of the Prophet sufficiently shows: and that Cyrus marched through Assyria unto Babylon is apparent, by Herodote, lib. 1. The words therefore may well thus be rendered, as they lie in the Text, and according to the pointings of them there, *against the land*, (or, *this land*; for the article is here demonstrative: as in that form; *the day*, for, *this day*, chap. 49.19,21.) from (or, by) *Merathaim* (a defect of the particle, as Gen. 4.1. Exod. 13.17,18.) *go up* (of which, see verse 9.) *against it*; (a redundancy elegant and vigorous; as Esay 8.13. *and by the Inhabitants of Pekod*; so is the particle used, Gen. 49.29. Job 29.19. or as some, *against them*: *el*, for *al*; as before, chap. 49.34. supposing it to be a city of the Chaldees, which Cyrus took in his way to Babylon. Thus Jeremy describes the course of Cyrus his progress toward Babylon, as Esay does of Sennacherib's march toward Jerusalem, Esay 10.20–32. Howbeit, because those names have some affinity in sound and letters with some Hebrew, or Syriack terms, the main shoal of Interpreters fetch another way, and takes them, not for proper names, but for names of common notion, and will have both to be spoken of Chaldea, or Babylon: and the former the Chaldee, whom the old Latin also follows, renders, *the land of those that rule*: as if it came from a Syriack term that signifies *to rule*: whence *Maran-abba* 1 Cor. 16.22. Others, *the land of rebellious ones*; from an Hebrew term that signifies to *rebel*, Lam. 1.20. the ancient Greek, *go up against the land of bitterness*; from a word, whence *Marah*, Exod. 15.23. Ruth 1.20. the latter likewise some make a noun, expounding it, *visitation*, or the land that is to be visited, ver. 27. Others make it a verb, rendering the words, *and visit her Inhabitants*: but that *her*, is not in the Text. A late learned Annotator coming after all, adds a peculiar Version of his own, thus rendering the whole passage; *Upon this land there is a double rebellion* (that is manifold, or much, as chap. 16.18. and 17.18.) *go up against her, and against the Inhabitants of visitation*: that is, such as are liable to visitation, as deserve to be visited. But leaving this with the rest to the consideration of others, I concur with the first.

*{waste, and utterly destroy after them, saith the LORD.}* That this injunction is given against Chaldea and Babylon is generally agreed: but about the last clause of it, some difference there is. Some refer those words, *after them*, to the places before mentioned; as if it were said, having done with them, subdued and sacked them, march on to Babylon. Others, and so some of the Jewish Commenters; pursue with the sword those that flee that none may escape; and draw hither those places, where God threatens persons, to *draw* and *send a sword after them*, Lev. 26.33. chap. 42.16. Ezek. 5.2. Others lastly, *destroy utterly the posterity*, or, *race of them*, as Dan. 4.11. and this seems the most probable. See Esay 14.20–22.

*{and do according to all that I have commanded thee.}* To wit, by a secret instinct; as 2 Sam. 16.12. 2 King. 18.25. 2 Chr. 36.23. Esai 10.6. See Esay 44.28. and 48.14. and chap. 34.22.

**Verse 22.** *{A sound of battle is in the land, of great destruction.}* Heb. *A voice of war*; that is, either *a report* of it; as Chap. 4.15. or, such *a noise*, as is wont to be raised in warlike conflicts. See chap. 48.33. and, *of great breaking*; as Chap. 4.6,20. and 51.64. See chap. 48.38. alluding withal to such a noise, as in the breaking down and fall of high buildings is wont to be heard. See chap. 49.21.

**Verse 23.** *{How is the hammer of the whole earth cut asunder and broken?}* Babylon that like a great hammer, or sledge, did subdue and destroy all the Princes and people of the world then known commonly in those parts. See Esay 14.4–7,12,16,17. chap. 51.20. Such an *hammer* is God's word compared to for the power and efficacy of it, chap. 23.29. and from such an one had that *Charles Martel* his name with the French.

*{how is Babylon become a desolation among the nations?}* Over whom she so domineered and tyrannized before. See ver. 12.

**Verse 24.** *{I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware:}* Or, *when thou wast not aware*; as chap. 34.1. I have caused you to be taken unawares, as a fowl in a snare, while it is feeding securely, and suspects no such matter, Eccles. 9.12. Luke 21.35. for the city was taken suddenly, when no such matter was expected, and while they were feasting and reveling; as Herodote relates. See Esay 47.11. Chap. 51.39.

*{thou art found, and also caught; because thou hast striven against the LORD.}* Against whom there is no defense, and from whom no escape, Prov. 21.30. Chap. 23.24. and 48.43,44. Heb. *hast mingled thy self with the Lord*: the term is used properly of joining issue at Law, or fight in the field, Deut. 25.19. 2 King. 14.10. Prov. 15.18. and 29.22.

**Verse 25.** *{The LORD hath opened his armory,}* Heb. *treasury*, or, *storehouse*: but well rendered *armory*; because a storehouse intended, not of blessings; as Deut. 28.12. but of judgments, though the same word be used of either; as God is said to *open the windows of heaven*, as well to pour down wrath, Esay 24.18. as to rain down a blessing, Mal. 3.10. but in the ambiguous, or comprehensive term of *treasury*, the Prophet is deemed by some to have some glance at the Treasures of the Temple, which her King had preyed upon, 2 Chr. 36.18. as if it were said that God would open the treasury of his wrath to be avenged on them that had pillaged the treasury of his Temple, 2 Chr. 36.18.

*{and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation:}* Or, *his weapons of indignation*; as also Esai 13.5. and *an array of vengeance*, Esai 59.17. and it is a figurative speech borrowed from the practice of Princes and States, who when any weighty expedition is intended, or invasion expected, are wont to set open the places of public stores, and to bring forth the arms for such occasions there reserved, 2 Chr. 23.9. Esay 22.8. as the former word was very comprehensive, so this much more. See on chap. 49.29. and is included in it as well *furniture, vessels*, and *utensils* of all sorts, as *instruments*, or *weapons*: whence it is also by some deemed, that some eye is here had to the holy vessels, as intimating that these *instruments of wrath* should be employed against them, for carrying away, and profaning the *vessels* of God's house, 2 Chr. 36.18. Dan. 1.3. and 5.3,22.

*{for this is the work of the Lord GOD of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans.}* It is not man's work, but God's, though men be made use of, and employed as instruments in it, Chap. 48.10. See on Esay 10.5,15. and 63.3. So ver. 15. The pronoun demonstrative, for the verb substantive: as there also.

**Verse 26.** *{Come against her from the utmost border,}* Heb. *Come to her* (as ver. 7.) *from the end*: that is, say some, from a remote place, from a far country; as Mat. 12.42. as intimating that no remoteness of place should hinder them from doing God's work, Esay 7.18. or, *from* the land's *end*; as ver. 41. For the Persians lay upon the Persian Gulf, and the Medes coasted upon the Caspian Sea. See Esay 13.5. which place parallel to this, helps to free & clear it from those forced constructions of the Jewish Master, of *coming upon her from her end*; when the term assigned for her standing is at an end; as chap. 51.13. or, *come upon her at end*; that is, set upon her suddenly at the one side of the city, chap. 51.31. the former, the ancient Greek follows, but with a disjoining of the Text. As also it excludes that new Interpretation of a learned late Writer, who expounds it in a notion of *universality*, but agrees not with himself in the particular application of it: for in one place he would have it meant of an universality of persons, and renders it, *Come all of you together*; as, says he, it is taken, Gen. 19.4. and 47.2. in another place, of an universality of place, and so it should be rendered, *Come on every side against her*; and so, says he again, it is taken both here, and chap. 51.31. Of which place, when we come to it; as also further concerning that of Esay on ver. 41.

*{open her storehouses}* Break open those houses, wherein her wealth and treasure lies locked up. The Hebrew word, here only found, does properly signify *granaries*: and so the Chaldee renders it; but the ancient Greek more generally, as ours here *store-houses*; and it is observed that the Hebrew word answering to our *treasury*, has a far larger conception, and takes in all manner of *stores*, whereof see on Chap. 41.8. so this of *granaries*, though in its original importing places of receipt for *stores* of *grain* and *victual*; yet does in likelihood here comprehend *treasuries*, places designed unto, and employed for the keeping of coin, plate, jewels, and treasure of all sorts; whereof Babylon had great abundance. See Esai 45.1,3. ver. 10.

*{cast her up as heaps;}* As men use to cast up earth and rubbish to raise the ground, when they are to make causeys; as Esay 57.14. and 62.10. make her of a goodly stately city, nothing but heaps of earth, stones and rubbish; as Psal. 79.1. Esay 25.2. and 37.26. See chap. 51.37. and this seems to be the genuine notion of the word, and the true sense of the Text: which one of the Jewish Masters laying this for a certain ground, that the word here used is never found, but in a notion of *lifting up*, so far backs: but in application of it goes another way, expounding it, not of the city itself, but of its wealth; as if it were said, heap up the spoils of the city, cast them together upon heaps. (See on Esay 17.11.) to which one of ours adds, heap them so up, as if you were to make a causey of them, make the heaps so broad, that men may walk many together abreast on them: and the Chaldee looking somewhat this way, *Consume her wealth, as the enemy is wont to do the heaps of corn* in the fields. The old Latin looking to that of Esai 62.10. renders it, *Take up the stones out of the way, and make heaps*: which is altogether here unsuitable.
