But our margin exhibits another reading, which many others embrace, *tread her down as heaps*: which some expound of the treading down of causeys, or materials cast up to raise them, thereby to flat them, and so make them even and smooth. Others, and so most of the Jewish Masters, of beasts treading on sheaves of corn to thresh out the grain; whom a learned Scholiast of ours following, renders it, *tread upon her, as on heaps*, (or, as some; *sheaves of corn*, from Ruth 3.7. where it seems used for the *mow*) and expounds it, As oxen tread the heaps of corn in the floor, Deut. 25.4. Mic. 4.13. See Esay 21.10. which I should willingly admit, the rather for the term of *granaries* before used, did I find the verb *salal* anywhere in that notion; which as yet I do not; and adhere therefore to the first.

*{and destroy her utterly}* Of the word here used, see on Esay 34.2. and 37.11. it is frequently used of some places in the land of Canaan that were utterly destroyed, Josh. 8.26. and 11.21.

*{let nothing of her be left.}* Heb. *let there not be a remainder to her*. See Esay 14.21,22. which may serve for a commentary upon this place.

**Verse 27.** *{Slay all her bullocks:}* Her great Princes and men of might. See Esay 34.7. The Hebrew verb here used might well be rendered, *sword them*, or put them to the *sword*: for the word *sword* in Hebrew comes from it.

*{let them go down to the slaughter:}* As Chap. 48.15. See there.

*{woe unto them for their day is come, the time of their visitation.}* As Chap. 27.7. and 46.21. So ver. 31. and the like, Ezek. 7.7.10,14.

**Verse 28.** *{The voice of them that flee, and escape out of the land of Babylon,}* The Prophet speaks this as if he heard the Jewish people that were got safe out of Babylon, and were now on their way homeward, how joyfully they congratulated one with another, and blessed God together for their delivery. The sentence is suspended, as in speeches full of passion and affection is not unusual. So Cant. 2.8. *The voice of my beloved*: and the very like we may see Esay 66.6. some to make the sentence entire, insert, *is heard*; rendering the Text, as here, so in Esay, *A voice*, there is heard: which though it be not necessary; yet I mislike not. But that of the Jewish Doctor is ridiculous, who would have this *voice*, to be the speech mentioned in the next verse: for Cyrus, says he, sent out his proclamation of liberty for the Jews to return to their own country, Ezr. 1.1. before that Darius came to sit down before Babylon; who thereupon many of them got by stealth out of it: and the words following, verse 29. are the speech of those Jews thus escaped, encouraging those of Darius his forces, to go on courageously in assaulting of the city, with assurance of success. But this may well go among other their groundless figments, whereof they have not a few.

*{to declare in Zion}* When they have gotten thither, and are arrived there, whither they are now bound, verse 5. See chap. 51.10. what manner of voice that there glanced at was; though it may also not improbably be understood of such, as having made shift to get before the rest to Jerusalem, should there make report of what had been done at Babylon. See ver. 8. and Esay 40.9. and 52.7.

*{the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance of his Temple.}* The vengeance executed by God for the direption and destruction of his Temple, 2 Chr. 36.18,19.

**Verse 29.** *{Call together the archers against Babylon; all ye that bend the bow, camp against it round about: let none thereof escape:}* God's speech, not the Jews, as the Jewish Masters would have it. See ver. 14.15. and the like, Chap. 4.17. Heb. *Make the shooters* (as Job 16.13.) *to hear* (as ver. 2. So Chap. 51.27.) *unto Babel* (for, *against* her: as Chap. 49.19,20.) *all treaders of bow*, as ver. 14. A learned Annotator for *shooters*, reads *many*: and the word may signify either. But the Version generally received fits the better here: *tread the bow*: as chap. 46.9. and 51.3.

*{recompense her according to her work: according to all that she hath done, do unto her:}* As ver. 15.

*{for she hath been proud against the LORD; against the holy one of Israel.}* The main cause of Babylon's fall, her proud and insolent carriage against God, ver. 31,32. chap. 51.1. Esay 14.13,14. Dan. 5.20,23. as of Ashur, Esay 10.11–15. and 37.23,29. and of Moab, chap. 48.26,29,42.

**Verse 30.** *{Therefore shall her young men fall in her streets: and all her men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the LORD.}* See the same Chap. 49.26.

**Verse 31.** *{Behold, I am against thee, O thou most proud, saith the Lord GOD of hosts,}* Or *I am coming against thee*, as Chap. 23.31,32. Heb. *unto thee*, as ver. 29. and, *pride*, for, *man of pride*; as Psal. 36.11. such God in special opposes, and sets himself against them, because by no sin do men more directly oppose him, Jam. 4.6. 1 Pet. 5.5.

*{for thy day is come, the time that I will visit thee.}* As before, ver. 27. there wants *wherein*; as Job 3.3.

**Verse 32.** *{And the most proud shall stumble, and fall, and none shall raise him up:}* Or, *And* that *most proud one* Heb. *man of pride*; as ver. 31.) *shall stumble and fall* (as Chap. 46.6,12.) *So as* (as ver. 3.) none shall be able *to raise him up*: the word taken in a potential notion; as Amos 7.2. See Eccles. 4.10.

*{and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it shall devour all round about him}* As Chap. 21.14. and 49.27.

**Verse 33.** *{Thus saith the LORD of hosts, The children of Judah, and the children of Israel, were oppressed together,}* Or, *were oppressed alike*: as the word is used, Deut. 12.12. though at several times, and by several adversaries: by the Assyrians principally the one; 2 King. 17.6. by the Chaldeans chiefly the other, 2 King. 24.12,14. and 25.11. for to the deportations of them especially do the words here relate. See ver. 17.

*{and all that took them captives held them fast, they refused to let them go}* They held them fast as having good right to them, or imagining that no power was able to rescue them. See Esay 14.17. and 49.24.

**Verse 34.** *{Their redeemer is strong, the LORD of Hosts is his name.}* Or, *But* (supplied, as Chap. 5.3. and 22.10.) *their strong avenger* (as Numb. 35.19,27. here alluded to. See Prov. 23.11. and Chap. 51.55.) *whose name is the Lord of Hosts*; as Chap. 32.28. and 48.15.

*{he shall throughly plead their cause,}* Heb. *will pleading plead*; as Esai 51.22. he will do it, not verbally, but really; not by speaking for them, but by righting of them, and revenging them on those that have wronged them. So Psalm 35.1. Prov. 22.23. Mic. 7.9.

*{that he may give rest to the Land, and disquiet the Inhabitants of Babylon.}* Rest to his people, that had been disquieted, Judge 5.31. Chap. 31.2. (where the same word is found) Esay 14.3. and vexation to those, by whom they had been disquieted, 2 Thes. 1.6,7.

**Verse 35.** *{A sword is upon the Chaldeans, saith the LORD, and upon the inhabitants of Babylon, and upon her Princes, and upon her wise men.}* *Sword*, for hostile invasion, doing execution upon them, as Levit. 26.25. ver. 16. the Princes and Counsellors of State are mentioned, as the chief stays of the State, (See Esai 3.2,3.) and such as might be most likely to escape, either by their power and wealth the one, or by their wisdom and policy the other. See Esai 28.14,15,18. *el*, for, *al*; as before, Chap. 48.11. and so afterward, ver. 36.

**Verse 36.** *{A sword is upon the liars and they shall dote:}* The word here used is ambiguous: it is used sometimes for *bars*, Exod. 25.14,15. whence some here would have it understood of great men in place, or power, that are as *bars* the chief strength and stays of a State: but of those before, and hereafter: sometime it signifies *a lie* and *a liar*, from a root that signifies *to devise*, 1 King. 12.33. and *to feign*, Neh. 6.8. So it is taken, Esay 16.6. Chap. 48.30. Job 11.3. and the Chaldean soothsayers and wizards are here so termed; as also Esay 44.25. See Esay 47.12,13. *dote*, be foolish, or play the fools; as Esay 19.13. Chap. 5.4.

*{a sword is upon her mighty men;}* Their Warriors: the chief for military affairs; as for civil those before, ver. 35.

*{and they shall be dismayed.}* Or, *broken in pieces*; as Chap. 1.17.

**Verse 37.** *{A sword is upon their horses, and upon their chariots,}* The hostile forces shall seize upon and spoil all their warlike provisions: so are *horse and chariot* frequently used, Psalm 20.7. and 76.6.

*{and upon all the mingled people that are in the midst of her,}* As Chap. 25.24. those of several nations that served under her, or sojourned in her, as Chap. 46.21. and 51.6. See Esay 13.15.

*{and they shall become as women:}* Full of fear, and void of courage, having no manliness in them, showing no manly disposition. Heb. *they shall be for women*, or, *to women*; as if they were turned into women; *they shall become women*; as, *to be unto desolation*, and, *to become utterly desolate*, are all one, Esay 1.7. and Joel 3.19. So also, Chap. 51.30. that which is said, *as women*, Esay 19.16.

*{a sword is upon her treasures, and they shall be robbed.}* See ver. 10.26. Esay 45.3.

**Verse 38.** *{A drought is upon her waters, and they shall be dried up:}* Cyrus, as he had dealt before with the river Cyndes in Assyria on his way to Chaldea, which he cut out into so many several channels, and made it passable for his people; so did he with Euphrates at Babylon, while he lay in siege before it, which by many outlets he so drained, that his forces had thereby free access without much difficulty to the walls of the city, and so came suddenly to surprise it. See Herodote, lib. 1. and chap. 51.32,36. there is in the words an elegancy arising from the affinity of sound in those two words, signifying *a sword* the one, and *a drought* the other, differing but in a vowel point only, which our English cannot express.

*{for it is the land of graven images,}* It is full of idols of all sorts, Dan. 5.4. as of the land of Israel, Esay 2.8. one sort put for the rest, as Esay 40.20. the pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive we have here also, as before, ver. 15.25.

*{and they are mad upon their idols.}* The Chaldee, with whom the ancient Greek, and old Latin agree, renders it, *they glory in them*; as Psalm 97.7. and a word very near to it, and springing from the same root for letters, is frequently so used. But I find it nowhere in this form, but in a notion of *madness*; as Chap. 25.16. and 46.9. and *madness* is used to express any vehemency of inordinate affection, whereby persons are strongly taken with, and carried headlong without reason, or discretion, unto, or after ought. See Act. 26.11. The word rendered *idols*, does properly signify *terrors*, Job 20.25. Psal. 88.15. there were a race of giantly people, thence termed *Emim*, because they were terrible and formidable to other near neighboring nations, Gen. 14.5. Deut. 2.11. Hence are the Chaldean idols here so termed, either, as some, in regard of the vast bulk, and giantlike shape and bigness of some of them, Dan. 3.1. or, as others rather, because they are terrible and formidable to their followers, as scarecrows are to birds and beasts, though being things contemptible and unable to do ought, Chap. 10.1,5. Baruc. 6.70.

**Verse 39.** *{Therefore the wilde beasts of the desert, with the wilde beasts of the islands, shall dwell there, and the owls shall dwell therein:}* Heb. *Ijim with ijim*: Whereof see on Esay 13.21,22. and 34.14. and, *daughters of the owl*: as Job 30.29. the most general term and form, where of that Fowl the Scripture speaks. Of Babylon's desolation see further Chap. 51.37. Rev. 8.2.

*{and it shall be no more inhabited for ever: neither shall it be dwelt in from Generation to Generation.}* Heb. *inhabit*, and *dwell*; as verse 13. Chap. 46.26. but of that manner of speech, see on Esay 13.20.

**Verse 40.** *{As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the LORD; so shall no man abide there, neither shall any son of man dwell therein.}* So Esay 13.19. See of Edom the same Chap. 49.18.

**Verse 41.** *{Behold, a people shall come from the North,}* As ver. 3.9. See Chap. 6.22. where the same things are said of the Chaldeans.

*{and a great nation}* As ver. 9. Chap. 6.22.

*{and many Kings}* Princes and Potentates, Associates and Assistants to Cyrus, subject to him, or serving under him, Chap. 25.14. and 51.27,28.

*{from the coasts of the earth.}* Heb. *from the sides of the earth*; as Chap. 6.22. and 25.32. and 31.8. that is, from the uttermost parts of it; as before, ver. 26. and this helps to back the received Version there: so, *from the uttermost parts of the earth* Mat. 12.42. as we would say, *from the land's end*; as far as any land that way was. So Psal. 72.8.

**Verse 42.** *{They shall hold the bow and the lance: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy: their voice shall roar like the sea, and they shall ride up on horses, every one put in array like a man to the battle against thee, O daughter of Babylon.}* *Bow* and *Lance*: The one to reach afar off, the other to pierce near at hand. See Chap. 6.23. where the same things are spoken of the Chaldeans, who were now to meet with their matches, and be dealt with themselves, as they had formerly dealt with others. See verse 15.29. Chap. 51.49. Esay 33.1.

**Verse 43.** *{The King of Babylon hath heard a report of them, and his hands waxed feeble: anguish took hold of him, and pangs as of a woman in travel.}* He has heard either the tidings of their approach, or the report of the surprisal of his city, Chap. 51.31. See the very same before, Chap. 6.24. and Belshazzar's condition, Dan. 5.6.

**Verse 44.** *{Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan, unto the habitation of the strong; but I will make them suddenly run away from her; and who is a chosen man that I may appoint over her? for who is like me, and who will appoint me the time? and who is that shepherd that will stand before me?}* See this whole passage opened at large, Chap. 49.19. where the same is spoken of Nebuchadnezzar's expedition against Edom, that is here spoken of Cyrus his expedition against Babylon. See the notes there.

**Verse 45.** *{Therefore hear ye the counsel of the LORD, that he hath taken against Babylon, and his purposes that he hath purposed against the land of the Chaldeans: surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitation desolate with them.}* See the very same, Chap. 49.20.

**Verse 46.** *{At the noise of the taking of Babylon the earth is moved, and the cry is heard among the nations.}* The same in effect, Chap. 49.21.

## CHAPTER 51

**Verse 1.** *{Thus saith the LORD, Behold I will raise up against Babylon, and against them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me a destroying wind,}* A Continuation of the prophecy against Babylon. The hostile invasion of the country; and surprisal of the city, is here set forth by a new resemblance taken from a gale, or gust of wind, both blasting, that spoils the fruits of the earth and boisterous, that sweeps and carries away all loose matter, not chaff, or stubble only, and such light stuff; but the corn itself also, and the weighty grain with it, ver. 2.

*{I will raise}* Heb. *I am raising*; as Esay 13.17. Chap. 50.9.

*{against them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me}* Heb. *unto* (*el*, for, *al*; as Chap. 50.29.) *the inhabitant of the heart* (that is, *the midst*; as *the heart of the sea*, Psalm 46.2. or, *amidst*, *within*; as Tyre is said to be situate *in the heart of the sea*, Ezek. 27.4. and so, *in the heart of the earth*, Mat. 12.40.) *of those that rise up against me*: the preposition swallowed up between the participle and the noun: as the like in the same term, Psal. 18.39,48. & 44.5. and 74.22. against the inhabitants of Babylon, which dwell in the midst of the land of Chaldea, in the royal seat and center of that State, and those people, that have carried themselves so rebelliously and insolently against me in the devastation of my land, the destruction of my Temple, and the deportation of my people, c. 50.11,17,24,28,29. and this I take to be the plain and genuine sense of these words, *against Babylon*, the city and state itself, *and against the inhabitants*; those that dwell in her thus described. But both the Jewish Writers, and others of note, do here find other mysterious and more abstruse senses. For some of the Rabbines, by a device of theirs, which they call *Athbash*, whereof see on c. 25.26. do out of the words *leb kamai, the heart of those that rise against me*, pick out *Casdim*, the Chaldeans. Others of them suppose a trajection in the text, and would have the words thus ordered, *against the heart of those that rise up against me, the inhabitants* of the land of Chaldea, before pointed to in Babylon: like that Esay 10.12. *I will visit upon the King of Assyria's great heart*. And the Chaldee goes somewhat the like way but swerving more from the text, *against the inhabitants of the Chaldeans people mutinous, haughty of heart, and goodly of stature*: as also the old Latin somewhat after the like strain; but more succinctly, and coming nearer to the text; *against the inhabitants thereof that have lift up their heart against me*: one of our prime Interpreters, *the inhabitants of the heart*; that is, those that dwell in and rest upon their own counsels, devices and courses. And a late learned Annotator, *against those that are secure in heart before me*; for the word says he, is *sitting*; and *sitting*, is a sign of *security*; and so one of the Rabbines sometime uses that word: and *Kamai* is here an abbreviation of *Kodomai*, and the Talmudists oft so use it. But where does the Scripture ever once so take it? or where find we in Scripture such a form as this, *dwellers*. or *sitters of heart*, for, secure ones, or persons that sit, dwell, or live securely? And to what purpose is it to have recourse to such forced and farfetched strains, when we have a plain and familiar sense, freely and of its own accord offering itself to us?

**Verse 2.** *{And I will send unto Babylon fanners that shall fan her and empty her land:}* As I sometime fanned and scattered my people by them, c. 4.11.1. & 15.7. so will I now fan them by the Medes and Persians, who shall empty their land of them, as they formerly emptied my land of her inhabitants, v. 35. 2 Chr. 36.20,21. See c. 48.12. & 49.32,36.

*{for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about.}* They shall so beset her, that none shall escape, c. 50.15,29. as they sometime beset Jerusalem, c. 4.17. Heb. *in the day of evil*: as chapter 17.17,18.

**Verse 3.** *{Against him}* that *bendeth, let the archer bend his bow, and against* him *{that lifteth himself up in his brigandine.}* So the Jewish Commenters well expound it, Against those that shoot with the bow, and those that appear in their armor among the Chaldeans, let those of the Medes and Persians that use the bow, bend it, and let fly their shafts at them. Heb. *el*, for, *al*; *against*, or *at*; as v. 1. and *tread*, for *bend*, because that is the end of it; as c. 50.14. Of the word rendered *brigandine*, see c. 46.4. shoot at soldiers of all sorts, whether in armor, or weaponed only without harness: there is a defect both of antecedent and relative; as Exod. 23.20. c. 2.8. Howbeit a learned late Writer thus renders the words. *Unto the bender, that bendeth his bow and to him that advanceth in his brigandine*, (to wit, those of either sort in Cyrus his army) thus says the Lord, *spare not her young men*, &c. and the word of *bending* is thrice repeated, implying that they should bend as deep as might be. And this way in part the ancient Greek seems to go: but taking no notice of the initial particle in the text, while it thus renders the words, *Let him that bendeth bend his bow, and let him that hath armor put it on.* But the former sense seems the more familiar, than either of these, and keeps closer to the express terms of the text, which the Chaldee, and the old Latin that follows it, not leaving only, but crossing, while instead of *el*, they render *al*, the negative or inhibitive particle, and render it, *Let not him that draweth the bow, draw it*, says the one; and *let not him that bendeth, bend his bow*, says the other; *nor let him go up in his brigandine.* One of the words of *bending* in the text, is by the Jewish Masters deemed superfluous. And it is observed by some, that they are willed to shoot at all, whether armed or unarmed, as not doubting but that their Arrows should pierce, wheresoever they lighted. See on c. 50.14.

*{and spare ye not her young men; destroy ye utterly all her host.}* This, *and*, controls the latter exposition of the foregoing branch, which makes this the beginning of God's speech to the enemies forces. See c. 50.30.

**Verse 4.** *{Thus the slain shall fall in the land of the Chaldeans, and they that are thrust through in her streets.}* Heb. *And* as c. 49.39.) *the slain* or *wounded*, (as c. 37.10.) *shall fall in the land of the Chaldeans*: there shall havoc be made of them, as well within the city, as in the country also abroad. See Esay 13.15. c. 50.30. A learned Annotator supposes a trajection in the text, and would have the words thus rendered, *And the chaldeans being slain shall fall to the ground.* But the distinguishing points in the original will not admit it.

**Verse 5.** *{For Israel hath not been forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of the LORD of Hosts;}* Heb. *Israel is not widowed* (a word in this form nowhere else found) *nor Judah* divorced *from his God, from the Lord of Hosts*: the latter word supplied in a congruous term; as 1 Cor. 3.2. *I gave you milke to drinke, and not meat to eat*: Neither is Israel a widow, that has lost her husband; nor is Judah as a woman divorced and put away, without hope of being taken home again, Deut. 24.4. Their husband lives still, and has not utterly cast off either, but will in his due time take them unto him again, though he have left them for a while, 1 Sam. 12.22. Esay 50.1. & 54.5,6. c. 3.1,8,14. Lam. 1.1.

*{though their land was filled with sin against the Holy one of Israel.}* This the Jewish Commenters understand of the Chaldeans country, and render it, *for*, or *but their land*, that is, the Chaldeans, *is full of delinquency* and sins *for* the evil that they committed against *the holy one of Israel* in his people. But this is somewhat a strange overstraining of the text: and yet want there not divers that go this way, rendering it, *because the Land of these men is full of guilt from the holy one of Israel*; contrary to that, that they presumed chap. 50.7. But this also seems to sound overharsh. Most others understand the words, *their land*, of the land of them both before mentioned, as well Judah, as Israel: but in the term following they differ; for some take the term *asham* here used in a notion of *delinquency*; as it is commonly used, Levit. 5.2. Num. 5.6. and render it as our Version does, albeit, that they have deserved to be irrecoverably cast off & cut off for their sins, wherewith they have fulfilled their whole land chap. 16.18. And some again, because the words of *sin* and *delinquency*, or *guilt*, are taken also for the penalty due thereunto, would have it so to be here taken, rendering the words, *for their land is full of penalty from the holy one of Israel*: it has received fully sufficient from him. So it should be as that Esay 40.2. But this also seems forced as well as the former. Others take the word in a notion of *devastation*: and although the noun here used, be not found elsewhere in that notion, yet is the Verb from whence it comes, Psalm 34.21. Esay 24.6. Ezekiel 6.6. & 25.12. Joel 1.18. and the tenor of the Text requires it here to be so taken; for it is word for word, *though their land hath been filled* (for it is a Verb, not a Noun) *with devastation from the holy one of Israel*; that is, though he have in his wrath caused their whole land to be wasted, and to lie thus waste for a long time together, c. 4.20,27.

**Verse 6.** *{Flee out of the midst of Babylon;}* See the same before, chap. 50.8. Though that was directed to God's people the Jews; This to me seems directed, not to them, (though most so take it, and the like speech be afterward made also to them, v. 45.) but to those in her, that were aiding and assistant to her, c. 50.16. v. 9.

*{and deliver every man his soul:}* Or, *himself*; as Psalm 3.2. Matthew 16.25,26. Heb. *deliver a man his soul*: Shift every one (as Chapter 49.5.) for himself, or for his life; as Genesis 19.17. c. 48.6.

*{be not cut off in her iniquity:}* Or, *lest ye be cut off in her penalty*, or *punishment*; as the word is used, Genesis 4.13. and 19.15. Some conceive this as an admonition to God's people, not to partake in Babylon's sins, lest they partake also with her in her sufferings; as Esay 62.11. Revelation 18.4. But I conceive it rather to be intended as before, of such, as taking her part, and standing for her, should perish together with her, Esay 13.15. chapter 50.37.

*{for this is the time of the Lords vengeance,}* As c. 50.15,25,27,28. So c. 46.10. v. 11.

*{he will render unto her a recompense.}* As Esay 59.17,18. and 65.6,7.

**Verse 7.** *{Babylon hath been a golden cup}* Such an one she has been hitherto; one by whom God has caused other people to drink deep of his wrath: but now her turn is come to drink deep of it herself, c. 25.26. the cup of which, c. 25.15. called *a golden cup*, as here, so Rev. 17.4. as most understand it, in regard of the great wealth and illustriousness of that Empire: resembled therefore by *an head of gold*, Dan. 2.32,38. and hence is Babylon called the *golden one*, Esay 14.4. Howbeit, the Jewish Doctors, by *a cup of gold*, (for so the words are; as *a crown of gold*, Psal. 21.2.) understand a cup of pure wine of the color of gold: as, *gold*, for pure yellow oil, Zach. 4.12. and *gold*, for clear wind, and fair weather, Job 37.22. But the former is more familiar, and seems the genuine notion of the word in this place.

*{in the Lords hand,}* As Psal. 75.8. and so, *take the cup from my hand*, c. 25.15. because he made use of that State as an instrument to execute judgment thereby upon others, and the cup there mentioned is expounded to be the Chaldean *sword*, c. 25.9,19.

*{that made all the earth drunken:}* With the Wine of God's wrath poured out by her hand, Chapter 25.15. Revelation 14.10. for that, Revelation 18.3. though the same words with this, bears another sense from this. See there: and that learned Annotator seems to be out of the way, who would have this meant of Babylon's enticing and drawing other Nations into association with her by her glittering show, and glorious state, unto their destruction.

*{the nations have drunk of her wine, therefore the nations are mad.}* That learned Writer renders it, *therefore they shall be mad*: they shall for their joining with her, suffer also and undergo such judgments together with her, as shall make them even *mad* withal. But it seems meant rather of those calamities that they had sustained from her, and by her, as the Prophet foretold they should, using this very term, where he spoke of this *cup*, chap. 25.16. and it might well be rendered, *therefore they are mad*; or, *so that they became mad*, or, *fared like mad men*; as chap. 46.9.

**Verse 8.** *{Babylon is suddenly fallen}* *Babylon is fallen*; as Esay 21.9. Rev. 14.8. and 18.2. as, *Babylon is taken*, chap. 50.2. *suddenly*, unexpectedly. See chap. 50.24. *in one hour*, Rev. 18.10. read Dan. 5.

*{and destroyed:}* Heb. *broken*. So chap. 50.23.

*{howl for her,}* Bewail her fall; as chap. 48.38. See Rev. 18.9–19.

*{take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed.}* *Take balm* (as chap. 8.22.) *for her grief*; as Lam. 1.12. use all the means you can to help her; but all will be to no purpose. See the like, chap. 46.11.

**Verse 9.** *{We would have healed Babylon: but she is not healed;}* Or, *could not be healed*: the verb in a potential notion, as the like, chap. 46.15. The words of those that had assisted her, and served under her: we have done our best to save her from destruction; but all in vain: there is no cure, or help for her; as chap. 46.11.

*{forsake her;}* Give her over, as Physicians do a desperate cure.

*{and let us go every one into his own country:}* Our only way and wisest course is to shift for ourselves, Esay 13.14. So chap. 46.16.

*{for her judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies.}* Her punishment and calamity is exceeding great and grievous, (as the term is used to express extraordinary eminency of ought, Psal. 36.5.) proportionable to her sin, Rev. 18.5. the like whereunto, see Gen. 18.24. Ezra 9.6. Jon. 1.2. too great to be holpen by any humane helps. The word *skies* in our Version some render *clouds*: which the learned Scholiast controls, because the word in his native notion signifies *small dust*, or, *fine powder*, Esay 40.11. whereas the *clouds* are *air*, condensated, or thickened: Our Version is the better and more exact; but that the word includes also the clouds, or cloudy sky at least, appears Psalm 18.12. and Prov. 3.20. *the clouds*, or *thick clouds*, *of the skies*, being mentioned in the one place; and, *the clouds*, or *skies*, said *to drop down dew* in the other.

**Verse 10.** *{The LORD hath brought forth our righteousness:}* The speech of God's people, acknowledging God's mercy and goodness, yea, & righteousness also in righting them upon their cruel oppressors, and owning thereby the religion professed by them, and their relation therein to him. So Psal. 37.6. Mic. 7.9.

*{come, and let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God}* As inciting one another to praise him for it. See chap. 50.28. So Rev. 15.3,4. and 16.5–7. and 19.1,2,5.

**Verse 11.** *{Make bright the arrows:}* Heb. *Make pure*: as chap. 4.11. *polish*; as, *a polished arrow*, Esay 49.2. whet the heads of them, that they may pierce the deeper, Psal. 45.5. See Ezek. 21.21. Howbeit, one of the Rabbines renders it, *feather the arrows*: deriving it from a word that signifies *a feather*, Job 39.16. Esai 40.31. feather them well, to make them fly, Job 39.26. but the former is sure the righter. The words of God, as some, yea, the most, to those that were to come against Babylon; as Chap. 50.14,15. But I suppose rather with some other, though fewer, that they are spoken in way of derision to the Babylonians, as calling upon them to make all the preparation they can, against the Medes and Persians that are coming against them; as intimating what need of such preparations there would be: but implying withal, that all the strength and means they could make would not be able to secure them. See the like in like manner delivered, Esay 21.5. and again here, ver. 12. and this the very course of the context does abundantly confirm. See the like also, chap. 46.3,4.

*{gather the shields:}* Heb. *fill the shields*, get them altogether, make up the full number of them; see that none of them be missing. So, *a fullness*, for, *a full assembly*. Esay 31.4. and, *he filled* the foreskins (that is, delivered them in full tale) *to the King*, 1 Sam. 18.27. it is implied that all got together would be little enough for the employment that should need them: the word *shelet* here used comes near home to our *shield*, which in likelihood came at first from it.

*{the LORD hath raised up the spirits of the Kings of the Medes.}* The reason why such great preparations are requisite; because there is an army of Medes and Persians coming against Babylon, and that by a divine instinct. See the same form, Ezra 1.1. and of this further, ver. 28.

*{for his device is against Babylon to destroy it:}* Or, *thought*; as Job 42.2. or, *contrivement*: taken in the better sense; as Prov. 1.4. and 3.21. though it be mostly in the worse. See ver. 12.29.

*{because it is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance of his Temple.}* See chap. 50.28. ver. 6.

**Verse 12.** *{Set up the standard upon the walls of Babylon:}* About this whole passage again Authors dissent. For the Jewish Commenters, whom some other also follow, conceive this whole speech, as that also, ver. 11. to be directed to the Medes and Persians, inciting them to use all possible industry and diligence in besetting and assaulting the city of Babylon; and would have this first branch meant; some, of marching with their ensigns displayed *towards* Babylon: because the Hebrew is *el*, that is, *unto* Babylon: but it has been formerly observed that *el* is oft used for *al*, *upon*; as chap. 48.11. and 50.35,36,37. And others therefore understand it of setting up their banners on the top of their walls and towers, in token of conquest and triumph, when they have taken it: like that, Psal. 74.4. But to omit that the words run then in a preposterous tenor, inciting to triumph in the first place; and to sedulous, vigilant, and cautious courses for surprisal in the second; the course of the context carries it clearly the contrary way. And others therefore rather deem the words directed to the Babylonians, in an Irony, advising them to use all the care, diligence, and caution they can, to secure and safeguard themselves and their city against the enemies assaults, implying, say some, that they should not want either courage to stand to it, and make their party good against the adversary, or means sufficient, as they suppose, to oppose them: but withal, as the most, that all their endeavors would not avail ought; or, as a late learned Writer conceives, twitting them with their remissness and recklessness, that little regarding the enemy set down before them, as if they were safe enough, & sufficiently secured against him, by the river that ran round about them, neglected the means of defense, and gave themselves to jollity and reveling, which they were deep in, what time by occasion thereof, the city was taken. See on ver. 39.41. and this seems backed with that Esay 21.5. in which place the Prophet joins these two together: and those that apply the passage to the Chaldeans, expound this first member of it, of an ensign to be set upon the walls, to bring up thither those forces that were to be employed for the defense of the place, and repulse of assailants, and to keep them together in such employment.

*{make the watch strong; set up the watchman:}* So, *watch in the watch-tower; set a sentinel*, or *watch-man*, Esay 21.5,6.

*{prepare the ambushes:}* Heb. *liers in wait*; that is supplies: such as not appearing upon the walls, but keeping out of sight, might be ready at hand to relieve those, as occasion should be, that were there employed.

*{for the LORD hath both devised, and done that which he spake against Babylon.}* Or, *hath both contrived, and done*, or *will do*. See Esay 14.24,26. Chap. 50.21. Heb. *also*, in both members; as Chap. 14.18. and *el* for *al*, either *against*, or *concerning*; as Chap. 50.1. See the like, Lam. 2.17.

**Verse 13.** *{O thou that dwellest upon many waters,}* The city of Babylon was situate upon the great river Euphrates, that ran both about it, and through it: to which is added, its ruling over many great nations in the other Babylon represented by it, Rev. 7.1,15.

*{abundant in treasures:}* Gathered from those nations, whom they had spoiled and pillaged, and made tributary to them, 2 King. 24.13. 2 Chron. 36.18. Esay 39.6. and 45.3. Chap. 50.10.37.

*{thine end is come,}* As Ezek. 7.2,3,6. Amos 8.2.

*{and the measure of thy covetousness.}* Heb. *the cubit of thy lucre*, or, *oppression*, or, *covetousness*. The *cubit* was the most common measure in dimensions of length, breadth height and depth among that people, Gen. 6.15. Exod. 25.10. it was taken, and so termed, as by the Greek term more plainly appears from the former part of the arm, reaching from the top of the middle finger up to the elbow. Hence some of the Jewish Doctors expound it, *the arm*, that is, *the might* and *power*, (for so is the word *arm*, commonly used. See Chap. 48.25.) wherewith you have formerly subdued and kept down others, is now come to an end. But other of them take it rather in a notion of *measure*; yet the word following these also expound diversely; some, *the measure of thy covetousness*; because the word seems so used, Exod. 18.21. Some; of *thine oppression*; because it is found joined with *oppression*, Ezek. 22.12. and these understand it of that recompense and retribution, that God would mete out to the Babylonians, for their insatiable avarice, exercised in the spoiling of other people, Esay 14.20. and 33.1. Chap. 50.15,29. Others, the time set and measure out for her *visitation*, so the Chaldee; as Chap. 50.31. or, as another Jewish Master, whom the old Latin concurs with, *of her destruction*, because the word that it comes of signifies sometime *to cut off*, or *destroy*, Job 6.9. Esay 38.12. But the word properly signifies *lucre*, or *gain*, 1 Sam. 6.3. Psal. 30.9. Esay 33.15. Chap. 22.17. Ezek. 33.32. And I conceive that the words may well be rendered, *the list*, or, *limit of thy gain*, or, *gettings*. The set stint and term of time, that God has precisely limited and designed to allow you, wherein to proceed in the feathering of your nest, and enriching yourself by the spoils of other people; and which therefore you cannot exceed, is now expired and come to an end. See somewhat the like, but in a divers notion, taken from another kind of measure, Gen. 15.16. Zach. 5.6–11. Mat. 23.32. 1 Thes. 2.16.

**Verse 14.** *{The LORD of hosts hath sworn by himself, saying,}* Heb. *by his soul*; as Amos 6.8. See verse 6. a supply of the term, *saying*, as Chap. 50.5.

*{Surely, I will fill thee with men, as with caterpillars,}* Heb. *but if*; that is, *unless*; as Gen. 32.26. Esay 55.10. the usual form of an oath. See Chap. 44.26. and 49.13. for, *if not*; and, *but if*, or *unless*, are in effect and force all one. And the learned Scholiast therefore, who here makes another unusual supply, and gives the particles other notions, while he renders it, *Certain it is that though I fill thee with men as with locusts*: which he expounds of furnishing Babylon with great multitudes of auxiliary forces, (because of Nineveh the like is said, Nah. 3.15,17.) does herein leave a plain beaten road, to step aside into a more uncouth, and solitary bypath. It is generally expounded both by the Jewish Doctors and others, of the enemies soldiery, for their vast multitudes compared to locusts, that should fill her whole country first, and city afterward also; and so afterward again, ver. 27. The word here used is a kind of *locust*; as appears, Psal. 105.34. compared with Exod. 10.4,5. so called, because they *lick up*, and destroy all before them, Nah. 3.15. amiss rendered *caterpillar*, in the Psalm, and *canker-worm*, in the Prophet, for it is there said *to fly*. And to multitudes of locusts are such vast companies commonly compared, Judge 6.5. Chap. 46.23. Nah. 3.15,17.

*{and they shall lift up and shout against thee.}* Or, *that shall* (as Chap. 50.9.) *utter* (Heb. *a giver*; as Deut. 26.5.) or *cry aloud*, (as Esay 13.22.) or *sing* (as Hos. 2.15.) *a shout* (as Chap. 25.3. & 48.33.) *against thee*, or *over thee*; as Esay 31.4. an allusion, says a Rabbine in the words of *singing* and *shouting* to such *songs* and *shouts* as the country peasants used amidst their treading of grapes for wine in the vintage, and at the bringing in of their wines and fruits. See Esay 16.9. Chap. 43.33.

**Verse 15.** *{He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his understanding.}* Or, Even *he that made* the *earth*, &c. for the word of *making* here is a participle, not a verb; and so the other two, that *established*, and that *stretched out*. He it is, that has sworn it, and is able to make good what he has sworn. See the very same passage, Chap. 10.12. The particle is supplied; as Job 15.26. Psal. 119.41.

**Verse 16.** *{When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens, and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth, he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures.}* Or, *At the uttering of whose voice*, &c. The demonstrative for the relative; as Exod. 8.20. Job 3.15. Chap. 46.18. and 48.15. See of the whole verse, Chap. 10.13.

**Verse 17.** *{Every man is brutish by his knowledge: every founder is confounded by the graven image: for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.}* This passage is here inserted, to discover and control the foolish vanity of the Babylonians, that relied upon their idols for protection and safeguard; and to show how unable they were to bicker with the true God or to stand before any, that should come furnished with power and commission from him. See the whole, Chap. 10.14.

**Verse 18.** *{They are vanity, the work of errors; in the time of their visitation they shall perish.}* See the same, Chap. 10.15.

**Verse 19.** *{The portion of Jacob is not like them: for he is the former of all things, and}* Israel is *{the rod of his inheritance: the LORD of hosts is his name.}* See Chap. 10.16.

**Verse 20.** *{Thou art my battle axe, and weapons of war:}* Or, *Thou hast been my hammer.* So was the word rendered, Chap. 50.23. and it signifies such a weighty one as is able to break statues, and to make them fly asunder, as the root it comes from, properly signifies, Psal. 2.9. Esay 27.9. thence also *an instrument of dissipation*, or destruction, Ezek. 9.2. See Chap. 23.29. Howbeit, some suppose it here to signify more specially such a warlike weapon, or spiked pole-ax, as horsemen make use of in fight; therewith to batter and break the armor, helmets, and harness of those they deal with; and *warlike weapons*; a defect of the copulative, as Esay 56. chap. 3.21. Or, *As an hammer* have you *been unto me*, *and as warlike instruments*: a defect of the note of similitude; as chap. 5.8. and 26.18. and 50.6. Howbeit, the Chaldee renders it, *how breakest before me the city*, wherein *the weapons of war* are: and both the ancient Greek and the old Latin somewhat to the same purpose; *Thou dissipatest* or *breakest asunder*, for *me, the instruments of war*. They seem to have taken the word here used, not for a noun, but for a participle, the one differing but in a tittle from the other, and consequently in the sound of a vowel; which in verbs of this form does oft vary and interchange: though in the participle seldom, if ever. Our Version seems to go with those few, that understand it of Cyrus, whom God intended so to use and employ. See Esay 41.2. and 45.1,2. But the most understand it rather of the Babylonian King, who was in God's hand, as the Assyrian before him had been, Esay 10.5. and they render the words all along therefore not in the future, but in the time past.

*{for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms:}* Heb. *and*; which those retain, who admit the latter Version: but there want not that render it, not *with thee*, or *by thee*, but *in thee*: and turn the copulative into a discretive; as if it were said, *But I will* now *break asunder the nations*, that are *in thee, and destroy the kingdoms* that are *in thee*, or under you: which latter clause the Greek renders, *I will take away the Kings out of thee.* But our Version seems herein the righter: the copulative is oft used in a causal notion; as Chap. 48.27. & 49.37. and it renders a reason why Babylon was said to be God's *hammer*, or wherein like unto such *an hammer*, as the word before imports, taken from the proper notion of the verb here used, from whence that term is deduced. Only the words would be read in the time past; *I have broken asunder & I have destroyed*; unless, says a Rabbine, this prophecy were penned by Jeremy before Nebuchadnezzar's conquests of those several countries: whereof Ch. 46–49. See Ch. 50.23. But whether it were penned before a good part of his conquests, or no, as it is not unlike it was; (for a copy of it seems to have been sent in the time of Zedekiah, while the Jewish State yet stood unto Babylon. See ver. 59–64.) the Prophet throughout this whole Prophecy speaks of Babylon, as having subdued all those nations that were to come under the yoke of that Empire and now drawing on to her downfall.

**Verse 21.** *{And with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider, and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider.}* Or, *by thee have I broken*: for it is the instrumental *beth*, as they term it, and spoken as in the time past; as before, ver. 20. and so also ver. 22,23. As before all warlike weapons and instruments, ver. 20. so now the Warriors themselves, with their *horses* and *chariots*; as Chap. 50.37. This enumeration of particulars has much emphasis in it, both here and there; as also, Chap. 50.35–38.

**Verse 22.** *{With thee also will I break in pieces man and woman, and with thee will I break in pieces old and young; and with thee will I break in pieces the young man and the maid,}* Or, *By thee have I broken*, &c. as before ver. 21. and so also ver. 23. both sexes and all ages. See 2 Chr. 36.17. Heb. *and*, as before; and so ver. 23.

**Verse 23.** *{I will also break in pieces with thee, the shepherd and his flock; and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman, and his yoke of oxen; and with thee will I break in pieces captains and rulers.}* People of all sorts, and of all ranks. So chap. 50.16,27,35–37. The former two, the support of a state, for provision of sustenance, 1 Chr. 27.25–31. 1 King. 4.21,22. Eccles. 5.9. The two latter for protection, safeguard, and government, 1 Chr. 27.32–34. Esay 3.1,2,3.

**Verse 24.** *{And I will render unto Babylon, and to all the Inhabitants of Chaldea all the evil that they have done in Zion in your sight, saith the LORD.}* This Version fits well with the sense of those, who understand all that went before of Cyrus: who also some of them supply from the former, *And I will by thee render* to Babylon. But those that conceive it, as the most do, to be intended of Babylon, take the copulative here in a discretive notion, and render it, *But* (as ver. 9.) *I will render unto Babylon*, &c. Though I have made use of you for the punishing of many nations, and of mine own people in particular, yet will I now at length execute judgment also upon you for your insolencies against me, and your cruelty showed unto my people. So Esay 47.6,8. Chap. 50.15,29. See the like of the Assyrian, Chap. 10.5,6,12. those words *in your sight*, (wherein God turns his speech unto his people) have reference not to *the evil done* though next before mentioned, but to the evil returned, and the term of *rendering* though more remote as if he had said, You that are now in captivity at Babylon shall survive to see this judgment executed upon her. So Psal. 79.10.

**Verse 25.** *{Behold, I am against thee,}* Or, *I am coming against thee*; as Chap. 50.31. and *el* here, for, *al*; which yet the old Latin retains rendering it *unto thee*.

*{O destroying mountain, saith the LORD,}* A *mountain* is Babylon termed, not for her situation, as if it had stood upon an hill; for it was built on a plain Gen. 11.2,9. and so seated that it had abundance of water round about it, ver. 13. but it is so styled, as some, in regard of the height of its power and eminency, wherewith it did, as *a mountain*, overtop other cities, countries, and kingdoms. Or, as others, in regard of its high and stately palaces, lofty Towers, and strong Fortifications: that, as Berosus reports of them, resembled *high mountains*; and appeared as such to folk afar off: by means whereof it seemed to reach as high, and to be as impregnable, as if it had stood upon some great and high mountain. Hereunto may be added the strange height of her walls: whereof further on verse 53. and those stupendous orchards, or gardens, with groves and walks, furnished with variety of goodly tall trees, and erected on arches aloft far from the ground, that made the city show afar off, like some Lebanon, or other forest-like mountain: whereof Diodore, lib. 2. cap. 2. See the like expression chap. 22.23. Zach. 4.7. and 11.1. yea, so says the Jewish Doctor, *the mountains of Gilead*, for their strong holds, Amos 1.13. which is not improbable.

*{which destroyest all the earth,}* And well therefore deserves the title of *a destroyer*. See Esay 14.16,17. and Chap. 50.11.

*{and I will stretch out mine hand upon thee,}* Or, *against thee*; as chap. 6.12. and 15.6.

*{and roll thee down from the rocks;}* From your strong Holds and Forts, and from your lofty Towers that seem to threaten heaven, Gen. 11.4. Dan. 4.11,30. See ver. 53.

*{and I will make thee a burnt mountain.}* Or, *a burning mountain*: alluding to those mountains of sulphury matter; such as Montgibal in Sicily, Soma in Italy, Hecla and Hogla in Iceland, that burn continually, and with the ashes and cinders at sometimes belching out from them, waste and spoil all the country near to them: Of which kind there was a field also sometime in that region continually burning; as Strabo, lib. 16. and Pliny, l. 2. c. 106. report: or to the heaps of ashes and cinders, that cities and towns ruined and burnt down to the ground, are wont to leave behind them, Chap. 50.26. ver. 37. Heb. *I will give thee* (as Ezek. 22.4. and 35.3.) *unto*, or *for*. (as Chap. 50.23. and so ver. 29.43.) *a mountain of burning*: as, *a land of burning*, Deut. 29.23.

**V. 26.** *{And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations;}* That is, as some, there shall not remain any stone of you that may be useful for building: or, as others, there shall be nothing left of you, whereon some hope or attempt may be to raise up a new state again; or you shall never be reedified: that which the words following confirm. The Chaldee by *corner stone* understands a *King*, by *foundation stones*, *Princes.* But that seems overcurious. These two sorts of stones are mentioned, because of special note and principal concernment in building, Psal. 118:22. Esay 28:16. Zach. 10:4. Eph. 2:22. Rev. 21:12. The verb is indefinite, and may well therefore be rendered, *There shall not a stone be taken off thee, &c.* as Luk. 12:20. & 16:9.

*{but thou shalt be desolate for ever, saith the LORD.}* Or, *for* (as ver. 5.) *thus shalt be.* Heb. *desolations of perpetuity,* or, *perpetual desolations;* as chap. 25:12. Ezek. 35:9.

**V. 27.** *{Set up a standard in the land; blow the trumpet among the nations:}* The *standard,* and *trumpet,* both to call people together, that are to serve and be employed against Babylon. Of this of the one, see Esay 5:26. & 13:2. Of the latter, chap. 4:19, 21. & 6:1.

*{prepare the nations against her:}* Heb. *sanctifie;* as Esay 13:3. chap. 6:4. ver. 28.

*{call together against her the Kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz.}* Heb. *make to hear against her* (as chap. 50:29.) *the kingdoms;* that is, people out of those kingdoms; as Esay 13:4. The two former of these the most writers bring within the compass of Armenia. Of the former mention is made in Moses where the ark is said to have rested on the mountains thereof, after that universal deluge, Gen. 8:4. See on Esay 37:38. And for the latter, to wit, *Minni,* the Chaldee here has also *Armenia:* which country divers learned men suppose to be termed by a word compounded of two other, either *Aram* and *Minni,* (because Syria was sometime deemed to take in Armenia, as Strabo, lib. 1. & 12. Pliny, lib. 5. cap. 12.) or of *Har* and *Minni,* as the more mountainy part of *Minni;* and under these two terms therefore conceive to be comprehended the higher and lower Armenia; nor want there of them who deem *Minni* to be the same country, which Nicholas of Damascus calls *Minyas,* on a mountain above which in Armenia, he says that one arrived in an ark at the time of the deluge. See Joseph's *Antiquities,* lib. 1. cap. 4. *Ashchenaz* are a people descended from Japhet, whose son's son by Gomer his eldest son was so called, Gen. 10:3. 1 Chr. 1:6. Their seat seems to have been within Asia the less in Bithynia and Phrygia, where the Ascanian gulf, and lake, and river, and city, and region, all of that appellation are found. See Strabo, lib. 12. & 14. Pliny, l. 5. c. 31, 32. and that out of these parts Cyrus having subdued them, took soldiers along with him to serve under him in his expedition against Babylon, is related by Xenophon, lib. 7.

*{appoint a captain against her:}* So the Jewish commenter, one of them, following the Chaldee, expounds it as a military term and office, *a captain:* though another of them, *a Prince;* because the latter syllable of the word is in a manner the same with the Hebrew term that so signifies. And because the former part of the word in Hebrew signifies a little one: hence, some critics overcuriously descanting upon it, would have it to import *an inferior Prince,* or one set over the meaner sort: and the old Latin therefore in Nah. 3:17. where the same word is used in the plural form, renders it, *little ones.* In this it retains the word as a proper name of a person, as some would have it, of a place, or people, as some other: which because it is singular here, some would have it to denote therefore *a Generall:* and this, say some of them, must needs be Cyrus: but another controlling that conceit would have it to be *a Lieutenant Generall* under Cyrus, that may rule the army by direction from him, and may from time to time acquaint the several regiments with his mind and pleasure: and would have the word to import *a Prince of instillation.* or *interpretation,* from an Hebrew word that signifies *to distill,* or *drop,* applied sometime to teaching, preaching, and prophesying, Job 29:22. Mic. 2:6, 11. But the word seems to be a foreign term, and these strained interpretations rather witty than weighty. Some would have it to signify *an army;* building on the old Latin, that bids, *Muster Taphsar.* The Greek renders it *βελοστάσεις*, that is, engines to cast arrows or darts. A learned annotator would have it a Persian word, but of the Hebrews, corrupted, partly by transposition, and partly by transmutation of letters, from one that is used, Esth. 9:13. and to be the same with that which by the Greeks and Latins is called *Satrapa:* and would therefore have the meaning to be, *set a satrapa over it;* make it, of a kingdom, *a satrapy;* that is, *a Province:* for the *Satrapae* were governors of provinces. Thus it should be herein not unlike that of Rezin and Pekah concerning the son of Tabeel, Esay 7:6. But not to insist on any debate about the deduction of the word, though more probable than any of the former, yet *tiphsar* from *Achashdarpan,* not so easily brought about: the whole tenor of the prophet's speech here, both in the words next before, and those that immediately follow after, is concerning the mustering of forces against Babylon, not concerning her, as being not yet dealt with, much less subdued. Amidst this great variety I shall make bold to suggest mine own thoughts. I conceive with those Jewish masters above mentioned, that the word signifies *a Captain,* and to be a term of some military prefecture: and so it seems to be taken, Nah. 3:17. for elsewhere, save here and there, it is not found in Scripture. But in one of the Chaldee paraphrases it is said to be taken for *Angels,* that are as *captains of Gods host,* Gen. 32:1, 2. Josh. 5:14. and our version in Nahum well renders it *Captains;* for of military men it is spoken: and so might it very well be rendered here; for the word is collective; as the word *horse* in the next clause: and the text to me seems clear and plain to this purpose, *set up captains* or, *Commanders against her;* to wit over those forces, that you shall gather together out of the nations before-mentioned: for in vain does that great man press this place, to exclude Darius, and to back his strained interpretations *Kings* for a *King,* v. 11, 28. where see further there.

*{cause her horses to come up as the rough caterpillers.}* That the word *horse* is here collectively taken, as Psalm 76:6. is not to be doubted: and that the word rendered *caterpillers* (singular also but taken collectively; as Psalm 105:34.) does signify a kind of locusts, has been showed already, on v. 14. The question is here only in what regard these *horses* are compared to *locusts,* or such a kind at least of them, as this term imports: and here some would have them to be intended like them for multitude, and render the words, *bring on,* or *bring up,* (as Exod. 8:1. 1 Sam. 19:15. sometime a military term. See on chap. 50:21.) *horse as locusts,* for number, or numberless rather; as Psal. 106:34. so it was used here before, verse 14. and so both this and the like, Nah. 3:15, 17. Others would have the resemblance to consist in the motion of either; *make the horse to rise like locusts;* that is, *to prance,* or *to curvet,* or to leap and run, as locusts use to do, skipping and flying from place to place, either by shorter jumps when they remove not far, or by longer flights, as when they pass sometime over-sea. Of the motion of the locusts, see Joel 2:4, 5, 7, 9. where they are compared to *horses,* as *horses* here to them: and of *horse* and *charets,* Nah. 3:2. The former way the Greek goes, the Chaldee the latter. I conceive the former here intended, though the latter not improbable. But there is an epithet given here to this kind of locusts, concerning which there is some diversity of opinion, and from which some draw other resemblances. The word *rough,* that our version yields, is by the Jewish commenters approved, pointing us to the places, where the word it comes of does so signify, Job 4:15. Psal. 119:120. and in these places alone it is found. Nor do I see why it should be rejected, the original of the word backing it, and the relations withal concurring of those that write of the several kinds of *locusts,* among which they affirm some to be *rough.* Yet the Chaldee here renders it, *glistering;* as some kind of flies also do, as well as the glowworm: and this some would apply to the horsemen's glittering armor, or the trappings of their horse. See Rev. 9:7. The Latin renders it, furnished with *stings,* or *prickles;* and that some such thing the male locusts have in their tails both Aristotle, lib. 5. cap. 28. and Pliny l. 11. c. 29. affirm; and hither also some would draw that, Rev. 9:3, 10. and those would have these resembled to such locusts, as those in John, for the mischief they should do to men: only they question whether this attribute should belong to the *horse* or the *locust,* which will come much to one. Lastly, a late learned annotator renders the word *wasting;* and seems to ascribe it to the horse, *wasting as the locust:* and of the locusts laying all waste before it, there is no doubt, Psal. 105:34, 35. Joel 2:3. Nah. 3:16. for the word, says he, written with *shin,* signifies to *waste* and *destroy;* but the Chaldee dialect turns *shin* into *samec:* the learned man seems to have read *shamad.* for *samar,* the letters being much alike. Howbeit, herein I concur with him in that he takes *horse* collectively for *horses;* and *horses,* for *horsemen.*

**V. 28.** *{Prepare against her the nations.}* Heb. *Sanctifie;* as before, v. 27. but here repeated to add the further vigor to it, again.

*{with the Kings of the Medes, the captains thereof, and all the Rulers thereof, and all the land of his dominion.}* Either together with the nations before-mentioned, ver. 27. that were to serve under them; or, simply, *the Kings of Media,* Darius and Cyrus; as vers. 11. for that great man seems very much here out of the way, who to exclude Darius from any copartnership with Cyrus, would have *Kings* to be taken for *King,* both here, and before, ver. 11. the particle seems to note only the nouns coming in regiment after the verb *Sanctifie,* to which it has reference: and it is not amiss therefore omitted in the members ensuing; though here also in the text, the meaning is, employ all the power you can make against Babylon.

**V. 29.** *{And the land shall tremble and sorrow}* The people of Chaldea quake for fear, and be in pain, as a woman in travail: so the word properly signifies. See Esay 13:8. Chap. 50:43.

*{for every purpose of the LORD shall be performed against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon a desolation without an inhabitant.}* See Esay 14:27. Chap. 50:3. verse 1, 12, 62. the noun plural put in a distributive notion, joined with a verb singular; as Esth. 9:23. Prov. 14:1. Joel 1:20.

**V. 30.** *{The mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight; they have remained in their holds;}* They have no heart to fight, they dare not stir abroad; as the Philistines of the Israelites, 1 Sam. 14:11.

*{their might hath failed,}* So some of the Jewish critics, deriving it from a word that signifies *to fail,* Esay 19:5. or *to wax faint,* Esay 14:17, 17. but some other of them expound it, *their courage is gone;* fetching it from a word that has a notion of dislocation in it; as having reference to a limb put out of joint and removed, Gen. 32:32. so it would rather be, *their courage is shrunk;* as it is there rendered, or *it is lame,* and *halts,* as it is said there of Jacob, verse 31. The former seems the genuine.

*{they became as women:}* Heb. *they are unto women;* or, *they are become women:* they are so affected, so timorous and heartless, as if they were turned into women; as if they were not men, but women indeed; the phrase is the same with that, Exod. 4:3, 4. So Esay 19:16. Chap. 50:37. Nah. 3:13.

*{they have burnt their dwelling places.}* Or, *her dwellings are burnt:* for the verb is indefinite; as the like, chap. 49:28. and as verse 26.

*{her bars broken.}* The bars of the gates, as well of her forts and palaces, as of her city: all fly open before the enemy, and all lie open to him: her gates are all broken open, as is wont to be, when the bars are broken wherewith they were kept fast shut, Psal. 107:16. & 147:13. Prov. 18:19. and the enemy become master and commander of all. See Esay 45:2.

**V. 31.** *{One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the King of Babylon that his city is taken at one end,}* Heb. *A runner to meet a runner shall run; and a reporter to meet a reporter.* Or, *A post shall run meeting a post; and a messenger meeting a messenger. A post,* and *a post,* for, *one post* and *another;* and *a reporter,* or *messenger* the like: as *day to day;* and *night to night;* for, *one day to another,* and, *one night to another,* Psal. 19:2. and, *to meet,* for, *meeting;* or, *in meeting;* as 1 Sam. 25:34. *unlesse thou hadst made haste, and hadst come meeting me:* and of this use of the particle, see chap. 55:8, 9. & 38:4. & 44:5, 17. The meaning is, says the Jewish commenter, there shall come post upon post, and messenger upon messenger, that as one goes away, he shall meet with another coming; and all to bring word to the king of the surprisal of the city, (Heb. *to report,* or, *declare to the King of Babel*) *that his city is taken from the end,* or, *at the end:* as, *at my right hand,* Psal. 16:8. & Exod. 37:8. *at the end on this side,* and, *at the end on that side;* *that his city is taken at the one end;* as our version renders it; and the like is again, verse 46. and yet there needs not here that restrictive supply; *at,* or, *on the end,* or, *edge* of it, is enough; for whether it were taken by assault made on the one side only; or, on either side at once, (as a learned interpreter would have it, both where the river entered into the city, and where again it passed out) *at,* or, *on the end,* or, *skirt* of it, it was. For whereas a learned annotator would have it expounded, *his city is taken from end,* that is, *it is all taken, the whole city is taken;* and adds withal, that this is *a most manifest place,* to prove that acception of this form, which he attributes hereunto, to wit, a notion of *university,* or, as we use to speak, *universality:* that which, I suppose, no one place produced by him proves, and this here least of any: that the term imports precisely, *from the end,* or *extremity,* cannot be doubted, much less denied. Now because *the end,* or extreme part of a company may be the best, or chief, one way, the worst and meanest another way; hence the word is used sometime for the chief: as where it is said, that Joseph took *of the end* (the better end) *of his brethren,* the chief of them, *and set them before Pharaoh,* Gen. 47:2. sometime for the meanest; as where it is said of Jeroboam, that *he made Priests of the ends* (of the fag ends, as we say) *of the people:* of the *meanest* of them, 1 Kings 12:31. and the word is plural here, which was singular there, where applied, as may seem to the better part. As for that of the Sodomites, Gen. 19:4. *the whole people from the end:* the universality is in *the whole people, young and old,* the place or places from whence they came, noted only in the word *end,* or *quarter;* as it is sometime not amiss rendered. So Esay 56:11. *every one from his quarter:* and of the Danites, *from their quarters.* Judg. 18:2. and if it be rendered as our version does it, *from every quarter:* the universality will be, not in the word *quarter,* but in the note of generality supplied; as 1 Sam. 30:8. Esay 30:17. but I should rather render it *from* each one's *quarter;* as in distributive notions is wont to be expressed. See Esay 2:20. & 16:19. So Numb. 11:1. *fire was kindled, and devoured in the quarter,* or *quarters* (the word being taken collectively) *of the camp.* And for that, cap. 50:26. enough was said of it there. Yet will I not deny but that this form may sometime signify *from among;* as the Chaldee renders it, Ezek. 33:1. and if any shall deem it so to be taken, either Gen. 47:2. or 1 Kings 12:31. I shall not contend with him. But that implies not an *universality,* which this learned man strives for: nor do I see any color of ground here to admit it: nor can it be so taken, but where it has some other noun after it to rest on, as in those places it has; nor yet in such case neither, where it passes on to some other *end,* or *extreme;* as Gen. 47:21. Exod. 26:28. & 36:32. But could his exposition of it here be made good, and the matter of the message brought to the king, thus by post after post, were, that *his whole city was taken,* it would much conduce to strengthen the opinion of a late writer of great note, who building upon a relation of Berosus a Chaldee writer, reported by Joseph the Jew, *against Apion,* lib. 1. maintains very stiffly, that when Cyrus was marching with his army towards Babylon, the king of Babylon whom he called Nabonidus, went forth to meet him, with such forces as he had: but being worsted by him, fled with some few to a town called Borsippus, whither Cyrus having taken Babylon, and given order for the demolishing of the walls thereof, afterward pursued him, and having there taken him, gave him his life, and bestowed the province of Carmania upon him. And he presses this place very hard for the further proof of this story: for what needed, says he, such posting to the king; who ever he was, to acquaint him with the surprisal of the city, if he were at that time in the city, and not rather in some remote place? And indeed if the whole city had been taken, as that learned annotator would have it, the king and his court needed not be informed of it by messengers, they would have seen themselves in the midst of the broil. But this relation neither sorts well with these passages of the prophet in this place; and it is far otherwise, and more agreeably to the prophet's discourse, related by Herodotus, lib. 1. who wrote near two hundred years before this Berosus, and received what he wrote hereof from the Chaldeans, as also by Xenophon, lib. 7. that wrote about an hundred before him: neither of them make mention of any such flight of the Babylonian king to Borsippus; and the latter of them expressly mentions the murdering of him in his palace at Babylon: whom if Cyrus had dealt so kindly with, as Berosus reports, or had he heard of any such thing, he would not have failed to have inserted it into Cyrus his life, whom for his humanity and kind usage of those whom he conquered, he strives by all means and upon all occasions to extol. And for the *post upon post,* or *runner upon runner,* as the Hebrew has it, coming one upon the neck of another to bring tidings to the king's court of the taking of the city, we need not remove king or court out of the city, to some more remote place, if we do but consider, first what kind of messengers it is that the prophet here speaks of; for neither are they *horsemen,* such as those, 2 Kings 7:14. & 9:18, 19. sent out for scouts; not *Persian posts,* (as that learned writer expounds the term here used) disposed into certain stages, (whence ours have their name) to dispatch messages and intelligences with speed; but as the word is plain, *curriers,* or *runners, foot-posts,* as we use to speak; such as Ahimaaz and Cushi, 2 Sam. 18:19–23. and again if we shall take notice of the strange largeness and amplitude of the city, even within the walls, in regard whereof Aristotle therefore in his *Politicks,* lib. 3. cap. 2. says, that it deserved the name rather *of a country* than of *a city:* and withal what both he and Herodotus also report, the one of them, that the *utmost* parts of the city, *the ends,* as our prophet speaks, were taken, while those that dwelt in the midst were wholly ignorant of it, having heard nothing at all thereof, but went on with their reveling, (for at one of their drunken festivals it was taken) see on verse 39, 41. the other from some other ancient historians, that it was *three days* after it was taken, before tidings came of it to some part of the city. And thus much may serve to clear this place both from those forced expositions of the terms therein used, and the removal of the ground thereupon laid, to thwart the received opinion concerning Cyrus and Darius their joint surprisal of Babylon, conjoined with the slaughter of the king of Babylon, Dan. 5:28, 30, 31.

**V. 32.** *{And that the passages are stopped:}* Or, rather, *taken,* as verse 41. or, *seized,* or, *surprized,* as chap. 48:41. the *passages;* that is, such places by which from the river Euphrates there was ordinarily entrance into the city: as one of the rabbis expounds it: who adds also not amiss, that by the *passages,* is consequently understood the *forts* and *towers* situate in those places, to inhibit enemies from entrance; as of Moab, chap. 48:41. or, as others, not unlike to that, Judg. 12:5. where it is said, that *they took the passages of Jordan,* that is, the places by which men usually passed over it: so here *passages are taken,* whereby the river Euphrates is, or may be, passed over: and this way if we take it, it may be rendered, *passages have been deprehended,* or *discovered,* or *found out:* as the word is used of the wife suspected of disloyalty, *it is hidden from her husbands eyes, and she hath not been deprehended;* that is, discovered, found in the deed, or, as our English renders it, taken with the manner. Numb. 5:13. By diverting and draining of the rivers there, have been passages made and discovered, whereof use has been made for the taking of the city.

*{and the reeds they have burnt with fire,}* That which is here rendered *reeds;* the Jewish commenter expounds *great rushes;* deriving it from a word that signifies *a rush,* Job 8:11. and making it the same with that rendered *a bulrush,* Esay 58:5. and these, says he, Cyrus his soldiers burnt down, that they might not hinder their access to the walls of the city; but the words are not the same: and it would rather be rendered with the old Latin, *meers,* or *pools.* So the word is commonly, yea, generally, used; as Psalm 114:8. Esay 14:23. & 19:10. & 32:6. & 41:18. & 42:15. Nor need we, with that Jewish critic, have recourse to the Arabic, who suggests, that in that language, the word signifies *a fort;* and would have it so taken here. The meaning is, that Cyrus had by draining so dried up the meres, that were about Babylon, that they were as if they had been wasted, and burnt up with fire. And hither some think that of Esay has some reference, Esay 44:27, 28. For as for that which some surmise, that Cyrus his soldiery might fire the reeds, rushes, flags, and such sedgy stuff as grew in those meery places, thereby to harden the ground, and make it the more passable, to me seems very improbable; considering how suddenly the attempt was to be made, and how covertly to be carried, whereas this would have retarded the enterprise, and partly with the smoke of the green, rushy, and sedgy matter have smothered and choked the assailants: partly by the flame and crackling of the drier reedy stuff have discovered them, and given notice of their approach unto those in the city, who might as easily then, as Herodotus observes, have taken them as fish in a purse-net.

*{they have burnt}* That is, *the enemies:* which some make so bold with as to thrust into the text: but that is not so well done: the verb is indefinite; and may best be rendered in a passive form: *the meeres are burnt up.* See on verse 26.

*{and the men of war are affrighted.}* Daunted, and dismayed with the sudden irruption of the enemy, whom before they slighted, little deeming or dreaming of any such passage for them or means of surprisal by them. See verse 30.

**V. 33.** *{For thus saith the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel;}* As chap. 50:18.

*{The daughter of Babylon}* As Psalm 137:8. Of the term, see Esay 47.

*{is like a threshingfloor; it is time to thresh her:}* Or, as some render it, *in the time that he thresheth her;* that is, what time it is wont to be threshed, as some, taking the word indefinitely. So there should be a defect both of the particle *in,* and of the relative *that:* but the Jewish master takes it rather for an infinitive, in the time of threshing it; the word signifies *to tread:* but *to tread,* both in Hebrew and Syriac, 1 Cor. 9:10. is used for *to thresh,* says a learned writer, and of the Syriac he gives an instance: but none of the Hebrew, in which it is used for *treading* of grapes commonly; as Esay 63:2, 3. Chap. 48:33. and of olives also sometime, Mic. 6:15. but of corn, for *threshing,* or, *treading* it out, I find not where it is used. Yet thus also some of the Jewish commenters, here expound it, Babylon is like a floor full of sheaves; the time of threshing her approaches; or, when the time of it, to wit, of the floor, (for the word of *floor* is in Hebrew feminine) approaches. But to speak properly, the *floor* is not said to be *threshed,* but the harvest of corn in the floor, whereof there is no mention in the text. And I concur therefore rather with those, that take the word in its native and most usual notion, for *to tread,* as Judg. 20:43. conceiving it to have reference to the usual manner of preparing and fitting of floors for threshing against harvest time, by new laying, and claying, or plastering of them, and then treading them down to make them, as well firmer as evener. So the meaning will be; the city and state of Babylon must be thrown down and leveled, made even and plain, verse 25. as a threshing floor against harvest time, that her princes and people may be threshed in her. See Esay 21:10. Joel 3:14. Chap. 50:26.

*{yet a little while,}* As Esay 10:25. & 13:22.

*{and the time of her harvest shall come}* Not for her to reap, but to be reaped and cut down: her sin being come to the height, ver. 13. Gen. 15:16. she is now ripe for judgment, ready to have her princes, people, and partakers cut down and threshed in her. See Joel 3:13. Rev. 14:16.

**V. 34.** *{Nebuchadrezzar the King of Babylon hath devoured me,}* God's people's complaint of the Chaldeans' cruelty exercised upon them. Heb. *hath eaten me,* or, *eaten upon me:* as of Ashur, chapter 50:17.

*{he hath crushed me;}* Or, *bruised;* as chap. 28:25. or, *broken me:* as chap. 50:17. *hath boned me.*

*{he hath made me an empty vessel:}* See of Moab the like, chap. 48:12. and Babylon at length served alike herself, verse 2.

*{he hath swallowed me up like a great dragon,}* Or, *a whale:* as Psal. 44:19. & 74:13. that swallowed down the lesser fish and fry as by shoals. Habb. 1:13, 14. So Psal. 124:3. Esay 49:19.

*{he hath filled his belly with my delicates,}* He has filled his treasuries with whatsoever matter of special price or worth, he could find in me, Esay 39:4, 6. 2 Chron. 36:18. Lam. 1:10. See the like expressions, Job 15:20, 23. See also verse 44.

*{he hath cast me out.}* As men cast away some vessel when there is nothing left in it, nor itself, of further use, or much worth. See chap. 22:28. Lam. 4:2.

**V. 35.** *{The violence done to me, and to my flesh, be upon Babylon, shall the inhabitant of Zion say; and my blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea, shall Jerusalem say,}* God's people's complaint of the Babylonians' harsh and cruel usage of them: (whereof see 2 Chr. 36:17. Esay 47:6.) and either a prayer for, or prediction and profession of God their avenger's (chap. 50:34.) just judgment upon them for the same: so Psal. 137:8, 9. It is an intimation at least that the cruelty showed them, and their blood shed by them, did of itself cry to God for vengeance against them, as Gen. 4:10. See Habb. 2:11, 12. Jam. 5:4. Rev. 6:9, 10. *Sion* and *Jerusalem* are here one and the same; as Esay 4:4.

*{violence done me}* Heb. *my violence;* as, *my wrong,* for, *the wrong done me,* Gen. 16:5. and, *the violence of Jerubbaals sons,* for, the violence done to them, Judg. 9:24. and, *the violence of the children of Judah,* for, that showed to them, Joel 3:10.

*{my flesh}* As Mic. 3:2, 3. where this word is also used; and he seems to persist in, or have an eye at least, to the former resemblance of a ravenous beast, tearing the flesh of that he preys on. The Jewish masters, some of them distinguish the terms here somewhat overcuriously, *the spoil of me,* in the rapine of my goods, *my flesh,* in those whom they hold in captivity and thraldom: *my blood,* in those that have been slain by them. Some for *flesh* read *remnant;* as the like word is used in *Shear-Jashubs* name, Esay 7:3. but the words differ in a vowel.

*{my blood}* The guilt of, and vengeance for, that blood of my people that has been shed by them. See the like, Mat. 27:25.

*{inhabitant}* Heb. *inhabitresse;* for people that sometime inhabited there; as chap. 10:17. & 48:19. speaking of them, as of a damsel, Esay 1:8.

**V. 36.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD, Behold I will plead thy cause, and take vengeance for thee,}* God's answer to his people's cry; *I will plead thy cause,* not by words, but by deeds; by righting the wrongs by her done you, and executing judgment upon her for you; as chap. 50:34. So verse 40. Psalm 35:1. & 43:1. Lam. 3:58. Mic. 7:9. Heb. *avenge thy vengeance;* that is, the spiteful wrong and cruelty offered unto you: as Lam. 3:60. See before, on verse 35.
