*{and I will dry up her sea, and make her springs dry.}* *Her sea;* that is, her great stream of the river Euphrates; so that it shall no more stand her in stead, than as if the springs that fed it were clean dried. See verse 32. *sea,* for, *river,* or, *lake,* Mat. 4:13, 18. & 8:14. & 17:14. Joh. 21:1. as *river,* for *sea,* Jon. 2:4. See Esay 21:1. & 44:27.

**V. 37.** *{And Babylon shall become heaps,}* See chap. 50:39.

*{a dwelling place for dragons,}* So Esay 13:22. & 34:13. Chapter 49:33.

*{an astonishment, and an hissing without an inhabitant.}* As chap. 25:9. and 40:17. So chap. 50:3, 13, 39, 40. Verse 41, 43, 29.

**V. 38.** *{They shall roar together like lions; they shall yell as lions whelps.}* These words some of the Jewish masters understand of the Medes and Persians, like fierce lions, with hideous shouts, and outcries breaking in upon the Babylonians; as Esay 5:29. Chap. 2:15. See verse 14. Other of them, of the Chaldeans, and their outcries forced from them by extremity of pain and grief, when the enemy should break in upon them: because of such mournful outcries the word is found sometime used, Job 3:24. Psal. 22:1. & 32:3. & 38:8. But I concur rather with those of our writers who understand this passage of the Babylonians roaring and reveling in their drunken festival, at which their city was surprised. Of which, Herodotus, lib. 1. Xenophon, lib. 6. before on verse 31. and again on verse 41. and this way the very next words direct us, verse 39. The latter word rendered *yel,* is nowhere else in Scripture found in this notion; though some of the Jewish masters would have it so taken, Zach. 2:13. the Chaldee renders it, *they shall lift up their voyce on high:* and the Jewish commenters upon the place tell us, that it signifies properly the *braying of an asse:* and is so used among the Talmudists. To which some add, that it is sometime used also with them of *camels:* that the braying of asses is a very uncouth noise is well known; nor is a camel's like to be any other; but a lion's roaring mixed with an ass's braying must needs produce a very hideous noise indeed: such as may very fitly be used to express such confused shouts and clamors, as are wont to be rife among reveling companies overmastered with wine. Howbeit, because the word in Hebrew is used commonly for *to shake off;* as Esay 33:9. or, *to shake;* as Neh. 5:13. Esay 33:15. Hence, the ancient Greek renders it, *they rouze up themselves;* and the old Latin, *they shake their shaggy hair,* as young lions use to do: and as with swaggering folks is not unusual: and some of ours, which our margin exhibits, *they shake themselves.* Our ancient versions had it, *As young lions when they are angry so shall they bestir themselves;* that which seems to look this latter way. But the former seems the more probable.

**V. 39.** *{In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the LORD.}* Or, *When they are hot I will dispose their drinkings.* When they are heated with drinking (as Esay 5:11.) I will temper and tender them such a potion, as shall make them so drunk, as they shall sleep their last, even an everlasting sleep with it: and a learned man observes, that as *to give,* is used for *to put;* so *to put* is used sometime for *to give;* as Gen. 4:25. and according to this interpretation of the term here, it should be rendered, *I will give their feasts,* or, *I will give them feasts:* but neither in that place of Moses does the word necessarily so signify; and here it seems to be somewhat harsh. Our last version is, *I will make their feasts,* and so the ancient ones, *I will make them a dinner:* the learned scholiast, *I will set on their potions.* Others of prime note before him, which to me seems fittest of any, *I will dispose their drinkings,* or, *their banquettings:* for the word may have a notion of *drinking* in it; and drinking is in banquets deemed a principal matter; whereof both in Hebrew and Greek they have their appellations; yet the word does generally signify a banquet, though to the *wine,* therein plentiful, respect be more peculiarly here had. And in this passage there seems to be a twofold reference: first of all to that great magnificent banquet that Baltazar made to his grandees; Dan. 5:1. and to that revelling festival that at the same day was for divers days kept throughout the whole city, that gave Cyrus his forces the greater opportunity suddenly to surprise it, when the people of all sorts were deep generally in drink, as Herodotus, lib. 1. and Xenophon, lib. 7. See Esay 21:5. And secondly, to that *wine-cup of wrath,* that God had threatened to temper for them, and tender to them, so as they should not refuse it, chap. 25:15, 16, 26, 28.

*{make them drunk}* With another manner of wine, than that they feast with and in another manner affecting them, than that is wont to do: such a wine as shall fill them with dread and astonishment: such as shall make them mad indeed, and at their wits' end, chap. 25:16. See the effects of it in Baltazar, Dan. 5:6.

*{that they may rejoice.}* Or, *make merry,* or, *revell in;* as Esay 22:2. for the word signifies properly *a skipping,* or, *leaping;* and by such like motions an expression of merriment and jollity, *that they may revell it, and sleep their last;* for *that while they are revelling it, they may sleep their last.* So the Jewish commenter, that after they have revelled, and drunk themselves drunk with their concubines in the vessels of God's temple, they may be cast into such a sleep, as they shall not awake out of it again. Dan. 5:1–4, 30. a syntax, not unlike that Rom. 6:17. *God be thanked that ye were the servants of sin, but have yielded obedience, &c.* for, that though you were such sometime, yet it is otherwise with you now; you yielded now obedience to the doctrine of Christ. The Chaldee is supposed to have found here another reading, rendering it, *they may not be swallowed,* but *faint,* as that word signifies, Esay 51:20. Amos 8:13. and both the ancient Greek and old Latin, *that they may be cast into an heavinesse* or *sleep.* But to attempt to alter the text here is neither safe nor needful.

*{sleep a perpetual sleep}* Heb. *a sleep of perpetuity;* as verse 57. *the sleep of death,* Psal. 13:3. Job 7:21. Esay 26:19.

*{and not wake}* As after ordinary sleep men are usually wont to do, Psal. 3:5. Chap. 31:26. but continue their sleep, being once surprised with it, until the heavens be no more. Job 14:12. until the last day, when all shall be awaked with the sound of the trumpet that then shall be blown, Joh. 5:28. 1 Cor. 15:51, 52. The Chaldee renders it, *and shall not be quickened in the world to come;* a spice of that Jewish conceit, which some of their doctors are tainted with, that wicked men shall never rise again, abusing to that purpose those passages, Psal. 1:5. Esay 26:14. the Scripture elsewhere expressly clear against them, Mat. 13:39, 41. & 25:30, 31, 46. Joh. 5:28, 29. Yet true it is, that they shall never rise out of a state of deadly sleep and death again: for they rise to pass from death to death, from the first death to the second death, not to shake off death, but to enter into a further and far deeper degree of it. Rev. 20:6, 14. See the same passage again hereafter, verse 57.

**V. 40.** *{I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with the he goats.}* Or, *I will throw them down,* or, *lay them along,* (as Esay 10:13. & 43:14. Ezek. 26:20.) *like rams.* (See Esay 34:6.) *to the slaughter,* (as ch. 12:3. & 48:15. & 50:27.) *like ewe-rams and great he-goats;* as Deut. 32:14. Ezek. 27:21. for these two latter terms properly and more peculiarly import, the one the choice and chief of *rams,* from their *strength* so termed: as the other the bigger and larger sort of male-goats. See Esay 14:9. chap. 50:8.

**V. 41.** *{How is Sheshach taken?}* Some conceive it spoken in way of lamentation. Others, in way of admiration. Others again of both jointly; both as bewailing Babylon's fall, and withal wondering by what means or power she could in such manner be thrown down. See the like, chap. 50:23. Of the name *Sheshach* which Babylon is here titled, somewhat has been already hinted, on chap. 25:26. The name is taken from an idol in no small request with them, in honor of whom they observed a festival every year divers days together not unlike to the Greek and Latin *Saturnalia,* and our wonted *Christmas holy dayes,* wherein every man had liberty to do what he listed, the masters were at their servants' command, they had in every house a master of misrule, whom they called *Zoganes;* and all that time for some five days, which from the name of their idol, whom they thus honored, were called the *Sesacean,* or the name being in common speech cut shorter, the *Sacean dayes;* they abandoned themselves generally night and day (for in such liberty, or licentiousness rather, how could it be otherwise?) unto all excess and extremity of reveling and riot. This is reported by Athenæus in his *Supper-Sophisters,* or *Table-discourses,* lib. 14. out of Berosus his *Babylonian,* and Ctesias his *Persian* stories: as also Dion Chrysostom, in his fourth oration of *Kingly power,* mentions it. And at the time of this feast, (for the same by all circumstances it seems to have been) when the whole city was in this posture of reveling and routing, and the people as well great as small drowned in drink, did Cyrus take his opportunity to seize upon the city as the authors before-mentioned, both Herodotus and Xenophon report: and the prophet therefore the rather calls Babylon by that name, as pointing with the finger to that very time, in which that state was to receive its fatal blow. Nor is it unlikely, as that during the time of this festival (according to that Prussian writer's relation) besides their household masters of misrule, they had one, whom they made a public spectacle of, for having made choice of some notorious malefactor or other condemned to die, they arrayed him as a king, and set him in a chair of estate, allowed him a table royally furnished, officers to wait on him, and concubines to make use of at his pleasure; and thus he passed the time so long as the festival lasted; but that expired, they stripped him, whipped him, and hanged him: so that the king, to add the more grace to their idol-festivity, might over and beside the general revels, make that solemn invitation of his great ones, and give that royal entertainment unto them at that supper, which he then little thought should be his last, Dan. 5:1, 30. wherein by Gaizatas and Gobrias, two of Cyrus his commanders, and their followers, he was slain, in revenge of some wrongs formerly done to them and their friends, as Xenophon relates it. Nor fell it out much otherwise with King Baltazar, than with that mocking king in the close of his royal banquet.

*{and how is the praise of the whole earth surprised?}* That city so famous over the whole world: *praise,* for, matter of *praise;* as Esay 61:11. & 6:7. So chap. 49:35. Lam. 2:15.

*{how is Babylon become an astonishment}* As ver. 35. rendered *desolation,* chap. 50:23.

*{among the nations?}* Over whom she before tyrannized; as chap. 50:23. where is the same in effect with this here.

**V. 42.** *{The sea is come up upon Babylon: she is covered with the multitude of the waves thereof.}* An answer returned to the former question. That it is not to be marvelled, if Babylon be thus surprised and spoiled, when a whole sea of hostile force is broken in upon her, and has with numberless multitudes overwhelmed her. See the like expressions, Esay 8:8. & 59:19. Ezek. 26:3, 19. Lam. 1:15. See also verse 4.

**V. 43.** *{Her cities are a desolation, a dry land and a wilderness, a land where no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man passe thereby.}* This some restrain to Babylon as consisting of two cities, the inner and the outer, divided by the river Euphrates running between them. But the most rather understand it of the other inferior cities, called *hers,* as being the mother-city to them (as also the cities of Judah are called *Jerusalems cities,* chap. 34:1.) and were to undergo the like with her, chap. 50:3, 12, 13, 39, 40. as also the whole land was to do verse 29. The like descriptions of desolation, see chap. 2:6. & 9:12.

**V. 44.** *{And I will punish Bel in Babylon,}* Heb. *I will visit upon* (as chap. 40:18.) *Bel.* Babylon's chief idol: whereof, see on Esay 46:1. Chap. 50:2.

*{and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up,}* Heb. *his swallowing.* The spoils of the Babylonians, whereof they had fleeced other people: ascribed to their principal idol *Bel,* either because they attributed their conquests and successes in war to him, Hab. 1:11. as the Philistines did theirs to their Dagon, Judg. 16:23. and the Ammonites theirs to their Camosh, Judg. 11:24. or rather because of their booties and spoils taken by them, rich presents were usually offered unto that idol. To which purpose Eusebius in his *Evangelical preparative,* lib. 9. cap. 40, 41. relates out of Abidenus an ancient Greek writer, that Nebuchadnezzar adorned and furnished the temple of Belus very plentifully with such spoils as he got in war: and the sacred records inform us, that the precious vessels of the temple of God at Jerusalem were thence carried away by him, 2 Chron. 36:18. and put into the temple of this his idol, 2 Chron. 36:7. Dan. 1:2. which he had swallowed down, verse 34. was afterward constrained to cast up again, that they might be restored to their due and proper place Ezra 1:7. & 5:14. See Job 20:12–15. But of the rich furniture of this *Bels* temple at Babylon, see Diodorus l. 2. c. 9.

*{and the nations shall not flow together any more unto him;}* They shall not flock to Babylon as they had wont to do, when she was in the height of her imperial state; nor resort to *Bel* their idol and to his temple, with presents as formerly they had done. See the contrary to be practised at Jerusalem, by God's people, after their return from captivity, chap. 31:12. and of the nations under the Messias, Esay 2:2.

*{yea, the wall of Babylon shall fall.}* Heb. *also: wall of Babel shall fall;* on the strength whereof she so much relied. See chap. 50:15. and hereafter, verse 53, 58.

**V. 45.** *{My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver every man his soul from the fierce anger of the LORD.}* That is to be poured forth upon Babylon. Of the terms whereof, see on ver. 4, 8. And this some understand of danger by staying in Babylon, till Cyrus his forces come, as advising and admonishing the Jews that there were, to get away before: but this seems not to fit so well with what followed. Others of prime note, not to stay in Babylon, when liberty was once published, as many might desire to do, being loath to leave a place and that very delightful, where they had so long lived, and where they might now abide free from their former bondage; and choosing rather now to continue there where they had built and planted, chap. 29:5. than to remove to their own land, that had lain long time waste and desolate, and wherein they were to begin as it were a new world again: and this I take to be the genuine intendment and scope of the place: for the wrath of God was not all at once poured forth by Cyrus upon Babylon, as appears in that Darius continued in it for some space of time: the royal seat of the empire, but was afterward to be further inflicted upon it; and howsoever God should secure them at Cyrus his surprisal of it, albeit they were found there; yet he might justly leave them afterward to ensuing destruction, if having liberty to depart, they should still desire and deem it better, to abide there among heathen people, than to return to serve God in their own country again. See also the like admonitions of leaving Babylon before, c. 50:8. v. 6. So Rev. 18:4.

**V. 46.** *{And lest your heart faint,}* Or, *And see that your hearts faint not;* or, *let not your hearts faint;* be not fainthearted: a defective speech: the like whereunto, see Gen. 3:22. Exod. 13:17. Deut. 8:12. Esay 36:18. Heb. *be soft,* or *tender,* as Esay 7:4. 2 Kings 22:19. Job 23:13.

*{and ye fear the rumour that shall be heard in the land:}* The rumor or report of Cyrus his preparation to come against Babylon: his they are encouraged not to fear, which they might the rather do, because they had by this our prophet been formerly willed to pray for Babylon's prosperity, their own safety and tranquility being wrapped up in its peace, c. 29:7. but this, says the Jewish commenter not amiss, to assure them, that God in his providence would so dispose it, that Cyrus his access should be no way prejudicial unto them. For that of a learned writer, that this should be disjoined to the foregoing advice, v. 45. to admonish them that yet they should not make so much haste as to get out of Babylon, upon the first report coming of Cyrus his intendment for Babylon, but stay till such time as God should further acquaint them with it: seems not to suit so well with the rest of the context.

*{a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour,}* Or, as some, *for* as v. 20. or, *when* (as ch. 34:1.) *a rumour shall come in one year,* (a defect of the numeral, as v. 31.) or *this year, and a rumour after that in another* (supplied, as c. 32:20.) or *in the next year;* that is as some, in general; there shall come rumors frequently, or year after year. But some more distinct report will come one year of Cyrus his preparations for war, and that might take him up no less time than a twelvemonth for such an expedition, as this against Babylon the head city of that vast empire, was in reason required to be. The next year comes the report of his setting forward, and being now on his way toward Babylon; but that year was spent in his march through Assyria, where there were passages proved troublesome; and the draining of the river Gyndes, to be revenged on it for the loss of an horse of special note, and much account with him, drowned in it, took him up much time, as both Herodotus and Xenophon report: for in the third year having pierced into Chaldea, he came and sat down before Babylon, and gave not over the siege thereof until he had surprised it. Nor does the Jewish master here go far from them, who expounding the place tells us that Belshazzar reigned three years, and in the first year of his reign a report should come to Babylon of Cyrus his intendment against it; and in the second of his reign the same should be renewed; but in the third year he should come indeed.

*{and violence in the land}* Or, *then* (so some render it, as chap. 47:2. that is, in the third year) shall *violence be on the land.* That which the Jewish doctors, and most other also expound of the Medes and Persians harassing the land of Chaldea: and a learned writer would have understood by the word here used, the *reward,* or *recompence* that should from God be inflicted upon the Chaldeans for the *violence,* or *wrongs,* done to his people, v. 35. (See v. 34.) as the word, says he, is taken Psalm 7:16. But the plain and proper sense of the word, does well enough here. Though those seem to go further out of the way, who taking the word so apply it to the Chaldeans' persistence in their oppressions of God's people, remitting nothing of their rigorous courses towards them but enhancing them rather, as Pharaoh did with them in Egypt, Exod. 5:6–9. and that this was it against which God here endeavored to confirm them.

*{ruler against ruler.}* That is, Cyrus against Belshazzar or Baltasar, as in other languages he is commonly termed. But some render the words, *ruler upon ruler:* expounding it of the frequent change of rulers in a short compass of time, first, Baltasar, then Darius, then Cyrus: and this way the Jewish commenter, and a prime writer of ours seem to go: and because such changes are wont to breed much trouble, the rather therefore against this in particular God here heartens his people, assuring them that these shiftings should no wise prejudice their safety; the new kings successively should rather help and favor, than hurt them or hinder their welfare.

**V. 47.** *{Therefore behold the days come, that I will do judgment upon the graven images of Babylon,}* This version of the particle agrees well with those that expound the foregoing words of the Chaldeans' persistence in their oppressions of God's people. But I suppose it would rather be rendered, *Moreover,* as chap. 23:7. Heb. *the dayes coming, and I will visit upon* (as chap. 48:12. vers. 44.) *the graven images of Babylon:* one sort of images put for all, as chap. 50:38. See the like hereunto, Exod. 12:12. Chap. 43:12, 13.

*{and her whole land shall be confounded;}* *The whole land,* for the inhabitants of the whole land, as Psalm 66:3. they shall be at their wits' end, unable either to act, or to advise ought, Esay 66:5. the same again hereafter, v. 52. *shall be confounded,* or *abashed,* which in sound also agrees with the term in the text; or ashamed of their idols that were not able to protect them. See Esay 1:29. c. 50:2.

*{and all her slain shall fall in the middest of her.}* Or, *shall ly.* Or, *lye fallen in the middest of her;* as 1 Samuel 31:8. Lam. 2:21. A learned late writer would have it rendered, *all her dancing ones,* or *dancers, shall fall in the midst of her:* and, says he, the word is used, Judges 21:21, 23. 1 Sam. 3:6. & 1:11. 1 Kings 1:40. and is by the Greek in these places so rendered: which would well fit with Herodotus his relation, who reports in express terms, that the Babylonians were dancing, and in merriment passing the time away, what time their city was surprised. But the terms, though rising from the same root, yet are not the same.

**V. 48.** *{Then the heaven, and the earth, and all that is therein, shall sing for Babylon:}* Heb. *And;* as v. 46. and, *over Babylon;* as Esay 63:5. or, *for;* as chap. 47:4. All the creatures in heaven and earth shall seem to rejoice at the ruin of Babylon; as eased of the heavy pressures that the whole world had sustained by her tyrannical dominion. See Esay 14:6–8. Chap. 50:23. verse 23–25. or, as applauding of God's just judgment, in avenging of the wrongs done his people by her. See Esay 14:3–5. & 44:23. & 49:13. and the like expressions, Psal. 96:11–13. and 98:7–9. Howbeit, they seem somewhat too curious, who by *heaven* here understand the angels; by the *earth,* the Jews and other nations abroad: the outward face of the whole visible world is commonly in Scripture by these terms described, Psal. 69:34. Esay 1:2. & 45:8.

*{for the spoilers shall come unto her from the North, saith the LORD.}* Or, *When;* as chapter 10:2. See c. 40:3. and verse 53, 55, 56.

**V. 49.** *{As Babylon hath caused the slain of Israel to fall: so at Babylon shall fall the slain of all the earth.}* Not of the city alone; but of the whole country: and there is in the words a reason rendered of what was before mentioned, that Babylon's people should be slain and lie slain in the midst of her, because she had dealt so with other people before, with God's people more specially among the rest, chap. 4:27, 29. And this version is backed with the ancient Greek, old Latin and others of ours. As for that, which some other of prime note suggest, *Both Babylon must fall, O ye slain of Israel, and with Babylon shall fall the slain of all the land,* seems overstrained, and not to come so freely, without some force, from the text. Heb. *also:* and, *also,* for, *As,* and *so;* as somewhat the like, Psalm 49:2. chapter 14:18. & 23:11. and *to fall,* for *to make to fall,* says that learned scholiast; as Numb. 2:22. but the vowel points are not there the same.

**V. 50.** *{Ye that have escaped the sword, go away, stand not still:}* Or, *stay not.* Heb. *stand not;* as Gen. 45:1. Chapter 4:6. You that have escaped the sword of the Chaldeans; as those of the Egyptians, chap. 31:2. Or rather, you who by God's gracious provision, and powerful protection abiding in Babylon, at the time of its surprisal, have escaped the sword of the Medes and Persians, make no stay, when you have liberty to be going, once granted you; let nothing retard you from setting speedily upon return to your own country. See on v. 25.

*{remember the LORD afar off, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.}* Heb. *come up upon the heart;* as chap. 3:16. Think upon God, and the seat of his solemn service, the temple at Jerusalem; though you be now in a place of much distance from it, chap. 4:16. Esay 39:3. let the remembrance of him and it, draw your hearts and affections thitherward and entice you to hasten thither, Psalm 102:14. & 137:1, 5, 6. c. 50:4, 5. A learned annotator, with some others, makes this the intendment of it, to show them, what meditations they should have, when they were upon the way homeward; expressed more fully in the words following, v. 15. which to bring on therefore the more smoothly, he subjoins here a supply of the word, *saying.* I conceive rather as before.

**V. 51.** *{We are confounded, because we have heard reproach, shame hath covered our faces.}* The complaint and lamentation of God's people, being put in mind of Jerusalem the wonted seat of God's service, at the very mention of it, and the remembrance of its present condition; bewailing the reproachful language and carriage of the adversary even against God himself, occasioned by the deportation of his people, and the devastation of his temple: of which kind of insolent and despiteful language, see Deut. 32:7, 8. Ps. 42:3. & 115:2. Esay 10:10, 11. Ezek. 36:20. and the like laments in the same terms some of them, see Psal. 31:11, 13. & 69:7. & 44:15, 16. & 89:50, 51. & 123:4. & 137:1–6. As those interpreters of note, and that learned annotator before mentioned, annexed a supply to the latter part of the foregoing verse to carry on their supposed connexion of it with this. So a learned scholiast prefixes another supply in the front of this, to wit, *If ye shall say,* as if it were spoken by way of preoccupation, as if they should say, how can we remember Jerusalem, when we cannot do it without much shame and confusion; so it should be not unlike that, Psal. 137:4. But this also seems needless as well as that, and to strain the context without cause.

*{for strangers are come into the Sanctuaries of the Lords House.}* Or, *Because* (as c. 30:12, 15.) *strangers* (who were not to set foot into your sanctuary, Num. 1:51.) *have come in upon it* (have not only entered into your temple, Lament. 1:10. but have come in hostile manner upon it; as v. 42. *the sea is come in upon Babylon, the spoiler is come upon her,* verse 56. *the Sanctuaries of the Lords house:* both the holy place, the body of the temple; and the Holy of Holies, or the most holy place; the oracle wherein the ark was seated, on which God, as on his royal throne, or in his chair of estate, was said to sit between the cherubs, and there was wont to be consulted with Exod. 25:22. Num. 7:89. Psal. 80:1. or, as the Jewish commenter, upon the house, consisting of those two, as one entire frame; and the courts with the buildings about them, as another: yet both comprehended in the name of *Sanctuary,* or *Temple.* (See chap. 36:6.) and have burnt them down and demolished them, 2 Chr. 36:19.

**V. 52.** *{Wherefore behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will do judgment upon her graven images,}* In consideration of these lamentable complaints of my people, as Psal. 12:5. or in regard of these insolencies committed against me in the devastation of mine house; I will be avenged both on the Chaldeans themselves, and on their idols, (together with their temples too; as chap. 43:12, 13.) which shall not be able to save either themselves, or their servers. See the same before, verse 47.

*{and through all her land the wounded shall groan.}* Their idols being not able either to deliver, or to relieve their people that depend upon them, to preserve them from wounds, or to relieve them of their pains, and much less to save their lives, see v. 49.

**V. 53.** *{Though Babylon should mount up to heaven,}* Though her walls were as high as heaven; as they speak, Gen. 11:4. Deut. 1:28. and they are reported to have been of a stupendous height, *two hundred* foot, says Pliny, lib. 6. cap. 26. *cubits,* and those *royal* ones, an hand's breadth longer than the ordinary, says Herodotus, lib. 1. though Strabo, lib. 16. and Diodorus, lib. 2. say, *fifty cubits* only between the towers, and at the towers *threescore.* See the like expressions, Obad. 4.

*{and though she should fortify the height of her strength,}* Though she raise her fortifications as high as heaven: so some, following the old Latin, that renders it, *Though she establish in the lofty place her power;* that is, set it, or settle aloft in heaven, in Scripture so frequently termed, Esay 24:18. & 32:15. Chap. 25:30. Lam. 1:3. but the word is here in a contracted form, resting in regiment upon the next. The meaning therefore seems rather, though she make their strength equal with, and proportionable to, their height.

*{Yet from me shall spoilers come unto her, saith the LORD.}* Yet for all her height and strength shall those come unto her, that coming with commission from me shall not fail to plunder her, verse 48. No height or strength can secure against God, or those that come furnished with power from him. So again, ver. 55, 56. a defect of the discretive, as chap. 25:1, 10.

**V. 54.** *{A sound of a cry cometh from Babylon,}* A loud outcry; as Esay 65:19. Chap. 48:3. the speech is abrupt, the verb wanting, as Esay 66:6.

*{and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans.}* Or, *and of great destruction.* Heb. *breach,* or, *breaking;* as chap. 50:22. See chap. 6:1. & 48:3.

**V. 55.** *{Because the LORD hath spoiled Babylon,}* Or, *For* (as verse 5, 27.) *the Lord will spoyle Babylon,* by them that shall come with commission from him, verse 53. Heb. *is spoyling;* about to do it, as chap. 25:36.

*{and destroyed out of her the great voice,}* Thus the most, both Jewish and others, understanding the place, some of that streperous noise, that is wont to be in places where great concourse of people is, Esay 13:4. and such was no doubt in Babylon, being so populous, and having such resort unto it out of all parts, v. 44. Others, of those confused clamors, that their roarers and revellers made at their drunken meetings, verse 38, 39. See Esay 22:3. which God, whither way we take it, would now still and lay, by bringing those in upon them, that should either make them change their note, or silence their multitude. See Esay 16:9, 10. & 22:12. & 25:5. Chap. 48:45. But some interpreters of note conceive it to be spoken of the enemies breaking in with shouts and clamor upon them, rendering the words, *and he will destroy* her strength (supplied from verse 53.) *out of her* with *a great noise:* the particle designing the manner of doing ought, omitted; as oft it is, Esay 34:2. Chap. 23:28. and the words following seem to carry it this way. See Esay 16:9. with chap. 48:32, 33. Amos 1:14.

*{when her waves do roar like great waters, a noise of their great voice is uttered.}* Heb. *and* (which some render, *for,* as verse 20.) *their waves shall roar like great waters,* or, *like many waters: the noyse,* or, *shout of their voyce shall be given out,* or, *when the shout of their voyce* (that is, their loud shoutings) *are given out:* the particle of time wanting; as chap. 8:18. Esay 17:6. & 18:10. & 41:17. the waves of that sea, which shall break in upon her, verse 51. shall make an hideous noise, such as the waves of the sea are wont to make, when they beat upon the rocks, or rush in with violence upon the land, having either broken through, or got over the seabanks. See the like expressions, Esay 5:30. & 17:12, 13. See the term of *giving out a voyce,* chap. 2:15. & 10:13.

**V. 56.** *{Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon,}* Or, *For* (as verse 55.) *the spoiler* (as v. 53.) *is come upon her* (as v. 42, 51.) *upon Babylon:* a redundancy, but such as makes the sentence more vigorous; as Esay 8:13. & 48:6. Prov. 5:21. Hab. 1:11.

*{and her mighty men are taken}* Unawares, when they little dreamed of any danger. See verse 39, 40.

*{every one of their bowes is broken,}* Heb. *their bows is broken;* a distributive form; as Esay 26:19. Joel 1:14. their strength is utterly spent and gone; as chap. 49:35.

*{for the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite,}* As, *the Lord of vengeances,* Psal. 94:1. Heb. *rendring render,* or, *requiting requite;* as Exod. 21:36. & 22:2. See verse 6, 24. Esay 59:18.

**V. 57.** *{And I will make drunk her Princes, and her wise men, her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men, and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake,}* I will make them all drunk with the wine of my wrath, chap. 25:26. Yet withal alluding to that drunken feast, at which they were to their utter destruction surprised and slain. See verse 63. and of the terms here used there: the enumeration of several sorts, of those of principal note especially, makes the sentence more emphatical; as Esay 3:2, 3. So chap. 50:35–37. Verse 21–23.

*{saith the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts.}* As ch. 48:15.

**V. 58.** *{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts, the broad walls of Babylon}* Or, *the walls of broad Babylon:* of the amplitude of the city, see on verse 31. Strabo lib. 16. says the compass of it within the walls was *three hundred fourscore and five* furlongs; and Diodorus, lib. 2. with some abatement, *three hundred threescore and five;* just so many as days in the year: but Herodotus, lib. 1. says, *four hundred and fourscore furlongs:* with whom, Pliny agreeing, lib. 6. cap. 26. says, *threescore mile.* And for the *walls* of it, it is reported by Herodotus, that they were *fifty large cubits* broad: though Pliny transcribing him, instead of *cubits* says *feet.* So broad they were, as Strabo and Diodorus agree, that two chariots drawn with four horses on breast, might easily meet on them, and leave space enough on either side vacant. Of the height of them, see before on verse 53.

*{shall be utterly broken}* Or, *made naked.* Heb. *shall in breaking down be broken down;* or, *shall in making bare be made bare;* for the word is ambiguous: the root at least whence it springs. The Jewish masters say it is taken in a notion of *demolition,* or *breaking down,* Esay 23:13. where our version has, *raised it up,* but they, *ruined it;* and so say they here. But the ordinary use of the word is frequent in a notion of *stripping,* or *making bare:* Esay 32:11. Lam. 4:21. Habb. 3:9. Zeph. 2:14. (See chap. 17:6. on the word, *heath*) and in this notion here taken, as by divers interpreters of the best note it is, it will in effect come fully home to the former: for the *wall* is said to be *laid bare* in a figurative form of speech; not so much when it is destitute of defendants, but when it is razed and her foundations are laid naked, and the ground made level on which it before stood. So Psal. 137:7. a place parallel to this, *make it bare, make it bare, to the foundation:* well rendered, *raze it;* for when the walls are razed, both the ground it stood on is made bare, and the town it environed is laid naked. As thick therefore and as strong as her walls were, yet God threatens and foretells that they should be razed: and Berosus reports that Cyrus took order for the demolishing of them. Yet were they not then wholly razed, but then in part ruined, and utterly afterward. See on chap. 50:15. it is thrice repeated to give the stronger assurance of it; because it would be deemed a matter incredible. See verse 44.

*{and her gates shall be burnt with fire;}* An usual form in describing the devastation of a city, Neh. 1:3. & 2:3, 13, 17. Chap. 17:27. Lam. 1:4. & 2:9. Ezek. 26:2. The gates of Babylon were built with stately and lofty arches, proportionable to the walls, as Diodorus reports: an hundred there were of them, as Herodotus says, with their posts and hinges all of brass,

*{and the people shall labour in vain, and the folk in the fire, and they shall be weary.}* Or, *thus,* (as verse 4.) *shall the people take pains for vanity, and the folk, untill they tire themselves for the fire;* that is, as some of the Jewish commenters, people shall use their utmost endeavors to save Babylon from destruction; but all in vain, and to no purpose, verse 9. for with fire and sword shall it be consumed, and all those together with her that do aid and assist her, v. 4, 47. Or, as other of them rather, it shall then appear, that all the pains that people have taken, wearying and tiring out themselves, about the building of Babylon, have been but labor in vain, and produced nothing but fuel, matter only to feed the fire, verse 25. so are some said to *breed children for the sword,* Job 27:14. and Ephraim, *for the murtherer,* Hos. 9:13. See the same expressions, Habb. 2:13. A learned annotator supposes a trajection in the text, and would have it thus rendered, *The labours of the people and folk that have been wearied* (with building thy walls) *shall come to nothing by the fire.* But this both disturbs and disjoins the text overmuch.

**V. 59.** *{The word which Jeremiah the Prophet commanded Seraiah, the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah;}* To this prolix prophecy against Babylon is subjoined a course taken by Jeremy at God's appointment, for the copying of it out, and conveying of a copy of it unto Babylon, verse 59, 60. there to be read unto the Jewish captives abiding there, verse 61. and after solemn protestation made of God's purpose to put in execution the matters therein menaced, verse 62. to be sunk in the river Euphrates, verse 63. as a sign and seal of Babylon's irrecoverable downfall, verse 64.

*{The word}* Or, *thing,* or, *matter;* as Exod. 16:16.

*{Jeremiah commanded}* Gave in charge from God.

*{Seraiah}* Of this Seraiah we read nothing elsewhere: but of another of his name then high priest, chapter 52:24.

*{when he went with Zedekiah King of Judah into Babylon in the fourth year of his reign;}* So, out of their annals one of the Jewish commenters tells us, that Zedekiah went to Babylon, and this Seraiah in company with him, and returned thence shortly after to his kingdom again: but others rather render the text, *when he went for,* or, *on the behalf of Zedekiah.* So one of the rabbis; or, as others, *from Zedekiah:* and so the ancient Greek, and the Chaldee: and so the particle is used, Gen. 4:1. & 44:4. & 49:26. Exod. 9:29. sent in embassage by him to the king of Babylon to treat with him about affairs of state. Hence it appears that this prophecy against Babel was penned seven years before the subversion of the Jewish estate. See c. 39:3.

*{and this Seraiah was a quiet Prince.}* Or now (as chap. 37:4.) *this Seraiah was* (as the Hebrew has it) *Prince of Menucha:* which some take to be the proper name of a place, whereof this man had the rule and charge: as some also suppose it to be, Judges 20:43. but this is of a place in Judah, whence the *Menuchothites,* 1 Chron. 2:52. Others, whom our translators follow, make it an attribute intimating the man's disposition, *a Prince of rest,* one that lived peaceably and quietly, as Solomon is called *a man of rest,* 1 Chron. 22:9. or one that labored to make peace, and mediated for reconcilement between Zedekiah his master, and the Chaldean monarch. Others again would have it to be the name of an office; and of these, some, the king's familiar favorite, with whom he used to recreate himself, when he had times of leisure and liberty of rest from other more serious affairs. Some, the *Lord Chamberlain,* he that had the charge of the king's resting place, or bedchamber. Others, that he was *Lord chiefe Justice of peace:* one that by such forces as he had the charge of, was to see the public peace kept and maintained, and so procure rest unto the state. The Chaldee deriving it from another root, expresses it by a term used of him, Esay 18:7. answering to the Hebrew *minchah,* that signifies *a present,* and renders it, *the master of gifts,* or *presents,* and so the ancient Greeks also: that which some understand of *presents* brought to the king, who were by such an officer to have access. Others, of *gifts,* or *donatives,* bestowed by the king, either on the soldiery or commonalty, which this man was by virtue of his office to dispose of. The old Latin renders it, *the Prince of Prophecie:* which Popish writers to little purpose strain their wits to make somewhat of. Amidst this variety and uncertainty, the two first seem most probable; and of the twain, that to me seems the more, that our versions generally pitch upon, being backed with an instance of the same stamp, and seems to have been here specified, to intimate that this Seraiah was none of those factious and turbulent courtiers, that opposed God's prophets, and disturbed them in the execution of their ministry, and one therefore not unfit for such an employment as this.

**V. 60.** *{So Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come upon Babylon: even all these words that are written against Babylon:}* Or, as some render it, *After that he had written in a book.* Heb. *And* but so is the copulative sometime used; as Exod. 14:21. & 16:20. Leviticus 9:22. and the noun for the pronoun, as again, verse 61. and *in one book,* for *in a book;* as *in one pot,* for *in a pot,* Exodus, 16:33. and *words,* for *things;* as Deuteronomy 30:1. and *el,* again in the first place, for *al upon;* as chapter 50:35, 36. and *el* the second time, for *al,* either *concerning,* or *against;* as chapter 50:1.

**V. 61.** *{And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, When thou comest to Babylon, and shalt see, and shalt read all these words,}* Or, as some render it, *and shalt have seen,* or, *beheld* the city (as his disciples did the temple, Matth. 24:1, 2. and Christ himself Jerusalem, Luke 19:41.) *then shalt thou read all these words,* or *thou shalt then looke upon* this book, or roll, *and shalt read all these words* or *things;* as v. 6. *out of it;* as Neh. 8:13. *and,* for *then;* as chapter 47:2. and *words* for *things:* as v. 60. Howbeit, it is not likely that Seraiah should read this in some public place where the Chaldeans should hear it: so, nor is that probable that some of note have, that he was to read it only privately in some closet apart by himself: for why that there, rather than before he set out, or when he was on his way thither? but that he was to read it unto his countrymen, the Jews, who had together with Jeconiah about four years before been carried captive thither, 2 Kings 24:12, 14. in some private house, whither, as to an ambassador coming from Zedekiah, that held from the king of Babylon, 2 Kings 24:17. they might have free access.

**V. 62.** *{Then shalt thou say,}* Or, *And shalt say:* if we follow the latter version before-mentioned, v. 61.

*{O LORD, thou hast spoken against this place to cut it off, that none shall remain in it, neither man nor beast, but that it shall be desolate for ever.}* In the Hebrew text *el,* again, for, *al, concerning,* or *against;* as verse 60. and *from man even unto beast;* as chapter 50:3. and *desolations of perpetuity;* as verse 26. chapter 48:34.

**V. 63.** *{And it shall be when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the middest of Euphrates.}* On the banks whereof Babylon was situate: *into the midst* of it, for *into it;* as *out of the midst* of it, for *out of it,* verse 6. In like manner is *a mill-stone* said to be cast into the sea, to represent the irrecoverable downfall of the spiritual Babylon, Revelation 18:11.

**V. 64.** *{And thou shalt say, Thus shall Babylon sink and not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her:}* See Esay 26:14. ch. 50:39, 40. v. 26, 39.

*{and they shall be weary.}* That is, says the Jewish doctor, they shall not be able to hold out against Cyrus: or, as others rather render it, *though they weary themselves:* as Esay 40:30. verse 58. the copulative in a discretive notion; as Esay 10:5. & 49:5. Though they take never so much pains, even till they tire out themselves, in endeavoring and striving to raise and restore her again: as of Edom, Mal. 1:4. Those that render it; *and they shall flee away,* as Job 20:8. Psal. 90:10. mistake the root.

*{Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.}* That is, as some, thus far concerning Babylon, as before; *Thus far concerning Moab,* chapter 48:47. Or as others rather, thus far of the prophet's own writing, for the chapter following seems to have been afterward added unto this book of his prophecies by some other holy man of God, (as the last chapter to the writings of Moses) for the further illustration and fuller confirmation of some things therein contained. For that which one of the Jewish masters would have to be the meaning of it, that after he had finished this prophecy against Babylon, he prophesied not, is apparently controlled by the inscriptions of some other of the prophecies in this volume recorded, that are of later date than this. See chapter 32:1. & 33:1. & 34:1. & 37:5, 6. & 42:7. & 43:8. & 44:1.

## CHAPTER 52

**Verse 1.** *{Zedekiah was one and twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, and his mothers name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.}* This chapter is supposed to have been written by some of those that lived in captivity at Babylon. The principal matter of it is concerning Zedekiah's wicked reign, v. 1–3. the siege and sacking of Jerusalem, v. 4–23. the slaughter of some chief ones, v. 10, 24–27. the deportation of the rest, v. 28–30. and the enlargement of Jehoiachin, verse 31–34. the most of it is related, 2 Kings 24. and 25. 2 Chronicles 36:1–18. Heb. *reigned,* for *began to reign;* as 2 Kings 21:1. & 22:1. See 2 Kings 24:18.

**V. 2.** *{And he did that which was evil in the eyes of the LORD,}* That is, displeasing to him; as 2 Sam. 11:28. See 2 Kings 24:19. 2 Chr. 36:12.

*{according to all that Jehoiakim had done.}* Of whom see 2 Kings 23:37.

**V. 3.** *{For through the anger of the LORD it came to passe in Jerusalem and Judah, till he had cast them out from his presence, that Zedekiah the King rebelled against the King of Babylon.}* According to this version, God punished his foregoing evil carriages, verse 2. by giving him up to his own perverse will, and permitting him to persist in a rebellious course against him, who had made him king, and unto whom he had sworn loyalty, to the ruin of himself, and the whole state together with him. The like whereunto, see Psal. 81:11, 12. Rom. 1:21, 24, 26, 28. Howbeit, I conceive the words may be thus rendered. *Yea, unto the anger of the Lord it was against Jerusalem and Judah—that Zedekiah rebelled against the King of Babylon. Yea,* so the particle is used in way of exaggeration, Esay 22:13. Chap. 14:5, 18. *unto the anger of the Lord;* as *add iniquity unto their iniquity,* Psal. 69:27. where the same particle is used, *it was;* it accrued, it was added further thereunto; as 1 Kings 13:34. compared with chap. 12:30. *against Jerusalem and Judah,* as Psal. 78:21. and 106:40. Esay 5:25. *that* (Heb. *and;* as c. 48:12. and 49:2.) *Zedekiah rebelled against the King of Babylon;* that which God takes so heinously, as being such a transgression, as should both surely and most severely be avenged, in regard of his oath therein falsified, and God's name thereby scandalized. See how eagerly God insists upon it, with oath upon oath, to punish him for the breach of his oath, Ezek. 17:15–21. See this also in the story, 2 Kings 24:20. 2 Chr. 36:13.

*{cast them out from his presence}* Heb. *face;* as Psal. 139:7. out of that land wherein they had formerly enjoyed the special presence of God in his house, word and worship, Psal. 42:2. and 84:7. So 2 Kings 23:27.

**V. 4.** *{And it came to passe in the ninth year of his reign in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it, and built forts against it round about.}* See 2 Kings 25:1. Chap. 39:1. Hence arose the fast of the tenth month, observed during the time of the captivity, Zach. 8:19. because in it the siege of the city began.

**V. 5.** *{So the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.}* Heb. *And;* as chap. 37:21. the siege continued an year and an half. See vers. 7. and the same with this, 2 Kings 25:2.

**V. 6.** *{And in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, the famine was sore in the city.}* This occasioned the *fourth months fast,* Zach. 8:19. because in that month the city was surprised and sacked.

*{so that there was no bread for the people of the land.}* Heb. *and;* as Chap. 50:3. See 2 Kings 25:3. Chap. 38:9. none for the common sort of people; as Chap. 26:23. whatsoever remainder of store some great ones might have.

**V. 7.** *{Then the city was broken up,}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 47:2. It was taken by storming, some of the gates being broken open, and the walls battered, or scaled. See 2 Kings 25:4. Chap. 39:2, 3.

*{and all the men of war fled, and went forth out of the city by night, by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the Kings garden, (now the Chaldeans were by the city round about) and they went by the way of the plain.}* See on Chap. 39:4. 2 Kings 25:4.

*{which was by the Kings garden}* Or, *which were:* to wit, *walls.*

**V. 8.** *{But the army of the Chaldeans pursued after the King, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 50:24. 2 Kings 25:5. Chap. 39:5.

**V. 9.** *{Then they took the King, and carried him up unto the King of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath: where he gave judgment upon him.}* Or. *brought him unto him:* as Chap. 39:5. See on Chap. 51:27. Heb. *And;* as vers. 7. and, *spake with him judgements;* as Chap. 4:12. and 39:5. 2 Kings 25:6.

**V. 10.** *{And the King of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes:}* Caused them to be slain, as 1 Kings 19:17. and so hereafter, and vers. 11. See 2 Kings 25:7. Chap. 39:6.

*{he slew also all the Princes of Judah in Riblah.}* See Chap. 39:6.

**V. 11.** *{Then he put out the eyes of Zedekiah,}* Heb. *And* (as verse 9.) *he blinded the eyes of Zedekiah;* as Chap. 39:7. 2 Kings 25:7.

*{and the King of Babylon bound him in chains and carried him to Babylon,}* Or, *fetters of brasse;* as Lam. 3:7. So 2 Kings 25:7. See Chap. 39:7.

*{and put him in prison,}* Heb. *gave him* (as 2 Chr. 16:10. *into the house of the wards,* or *custodies;* as a prison is also termed by a word of the like notion, Genes. 42:7. Matt. 14:3. and this seems rather the proper notion of the term, as Chap. 37:13. Ezek. 44:11. than, as a learned annotator would have it, *the house of inquisitions.*

*{till the day of his death.}* A defective form, *put in the prison till the day of his death,* for, put him in, and kept him there till he died: as. *bruise it upon* the boil, for, bruise it, and lay it upon the boil, Esay 38:21. See more the like there. See this before menaced to Zedekiah, Chap. 32:5. Ezek. 17:16.

**V. 12.** *{Now in the fifth month,}* Heb. *And;* as Chap. 30:4. Hence *the fast of the fifth moneth,* Zach. 7:3. and 8:19. for the burning of the temple.

*{in the tenth day of the month}* It is said, 2 Kings 25:8. *on the seventh day.* The one of the two says a learned annotator, doubtless erroneous: but of that there is no necessity. The one may point to the day of the captain's arrival at Jerusalem: the other to the day wherein he set fire on the temple: which also though it were fired on the seventh day, yet might not be burnt down before the tenth. Either, rather, than what another suggests, that he might set forth from Riblah upon the *seventh day,* and arrive at Jerusalem upon the *tenth.* But howsoever, that learned annotator is doubtless himself in an error when he says that Joseph the Jew assigns it *the ninth:* for he in his *Antiquities,* lib. 10. cap. 11. says expressly it was *in the new moon;* and that is neither *seventh,* [illegible], nor *ninth,* but the *first.*

*{(which was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar King of Babylon}* See Chap. 25:1. and 32:1. So 2 Kings 25:8.

*{came Nebuzaradan Captain of the guard,}* Or, *Provost-Marshall:* so vers. 14. &c. See of the term, on Chap. 39. vers. 9.

*{which served the King of Babylon into Jerusalem}* Heb. *stood before him;* as 1 Kings 10:8. and 17:1. Prov. 22:29. It is said simply *a servant,* 2 Kings 25:8. which shows the relative here omitted, as chap. 50:5. to have reference to the captain, not to the guard, which in the Hebrew is not ambiguous.

**V. 13.** *{And burnt the house of the LORD, and the Kings house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and all the houses of the great men burnt he with fire.}* If *he burnt all the houses of Jerusalem* one and other, to what end is mention made of the great ones' houses after apart? But the words would be rendered, *all the houses of Jerusalem, even every house of any great one* (Heb. *house of great;* that is, noble, or rich, as Gen. 24:35. and 26:13.) *chap. 41:1. he burnt.* So that the copulative here is not in a notion of distinction, but of restriction rather, and further explication; as if it had been said, when I say, he burnt all the houses of Jerusalem, my meaning is not, that he burnt all the sorry dwellings of the meaner sort; for of those he spared some for such as should be left to husband the land thereabout; at least, regarded not so much the demolishing of them, being no grace, or ornament much less strength to the city: but that he burnt down all the great men's stately buildings, together with the king's palace, and God's temple, all the strong and graceful edifices, that were in any part of the city: though it is not unlikely but that many others of less note standing near them, were burnt down together with them. See the like use of the particle again, vers. 15. and such additional restrictions, Ps. 73:1. and 145:18. For those great masters seem to shoot wide here, who would have by this term intended, either their *Chappels,* or their *Schools,* because God was by praise and prayer magnified in the one, and the law by the lectures of their doctors in the other.

**V. 14.** *{And all the army of the Chaldeans that were with the Captain of the guard brake down all the walls of Jerusalem round about.}* They dismantled the city that it might not be a place of strength to secure any that might rise again. So 2 Kings 25:10. Neh. 1:3. Ezr. 4:12, 13, 15, 16. Lam. 2:18.

**V. 15.** *{Then Nebuzaradan the Captain of the guard carried away captive certain of the poor of the people, and the residue of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to the King of Babylon, and the rest of the multitude.}* Heb. *And,* as ver. 9, 11. So 2 Kings 25:11. See Chap. 39:9. and 51:34.

*{of the poor of the people, and the residue,}* Or, *even the residue;* not of the people of the whole land in general; but of those that were found in the city; as before, ver. 13.

*{the rest of the multitude}* the word rendered *multitude* is in the story of the Kings *hamon;* here *amon:* as Chap. 46:25.

**V. 16.** *{But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left certain of the poor of the land for vinedressers, and for husbandmen.}* Heb. *And,* as vers. 8. See 2 Kings 25:12. Chap. 39:10.

**V. 17.** *{Also,}* Or, *Moreover,* as Chap. 39:7. Heb. *And.* See 2 Kings 25:13.

*{the pillars of brass that were in the house of the LORD,}* As the prophet had foretold it should be, Chap. 27:19, 22. of these pillars, see 2 Kings 7:15.

*{and the bases,}* Ten in number, that stood under the lavers. See 1 Kings 7:27, 38. 2 Chr. 4:14.

*{and the brasen sea that was in the house of the LORD}* See 1 Kings 7:23.

*{the Chaldeans brake, and carried all the brass of them to Babylon.}* They broke them for the more easy and convenient carriage of them; as the Chaldean idols were dealt with by the Medes and Persians, Chap. 50:2. Esay 46:1, 2.

**V. 18.** *{The Caldrons also,}* Heb. *And,* as Chap. 39:6. but *Also* does well here; and better than before, vers. 17. of such *caldrons,* see Exod. 7:3. it is rendered *pots,* 2 Kings 25:14.

*{and the shovels,}* Instruments they were wherewith to remove the ashes from the altar of burnt-offerings, Exod. 27:3. for they were of brass, 1 Kings 7:45. and they have this name from a term that signifies *to remove,* and *do away,* Esay 28:17. in regard whereof some render it *besums,* or *brooms;* but that not likely: they would never be at the trouble to carry besoms to Babylon. The ancient Greek and old Latin render it here *flesh-hooks;* but without ground.

*{and the snuffers,}* The ancient Greek retains the Hebrew term, though misplaced: the old Latin renders it *Psalteries;* and the Jewish masters some of them make it some instrument of music: and the word indeed comes from a root that is of various conception, and signifies very frequently to make music by *playing* on some instrument; and for such musical instruments, is a word very near to this frequently used. But what should such instruments do here, among brazen *caldrons* and *shovels?* The word is indeed rendered *snuffers:* as here, so 1 Kings 7:50. 2 Kings 12:13. 2 Chron. 4:22. and being so taken, it may come from another acception of the same root, whereby it signifies properly *to prune,* and by *pruning,* to trim trees and plants, and consequently by a metaphorical use of its lamps: whence the *snuffers* might have their name; for that they pare off the superfluous part of the wicks, as *pruning hooks* (from hence in Hebrew so termed, Esay 2:4.) do the superfluities of plants: but those *snuffers* belonging to the lamps were of gold; as by the places above pointed to appears: whereas these were of brass, and are reckoned among those implements that belonged to the brazen altar: and I conceive therefore it should rather be rendered *tongs;* though by another name also so termed from a root that signifies *to take;* because by them men are wont to take up quick coals, and the like, from the fire on the hearth, or in the chimney, Esay 6:6. and yet is the same word used also for *snuffers;* so termed, because they lay hold on the wick, and take it by the end to raise it up: and it is so rendered in our version among the implements which belong to the lamps, Exod. 37:23. nor see I on what ground the same interpreters turn them elsewhere into *tongs,* Exod. 25:38. and Num. 4:19. whereas the very word next ensuing, in all the three places, to wit, *snuff-dishes,* does evidently show the word before it, to intend no other than *snuffers:* (and indeed what use is there of tongs about lamps?) the very selfsame thing being spoken of in all those places. Howbeit, in Solomon's temple, it seems, that there were instruments of two sorts, that were used about the lamps, the one to raise up the wick, called by this latter term, and another to snip it off, designed by the former: for both the terms are found distinctly mentioned, 1 Kings 7:49, 50. 2 Chron. 4:21, 22. though but one of them in Moses: and *tongs* seems no fit term for either. But as the word that signifies *tongs* properly, is used also for *snuffers,* in regard of some general notion designed in that term, common to either; so the word that most usually signifies *snuffers,* seems both here, and 2 Kings 25:16. used for *tongs,* in regard of that common use there is of them to trim lights with the one, and fire with the other. A learned scholiast would have it to signify *flesh-hooks;* so termed says he, because they *cut* the meat: but the office of such instruments is not to cut or mince meat, but to take it up only: So that neither observation, nor notation, backs this his interpretation; wherein I suppose he walks alone.

*{and the bowls,}* So is the word rendered, Numbers 7:13. and oft in that chapter: or *basons,* as it is rendered 2 Kings 12:13. Neh. 7:70. The word is used sometime for *a bowl* to drink in; as Amos 6:6. and such in likelihood were those that were in the temple and tabernacle, for the receiving of the wine or drink-offering, and pouring it out upon the sacrifice: sometime for *a bason:* such as were those that were used to receive the blood of the sacrifices so called, say the Jewish critics; because out of them the blood of the beast sacrificed was sprinkled, part of it upon the altar, the residue being poured down at the foot of it. Now these, whether *bowls* or *basons,* (for the word comprehends both) were some of them of brass, as those that Hiram cast for Solomon, 1 Kings 7:45. and those that Moses made for the brazen altar, Exodus 38:3. Numbers 4:14. some of silver, as those that the twelve princes gave, Numbers 7:13, 85. some of gold, belonging to the altar of incense, 1 Kings 7:50. 1 Chronicles 8:17. those of brass are here spoken of; the other, Verse 19. See there.

*{and the spoons,}* Or, *ladels.* or *cups,* or *dishes;* for they were some of them to put incense in: and are so called, because they were hollow, resembling the *palm,* or hollow of the hand. These seem to have been brazen *ladels,* used about the caldrons before mentioned, belonging to the service of those sacrifices, whereof part used to be boiled: and of this sort I conceive those to have been distinguished from the vessels of gold and silver, 2 Chron. 24:15. Other there, though rendered *spoons* in our versions yet indeed *cups,* or *dishes* rather, in which the incense was placed on the showbread, Num. 4:7 & 7:14, 86. and those were of gold, as all implements belonging to that table were, Exodus 25:29. & 37:16. 1 Kings 7:50. 2 Chr. 4:22.

*{and all the vessels of brass,}* That is *the rest* of them; as Chapter 43:2, 14.

*{wherewith they ministered, took they away.}* That is, wherewith service had wont to be performed: for the verb is indefinite: as chap. 5:26.

**V. 19.** *{And the basons,}* This is omitted 2 Kings 24:15. The word is used sometime for *a bason,* or *a piece,* as we term it: so where the blood of the Paschal lamb is said to be received in such, Exod. 12:22. and that such both of gold and silver were used about the service of God in the temple, appears, 1 Kings 7:50. 2 Kings 12:13.

*{and the firepans}* Or *censers;* as the word is rendered, Numbers 16:17, 37, 38. These were some of them of brass, belonging to the brazen altar, Exodus 27:30. & 38:3. Numb. 16:39. But one such at least belonging to the golden altar of gold, Lev. 16:12. compared with Heb. 9:4. & Rev. 8:3, 5. and others, so termed, not so much from the use, as from the fashion of them, belonging to the lamps, rendered commonly *snuff-dishes;* because they stood by the lamps with sand in them, therein to bury the snuff, so oft as occasion was to snuff them. Of these, see Exod. 25:38. & 37:23. 1 Kings 7:50. 2 Chr. 4:22.

*{and the bowls,}* Such of them, as were of silver, or gold. See on Verse 18. There were of these an hundred golden ones made by Solomon for the service of the temple, 2 Chronicles 4:8.

*{and the caldrons,}* Or *pots:* this is not mentioned, 2 Kings 25:15. but in the verse only before going; and whether any such silver *pots.* or *posnets* might be used in the temple, some doubt may be made; though we read of some golden *flesh-hooks,* 1 Chr. 28:17. which yet one of the Jewish doctors supposes to denote there some other implement that did belong to the table, and would have to be the same with the last here mentioned. But the scribe having the former verse in his eye, when he was writing, might put that again here that he had there. See the like acknowledged superfluous insertion, c. 51:3.

*{and the candlesticks}* Whereof, being ten in number, see 1 Kings 7:49. 2 Chr. 4:7.

*{and the spoons}* Or *dishes,* or *incense-cups.* See on v. 18.

*{and the cups}* So the ancient Greek and old Latin render it. That by the term some implement is designed appertaining to the table of showbread, is apparent from Exodus 25:29. and Numbers 4:7. And whereas there are two terms there joined together, this and another, the Jewish masters some of them tell us, if we may believe them, that thereby are designed certain golden *pipes,* or half pipes rather, like to cleft reeds, or canes, and *props* or shores made somewhat after the manner of a fork: and whereas the loaves or cakes of showbread were to be set on two rows, six in either row one upon another, these half-pipes were to be laid three of them between every other cake, to make free passage for air between them, and so to keep the bread from molding; and that those forked props or shores were to keep up these half pipes, and enable them the better to bear up the weight of the bread: and that hence the term here used has its name; because these pipes or half pipes kept the bread *pure* and free from growing moldy. But some of them of no small note herein dissent from their fellows; nor is there among those of them, that go this way, an entire agreement: for some of them would have this here mentioned the *pipes,* and that other the *props:* others of them would have that to be the *props,* and this the *pipes:* and some of ours, because the root it comes from has a notion of making or keeping *pure,* or *clean,* conceive thereby to be meant *besoms,* and so render it: but of that somewhat was said upon occasion of another term on Verse 18. and of silver and golden *besoms,* I remember not to have read. By those places of Moses pointed to, and compared together it appears, that the use of them both was one and the same, *to wit, to cover the Table,* (so the words are expressly in both places) that is, the things set upon the table, to wit, the bread, and the incense, which stood both upon the table in two *Chargers* the one; in two lesser dishes the other: which how those *pipes* or *props* may be said to do, is beyond my shallow capacity. But these were then both in nature of *covers,* if Moses may be believed: and it may (as to me seems) not improbably be conjectured, that the one was of a larger size or breadth, flat-bottomed, not unlike to our plate-trenchers; that it might both cover the uppermost loaf, or cake, (which was in likelihood of some good breadth, containing, as each of the rest, *two ten parts of an Ephah,* Leviticus 24:5. of which measure, see on Esay 5:10. that is, *two Omers,* Exodus 16:16.) and have the incense-cup, or dish, also set on it: the other of less compass to cover the incense, which in a cup or dish, stood on the uppermost loaf or cake of either row, Leviticus 24:6. both for use at least, if not for fashion, not unlike to such sort of covers, as we have oft for greater glasses and standing cups, the one, the other to those brazen plates made of those mutinous ones' censers, to cover the altar. Numbers 16:38, 39. nor is this use of them unsuitable to the term given the one of them, that is here mentioned: for by means hereof both the bread and incense were kept clean, and free from dust or ought else that might casually fall on them. But this my conjecture, I shall leave to the learned; resting ready to yield unto any, that shall produce and render some more probable matter.

*{that which was of gold in gold, and that which was of silver in silver, took the Captain of the Guard away.}* Heb. *what gold gold, and what silver silver:* that is, as some, whatsoever was of gold, or silver: such repetitions sometime importing an universality: as, *man man,* for every one, Lev. 15:2. and *day day,* for every day, Psal. 61:8. & 68:19. and *morning morning,* for every morning, Esay 50:4. or, as others, those of gold apart by themselves; and those of silver apart by themselves: and both of them entire as they were; not broken as the brazen ones were, verse 17. See the same, 2 Kings 25:15.

**V. 20.** *{The two pillars,}* Or, As for *the two pillars;* (the nominative put absolutely: as the like, Psalm 18:30. & 104:17.) the one called *Jacin,* the other *Boaz,* 1 Kings 7:15, 21. 2 Chronicles 3:15, 17.

*{and one Sea,}* Hebr. *and the one Sea.* See Verse, 17.

*{and twelve brazen bulls,}* Heb. *and the twelve Bulls of brasse.* Whereof see 1 Kings 7:25.

*{that were under the bases,}* There is some doubt here moved how the *Bulls* should be said to be *under the bases,* when as they were under the *Sea,* and the *bases* not under it, but the other lesser lavers, 1 Kings 7:27, 38. To which is answered by one, that the nethermost parts of the sea are here meant by the word *bases:* by a Jewish doctor, that the meaning is, *they stood below* by, or beside *the bases:* by a third, that there is in the text a defect thus to be supplied, *the twelve Bulls that were under it,* (to wit, the sea,) *and the bases,* before mentioned, v. 17. The *bases* are omitted, 2 Kings 25:6.

*{which King Solomon had made in the House of the LORD:}* All *which,* as well pillars, and sea, and bulls, as bases, Solomon has made; That is, procured, or caused to be made: as *he built the house,* Acts 7:47. and this is added to show, as a Jewish doctor observes, that they were the very same that Solomon had made; having not been altered, or embellished: as some other things about the temple had been, in some former kings' reigns, 2 Kings 16:17, 18. and 18:16. Yet it is expressly said, 2 Kings 16:17. of Ahaz, that *He mangled the borders of the Bases, and removed the Lavers from off them:* As also that *He took down the Sea from the brazen Bulls that were under it.* But Hezekiah his son and next successor, in likelihood repaired the one, and restored the other again.

*{in the House of the LORD}* Either, *in the House of the Lord,* which, (to wit, pillars) *Solomon made:* and so there should be a trajection in the words of the text as the like, Chapter 32:9. Or. *for the House of the Lord:* for they were not made in it, but *in the plain of Jordan,* 1 Kings 7:46. for it. So is the particle used, Nehemiah 5:3. and 13:14. Est. 4:7. Jeremiah 15:13. See Verse 21.

*{the brass of these Vessels was without weight.}* Heb, *of the Brasse of them,* to wit, *of all these Vessels, there was no weight:* the quantity was so great, that they could not well or easily be weighed; or that they regarded not the weight of them, they were not willing to stand to weigh them. See 1 Kings 7:47. 1 Chronicles, 22:3, 14. 2 Chronicles, 4:18. and the like syntax, Chapter 51:56. and the same in effect, 2 Kings 25:16.

**V. 21.** *{And concerning the pillars,}* Heb. *And the pillars;* as verse 20.

*{and the height of one pillar was eighteen cubits}* This agrees with what is related, 1 Kings 7:15. where the making of them is mentioned: as also with 2 Kings 25:17. where the same story with this is reported. But in 2 Chronicles 3:15. parallel to that, 1 Kings 7:15. the pillars are said to be *thirty five cubits* long: for so the words are there, *he made* and placed, or to be placed *before the house* (a complexive form of speech, for they were not there made, but in the plain of Jordan, 2 Chronicles 4:17. though to that place they were designed, and there they were placed, 1 Kings 7:21. See of the like on verse 11, 20.) *two pillars thirty and five cubits in length.* These seeming differences to reconcile, some have recourse to the diversity of cubits, which (say they) were of two sorts, the civil or common cubit, consisting of one foot and an half six hand breadths twenty four finger breadths, and eighteen thumb-breadths; and the sacred or holy cubit, that consisted *of an hand-breadth,* or *foure fingers* more than that other, Ezekiel 40:5. & 43:13. that which exactly agrees with what Herodote reports of the *royal cubit* in Egypt, that it was three thumbs breadth longer than the ordinary cubit, and the computation, say they, is made by the civil or common cubit in the one place, by the sacred in the other. But because this computation will not serve to bring up the less number to the greater; for an hand's breadth added unto each cubit will not raise eighteen, to above 21. which comes far short of thirty five. Some tell us of a third sort of cubits that was of a double length to the common cubit, called the *chief cubit,* 2 Chronicles 3:3. and *the arm-hole cubit,* because it reached not from the top of the hand to the bending of the elbow, as the common cubit, but up to the arm-hole, Ezekiel 44:8. And this being admitted, might indeed bring us home to the longer measure, and a little also beyond it, a cubit over either in the greater (say they) omitted, because it belonged to the basis; or in the less number, though but seventeen and an half indeed, added to make up a full number. But [illegible] places produced for it are both ambiguous, the latter [illegible], on which the main weight of this conceit lies; and by the word rendered *arm-hole,* some interpreters of prime note conceive some part of the building itself to be meant, which they render *a wing.* Certain to me it seems, that no other cubit can there be meant, than that which was before mentioned, chap. 40:5. where the angel is said to have had in his hand *a measuring cane, reed* or *rod of six cubits, by the cubit and an hand-breadth;* and here, as having an eye to what he had there said, he says, that *the foundations of the side chambers* were *the fulnesse of the reed of six cubits:* that is, full as long as that measuring cane of six cubits: and what cubit can there be any reason to imagine here intended, other than that so spoken of at first, and after repeated again? which may also justly be deemed to be the same with that *chief* one mentioned in the dimensions of Solomon's temple; if the word at least be there so to be rendered, whereof some also make doubt. This therefore unless better ground could be produced, will hardly here help us. Some other therefore have recourse to the fabric of the pillars. These *pillars,* or *columns,* says a learned writer, consisted of five parts, *a square* table at the bottom, *rundle* or round basis upon that, the *shaft,* or main body; the *head,* or *Chapiter,* and the *crown,* or *pomel.* Unto which five I suppose a sixth may well be added, the square border on which the pomegranates were: whereof see on verse 23. Now, says this learned man, the shaft or the main body of the pillar was of *eighteen cubits* mentioned in the one place: the square table and round basis below, together with the chapiter and coronet above, made out between them the other seventeen; and these altogether with the shaft, make up the thirty five related in the other. The Jewish doctors go a third way. The one place, say they, speaks of either pillar apart; which were either of them of eighteen cubits, in the shaft or main body; besides the chapiters, the measure whereof is reported by itself, 1 Kings 7:16. the other place speaks of them jointly together, as they were cast at first in one entire body, though after divided into two; and one cubit, say they is not expressed in the whole number, because it was divided between them, and went with either to the making up of the chapiter on the top, and to back this their opinion, they press the word of *length* used in the text: for it says not, say they, *the height of the pillars,* as in other places, where they are spoken of as they stood, but *the length* of them, because he speaks of them as lying yet along on the ground in the place where they were at first cast. Either of these two last seem to carry some good probability with them.

*{and a line of twelve cubits did compass it,}* Heb. *a thred* (as Genesis 14:23. rendered *a line,* 1 Kings 7:15. *a cord,* Eccles. 4:12.) *of twelve cubits will,* or *would,* or *might compasse it:* the verb in a potential notion: as, *it will,* (for, *it would,* or *could) contain,* 1 Kings 7:25.

*{and the thickness thereof, was four fingers: it was hollow}* Before was the *perimeter,* or *compass,* (says a learned annotator) here the *diameter* or *bredth,* of the pillar: and here, says he, the scribes must of necessity be out: for *four fingers* cannot make *a diametient of eight cubits* in a column. But I doubt that this learned man is herein himself rather much mistaken: the purpose of the writer hereof, whoever he was, being not, as I conceive it, to give the *diameter,* or *breadth,* of the main body of the pillar, (what needed that when he had related the exact compass of it before, from whence the diameter might be easily gathered?) but to acquaint the reader with the *thicknesse* of the brass throughout the main body of the column; which though it were not entirely solid and massive, but *hollow* within, yet was the brass of it *four fingers thick,* which the diametient makes nothing at all. And this appears plainly by what is said of the *sea,* 1 Kings 7:26. & 2 Chron. 4:5. *the thicknesse* of it was *an hand breadth:* the very term here used though the measure a finger's breadth more in that than in this here, whereas both the *perimeter* and the *diameter,* or compass and breadth had been distinctly before mentioned, v. 23. in the one place, v. 2. in the other.

**V. 22.** *{And a Chapiter of brass was upon it, and the height of one Chapiter was five cubits}* The word rendered *Chapiter* signifies properly *a crown* or *coronet;* and so divers render it: that which is here said of it, however we shall term it, and its measure agrees with the dimensions thereof reported, 1 Kings 7:16. But 2 Kings 25:17. where the same story with this is related: this work *Chapiter* or *coronet* is said to be *three cubits* high, which falls two cubits short of this. This seeming difference the Jewish commenters thus reconcile: the chapiters, say they, were divided into two parts, the upper and the lower; the lower part next to the shaft of the pillar had no figures on it; the upper part above that was set out with figures and much curious workmanship: and this upper part only is respected in the latter story of the Kings, being of three cubits height: the lower of two cubits being let pass as belonging to the shaft. Some of ours more exactly divide the whole work above the shaft into three parts, the *chapiter* the *table,* and the *coronet:* and they assign to the *chapiter* one cubit, to the *Table* one and three to the *Coronet:* which therefore say they, considered together with the table, has four assigned it, 1 Kings 7:19. Others again divide it into the *Table,* or *square,* the *belly* and the *crown:* which I conceive to be the better division, and suppose, that the square or table with its rise, until it closed with the middle part, termed the *belly,* was of two cubits, omitted for that cause which the Jewish doctors give, as comprehended in the pillar, and the *belly* with the crown to make up the three cubits between them mentioned in the place parallel to this.

*{with network and Pomegranates upon the Chapiters round about, all of brass: the second Pillar also, and the Pomegranates were like unto these.}* Heb. *and;* for *with;* as c. 27:2. Ezek. 23:40. Of this *net-work,* or *wreathed work;* as it is rendered in the record of Kings: as also of these *Pomegranates,* see 1 Kings 7:17, 18. 2 Kings 25:17. and hereafter v. 23.
