**V. 23.** *{And there were ninety and six Pomegranates on a side, and all the Pomegranates upon the network were an hundred in all.}* There are here again some seeming differences both about the sum in gross, between this text and some others; and about the sums themselves here mentioned. Concerning the former we find it said, 1 Kings 7:19. that *the Pomegranates were in rowes two hundred about upon either Chapiter,* and 2 Chronicles 4:13. that there were *four hundred Pomegranates upon the two wreaths; two rowes upon either wreath.* But these seeming differences, for the sum in gross, are by general agreement thus reconciled; that there were *two rowes* of them on the top-works of either pillar, one over another and an *hundred* in either row, as is here said, and this place therefore to be understood, as if it were said, *an hundred all* in one row: and consequently, *two hundred.* as the former place says, in the two rows upon the one; *foure hundred* as the latter has it on both. There is a little more difficulty about making the two sums here mentioned to agree; for according to the words here thus rendered it might seem, that there were *ninety six Pomegranates* on each side of either *Chapiter,* or *Coronet* above mentioned, which would rise to the sum of three hundred eighty and four in all, for each either chapiter or row, which none of the former sums would admit: and whereas there is mention in the after sum of an *hundred only:* Unto this the common answer is, that the four that should go to make up the hundred that was in each row were out of sight, by reason that the pillar stood close to the wall, either of the porch, or the house; and the writer here mentions those alone that were in sight. Thus both the Jewish, and others: which yet seems not very satisfactory: for neither is it probable, that two such goodly columns erected, not to bear up ought, but for a grace and ornament to the house, should be situated so close to the wall, that the curious workmanship of them might not be conspicuous on every side: Nor again, do they take notice, either of the translation, or of the text, which may seem to raise the computation to such an excessive sum as was hinted before. In the Hebrew text, for that which is here rendered *on a side,* it is word, for word *Winde-ward:* That is, toward the four winds, or quarters of the world: as the word *wind* is used, 1 Chr. 9:24. Chap. 49:36. Ezek. 42:20. whence it may well be deemed that the *table,* or border on which the pomegranates were engraved, was square; albeit that the *belly* or main body of the chapiters were round; as the borders of the bases on which the lavers stood; set out with the like imagery, were square, although the mouth and main body of the bases were round, 1 Kings 7:29, 31. and that the pomegranates stood *twenty and four* on each side, to which number the four corner ones added to the number here mentioned, make up the sum of *an hundred* hereafter subjoined, and understood as before. And this I conceive to be the most probable way of reconcilement. For as for that apprehension of the late learned annotator, who would make but two sides of them, and would have *ninety six* in each row on either of those sides, which with the two parting ones in each row, being eight in all should make up the 400. neither does it suit well with the term of *wind,* unless we make but two winds: nor will it with that addition of those eight, make up that entire sum, unless four more be added.

**V. 24.** *{And the Captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief Priest, and Zephaniah the second Priest, and the three Keepers of the door.}* The historian returns from the spoils carried away, to some persons of note, that Nebuzaradan took away from Jerusalem, at his return from thence to Riblah, where by Nebuchadrezzar's appointment they were slain. Those mentioned in this verse, he took out of the temple; those in the next, out of the city. *Seraiah,* the son of Azariah, 1 Chr. 6:14. *the chief Priest:* another from him of that name mentioned Chap. 51:59. and *Zephaniah;* of whom, Chap. 21:1. & 29:25. *the second Priest:* the next in place to the chief priest, who upon any extraordinary occurrent restraining or disabling him, was to supply his place, Chap. 21:1. 1 Chr. 5:12. 2 Kings 23:4. *and three* (not *the three,* for there were many more of them) *Keepers of the door.* Heb, *threshold.* See Chap. 35:4. three select ones of those, it may be, that used to attend at the three gates, the east-gate, 2 Kings 11:6. 2 Chr. 23:5. Ezek. 44:1, 3. & 46:1. and the north and south gates Ezek. 36:7. which seem to have been the chief, and of most use. See the same, 2 Kings 25:18.

**V. 25.** *{He took also out of the city an eunuch which had the charge of the men of war,}* Heb. *And out of the city* (for the former out of the temple, Verse 24.) *he took an Eunuch,* or, *officer;* as Gen. 39:1. Esay 39:7. *one,* as chap. 51:60. *who was overseer of the men of war;* or, *the Muster-Master.*

*{and seven men of them that were near the Kings person,}* Heb. *that saw the face of the King;* as near attendants, standing before such, usually do. See the manner of speech, Matt. 18:10. In 2 Kings 25:19. there is mention of five only. But Joseph the Jew, lib. 10. cap. 11. has, as it is here, *seven:* two of them might be men of less note, and in that regard it may be, there omitted. Some of the Jewish masters say, that they were the two scribes, that belonged to the judges. But for this assertion they give no ground.

*{which were found in the city;}* Either were taken there; as Chapter 50:7, 24. or, simply, *that were abiding* there: as Esth. 1:4.

*{and the principal Scribe of the host,}* So the old Latin; but others rather with the Jewish commenter, *the Scribe of the Captain of the host,* or the general: the office that Joab had under David, 1 Chr. 27:34. alluded to Josh. 5:14.

*{who mustered the people of the land,}* Heb. *that hosted,* or, *armied,* if we might so speak: that made an host, or army of them, This some refer to the commander, that framed the people into an army, and so led them out to service: others, to the scribe, that enrolled and listed them for service: and this latter seems the right. See the like office, Esay 33:18.

*{and threescore men of the people of the land that were found in the midst of the city.}* Or, *that were* (as before, and Chap. 41:3.) *in the city;* as it is 2 Kings 25:19. the like see Chap. 51:7. & 50:8. Ezek. 3:24.

**V. 26.** *{So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them; and brought them to the King of Babylon to Riblah.}* Heb. *And.* as verse 5. See the same, 2 Kings 25:20.

**V. 27.** *{And the King of Babylon smote them, and put them to death in the land of Hamath:}* See Verse 10. and the same, 2 Kings 25:21.

*{Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land.}* Heb. *And.* as Chap. 51:4. But the copulative may well be retained here; or else it must have reference to what was before related, Verse 15. but this seems rather to look further backward than so, as appears, Verse 28. and to be in nature of an introduction, used as a passage to a new discourse, concerning such as either had been before, or were at this time carried away captive, containing the sum in general of the ensuing relation, Verse 28—30.

**V. 28.** *{This is the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried away captive in the seventh year, three thousand Jews and three and twenty.}* This was done in the short reign of Jehojacin related, 2 Kings 24:12, 14, 16. But there seems some difference between the relation of it here and there: for first what is said to have been done in Nebuchadnezzar's *seventh yeare* here, is said to have been done in his *eighth year* there. That which may easily be reconciled, as being transacted in the latter end of his seventh year, and about the beginning of his eighth: and so verse 29. the like thereunto, see 1 Kings 15:25, 28. and on Chap. 25:1. Another difference more difficult is in the number, which are but *three thousand,* and odd here, but *ten thousand* there, 2 Kings 24:14. and *seven thousand,* if not *eight thousand,* as may seem more to them, Verse 16. for it is there said; *and all the men of might seven thousand, and craftsmen and smiths, a thousand:* Which some so reconcile, as if the first number included the two latter; to wit, that of the *ten thousand, seven thousand* were *men of arms,* and a *thousand* of them *cunning workmen:* and this seems not improbable; because they were mentioned together with the gross sum in the same verse before. But for the reconciling of this and the former, both the Jewish writers and others give jointly this answer, that of that *ten thousand,* the *three thousand* and odd, were of the tribe of Judah, *Jewes* strictly so termed, the residue of the tribe of Benjamin, and some other that adhered unto them; which for ought I see must be admitted, and stand for good, unless some error have by the scribe's default crept into the account.

**V. 29.** *{In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty and two persons.}* That is, what time the city was taken in the *eleventh year of Zedekiah,* 2 Kings 25:2. said to be *the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar,* 2 Kings 25:8. from which place a learned writer would have to be corrected. But thereof there is no need: in the *eighteenth* expiring, and in the *nineteenth* then entering, may well stand together, as before, verse 28. Heb. *souls,* for, *persons,* as Exod. 1:5. Chap. 35:6. So after Verse 30.

**V. 30.** *{In the three and twentieth year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty and five persons:}* This seems to have been done after that barbarous murder of Gedaliah, chap. 41:2. 2 Kings 24:25. to prevent some new rebellion. Heb. *souls,* for, *persons,* again, as before, Verse 29. and so in the next clause.

*{all the persons were four thousand, and six hundred.}* The whole number made up exactly from the several ones before particularly recited.

**V. 31.** *{And it came to passe}* Or, *Now* so it *was;* as chap. 36:22, 23.

*{in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehojacin King of Judah}* Or, *after the deportation:* so the particle seems here to import; as also, Esay 38:17. Ezek. 40:1. Dan. 11:6. six and twenty years after the dissolution of the Jewish state, 2 Kings 25:2, 8. when Jehojacin was now about fifty and five years old 2 Kings 24:8.

*{in the twelfth month in the five and twentieth day of the month,}* Here again comes some seeming difference between the relation of this passage here, and that in the history of the Kings: for what is said to be done on *the five and twentieth* day here, is said to be done on the *twenty seventh* there, 2 Kings 25:27. Now this to reconcile the Talmudists tell us a tale of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Evilmerodac; to wit, that when Nebuchadnezzar died and was buried, this son Evilmerodac was afraid to take the kingdom upon him, for fear lest his father should return, (either not being dead indeed, or risen again as he did before,) after his seven years' frenzy, Dan. 4:32, 36. and should then kill him, as he had done one of his sons before, whom he found then sitting upon his throne; though some of them say, (for they are not all in one tale neither) that it was this Evilmerodac that he found in his royal seat, and that he did but imprison him; but that he feared now, if he came again the second time, he would deal worse with him: and durst not therefore take the kingdom upon him, until he had seen his father's corpse taken out of the grave, and before his face cut in pieces and cast to the vultures, that flew away several ways with the gobbets of it; and that Jehojacin, (with whom he had been fellow-prisoner, whereby they were grown into some familiarity) then standing by him, told him that his father would then come again, when all those pieces of him, that the vultures flew away with, should meet together in that place again: and that thereupon he released him from his imprisonment: And thus after all this long tale told the knot is readily untied, and they will show you how: for, say they, Nebuchadnezzar died the *five and twentieth* day of the month, and was buried on the *six and twentieth:* (they made haste belike to be rid of him) and on the *seven and twentieth* day his corpse was taken up, and used as we have heard, to fulfill that prophecy of Esay 14:19. and Jehojacin withal released. And how helps all this, if all of it were true, to assoil the doubt? One of them therefore a little wiser than his fellows; though he relates their story too, tells us, this enlargement of Jehojacin was resolved upon, and order given for it on the twenty and fifth day, though not put in execution till the *twenty seventh;* and this our interpreters also approve: nor is it either unreasonable or incongruous to allow a day intervenient, for the fitting of one in such a condition for a suitable receipt.

*{that Evil-Merodach King of Babylon, in the first year of his reign,}* Heb, *in the year of his Kingdom;* that is, in the same year wherein he came to his kingdom: as, *in his reigning,* or, *when he reigned;* that is, when he began to reign, verse 1. and so it is, 2 Kings 25:27. *in the year of his reigning:* well rendered there, *that he began to reign.*

*{lifted up the head of Jehojacin King of Judah,}* *To lift up the head,* is sometime used for *to advance, set up,* or *above:* as *thou liftest up the head,* Psalm 3:3. & 18:43, 48. and *he shall lift up the head,* Psal. 110:7. but sometime it signifies *to survey* and *take account of;* or upon survey, to take special notice of, be it for good or evil. So it is said of Pharaoh, that making a solemn feast upon his birthday he took a list of his servants, and among the rest he *lifted up the head* of two of them then in restraint, that is, he took special notice of them both, but to contrary purposes, to release and restore the one of them to his former place, and to execute the other, Gen. 40:20—22. In the former sense the word is not here to be taken, (for he did not advance him before he released him) but in the latter taking a list or survey of such princes as his father Nebuchadnezzar had left under restraint at his decease, he took special notice of Jehojacin among the rest.

*{and brought him forth out of prison.}* Heb. *out of the house of restraint;* as Chapter 37:15. See verse 33. much dispute and debate there is among writers, what the reason should be why that Chaldean king should show Jehojacin this kindness: and the Jewish masters tell us, as was hinted before, because he and Jehojacin had been sometime fellow-prisoners: but that relation is of as much credit, as any other tales that they tell. Some other say it was done in regard of his voluntary yielding himself unto Nebuchadnezzar, 2 Kings 24:12. whereunto some add, that he did so by the advice of Jeremy, which God would hereby make to appear that he approved of. But neither do we read of any such advice given by Jeremy to Jeconiah, though to Zedekiah he so did, chap. 38:7, 8. But it may well be thought rather that he did it by his mother's direction, by whom he was in other things in likelihood too much led. Nor did Nebuchadnezzar, unto whom he so yielded himself, ever show him any such favor so long as he lived. Others would have it again so disposed by God's special providence to fulfill Jacob's prophecy, concerning the continuance of the scepter with Judah until the coming of the Messias, Gen. 49:10. which had failed, say they, had not Jeconiah been set at liberty to be head of the captivity, in which heads, him and his issue after him being of that stock, the government was continued. But what answer will these men then give to the Maccabee commanders, who were of another tribe, and yet that prophecy by their government not frustrated? Nor does this therefore give any satisfactory reason of this kindness showed by Evil-Merodac to Jehojacin. If conjectures may be given in a business so uncertain, I should suppose that Jehojacin being a youth of eighteen years when he was brought captive to Babylon, 2 Kings 24:8. and it may well be, well favored, and comely withal, and one that had been king of one of the kingdoms of special note and name in those times. Evil-Merodac being also but a young stripling then, might take some liking to him, and set his affection upon him: and howsoever, during his father's life, he could not in this kind show it, yet did it, when he had power so to do after his decease. But whatsoever the ground or occasion on man's part was, which is not easy to define, thus God made good, what the Psalmist, whosoever he were, with thankfulness, to the amplification of God's mercy to the people, acknowledges, that God gave him, and others of them at several times favor in the sight of those, with whom they were under restraint, Psalm 106:46. See chap. 15:11. Daniel 1:9. and 2:48, 49. and 3:30. and 6:2, 28. Nehe. 1:11. and 2:8. Acts 7:10. In the book of Kings, this is delivered in a more concise form, but in Scripture very frequent, *he lifted up his head out of prison,* for *he lifted up his head* and took or brought him *out of prison:* as more fully here we have it. So, *thou hast loved,* or *affected my soul from the pit,* for *thou hast loved,* or *affected my soul* and delivered it *from the pit,* Esay 38:17. See the like, v. 20.

**V. 32.** *{And spake kindly unto him,}* Heb. *spake good things with him;* as c. 12:6. So 2 Kings 25:8.

*{and set his throne above the throne of the Kings that were with him in Babylon.}* Divers whereof it seems Nebuchadnezzar his father had with him there; before whom he gave Jeconiah the precedency, as some think, in regard of the great fame of his ancestors David and Solomon; but might as well be out of some other private respect, or affection to his person.

**V. 33.** *{And changed his prison garments:}* Heb. *the garments of his restraint;* or, *his garments of restraint:* that is, of *the house of restraint:* as it was more fully, Verse 31. *the prison.* So 2 Kings 25:29. The like is said of Joseph, when he was to appear before Pharaoh, Genesis 41:14. because it was not fit for him to come into the king's presence in such sorry raiment as in the prison he wore. But there seems more than so implied in it here; to wit, that instead of such raiment, as had formerly been allowed him, while he was under restraint, he had apparel now allowed him suitable to the condition of one of his quality, a prince living at liberty: As is it said, of Joseph afterward, that the king put him into *a vest of fine linnen,* Gen. 41:42.

*{and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life.}* Either he mealed frequently with him; (so some) as did Crœsus with Cyrus: he was constantly at table with him, as was David with Saul, 1 Samuel 20:3, 27. or he had a table in the king's court prepared of course for him. See of Mephibosheth the like, 2 Sam. 9:7.

**V. 34.** *{And,}* or, *for:* the copulative in a causal notion, as Chapter, 51:22. because in these words is contained a further confirmation, and fuller explication of what before had been delivered verse 33.

*{for his diet}* Or, *as concerning his provision:* that is, the provision made for him, or assigned him: for it is a nominative absolute, as the like before, Verse 20, 21. The word signifies properly, that which the Latins call *Viaticum,* provisions for a journey; as does also the Latin *commeatus;* Whence our English *meat:* though restrained sometime to *vitail;* whence it is used for *a meal,* Proverbs 15:17. See on Chron. 40:5. here it may well be rendered *provision:* though, having reference chiefly to diet, yet including also all other ordinary accommodations together with it.

*{there was a continual diet given him of the King of Babylon,}* Heb. *a provision of assiduity;* that is, *a daily,* or *constant provision:* as *a sacrifice of assiduity,* for *the daily,* or set constant *sacrifice,* Ezra 3:5.

*{every day a portion,}* Heb. *word,* or *matter,* (as Chapter 38:27.) *of a day in its day.* See the very same forms, Exodus 5:13.

*{until the day of his death, all the days of his life.}* The like manner of forms of speech conceived in the positive and privative, or affirmative and negative conjoined, and both intimating one and the same thing, is in Scripture very rife, and adds some emphasis to the things so related. See Genesis 40:23. Deuteronomy 9:7. 1 Samuel 1:11. Psalm 118:17. John 1:3, 20. and 3:15, 16. 1 Thess. 5:6.
